fields.name: FISH Maritime Fixtures and Fittings Thesaurus

fields.value: An instrument strung with metal pieces which sound when shaken.
A workshop in which carded wool was passed through heated combs to straighten and separate the long and short fibres prior to spinning. Associated with the worsted branch of the textile industry.

A type of waterwheel where the incoming supply of water leaves a launder near the top of the wheel, and drops onto the paddles or buckets of the wheel which rotates in the reverse direction to that of the incoming flow.
One of 12 roadside crosses erected by Edward I in memory of his wife, Eleanor of Castile, the most famous being Charing Cross in London.
A vessel for maintaining the buoys, hawsers and netting of a boom defence.
A plan with four foils radiating out from a central point.
A circular construction at the intersection of two or more roads to aid the passage of vehicles from one road to another.
A barrier used to close an opening, usually hinged and often hung within a supporting frame.

Low-grade cast iron in the form of balls or spheres, produced in small workshops and exported across the North Sea and Baltic region. Particularly associated with 16th century Sweden. Also spelt "oszemundt" and other variants.
A type of guildhall belonging primarily to the London livery companies, but also found elsewhere in the country, so called because of the livery worn by members of the guild.

Animal, vegetable and mineral remains including edible materials, drink or residues and unworked imported objects which have been retrieved from archaeological contexts. Also soil samples taken for environmental analysis.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
A settlement, usually enclosed, on a sloping hillside containing a number of oval or circular scopped house floors separated by walls or unexcavated ridges.
A stone ring built to enclose and sometimes revet a burial mound or cairn.

Satellite craft belonging to a larger vessel, usually a rowing vessel; used to pick up or set down passengers or crew when lying offshore, or stowed on board as the "long boat" or "jolly boat" for lifesaving purposes.
A workshop or factory where bronze articles are made by casting molten metal into moulds.

A covering of thin copper plates secured, on top of a layer of tar and horsehair, to the bottom of wooden ships to protect the hull against weeds, barnacles and especially Teredo navalis, a wood-boring worm prevalent in tropical seas.
A protective earthen mound, often the main defence of a fortification.
A cargo vessel designed to carry goods packed in large containers that can be loaded directly onto trains or lorries.
A musical instrument producing sound from its own body.
A cleansing agent, manufactured by reacting natural oils and fats with a strong alkali. Nowadays, formed into bars with added colouring and perfume.
An object made of two verticals with rungs between for ascending or descending.
The shaped projection on the top of a newel post or at the apex of a gable.

A small three-masted lateen-rigged vessel used exclusively in the Mediterranean from the 16th to the 19th century. Its hull was similar in form to that of a polacre but with an extended bow and stern.
A building or site for the industrial manufacture of locks.
Not to be used for indexing. Broad term to assist retreival of all monuments where non-physical evidence is recorded.
A stone commemorating the date of a specific event.
A hand held instrument for producing a current of air for cooling the user. It is both a practical and a fashion item.
A long spear with a double barb where one barb is longer than the other.
A bottle with a narrow neck used for wine, oil etc.
A purpose-built building with a tower used for the drying of parachutes.
A site from which troops could be embarked onto transport vessels prior to the D-Day landings can also apply to muster/departure points from which troops embarked for their journey to the Front.
A square, hewn or worked, high class freestone which can be 'freely' cut and is laid in horizontal courses with vertical joints.
A farmstead where the house and working buildings are attached and in-line. Can include Bastles, Longhouses and Laithe houses.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
A building used by an organization instituted to promote the needs and rights of the blind.
A roof, circular in plan, usually semicircular in section, over a circular, square or polygonal base.
Twin bars riveted together which can open and close allowing it to grip objects, usually to lift and move them.
Use for vessels registered in England

A rectangular or trapezoidal non-megalithic stony mound of Neolithic date, with human remains in cists rather than a large chamber. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
A liquid used to provide a protective or decorative cover to a surface.

A tall building, either round, square or polygonal in plan, used for a variety of purposes, including defence, as a landmark, for the hanging of bells, industrial functions, etc. Use more specific type where known.
An object with a ceremonial or symbolic function. Multiple index with specific object where possible, eg for a ceremonial battleaxe index as ceremonial object and battleaxe.
Buildings and works around a mine shaft with an artificial embankment on which the winding gear etc, is located.
A flask with a hollow ring-shaped form. (Source: MPRG)
Elastic polymeric substance made from the latex of a tropical plant or synthetically
Collection of artefacts recovered during archaeological investigation of a site.
Writing implements; formerly quill pens made of bird feathers, and in more modern times fountain pens made of various materials with metal nibs, both used with ink to write.
A horizontal, stationary steam engine with two cylinders in line, one behind the other, the steam passing through each cylinder in turn.
The administrative office of a commercial concern.

An overview of the historical and architectural development, character and heritage assets of a settlement or area.  An HAA may result in the creation, at varying levels of intensity, of individual site-based records informed by area context.
An artificial mound of earth outside a ditch or wall intended to deflect or absorb cannon fire.
Colour positive print developed using a dry process.
A utensil used to pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A peat-based garden where various types of heather are grown.
Monument known only from primary documentary sources eg books, maps, legal records, where no physical evidence exists. Use also where a monument has been planned but never constructed.
A Saxon quoin consisting of alternating horizontally and vertically laid stones.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.

A core which has two opposing platforms. One end serving as the main platform for the removal of blades - the other being used to straighten the face of the core and correct knapping errors. Removals are taken from the full circumference. (Source: SARC)
An instrument which creates a buzzing noise.
Collective term for the North and South Wales groups of slate. Hard, fine grained, metamorphic rock, with varying dark shades.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around three sides of a yard which is open to one side.
A mixed house of nuns and religious men of the Benedictine order.
A large communal room within a college complex used for functions, assemblies, examinations etc.
A residential home for children with physical and/or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues who need medical intervention and/or care provided by registered nurses.
A house built by a local authority.
A jug with a sinuous profile where the rim, girth and base are of roughly equal diameter, and the neck and lower body are narrower.(Source: MPRG)
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply for domestic use.
A structure which protects an area of ground from the weather.
An institute provided by a regiment for the improvement of the soldiers and to reduce excessive drinking.

A machine tool for producing large flat surfaces on metal objects. It comprises a large work table which slides backwards and forwards along a substantial guide bed, passing under a stationary bridge containing a fixed tool.
The lowest part of a structure, such as a pier, or the section of an order on which the shaft of a column sits.
A space used for the storage of chemicals.
A Monument whose presence is inferred from artefacts found in stratified below ground deposits, as distinct from surface collection or chance find.
A room in which public or private auctions are held.
A machine used in the silk industry for applying the final twist  to silk threads to make them suitable  for weaving into a fabric.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A parterre consisting of square beds containing ornamental plants often laid out in intricate patterns mimicking embroidery.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
An enclosure, usually private, used for burial. Often found within a cemetery.
Paste or cake of the fruit of the cacao-tree, sweetened with other substances and used to make beverages or confectionery.
A site, including an airfield and customs house, where air passengers embark and disembark.

A building used for storing Sulphur, a highly inflammable chemical element used in the manufacture of matches, gunpowder and sulphuric acid. It is also used in bleaching, for vulcanizing rubber and as a disinfectant.

An excavation technique that involves the machine stripping the topsoil/subsoil from the area to be excavated, plotting observed features onto a site plan and then partially or fully excavating those features.
A building or area where stone is stored for industrial or agricultural use.
A stationary winding steam engine positioned at the top of a railway incline for hauling up trains and locomotives.
A substantial bank and ditch forming a major boundary between two adjacent landholdings. Most date from the late Bronze Age and Iron Age.
Remains of parasitic or free-living worms of the phylum Nematoda, characterized as having slender, cylindrical unsegmented bodies. Cysts of Heterodera commonly occur archaeologically
Use for the remains of any part of a mollusc. Use more specific term if known.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of five 10ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 11137/41.
An unconsolidated geological deposit sometimes iused as a bonding material in stone walls.
Accommodation, often in private houses or lodgings, provided for military personnel.
An object used in the sublimation process. It is pear shaped with both ends open.
A ship that is built and primarily intended for war.
A windmill with a rotating cap containing the windshaft, and a stationary body in the form of a tower.
The latex of plants tacky in its normal state and elastic after treatment. Used for a variety of purposes.
A sports arena with a steeply banked oval track for bicycle racing. There are outdoor as well as indoor velodromes.
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
Traditionally begins with the Roman invasion in 43AD and ends with the emperor Honorius directing Britain to see to its own defence in 410AD.
A residential establishment for retired armed servicemen and women.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A device for receiving and sending radio-transmitted signals into the atmosphere.
A flint tool with a convex top and flat base.

An unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting avtivities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools with a covering structure.
A sundial capable of giving an accurate reading of standard time to the minute.
19th century school for the daughters of clergymen.
A structure used for execution by hanging. Usually two uprights and a cross-piece, from which the offender is suspended by the neck.
Portable device that generate stable and consistent flame by combining flammable liquids or pressurised gases with a spark.

A clay-based ceramic fired at low kiln temperatures (c.800-1200 degrees). Essentially, earthenwares are porous and require glazing for most applications. This term has been used interchangeably with TERRACOTTA and with POTTERY
The part of an object by which it is held when in use, being moved or carried.
A building licensed for the sale of beer.

A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which panels of either pre cast concrete or corrugated asbestos could be slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation during WWII.
A system of artificial or natural drains and ditches used to drain off surplus water.

The measurement of the light emitted from sedimentary minerals, mineral inclusions in bricks, burnt flint or unburnt calcite when they are heated. The signal relates to their prior exposure to radioactivity. Used to date samples up to 500,000 years old.
Defensive fortifications such as ramparts, ditches and stone walls, built to defend a town or city.
The residence of a storekeeper of naval ordnance.

A fishing vessel which tows a dredger to gather oysters. This is an iron wedge shaped contrivance with a small net attached. Towed behind the vessel the iron wedge loosens the oysters and they fall into the net.
A type of 18th century public park, with refreshment houses, concert rooms, etc.
Recording of a complete broadcast television programme, for instance a documentary. For extracts such as items from news broadcasts use VIDEO CLIP.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
A rod or spindle, either fixed or rotating, on which a wheel or group of wheels is fixed.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
A small open container, usually with one handle, used for drinking.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.
A mollusc usually used as a foodstuff.
A building in which an organization or society is instituted to promote foreign languages in England such as French and German, etc.
A piece of machinery used to raise oil from a well.
A demasted old ship used for storing items.
An ancillary building in a factory or other industrial complex where manufactured goods are packaged.
Grounds, usually associated with a country house, laid out so as to produce the effect of natural scenery.
A flake produced from a carefully prepared core.
The limit line of a township.
A projectile fired from a bow.
Rendering material containing lime and sand spread on walls as a pliable mixture before drying to a hard surface.
A plate-steel water tank on a steel tower designed to hold 80,000 gallons of water. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 9526/41.
The skirting or projecting base of a wall.
The oldest form of iron, it is a tough, pure form of iron that can be fashioned into decorative items or shapes by hammering, squeezing or rolling.
An engineless aeroplane, designed to be towed aloft, that travels suspended by upward air currents.
Oil obtained from the liver of the cod, providing a rich source of vitamins A and D.
A building or room where items of pottery are manufactured. Includes handcrafted and machine made pottery.
A roof with four sloping sides, rising from four gables, joining at the apex like a pyramid.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two ranges at right angles to each other.
A building, structure or site used for the storage of charcoal.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.
An instrument played mainly by bowing the strings. Use narrower terms where known.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
An opening in a wall that is usually narrow on the outside but widens internally to allow a defender to stand and shoot through the loophole.

A perforated stone basin usually built into the wall of a church on the south side of the altar. Used for carrying away the ablutions (wine and water used to rinse the chalice, and wash the priests hands after communion).
Thin plates of slate, usually rectangular in shape, used as roofing tiles.

A building complex, usually including kennels and cages and built close to a port or airport, in which animals can be securely held, for a designated period, to ensure that they are not carrying any infectious diseases which could be spread to others.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one or more sides of an open cattle yard.
An internal combustion engine which uses a mixture of air and petrol as fuel, the combustion of which is by an electric spark.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.
A departmental building within a college or university where a particular subject is taught and administered.
A pit filled with rocks and metal, designed to be fired with an explosive charge.
A road block formed by placing curved rails, "hairpins", in sockets in the road surface.
A rafter set outside a gable to carry the roof beyond the wall face.

As this proposal may affect a heritage asset other than undesignated archaeology, we recommend that you seek the advice of your local authority conservation officer. The NPPF defines a heritage asset as ‘a building, monument, site, place, area or landscape identified as having a degree of significance meriting consideration in planning decisions, because of its heritage interest’. Designated heritage assets include listed buildings and conservation areas, which are legally protected under the Planning (Listed Buildings and Areas) Act 1990. Most works to listed buildings require listed building consent in addition to planning permission.
A mound used to elevate buildings associated with a fishery e.g. smoke houses, above the level of a flood plain.
Any of a large group of cold blooded vertebrates who live exclusively in water. Also can refer to the flesh of fish which is eaten.
An area of land which retains distinctive large-scale rectilinear land divisions characteristic of Roman agriculture. Generally aligned with the course of a Roman road.
Any church which bears signs of fortification. Churches on the Welsh and Scottish borders were often fortified, only allowing access to the tower from a single opening in the nave.
A pipe used for smoking where the smoke passes through water.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate an airfield and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
Use for vessels registered in Greece.
A long handled shallow pan used for frying.
The rod is also called pole or perch and equal to  5 1⁄2 yards
A furnace composed of two fire brick boxes: the fire was in the lower box and the upper box held the crucibles. Used in the manufacture of steel.
A vessel comprising of two or more bowls, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
Remains of any of the groups of animals characterized by having a bony or cartilaginous spinal column (backbone) and a well developed brain.
A church built within the bounds of a parish for the attendance of those who cannot reach the parish church conveniently.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, usually found at an observatory, through which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
A hard metallic element used in steels and magnetic alloys. Compounds containing manganese are used in glass-making and other industrial processes.
A common plan form of large medieval and sub medieval houses, with a hall range flanked by two wings; also found with only one wing.
A band of material, often leather, or a chain or similar worn around the neck of an animal for identification and or restraint. Where this is part of harness use the specific harness term.
A hinged or looped clasp that fits over a staple and is secured by a pin, bolt or padlock.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.
A calculating table or frame, specifically one in which balls slide upon wires. Used for the mechanical solution of arithmetical problems.
An establishment for the testing of eyesight, making up of optical prescriptions and the sale of spectacles.
A furnace for the calcining and roasting of a mixture of sand and fluxes as a preparatory stage in glass-making.
A nursery for infants, where they are taken care of while their mothers are at work.
A fictitious name, especially one used by an author. A pen-name.
A trap designed and used to catch fish.
Ore hearth specifically for the refining of silver.
An enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a promontory which projects into the sea.
A first-floor chamber, often serving as a parlour, bedchamber or private room, in a medieval house. Also a loft, rood-loft or garret.
A distinguishing emblem or mark, often worn to signify membership, achievement, employment etc.
A closely mown lawn used for the game of croquet.
Apparatus used for applying a mechanical force, or to perform a particular function. Use more specific type where known.
Salmon which has been pickled in vinegar or brine to preserve it.
A thin wooden slab or tile used in quantity as a roof or wall covering.
The limit line of a field.
The flesh of animals, either raw or cooked, used as food.
An establishment for the storage of food for use during wartime or similar states of emergency.
A basin or harbour, which is open to the tides. Vessels can only enter and leave at high tide and are stranded at low tide.
A large vessel with raised or applied cordons running horizontally on the body of the vessel.
A plan of a building where the entrance is in the gable wall.
A container, capable of being carried by hand, often for carrying such items as clothes, keys, money, etc.

A hexagonal pillbox, with an internal anti-ricochet wall and loopholes for fives light machine guns and one rifle. Originally designed to have 15in bulletproof walls many were built with 42in thick shellproof walls. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A large house dating from the 16th century onwards, built as a symbol of the wealth and status of the owner but not intended to be defensible unlike the castles and manor houses it replaced.
A wheeled passenger vehicle, especially one with four wheels and pulled by horses.
An excavation from which cobble stone is obtained.
Workshop for the construction and maintenance of boilers within an industrial complex.
A Mark 2B aircraft with which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A submarine built or adapted to carry mines and lay minefields.
A large kitchen garden enclosed by a substantial wall, not usually adjacent to its associated house.
A garden in which bees are kept.
A marker stone erected to indicate a claim to the rights, usually mineral, of an area.
A building in which sheep are sheared.
Mark 4 or the fourth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A holistic approach to urban character, using GIS to map areas of urban character and historical development, as a tool for managing future change in ways that are appropriate and sustainable.

A cable repeater station for the undersea telephone and telegraph cables. Repeater stations compensated for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.
A small bag or detachable outside pocket.
A form of thatching straw composed of stems that have been combed mechanically to remove grain and extraneous waste material without crushing the stem.
A hospital where Royal Naval personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A two storey building with a watch office on the ground floor and a control room above. Originally based on drawing number 12096/4.
The residence and office of an ambassador.
A flint blade or flake with retouch on one or both ends.

A circular bank in which trees have been planted for ornamental purposes or to create an enclosure. May exist purely as a bank which has been formed over the stumps of the trees which had been planted to form the enclosure.
An area of ground, set apart for the burial of the dead.
A cargo vessel constructed in the U.S.A. during World War II from prefabricated sections by welding.
The official residence of a bishop.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
A vessel or craft used for catching or harvesting marine life by a variety of methods, use specific method where known.
A small cushion into which pins are pushed for storage.
A portable writing-case or surface, especially one for use on the lap. May contain compartments for storing writing materials and paper.
The cutting or chopping part of an axe; bifacially worked, longitudinal section symmetrical, cutting edge  parallel to the direction of the hafted tool as swung.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
A curved moulding with a sharp edge running along its centre. So named as its profile resembles the keel of a ship.
A long, high-ceilinged room, usually extending the full length of an Elizabethan or Jacobean house and often occupying an upper floor, used as a promenade, place of entertainment etc..
A white powder used to colour medicines, paints etc.

Historic building assessment is an investigation to establish the character, history, dating, form and development of an historic building or structure to inform a strategy for its conservation, alteration, demolition, repair or management. This may also inform the preparation of Heritage Statements and/or Conservation Management Plans
A suburb of a town, especially Roman or Medieval, situtated or extending beyond its formal limits, usually demarked by defences.
A bay in a two storeyed house open to the roof to allow smoke to escape.
A place where two or more roads meet.
An order composed of elements of the Ionic and Corinthian orders.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A fortifed position, often including fieldworks or defensive structures, designed to keep enemy forces engaged to allow reinforcements to be mobilized.
Large fish, native to the North Atlantic and adjacents seas which has been fished since the Middle Ages.
A depression in the ground caused by the impact of a falling object, such as a crashed aircraft.
A path covered in a layer of water-worn or pounded stones.
A cast of a person's face taken after death.
The fat removed from the carcass of a whale or seal and used in the manufacture of cosmetics and as a fuel for tallow lamps.
A building where artisans could learn more about their craft, and the scientific and theoretical principles behind it, by attending lectures and the use of the reading room facilities.
Partial Shielded Self Propelled Mounting System
A place where goods are sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A piece of openwork fabric made from twine or cord, either natural fibre or artificial, forming a mesh used for catching birds, animals or fish or for holding other inanimate objects.
Armoured covering to protect the hand and wrist.
A signalling station which used a series of shutters to indicate various messages.
Begins with the dissolution of the monasteries and ends with the death of Queen Victoria. Use more specific period where known.
Containers of cylindrical form, traditionally made of curved wooden staves bound together by hoops of metal. Also includes modern plastic and metal barrels.
A piece of furniture containing shelves, cupboards or drawers for storage or display.
Frozen water. Prior to the invention of the refrigerator, ice was used to preserve food.
A dredger that works by the use of suction.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of silk.
A fixed basin, containing Holy Water, positioned near the entrance of a church, usually placed within a niche, on a wall or pier, or freestanding upon a pedestal.
A long ridge of earth, rocks or gravel primarily constructed to carry a roadway.
Use for vessels registered in India.
A rail or balustrade that separates the altar from the rest of the church.
A flag bearing a device, often carried on two poles or hanging from a cross piece. Usually used in processions.

A panel, board or device bearing an inscription, symbol or image, usually describing a function, name, location, instruction, or otherwise distinguishing the object or structure on which it is placed.
A hand operated machine for winding cotton and linen thread into balls - invented in 1802.
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.
Clothes worn against the skin and beneath other clothes.
A straight sided drinking vessel, usually with a wide mouth and without handles.
A pair of principal rafters with a tiebeam, usually with a collar.
A horizontal door within, and usually flush with surface of, a floor, ceiling or roof.

A building or buildings ranged around a courtyard on at least three sides. They occur in the Iron Age, as well as being an influential plan type of house from the 15th century onwards. Index with appropriate period.
A cast-iron or stone boundary post, obelisk or plate found on roads, railways, canals etc around London marking the boundary within which a duty was payable on coal.
A major horizontal timber spanning a roof space to connect a pair of principal rafters and prevent them spreading.
Hard semi-translucent ceramic material made out of kaolin, quartz and feldspar which is biscuit fired at around 1000 degrees Celsius and glaze fired at around 1300 degrees Celsius.
A long seat, usually made of stone or wood, with or without a back.
A large fork with wide spaces between its tines, used to throw grain etc into a breeze to separate grain from chaff.
A system of communication used in a house to summon servants or on board ship to transmit orders to the engine room.
A pumping station used in the production of hydraulic power, eg. in warehouse complexes, goods depots on railways, etc.
Mill for producing a smooth surface and edges on newly sawn timber.
The wood from trees of the type Quercus.
Very tough transparent sheeting often used for security glazing.
A heavy, smooth bore, long barrelled weapon, fired from the shoulder.
Wood used to produce a dye.
A site where the baiting of animals took place. Use more specific site type where known.
A prehistoric coffin made out of a hollow tree trunk.
A gable without a roof behind it.
Soft, pear-shaped fruits of the Ficus carica tree. They can be eaten fresh or dried.
A guard or cover put in front of a fire to prevent embers or flames setting fire to a building.
Removal of a sample from a vertical section generally using a U sectioned tin to extract an intact column of the observed stratigraphy. Used in the study of pollen, diatoms etc.
A collection of associated artefacts recovered from a single site.
A machine that can be flown in the air, now specifically an aeroplane or helicopter.
Coiled substance, usually metal or plastic, used to absorb shocks or in timepieces since it can stretch and return to its original shape.
A metallic rod attached to a high point on a building and leading to the earth for the purpose of conducting lightning away from the main body of the building.
A site where a body of troops is temporarily or permanently lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
A small house or cottage at the entrance to a cemetery, usually occupied by a caretaker or gardener, etc.
A building or room within a monastery in which the monks were allowed to warm themselves. The warming house was often the only place where a fire was allowed.
A Mesolithic type of mace head made of stone.
Use for places of worship. For later landscape features use, eg. GARDEN TEMPLE.
An establishment where the art of sword fencing is taught.
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
A three sided or U-shaped metal fastener on which the ends are pointed.
Generic term for the oolitic limestones quarried in Northamptonshire, Lincolnshire and Rutland. Varying in grain size from medium to coarse, and colour from cream to pale brown.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
A device, monogram or symbol incised in stonework by a mason as a means of identifying his work. Particularly common in Romanesque and Gothic buildings.
An instrument with a series of pipes at different pitches, the air being produced by bellows, and pipes selected by keyboard or sliders.
A structure of iron or wood, open below, running out into the sea and used as a promenade and landing stage.
A major warship equipped with a clear flat deck to provide a landing and taking off place for aircraft.
An artificial hill constructed in Tudor gardens, especially, to provide a good view.
A building in which newly made bricks are laid out to dry.
A site where clay pipes used for drainage are manufactured.
Unrefined oil used in the manufacture of petroleum.
A hospital devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.
A building and open area from which buses, usually those working local or regional services, begin or end their journeys.
An arcade providing shelter for perishable market goods which also provides protection from the elements for the occupants of the adjoining properties.
A mechanism used to transport minerals or granulated materials.
A military building from which the guns of a battery were directed.
A rod used to measure the imperial measurements of a pole or a perch.
Use for the remains of any part of an insect.
One of a series of small, rectangular blocks arranged like a row of teeth, projecting from the lower part of a cornice in many classical orders.
A model village built by a utopian society or group of artists.
View across roofs, generally in an urban context, showing details of roof and chimney construction.
A manufacturing site producing weaving shuttles for the textile industry.
A column in which the shaft is interrupted by stone bands.
A settlement carefully planned from its inception and usually constructed in an area which was previously undeveloped. Many new towns were developed following the New Towns Act 1946.
A building with a range of educational and recreational facilities for the exclusive use of its all-female membership.
A weapon, usually blunt, used to strike an opponent.
A site used for the small scale extraction and working of surface boulders.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of South-Eastern Command.

One in a chain of stations with semaphore shutters and telescopes which could relay messages according to a planned code. Used from the 1790s by the British Admiralty to speed up communications from London to the ports of Deal, Portsmouth and Plymouth.
An institution, sometimes attached to a hospital, where patients may receive treatment or health checks.
A container for pills or tablets.
A building, usually within the grounds of a school and often containing dormitories, used by pupils who board.
A small, single-masted merchant vessel, designed for maximum hold capacity and not for sailing ability.
An establishment where wine is produced.
Use for stationary railway carriage being used for a purpose it wasn't originally intended for - office, shelter, etc.

A cutting and thrusting weapon consisting of a blade and a hilt. The blade varies in length and width and the cutting edge can vary from being purely the point to being one or both sides or a combination of these.
A site, including buildings and structures, from which communication signals are transmitted.
For example allergic contact dermatitis, Barlows Syndrome, cutaneous melanoma, irritant contact dermatitis, MRSA infection, mummification and other related illnesses.

A complex of buildings at a seaport, comprising of a terminal building, landing pier and hangars, used for the embarkation of passengwers and/or freight on flying boat services during the 1930's-50's.

A well concealed structure, usually constructed undergound, intended for use by members of the Special Duties section of the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organization) in the event of invasion.

Single-engine, testbed monoplane built to Air Ministry Specification 43/37. Only twelve were produced, the first of which tested the Sabre I engine in 1940, and were used throughout the war. The cockpit could seat two observers behind the pilot.
A shaped and or carved stone.
A tall structure of any form, high in proportion  to its lateral dimensions, often rising in stages, freestanding or part of another building, often used in fortifications and churches.
A shop housing the business of a grindery dealer. Grindery are the tools and materials used by shoemakers and other leather-workers.

A house within a row. At first floor level a gallery which runs through the front of the building. Access to the gallery was gained by steps set at intervals along the row. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A building for housing, maintaining and repairing motor cars. Dating to the 1890s.
Concrete, containing bars or wires, which is compressed to greatly increase its strength.
An enclosed area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.

A funeral rite in which the human body is burnt, usually on a pyre, leaving fragmentary charred or completely combusted remains. Often found buried, occasionally in a container associated with grave goods.
A mass of stone or brick built against or as part of a wall to provide additional strength to it.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
A projection on the under side of a hinged choir stall seat providing support during long periods of standing.
A school conducted by members of a convent.
An elementary steam engine working on the atmospheric principle; often used downstream of an overshot waterwheel.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
A hand held long barrelled gun.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of products from metals.
An arcaded upper aisle, wall passage or blind arcade, usually occurring in large Romanesque or Gothic churches, above the aisle and below the clerestory.
A circular window with tracery or shafts radiating from the centre.
A factory where tobacco was ground to form snuff.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.
Small stones which have been rounded usually by the action of sea water.
Use for items of personal equipment used in a military context, eg AMMUNITION POUCH, PRIMING FLASK.
Two linked quadrangular open areas surrounded by walls or buildings.
A building, room or suite of rooms where books, or other materials, are classified by subject and stored for use by the library's members.
Houses specifically of nuns/canonesses or religious women.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for foxes.
A swimming pool restricted to the use of females only.
A barn belonging to, or associated with, a grange.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
The extraction of a limited quantity of wood for scientific analysis.
A storehouse using mechanical means of controlling temperature rather than ice or insulation.
Listed Building List Entry Legacy UID
Card printed with an image, often a photograph on one side, and space for a short message and a postal address on the other.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of sailors and/or their families. For Royal Naval seamen use ROYAL NAVAL HOSPITAL.
A prepared area of ground, often enclosed, used for the game of basketball.
A large tank where particles suspended in water, or other liquids, are allowed to sink to the bottom forming a sediment.
The horizontal piece of timber or stone forming the bottom of a window, doorway or other opening, usually and properly designed to throw off water.
A site where an army or body of troops is, temporarily or permanently, lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
A Cornish Medieval amphitheatre used for the performance of mystery plays and sports.
An ovolo moulding below the abacus of a Doric or Ionic Capital.
A tool used for weeding and breaking up the ground prior to planting.
Accommodation designed for the elderly, disabled, etc, as individual units.
A table made of stone, found in streets, parks, etc.
A piece of machinery used to convert energy of one sort (for instance steam) into motive energy.

An area of land owned by a developer, whether a private entrepreneur or a public authority, and divided into plots for leasing or sale to manufacturing or commercial concerns which may share some common services.

A prefabricated structure of cant sided lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed for use as barrack accommodation during WWII.
A deposit that forms the ground surface (when the evidence is collected), particularly a hard surface such as a floor or road.
A purpose built covered market hall, usually 19th century, although earlier examples do exist, eg. that at Abingdon, Oxfordshire c.1680.
A machine for the final reduction in cross sectional area of a cotton sliver into a fine roving preparatory to spinning high counts of yarn.
An ornamental receptacle to catch rainwater for birds to drink from and bathe in. Sometimes mounted on a column or plinth.
Lead which has been rolled into a sheet and often used as a roof covering.
A dining hall for the use of seasonal labourers.
A jar with roughly vertical body walls which in some cases may be slightly convex. (Source: MPRG)
One of a line of blocks on the floor of a building slip on which the keel of the ship to be constructed is laid. Also used in dry docks to rest a ship when a dock is pumped dry.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a wood or coppice
A shaped piece of iron perforated for nails and used on horses.
A mill used for the manufacture of walking sticks.
A building where timber was allowed to dry and harden, to render it fit for use as a working material.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A container, typically cylindrical with a narrow neck, usually for containing liquids.
A purpose built section of path linking two sections of a canal enabling a horse to be led over or around an obstacle such as a hill. Horse paths predate towpath tunnels.
A vessel which has damaged by a lightning strike and subsequently lost.
A container used to serve drinks and liquids.
A small cutting hook on a long handle.
A measuring rule used for cloth, with the imperial yard divided into quarters and nails (sixteenths), or using the now obsolete ell of 45 inches.
A sensing technique that consists of measuring minute variations in the gravitational pull of the Earth in order to detect gravity anomalies arising from voids and cavities within the earth.
A low stool for resting feet upon.
An instrument for viewing or measuring information on heavenly bodies.
A piece of wood or iron to secure ropes, etc to or on.
An opening normally in a door or window filled with diagonally set slats to provide ventilation.
A building or group of buildings in which communications signals, usually intercepted fro military purposes, are analysed.
A very small flint or other stone tool.
A trench dug in order to receive the foundations of a structure such as a stone wall etc.
An area of a site or building providing a stable base for the firing of artillery pieces.
A small bar raised or lowered by a latchlifter which is used to fasten gates or doors etc.
Documents relating to the planning, inception and management of a project.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A structure providing protection against the weather, situated on railway platforms.
A terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.
A building with first aid facilities to deal with accidents and other medical emergencies.
A hearth for roasting metallic ore, usually non ferrous, before smelting.
A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which wild animals are kept and reared for public exhibition.
A small container used to fill a lamp with fuel.
Armour designed to protect the foot.
A costrel with a cylindrical body and a centrally placed neck. One end is usually domed and the other flat. Two opposed strap handles or lugs may join the rim or neck and shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
The non-diagonal joint at the right-angled meeting of two stone mouldings.

A building or part of a building, sometimes attached to a religious community, where religious activities such as worshipping, meetings, teaching about the faith and conferences take place. It can also provide accommodation.
A specific type of Infrared photography that uses an airborne scanning infrared sensor to record differential spectrums of features both extant and buried.
A straight brace from rafter to collar in a common rafter truss.
A frame used to lift unco-operative horses off the ground during shoeing.
A stemmed cup used for holding the wine during communion.
An object designed to add curls to a wig.
A place of law to which debtors were taken for the recovery of monies by their creditors.
A tower built on a prominent part of an estate to provide panoramic views of the surrounding countryside.
Buildings and structures associated with a private aviation club undertaken as a leisure pursuit. Usually situated on or near an airfield.
A crane usually found at a marine or inland quay.
A well concealed structure, usually constructed underground, intended for use by members of the British Resistance Organization in the event of invasion.
Poles of timber, metal etc. used as masts, booms or yards on a vessel.
Steel coated in zinc, giving good protection against weathering.

An entablature often of great magnificence with bead and reel between fasciae of the architrave, frieze ornamented with continuous sculpture and cornice, with ornate coffers and richly carved modillions.
An antechurch which is transverse to the axis of the church and is covered or enclosed.
A walk, common in 18th century gardens, providing a view across the surrounding countryside.
A stick or rod with an attached lash.
A building for a society formed for the promotion of some branch of learning or science.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around two sides of an open cattle yard.
A platform scale set within, and flush with the surface of, a roadway, for weighing vehicles, cattle etc.
A maritime monument where the vessel remains are buried in the sea bed.
A building housing the instrumentation necessary for the observation and measurement of tremors generated by earthquakes.
A self-propelled wheeled vehicle that does not operate on rails, such as trains or trolleys.
A decorative panel worn over the chest and stomach by both men and women in the 16th century and later only by women.
An instrument of punishment, in which the offender was placed in a sitting position in a timber frame, with holes to confine the ankles and wrists between two planks.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief and can be of various materials. For freestanding sculptures see also Monument Types Thesaurus.
A local civil court first established during the 17th Century by local Acts of Parliament to deal with minor cases of debt. Based on a model established during the reign of Henry VII.
Short-range naval weapon with a low muzzle velocity.
Use for vessels registered in Brazil.
General term for documents that have been produced in large numbers for public sale or distribution.
The central division of a church, extending from the west end to the chancel or transepts.
A small carved or sculpted figure.
A brewing or baking house attached to a vernacular building, 16/17th century.
A room or office at a general practitioners' or veterinary practice, where patients or animals are seen and medicine dispensed.
Bank to let deer cross ditches, fences or roads, into, but not out of, a deer park.
An often secluded garden set below the level of surrounding ground, usually surrounded with terraces.
A room for servants, particularly where they would eat.
A simple flat-topped lid resembling an inverted dish but with no central knob or handle. (Source: MPRG)
Photographic negative on film. Use for all acetate material types.
A photographic print of a mononchrome image (composed of grey, black and white tones).
Buildings and sites associated with the printing and publishing industry.
Letters and parcels transported on behalf of the dispatchers by the postal services.
A covered chalice used for the Eucharist.
Buildings and structures associated with the use of animals to generate power.
A building in which a sport is played. Use more specific type where known.
A type of GARDEN HOUSE situated on an island in a garden lake or canal or, more generally, by any waterside.
An establishment where offenders who have committed the most serious crimes, e.g. serial killers, are confined.
A rotating wheel, horizontal to the ground, on which pottery is made.
18th-19th century stone-lined pit which held the balance bob for a pump-rod or flat-rod system. It includes examples where the surviving feature is a pillar for the bearing, rather than the pit.
A decorated screen behind an altar.
Loss of speech and other forms of speech disorder.
A room decorated, and furnished, in the style of the Chinese.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A building constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A device, often consisting of a cyclinder containing a piston or plunger, used to raise or move liquids or gasses by means of compression, lifting or suction.
A group of trees planted as part of a designed landscape.
A building or area where processes like bleaching, dressing, etc, are conducted under one roof.
A farrier's tool for paring a horse's hoof.
An enclosed cage used in a mine shaft to transport miners from the surface to the mine workings.
A decorative motif representing a palm leaf. Often painted, incised or applied in relief, can occur singly or as a repeating pattern.
A machine used to burn and desiccate rubbish.
Sites, buildings and structures associated with the prevention of an invasion by a hostile force.
An abbey or priory of the Trinitarian brethren also named Maturins.
Hospital For Fistula And Rectal Diseases

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.

Manmade structure for bathing or swimming that is located on the beachfront and filled by tidal waters. Similar to a LIDO, with the main difference being the extent of the built up complex around the pool.
A monument composed of plants or trees which are still extant. Especially relevant for park and garden features. For example tree avenue, orchard, rose garden and lawn.
A depot used for the unloading of coal.
A fort with a star trace plan, designed to increase the angles of fire.
The choir and sanctuary in the liturgical eastern part of a church appropriated for those who officiate during services.
A bridge manufactured from prefabricated sections.
Any material that records, holds and communicates information in a primarily visual manner.
A college where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
A building or site from which a lookout can be kept.
A mill for grinding or crushing bones, in the process of making bone china, for example.
A small ferry powered by steam or diesel engine, which pull vessel from one side of a river crossing along submerged chains.
A plot of land longer than it is wide, can include any structures on it. Typical of medieval towns.
A school where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
Ordnance, expended or otherwise, weapons, armour, personal effects, transport wreckage, or ship wreckage, left behind on the site of a terrestrial or naval battle.
An abbey or priory for monks of the Benedictine order.

Roman mid-first to third century AD S or reverse-S shaped brooch. Often enamelled, with its central section expanded for decoration, the brooch depicted stylised creatures derived from Celtic art. The pin was looped over the neck of the brooch.
A booth, cubicle or recess, often enclosed, in which a priest, usually screened from view, hears confessions.
A modern small factory or workshop, often in the form of a prefabricated shed.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the collection, distribution, sending and reception of mail.
Site for the disposal of unexploded ordnance, possibly attached to a bombing range.
An isolated barn, cow house or shelter shed with a hayloft. Typically found in areas where farmsteads and fields were sited at a long distance from each other.
An image created manually using paint or pigments, to record, illustrate or convey impressions.
A block of metal with a device cut into it, used to impress a coin blank.
A building used by teachers for in-service training.
A place where pieces of stone are crushed and ground.
Fifth Rate Ship Of The Line
A type of direct-acting, twin cylinder steam driven water pump.
Buildings and sites used for the production of inorganic and organic dyes, pigments and paints.
A small tank or cistern, often lead or cast-iron and sometimes ornamented, that collects rainwater from a gutter or channel prior to it being discharged.
Dating to the start of the third millennium CE/AD.  2001-2100
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and repair of ships and boats.
Explosive devices, usually of metal, placed in the ground or floating in water with the purpose of endangering enemy personnel or shipping.
An establishment where musical performances take place.
A column of the Ionic Order, set upon a base and characterized by its slender form.
A law court builidng established during the 1970's accommodating offices and courtrooms fro the Crown and County Courts.
A vessel with a single mast, fore and aft rigged.
Between 40¡N and mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal04
A simple, wind-driven water pump, also known as a windpump.
An area of plasterwork modelled or incised with ornamental designs or motifs.
A tall multi-storey block of flats, slender with a square plan.
A crane used for the refueling of coal-powered vessels.
Plaster which has been painted either for decorative purposes or to protect it.
A group of buildings and machines, usually situated close to the pithead,  enabling the rapid, mechanized loading of goods wagons with coal.
A place where manganese ore is extracted. Use with other ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A tower used for surveying, especially in civil engineering projects such as bridges.
Objects designed to be played with, often a model or miniature replica of something and especially for a child.
A small file for manicuring a person's nails with.
Goods, usually foodstuffs, which have been sealed inside canisters, usually made of tin or steel, to preserve them.
An office for the payment of wages, especially in industrial or commercial complexes.
A transverse vestibule at the west end of a church.
A wall cladding consisting of slates hung in overlapping rows.
A 19th century glasshouse built specifically for the fostering of camellias.
Building with underfloor kiln used for drying China Clay slurry prior to packing and transportation. Central feature of China Clay Works.
Use for vessels registered in the United States of America.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a dockyard and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
The period covering the reign of Edward VII. Do not use for the reigns of Edwards I-VI.
A factory where lace is manufactured.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A horizontal, supporting beam set above an opening in an external wall, a fireplace opening or in timber framed construction set forward from the lower part of a building to support a jettied wall.
An ornament at the top of a roof or spire.

A fastener made of a metal circle connected to a metal loop fixed to an object and used to fasten to another object by means of a button or a loop. The usage of these items is unclear, could include use for animals or for dress.
Specify in Descriprion whether currently managed, neglected, unmanaged or management not determined.

Generic name for a vessel used for work rather than for recreation, transportation, or military purposes. The vessels include tugs, barges, landing craft, dredgers and standby safety vessels. Use only were the exact type of vessel is unknown.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to the surface of a wall.
An alignment of trees planted as part of a designed landscape. For a belt lining a road use TREE AVENUE.
A garden building on an estate used by fishing parties.
The purpose of this object is unknown though it could be for surveying or it could be a charm.
A building combining a cow-house with crop storage space.
Unclassifiable site with minimal information. Specify site type wherever possible.

A short wide-beamed Dutch craft, often used as a fishing vessel or, in the 17th and 18th centuries, a privateer due to its manoeuvrability. Fitted with a ketch rig or variations thereof. Used extensively in the North Sea.
Loss of a vessel or aircraft primarily due to fire.
A long pillow, especially one used as an under pillow.
A plucked string instrument in which the strings pass over the soundbox and parallel to the sides of the instrument.
Any subsurface investigation conducted to assist with the technical rather than archaeological aspects of a proposed development or extraction scheme.
Central two-storeyed tower surmounted by an octagonal glazed control room giving a 360 degree view. Flanked by single-storey wings.
A weight used to sink a fishing line or a net in water.
A vessel used for the transport of troops, either during wartime or for garrison duties in peacetime.
A mounting or fixture attached to a cart.
A round object used in games.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specification (drawing number 6910/43). Similar in design to the ROBINS AIRCRAFT HANGAR but larger.
An engineering workshop for the manufacture and repair of springs.
A court of summary jurisdiction established, following legislation, in 1908 for the trial of offenders below the age of legal reponsibility.
A 19th century structure of various shape or material for the protection of troops in an emergency.
A decorative tile on the end of the cornice or eaves of a building to conceal the ends of tiles.
Use only for fragmentary wreckage washed up at the time of loss or subsequently: but not for complete hulls for which STRANDED or another appropriate manner of loss should be used.
Any form of fastener used to fasten a girdle together.
A crane consisting of a vertical tower or similar structure from which projects a movable boom, or jib, fitted with a mechanical hoist.
A niche in the corner of a structure.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.
A layer underneath the topsoil containing rubble or fragments of building material, e.g. mortar, tile, flint.
A large area, usually open-air, used for permanent, seasonal or regular shows, events or exhibitions.
A carved or moulded decorative projection adorning an object or, in the case of architectural features, the termination of a moulding or the intersection of ribs or beams.
A stone basin for containing holy water often set in inside walls of a church, especially near the entrance.
A threshing barn which also houses farm animals and is somethimes used to stotre grain, house carts and other functions.
A place where a group of people live together sharing accomodation and goods, forming their own community based upon common ideals.
The hard, heavy wood obtained from plants of the genus Guaiacum.
A flat slab of stone used to provide a level surface from which to measure the height of racehorses at a meeting, as part of the handicapping and anti fraud systems.
A castle built on a simple, rectangular plan, usually with a tower at each corner. This design became common in England after 1300.
A furnace used for smelting or re-heating of iron, either for casting or for further working.

To include areas of wet valley bogs, sphagnum bogs, fens (N.B. in areas such as the Fens and the Somerset Levels most land should be classified under Cultivated Land, Woodland or Grassland rather than Wetlands).
A sea within a sea, the Aegean consists of that part of the Mediterranean bordered by Greece and Turkey.
A military base for the training of SOE operatives in the skills and techniques required to survive in enemy-occupied territory.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
A ridge and furrow produced by a plough drawn between two steam engined vehicles, or a steam engined vehicle and a moveable windlass, standing on opposite headlands.
Medium to coarse grained metamorphic rock, colour being determined by its dominant mineral. Often used for floor and wall cladding.
A building or structure for the storage of processed minerals, chemicals or agricultural products, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A vertical structure usually with an Attic base or spira with slender and elegant design, with a capital decorated with acanthus leaves and an entablature rich in carved ornament.
An office where the administrative duties of a university are performed.

A club often with a dance floor or small stage and featuring entertainment generally of an improvisational, satirical, or topical nature which can be watched by the clientele whilst they drink and dine.
An employment exchange for unemployed labourers, servicemen, etc.
Seed of the cotton plant from which edible oil is extracted.

A form of axehead where the body is hollow allowing for insertion of the haft. Usually bronze or iron and of late Bronze Age or Iron Age date. Most examples feature a side loop to further assist hafting.
A factory used to manufacture fibreglass.
A device for catching fish, may be a portable or permanent structure, often a fence or row stakes made in a river, harbour, etc
A monument consisting of parallel banks, normally accompanied by ditches, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A building or structural plan with a U shape.
A bowl in which an offering is made.
Any vessel which has been hired or impressed for use by the Admiralty.
A cross erected in a village.
A piece of armour worn to protect the throat.
A monocular optical instrument possessing magnification for observing distant objects, especially in astronomy.
A building in which a parliament meets and conducts the business of government.
Demolition to the ground level of a building.
An inclined concrete ramp on which cars can move from one level to another.
A place of worship for Christian Scientists, a sect founded in the mid-19th century in America who believe that God is the only reality and can bring healing to humanity.
Ornament often with a hinged pin and catch, worn fastened to clothing.
A hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
A joint in which the end is shaped like a dovetail.

A square shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier. Small square enclosures (with sides of less than c.20m) have been interpreted as the remains of square barrows of Iron Age date.
A tool with a sharp tapering end used for piercing materials or as a weapon point.

Monument visible as substantial above ground remains, retaining evidence of architecture and materials, with walls partially or completely intact but with roof and interior walls substantially or completely destroyed.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of heart disorders and diseases.
A building or room for the storage of vegetables, particularly root vegetables, for human consumption.
A building which provides the centralized market for trading in stocks and shares and for raising capital for industry.
An area of ground belonging to a church, often used as a burial ground.
A machine for combing out wool, mohair and alpaca, removing short fibres and any extraneous matter, and laying  the long fibres more or less parallel  to each other.
The wood, stone or brick framework, lining a doorway, from which the door is hung.
Objects used to thresh and winnow crops.
A small outlying farm building, especially common in southern England, used to store ash (which was used as a fertilizer).
White coloured marble. Imported from France.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A stick used as an aid or accessory when walking.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is laid out in an approximately straight line, whether face up, face down, or on its side.
A light porous cellular rock, consisting of consolidated volcanic ash ejected from vents during a volcanic eruption.
A stone placed across a grave.
A passage that runs axially across the end of a hall with a screen between it and the hall and doorways to service rooms on the other side.
A wheel turned by water to generate mechanical power.
Microscopic living things, usually unicellular, occasionally multi-cellular. They lack cell nuclei.
A coastal site producing salt by scraping up salt-impregnated sand and silt, leeching out the salt to produce a concentrated brine, then boiling in 'saltcotes' (small huts containing lead pans)
Timber sawn into long, flat, pieces used for flooring etc. in buildings.
A steam vessel propelled by a pair of paddle wheels amidships or a single wheel astern, driven by a reciprocating engine.
A short timber supporting end of joists or rafters to facilitate an opening, such as a door or dormer.
A ring worn on a toe.
A vehicle used in warfare, racing or to carry passengers.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.
A vessel designed principally for the carriage of fare paying passengers.

Collective name for the oolitic limestone quarried in the Isle of Purbeck region, geologically classified into two main groups. Firstly, a fine grained whitish variety, Purbeck Portland, secondly a fossil-rich cream/gold to grey variety, Swanage Stone etc
A room or building housing the controls to a mechanized system, eg. in a power station, airport, etc.
A piece of armour used to protect the armpit.
For example chronic liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease, weight loss, liver transplant and other related illnesses.
A space or area that is outside a building.
A place of worship for the followers of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints

An astronomical instrument for telling the time at night. The date is set on the nocturnal then its pointers lined up with the Pole Star and the two primary stars in the Great Bear, thus allowing an approximate time to be read off.
Usually slag, a residue from burning stone, but can be used for vitrified bricks.
Buildings and structures associated with educational and artistic recreational activities.
Domesticated animals, derived from the wild boar, kept as a source of ham, bacon and pork products.

An ornamental (carved and/or painted) frieze carved into, or attached to, the planking either side of a vessel's bow carrying the vessel's name and often illustrating some aspect of the name, port/country of origin etc.
Establishments responsible for the research into and the design, development and manufacture of nuclear warheads.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.
A lustrous, malleable metal, which is resistant to corrosion. Tin is used in alloys such as pewter and used in the manufacture of cans for the storage of food.
A jug with a maximum diameter in the lower half of the vessel and with no discernible shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A modified Nissen hut, based on drawing number (2900/43), used for the repair packing and storage of inflatable liferafts.
A small gable above a hipped roof. Also used ornamentally, such as on a buttress or over a niche.
A plate in a crown post roof, supported on crown posts and bearing the collars.
A decorative building in the form of a dairy, used for recreation.

Recording and analysis of built structures utilising close observation as well as manual or electronic survey equipment such as GPS and REDM (Reflectorless Electromagnetic Distance Measurement). Includes research, fieldwork and a report.
The quasi-triangular area between, and defined by, the upper sections of a pair of adjacent arches, or between the curve of an arch and the angle of a surrounding frame or structure.
An object designed to add curls into hair.
NB currently Includes ISOMETRIC though this has a separate term.

A concrete hut produced by the Ministry of Works as a cheaper alternative to the BCF Hut as any suitable wall cladding could be employed in its construction. Usually used to form barrack blocks on airfields from 1944 onwards.
A Roman cremation burial in which the human cremated remains are placed inside or adjacent to a wooden casket, frequently decorated with lion-headed mounts and studs.
A horizontal member dividing a window into two or more lights.
A railway at a dockyard used for the transportation of goods to and from the dock side.
Development of a new area or extension to an existing area of mineral extraction, including associated buildings and works.
A pair of SHEER LEGS mounted on shore or on a SHEER HULK, used as a crane to hoist a mast and lower it into place on a ship.
A holding tank/pen on a river or seashore for raising and preserving fish and/or for catching them easily.
Including accommodation for animals, birds, reptiles and fish in captivity.
A high building at an airport from which air traffic is controlled by radio.
The approximate location at which stray finds of artefacts were found. Index with object name.

A type of steel framed transportable British military aircraft hangar developed from 1941onwards. The hangar had a steel frame, some versions used commercially available sheeting for cladding. It was similar to but smaller than the arcraft hangar type T2.
Iron in the form of rails eg. for use in the construction of railways.
A long, narrow ditch designed to carry water away from a waterlogged area.
A mould which is used to provide the shape of a piece of footwear.

A schedule of work set out in sufficient detail for it to be quantifiable, implemented and monitored. Can include contractual details relevant to the commissioning body. A project design may be a research proposal independent of the planning framework
A building where documents such as title-deeds, charters, etc, were kept as evidence of rights or privileges.
Rolled iron or steel formed into rails.
An arched or vaulted recess, within a tomb or catacomb, intended to contain a coffin or sarcophagus.
A vessel used for the laying and removal of buoys and other navigational markers.
A liquid derived from wood tar through a distillation process. Now used to describe timber preservative derived from coal tar.
A residence for a member of a religious community eg. Abbot, Prior, Manciple etc. For multiple occupancy use more specific term eg. DORMITORY.
A farm with a pond, river, lake or tanks where fish are kept and bred for commercial purposes.
A bowl used in magical ceremonies.
A school associated with a cathedral or college originally intended to provide a general education for their choristers.
A school in which instruction is given on a Sunday, especially such a school for children connected with a parish or congregation.
A place where oysters are bred for consumption.
A piece of ice or a floor, often within a building, used for skating.
A simple, single cylinder vertical steam engine with its cylinder mounted directly on a baseplate, driving an overhead crankshaft which is supported by two A-shaped frames

Blocks of solid concrete,in the form of truncated pyramids usually 3 feet square x 2 feet high which could be placed in rows to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Pimples were recommended for use on soft ground.
A heavily armoured capital ship with an armament composed entirely of large calibre guns and powered by stem turbines. In effect any battleship constructed after 1908.
A workshop in which saggars - fire clay boxes to protect ware from direct action of flame and gases during firing - were manufactured.
Solid bars made from pure tin.
An instrument where the note is made by air being blown over an edge.

A jar adapted by the addition of two handles. Handles may be horizontal or vertical loops or horizontal or curved lugs. Handles are nearly always opposed. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)

Based on the previous all-timber design 2423/39 and the temporary brick and timber design 518/40, the 8936/40 was built with pre-cast concrete slabs replacing the timber floors and staircases with only the balcony and watch office roof in timber.
Oil obtained from the flesh of the coconut and used in ointments, soaps etc.
An Anglo-Saxon brooch type dating from the 5th to 7th centuries AD and influenced by the Crossbow brooch, featuring a sprung pin and a head plate.
A building or other establishment used for the retail, making and repairing of jewellery.
An informal encampment, usually near a military establishment, set up as a public protest against that establishment or against some aspect of military policy.
Starshaped cairn with three radial arms of equal length, a monument unique to upland Northumberland. (Late Neolithic or early Bronze Age).
A small containment for drugs which can be ingested.
A levelled area of ground on which a barn is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a barn.
An area within a building (usually the barn or stable) for storing husks from the grain crop (chaff) for animal feed after it has been threshed and winnowed in the barn.
The partially enclosed western part of a chapel, leading to the chapel proper.
The part of footwear that touches the ground.
A plain moulding of semi-circular section.
The office or headquarters of a local police force, or of a police district.
The SI derived unit of concentration (of amount of a substance).
The main vertical axle running through the centre of a mill.
Obstacles, often semi permanent, which are placed on railway lines to prevent the enemy from using them. Set up during the defence of Britain.
A pediment with a gap at its apex, sometimes filled with an urn or other decorative feature.
Colour or dye, often in powder form, from natural mineral or vegetable sources (e.g. ochre) or created through chemical process (e.g. lamp black).
A flared bowl of medium to deep depth, with wide horizontal everted rim. These vessels may have a single handle. (Source: MPRG)
The top part of a column, often decorated.
Personnel serving with one of the three armed forces - army, navy or air force.
An area, often including a platform, used for boxing competitions.

Protective equipment, usually made of metal, to protect parts of the body, e.g. helmets, breastplates, or full suits of armour, to protect troops or individuals in warfare. Most examples date from the Middle Ages, obsolete from the 17th century.
A pipe used for smoking tobacco.
A semi solid mixture of complex hydrocarbons derived from coal or petroleum. Used as a waterproof binder or protective coating.
An abbey of Franciscan nuns also known as Minoresses or Poor Clares.
The bottom storey of a building, often below or partially below ground level.
The wedge-shaped block placed at the crown of an arch to consolidate the structure. Sometimes employed as a decorative feature.
An observation post for a naval officer in charge of a marine minefield.
A small shovel used with incense.
A mill where mustard is produced.
A high explosive, manufactured by absorbing unstable nitroglycerine in a material such as kieselguhr, a soft, earthy material.
A building in London belonging to one of four legal societies having exclusive right of admitting persons to practise at the English bar.
A room in which commercial or administrative activities are carried out.
A long staff, occasionally bound with metal, used as a weapon.
The lowest part, usually projecting, of a pedestal or the base of a column.
A designated area of water in which the perfromance of torpedoes can be evaluated.
