Single lap roof covering made of clay. Half cylinder in profile although one end is slightly wider than the other. A Spanish tile roof covering comprises under-tiles and over-tiles, the two have the same shape, but the under-tile is slightly larger.

Early to mid-1st century AD Bow Brooch with a P-shaped profile, a cylindrical or semi-cylindrical spring cover and a round or lozenge-shaped centre plate with a short bow above and a flat leg below, both of which are reeded like the Langton Down Brooch.
The intersection and space between the nave, chancel and transepts in a cruciform church.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A building for the storage of all stores supplied for naval service other than victualling and armament.
A heavy weight used to moor a ship.
Solid or viscous bituminous pitch of natural occurrence,or produced from petroleum mixed with sand or other aggregate filler, for use in roads or as a covering material
A tool, piece of equipment, container or other object used for or in fishing.
A building or complex where skins are prepared, with their hair still on, to make fur products.
Aquatic invertebrate animals whose outer covering is a shell, often 'farmed' to be eaten. Includes molluscs and crustaceans.
A type of stock exchange for tin which replaced the stannary courts in the mid 19th century.
Material hung from walls, excluding paper.

A wall within a lead mine surrounding a dressing floor, where waste from mining and smelting is deposited, to protect livestock from entering and consuming contaminated material and becoming poisoned, or 'bellanded'.
Remains of the animal group Crustacea: hard-shelled arthropods which are largely aquatic. Use for the remains of shrimps, prawns, crabs and lobsters, and also woodlice.
A written work issued at regular intervals, numbered consecutively with no intended or planned end point.
A type of spike, often on candlesticks.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.
General term describing any defence work where no more specific term is applicable.
An area where fish are naturally present, eg. part of a river.
A coastal site producing salt by boiling of unconcentrated seawater in a PANHOUSE, normally using coal fuel.  Foreshore BRINE TANKS may also be present
A large tract of land covered with trees and interspersed with open areas of land. Traditionally forests were owned by the monarchy and had their own laws.
A post bearing one or more signs indicating the direction, and often the distance, to specified locations or routes.
A stone, usually inscribed, laid during a ceremony to commemorate the founding of a new building

Medieval Fenland ditched field system where the land is divided into strips for agricultural production. The strips are separated by hand-dug wide shallow drainage ditches with the spoil thrown up to create a dryer ridge.
A place where pigs are reared.
Used to detach flakes from cores or tools.
A tool with a scoop end for digging up roots etc.
A building used by organizations or societies for the promotion of a particular profession through lectures, research, etc.
A weight made to be hung from a steelyard.
A room over the vestry of a church, often thought to have been where anchorets lived.
A place where (young) holiday-makers and hikers can be put up cheaply for the night.
An object for cleaning a pipe used for smoking.
A large shop supplying many kinds of goods from various departments.
Grains of rock fragment larger than coarse sand and finer than pebbles (diameter 2-4mm).
A bowl used in the marriage ceremony.
A ship of the line mounting between 46 and 64 guns
A restraining ring usually linked to another.
An area of ground in which horses can be exercised.
Hard white/grey coloured liassic limestone. Quarried on the Devon-Dorset border.
A portable timepiece capable of being worn on the wrist or carried in a pocket.
An area of hardstanding, surrounded on three sides by a protective wall or bank, used for parking aircraft, in a state of readiness, usually around the perimeter of an airfield.
A body of wax or tallow, usually formed into a long, thin, cylindrical shape enclosing a wick and burnt to produce light.
A hospital where people with learning disabilities receive medical treatment.
A stringed instrument usually with a triangular frame.
A basket for the storage and transport of fishing equipment. For the storage and transport of fish use creel.
A metal, stone or wooden projection with a flat upper surface to support a shelf, arch, statue etc.
A narrow container, especially one in which food or water for animals is put.
A container for the storage of rice.
Very hard, rough medium/coarse grained, pink to grey coloured granite. Usually found and quarried in Leicestershire.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
An object used in the harvesting or mowing of crops etc.
A crane or hoist within a building found mainly in the North of England. Can also refer to a projecting crane located above a loading slot.
A machine in which a heavy block of metal is used for beating, breaking or driving something.
A free-standing cross made of stone in the form of a cross with a ring surrounding the intersection. Often used as a grave marker
An 18th century cottage with a pottery kiln attached.
Use more specific term where available.
Access for survey or assessment limited to the exterior of existing buildings and structures.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
Floor cover in Roman time, where small cubes (tesserea) of one or more colours were laid in a geometric pattern.

A pair of timbers, or blades, usually curved, rising from a place at or near ground level to a point at or near the apex of a roof, forming an approximately triangular frame on which the subsidiary structure rests.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).
An object lying on the sea bed detected by marine survey equipment that emits and receives high frequency sound waves.
A building for the storage of ammunition and other military stores.
A small warship (often adapted from a trawler or drifter) used to hunt enemy submarines.
Glass used within a window, usually to protect from the elements, can permit a view through it or can be for decorative purposes.
Armour made up of interlaced metal rings.
A factory built as a pattern for improved design.
A hospital where patients would bathe daily in the sea or in indoor salt-water swimming baths.
Use for vessels registered in Malta.
Any vessel involved in the catching or transportation of whales.
A simple type of plant. For most of their lifecycle they exist as haploids (i.e. only one set of genes as opposed to two). Most have clearly differentiated stems and leaves.
An underground passageway for cables, pipes and pedestrians to allow passage beneath an over ground obstacle.

Sites, building, structures & features associated with the construction, maintenance & supply of maritime craft. Includes associated ancillary structures such as navigation aids, dockyards, wharves, etc; does not include vessels.
Use for objects made from coal or for stray finds of coal where the association with a wreck site is not proven and thus cannot be stated as either cargo or bunkers.
Several strands of string twisted together to form a strong thin rope, or thick string, though it has been used in the past as synonomous with rope particularly for ropes on ships.
The main gear wheel, which is engaged by a brake to halt or slow the machinery, mounted on the windshaft of a windmill.

Management Plans help pull together an understanding of significance to evidence the conservation and management of heritage assets. From this informed basis, plans are then used to develop programmes of repair, restoration or to draw up proposals for change. Management Plans should be structured to meet the needs of the specific property/site and designed to be used for every day reference by staff managing the site. Management Plans not only pull together and analyse the history of a site or landscape, they can also be an important record in their own right.
A photographic print of a polychrome image (composed of colours other than, but not exclusive of, black, white or grey tones).
The taking of photographs during informal site visits, which may be undertaken by amateur archaeologists or architectural students. More formal, detailed surveys should be termed Photographic Survey.

A biggest and plainest of the classical architectural orders, based upon a simplified version of the Doric Order. Sometimes called the Gigantic order, though not to be confused with the Colossal or Giant Order.
Rock of definite form and size, usually artificially shaped.
A multi-purpose farm building in an outlaying area of a farm.
The main axle projecting through the front of a windmill on which the sails are mounted.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting smaller, faster weapons such as Bofors guns or a single anti-aircraft machine gun, intended to engage fast low flying aircraft.

Flexible, synthetic, polymeric organic material formed by chemical synthesis usually in imitation of a natural substance. It can be moulded to shape, extruded or formed into a sheet from solid or foam material.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
A hospital for the treatment of diseases of the nerves and nervous system.
A power station used to produce electricity, fired by coal gas.
A vessel with two masts, rigged as a ketch, used for coastal trading.
An enclosed container to hold coals or logs of a fire.
An intially worked object, prepared to be made into a final product.
Container for the storage of unspecified materials.
Clay used in the manufacture of fire bricks.
A decorative feature in the style of a flower or plant. Use more specific term.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
A factory where pianos are manufactured.
A container used in the preparartion of food.
An unroofed structure, found on military airfields, protected by brick walls and earth banks for shelter during air raids.
Use for vessels believed to come from South America but where the precise nationality is not known.
A factory, or group of buildings, containing apparatus used to extract specific properties, e.g flavour or scent, from natural ingredients.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of five 10ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 17865/39.
Site and structures associated with the supply of clean water.
A room within a church or cathedral in which holy relics were kept.
A building in which apparatus registering the amount of gas consumed is housed.
A raised platform for the unloading of coal from waggons or other containers.
For example chronic heart failure, high blood pressure, congenital heart disease, heart transplants, rheumatic fever and other related illnesses.
A purpose-built residence for an artist, containing a studio.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
A raised platform, especially in a theatre or auditorium, for the use of performers or speakers etc.
A building where ambulances are housed awaiting emergency calls.
A mineral of copper, iron and sulphur and is the main ore of copper.
A steam engine driving a reciprocating air pump to provide air for a blast furnace.
A needle for making and mending nets, often forked at both ends.
A dispersed farmstead where the farm buildings and farmhouse are loosely grouped together within the boundary of the farmstead.
A highly-prized, hard, white, fine-grained dentine constituting the main part of the teeth of walruses, hippopotami and elephants. Used in the manufacture of ornaments and piano keys.
A staircase that rises  through only one storey and has treads and risers framed into square studs, one of them often on one side of a door-frame; it usually occupies a rectangular space.
An open area of prepared ground used for practising putting with golf clubs.

Unspecified Second World War anti-aircraft battery. There were three types of battery. The U2P and U20P had different arrangements of DFW55373 projector sites for the 20-barrelled 3" projectors. The U9P mounted 12-barrelled projectors.

Damaged, usually by weather or warfare, to such an extent that the vessel is in severe or imminent danger of being lost; i.e. a pre-existing condition of the vessel which contributes to the final wrecking event.
A metal pillar with a flashable lamp on top containing an emergency telephone for use by members of the public and by officers of the local police force.
Classical decorative motif of interlocking right-angled and vertical lines, usually applied as a continuous pattern.
A small building in which game is hung up and kept cool.
A tomb or memorial, resembling an altar, often with a recumbent effigy on top.
A place of worship for Jewish people.
A garden walk lined with yew trees and hedges.
A timber running above vertical posts, in the place of a wall-plate, within a timber-framed building.
Bordering the continents of Asia, Europe and North America the Arctic Ocean covers 5,426,000 square miles. Situated over the North Pole, much of the ocean remains frozen year round.
A small enclosure built onto the perimeter of a Roman fortress or fort.
A market where goods are bought and sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
Forms used in the recording of archaeological or other site investigations.
Reheating of iron from a finery, for rolling or slitting.
Equipment enabling a horse to be ridden or driven, eg. saddles, bridles, harnesses, stirrups etc.
An instrument whirled to produce sound by a piece of flexible wood hitting against a ratchet wheel.
A tool used to polish the surface of an artefact.

Fieldwalking is a rapid, cost-effective and relatively inexpensive technique which allows for ‘broad-brush’ archaeological prospection and landscape characterisation over large areas. It is most commonly employed as part of the archaeological evaluation stage of the planning process. It is particularly effective for locating Stone Age archaeology when undertaken at close-spaced intervals.
A classical order having a bell shaped capital that is decorated with laurel, olive or acanthus leaves from which CAULICOLI emerge. The shaft is usually fluted and the base is often an Attic base.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of explosives.
A site comprising a system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft. Use more specific type where known.
An aperture cut obliquely in a wall, usually of a chancel, affording a view between the high altar and the aisles or side chapels.
A construction of unknown function, either extant or implied by archaeological evidence. If known, use more specific type.
The burnt remains of a corpse.
A narrow means of access, often internal.
Small fragments of waterworn stone used in the construction industry.
Stone consisting of nearly pure silica, which can be used as a building material or knapped to produce flint objects.
An office used by a qualified pilot, expert in ship-handling and with local knowledge, who assists the captain or master to take a vessel in or out of a harbour or through narrow waters.
A form of stopper used to regulate the flow of liquid, often used in a barrel.
A tool for cleaning a person's nails.
A hospital department for the medical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders.
Waste products ensuing from the casting process.
A small building used by a gatekeeper.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A wheel with a groove in it for a rope or cord, used to raise heavy objects.
Boarding school for children of Travellers and Romany Gypsies while their parents were away on agricultural work
A piece of material that has been inlaid, or prepared and shaped for inlaying, in an object, decorative feature or other setting.
A mine used for the extraction on tin bearing ore.
Form of ore crushing machinery associated with tin mines often wooden and water-powered.
A metal girder, usually of iron or steel, embedded in the ground designed to obstruct the progress of hostile tanks or armoured vehicles.
Friary Of Friars Of The Sack
A ring containing a scarab shape.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
Moored barge providing a refuge for shipwrecked sailors or downed airmen, for example the air-sea rescue Cuckoo barges of WWII.
An old opencast iron ore site, which has been abandoned.
The recording and analysis of the fabric of a structure or bnuilding
An aerial lift in which cabins are suspended from a continuous cable between two towers which hold the winding mechanism. The cable may be supported by towers or pylons.
A handled tool with two or more prongs used for digging, cultivation etc.
A purpose-built building with a steel framed tower, based on drawing number (11595/42). Used for the drying of parachutes.
Carriages, locomotives and other vehicles used on a railway.
A heavy artillery piece consisting of a metal tube mounted on a gun  carriage.

A two-seat, general purpose biplane. The first to be designed specifically for an Army Co-operation role, it entered service in late 1927. Ended its service as a communications and advanced trainer aircraft.
Previously recorded as 'Modern'. Covers the period from 1901-2000.
A chapel for a private residence.
A giant figure of a man, animal or symbol carved on chalk hillsides mainly in southern England.
A triangular arrowhead retouched to form a central tang and lateral barbs. The sides may be straight or concave.
A building used for the accommodation of a military guard and/or the detainment of prisoners.
Deliberate sinking of a vessel, e.g. to prevent capture or to act as a blockship.
A early match made of a piece of wood and an inflammable substance, lit by friction between the inflammable substance and a rough surface.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
Pieces of leather connected to a bridle designed to direct a horse's vision straight forward only.
Grain, especially barley, prepared for brewing, distilling or vinegar making.
A hole dug in the ground to act as a, usually temporary, communal toilet facility.

An Iron Age round defended house, found mainly in the north and west of Scotland. Brochs have a tapering profile and thick, usually hollow dry stone walls which contain galleries, cells and a stairway, with guard cells at the entrance.
Used for boiling sections of willow for basket making, etc.
Fibres of wood reduced chemically or mechanically to pulp for use in the manufacture of paper.
A chamber attached to the sewer of a building to facilitate the removal of any blockage.
A medieval court for tin miners in Devon and Cornwall.

A blade attached to a shoe to glide on ice. It can be made of bone, and examples are known from at least as early as the Bronze Age. Metal blades have progressively replaced bone skates since the sixteenth century.
A photographic reproduction of written or printed material produced by using toner particles under heat and pressure to fuse a copy onto blank paper.
The remains of a manufacturing process.
A thin flat slab used to mix cosmetics on.
An industrial facility concerned with the manufacture of magnesium from magnesium hydroxide derived from sea water. Magnesium was used in the manufacture of aircraft.
A place of worship for followers of Sikhism.
A brick tower, based on drawing number (9290/42), usually added to an existing building. Used for the drying of parachutes.
A tool used to smooth wood. It has a flat surface with an adjustable blade protruding through it.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.
Small pieces of wood, tipped with a chemical composition which ignites when rubbed against a rough or, if safety matches, prepared surface. Normally contained within a small box.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
A purpose-built hall (usually 19th century) which was available for public hire and could be used for a variety of activities, eg. lectures, meetings, balls and concerts.
A report detailing the archaeological and architectural potential of a site or locality.
The lesser stalks springing from the principal stalks, or caules, within the decoration on a Corinthian capital.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canonesses.

Composed of a wide variety of substances and materials such as whole or broken bricks, cobblestones, flints, pebbles and sand which are set into hydraulic lime. Used most often to form external walls and is commonly found in the Brighton/Lewes region.
For the disposal of town refuse. Some 19th century plants were linked to a power station. Later ones incorporate INCINERATORS, recycling facilities, etc.

Buildings used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for buildings associated with military installations. For non-military, use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
Includes terms for components of site. See also terms in MINING INDUSTRY SITE grouping.
A hall built as a memorial to a particular person or event.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
Pipes manufactured from cast iron and used for a variety of purposes.
A small structure used to support strings on an instrument pushing them away from the body of the instrument.
A hangar for the storage and maintenance of dirigible motor-driven balloons.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
An ornamental grove, thicket or shrubbery pierced by walks.
An establishment where the theory and practice of medicine is taught.
A device in the form of a loop with a flat base hung on either side of a saddle to support the rider's foot.
A maritime monument where the hull structure and fabric of a vessel remain wholly or mainly intact.
A channel used for or formed by the conveyance of water. Can be natural, eg. a river or artificial eg. an aqueduct. Use more specific type where known.
A warship constructed of iron plate with its main armament mounted in a revolving turret on deck.
A structure, usually of brick, stone or timber, that encloses or defines a space or room.
A building housing a variety of facilities, such as theatres, galleries, concert halls, etc.
A small edge blown instrument with no finger holes, producing one note.
Form of dam, usually associated with ponds supplying water for blast furnaces.
Pinion which engages with the spur wheel and drives the millstones in a corn mill.
A place or path for walking in a park or garden. Use more specific type where possible.
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
A college founded for the education and betterment of the working classes. Lectures usually being held after the end of the working day.
A self-service dining room, especially for workers/employees; also in institutions, such as schools, hospitals, etc.
Generic term for fast sailing ships with schooner rig and fine hull lines.
A box in which one or more games are stored.
Regularly cultivated and re-seeded grassland (but not including temporary grassland within arable rotation - this would be classified under Cultivated Land).
An ornamental, commemorative tablet. Use with materials field when indexing.
A building where the administrative functions of a Trade Union are carried on.
An elevated area or platform in a synagogue where the person reading aloud from the Torah stands.
An appliance for holding an object while work is done on it, usually has a pair of jaws.
A small settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling with ancillary buildings.
A form of padlock with a cylindrical case and bolts and springs attached to spines.
Bordering the continents of Africa, Antarctica, Europe, North and South America the Atlantic is the second largest of the oceans, covering 31,736,000 square miles.
A curving metal band attached to the underside of the stock of a firearm, vertically enclosing the trigger to prevent accidental discharge.

A two-storey, brick construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A brick parapet on the roof differentiates it from 2328/39.
Supplies owned by, or for the use of, the government.
A large space in an underground tunnel, usually wider than the tunnel itself, used for storage, etc.
A golf course, usually situated on or near the coast, consisting of sand dunes with few trees or water obstacles.
A flush decked sailing warship with a single tier of guns.
A building where mineral jelly was stored. Mineral jelly was used as a stabilizer in the manufacture of the explosive, cordite.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a railway across low-lying land or water.
Material of unknown origin observed adhering to, or found within, an object of another material.
A cottage erected over a short period of time, by people who had no legal right to the land. Squatters were often tolerated by the landlord as they provided cheap labour.
A passageway, duct or pipe used for the conveyance of heat, gasses, smoke or air.
An item worn as clothing or in addition to clothes.
A building where lace was laid out to dry.
The nationality of a vessel according to its registration.
A sea within a sea, the Adriatic consists of that part of the Mediterranean which separates Italy from the Balkans and Greece.
A joint in which the tenon retains one or more of the original sides of the timber.
Glaucoma, diabetes, cataracts, retinal detachment and other related conditions.
A short stabbing weapon with a pointed blade. In Medieval period daggers served a dual function being also used as knives.
A device used to gauge the speed of a vessel at sea.
A raised platform from which an officer can address or review his troops.
A wall, usually of reinforced concrete, designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle
A band worn around the leg to hold up a sock or stocking.
A photographic frame of developed colour film which can be used to print a photographic image.
A tool used to remove shavings from an object.
Ornamental plasterwork applied to the exterior of a building, especially timber-framed houses of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries..

A bladed wheel attached to the rear, and at right angles to the main sails, of a windmill.  Connected to winding gear, the fantail would catch the wind when it changed direction, allowing the mill to move automatically into the wind.
A site where the magnetic signature of ships was lowered thereby making them less susceptible to magnetic mines.

A decorative emblem stating the name of a village or town and depicting aspects of the place's history of culture. Most signs are mounted on a post and usually errected in a central position near the church or village green.
A column, in the form of a female figure, used to support an entablature.
Weight used for weighing specific quantities and qualities of gold.

A confusing and baffling network of winding and intercommunicating paths, often bordered by high hedges or walls. Some early examples are believed to have had ritual uses. Use more specific type where known.
A purpose built tower used for the testing of helicopter rotor blades.

A timber building based around a sunken hollow, the floor of which may have been suspended above the hollow to counteract dampness. Grubenhauser are believed to date from the 5th to 8th centuries AD but may be earlier. Use Grubenhauser as plural.
A camp used for the accommodation of members of the Womens Auxiliary Air Force who undertook a variety of essential roles within the RAF to enable their male counterparts to fight more effectively.
A stone inscribed or marked with ogham letters used for a memorial
Former grade pending relisting. Approximately equivalent to Grade I.
A factory where lengths of soft, woollen cloth, loosely woven to retain heat, used as a bed covering, were manufactured.
Building housing switch gear to control electricity supply either to the National Grid, industrial or domestic premises.
A site inhabited by a modern order of nuns, founded in 1900 at Lanherne, Cornwall, following Carmelite traditions.
A building used to store navigational buoys.
A place where patients have X-Rays taken to highlight an illness or irregularity.
Use for the remains of a cargo which have been accidentally lost at sea, or purposefully dumped, and which consist the only physical evidence of a vessel.
A channel which feeds water from a reservoir into a canal when the water level gets low.
An article, but published as a separate item.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of ball sports.
A kiln where gypsum was dried to a state where it could be used as plaster of Paris or for the production of cement.
The residence of a master ropemaker.
An object representing the sun, made of bronze or gold usually dating from the European Bronze Age.
A block for mounting a horse.
A water-filled hole used for the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
A technique used to date obsidian (volcanic glass) of all ages and is thus not commonly used in the UK.
The hole through which the fuel for a fire is put to start and maintain the fire.

A stand by set house built with a steel-framed pitched roof. Built to drawing number 8760/42 it was intended to supersede all earlier designs and was cheaper to produce. Both the transformer and fuel tanks were located outside the main building.

An often squat building with thick, loopholed walls and a flat roof, designed to accommodate a variety of weapons, usually strategically positioned to cover a vulnerable point in a defensive system. Many were built to standardized designs.

Collective term for a hard, fine grained, dark coloured metamorphic rock, which splits easily; hence its common use as a roofing and flooring material, and a functional description for any rectangular, sheet, roofing material.
A hole occupied by a timber post or the void remaining after its removal, usually with packing.
A device for converting one voltage of alternating current to another voltage.
A structure for visually communicating the exact time to ships in anchorage. A ball slides down a mast at the top of the tower, usually at noon or one o'clock exactly.
A court established in England and Wales by Parliament in 1846 to decide minor civil disputes.
Mackerel which has been salted to preserve it.
An elevator used to raise locomotives.
A two panelled altar decoration that can be closed.
A craft built with the intention of demonstrating or advertising a novel design feature.
A small vessel attached to a larger vessel (usually a warship) for general harbour duties such as taking crewmen ashore or fetching supplies.
An establishment for the theoretical and practical training of nurses.
This includes all articles created to be used for personal care, hygiene, grooming and cosmetic activities.
A house to receive boat landings.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A place of worship for military personnel.

Use for the remains of internal parasites of vertebrates, including humans, such as flukes, tapeworm, including their calcified cysts, etc. Eggs of the nematodes Ascaris sp. (maw-worm) and Trichuris sp. (whipworm) are commonly reported.
The cover for a garderobe on which a person would sit.
A rack to hold smoking pipes.
A settlement located on or near to the shores of a lake. Buildings associated with lake villages are usually raised on piles to prevent them from being flooded.
A building or site used in the production of enamelled goods.
The principal longitudinal member or spine of a windmill sail, extending from the stock and supporting the sailbars.
A resource comprising of a group of items the parts of which may be separately described and navigated. [DC]
An image used to convey information, often as part of a larger publication or exhibition.
An educational establishment for the training of police cadets.
A horizontal timber usually at the bottom of a timber framed wall into which posts and studs are tenoned.
A piece of ground over which small arms or large artillery may be fired at targets. For rocket and missile firing use ROCKET TEST FACILITY.
A factory where putty, used as a means of securing windows and for setting plumbing fixtures, is produced from a combination of whiting and oil.
Factory producing asbestos sheeting and or asbestos fibre.
A building designed to house insects.

A round house indicated by the presence of a low, roughly circular bank of turf, earth or stone, which formed the base of the walls. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Where several occur together use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT.
A report that primarily details the results of a survey that was conducted using remote sensing techniques such as resistivity and magnetometry.
A gun using an explosive propellant to fire sharpened metal shafts, usually fired through water.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
Specify in Description using: cave, cliff etc.
A rope, cord etc used to hold or secure animals.
A building for the weighing or testing of metals, eg. at a mine site.
A vertical pillar or post, often shaped.
An establishment where offenders are confined. Use more specific type where known.
A three-sided structure for the production and storage of silage.
Wooden roof tile (traditionally oak) which is riven or sawn from good quality timber to a regular size and used as a roof and/or wall covering. Index with type of wood if known.
A small piece of timber occupying the angle between two other timbers.
A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.

Condition 	

No demolition or development shall take place until a stage 1 written scheme of investigation (WSI) has been submitted to and approved by the local planning authority in writing.  For land that is included within the WSI, no demolition or development shall take place other than in accordance with the agreed WSI, and the programme and methodology of site evaluation and the nomination of a competent person(s) or organisation to undertake the agreed works. 
	If heritage assets of archaeological interest are identified by stage 1 then for those parts of the site which have archaeological interest a stage 2 WSI shall be submitted to and approved by the local planning authority in writing.  For land that is included within the stage 2 WSI, no demolition/development shall take place other than in accordance with the agreed stage 2 WSI which shall include:
A.	The statement of significance and research objectives, the programme and methodology of site investigation and recording and the nomination of a competent person(s) or organisation to undertake the agreed works
B.	Where appropriate, details of a programme for delivering related positive public benefits
C.	The programme for post-investigation assessment and subsequent analysis, publication & dissemination and deposition of resulting material. This part of the condition shall not be discharged until these elements have been fulfilled in accordance with the programme set out in the stage 2 WSI.

Informative	

Written schemes of investigation will need to be prepared and implemented by a suitably professionally accredited archaeological practice in accordance with Historic England’s Guidelines for Archaeological Projects in Greater London. This condition is exempt from deemed discharge under schedule 6 of The Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015.
An establishment where deaf people receive education, training and social support.
The sculpted head, shoulders and breast of a person.
An object which has one or more holes through it. Use more specific term where known.
Ceramic vessels made from potash, sand, feldspar and clay which is biscuit fired at a temperature of around 1000 degree Celsius. Usually glazed in order to become watertight.
An axehead of early Bronze Age date, made of copper or bronze, which is flat on both sides and generally lacks side flanges or other hafting aids.
A storeroom for valuable goods, such as wine, oil and spices.

Inhumation rite in which charcoal is included with the buried corpse, possibly in an attempt to preserve the body. Thought to be associated with high status burials of the early medieval and medieval period.
Equipment used to create a mark, image or character in an object.
A native hardwood of the Beech family with hard and durable characteristics which traditionally made it appropriate for structural work.

A vessel used as the lower part of a distillation unit consisting of a round-bottomed vessel with walls sloping inwards towards the rim. Some examples may have an external flange to support the upper unit (ALEMBIC). (Source: MPRG)
An indoor or outdoor market where hay and straw is sold.
A window that forms a projection from the body of a building, extending down to ground level, forming a bay in the wall's interior.
A large, deep, manmade pool, usually with accompanying diving boards/platforms and forming part of a swimming pool complex.
Medium grained, hard, white/grey coloured stone consisting of quartz and often silica, produced by the metamorphosis of sandstone.
A malleable, ductile ferromagnetic metal widely used for structural and decorative purposes.

A series of parallel railway sidings on which goods wagons originating from different locations can be sorted or re-sorted into new trains before being despatched to their next destination or sorting points.
Use for vessels registered in the Isle of Man.
A bakehouse built in association with a group of dwellings who shared the baking facilities. Often found in model settlements.
A channel or casing containing and protecting wiring, piping etc.

A prefabricated structure consisting of six curved asbestos cement sheets that were bolted together, without a frame, creating a hut semi-circular in section. Used on airfields during WWII and manufactured from 1942 by the Turner Asbestos Company.
A hall used by the members of a trade union for meetings and social functions.
A modern piece imitating an ancient coin, such as a replica sold in a museum.
Waste material resulting from industrial manufacturing processes.
The wedge shaped end of a bridge pier designed to break the current of water.
A technique in which the date is deduced from the presence of fauna and/or flora considered to be characteristic of a given peirod of time or that gives and indication of a probable date.
A large tank used for training divers.
Articles, usually woven from coarse fibres or made from hard wearing materials (eg. rubber or cork) used to protect the floor or for lying, sitting or kneeling on.
Subsidiary settlement of lay brothers attached to some Carthusian monasteries.
A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.
An extract from a longer video film, used as an illustration.
A container with a human face appliqued onto it, often used as a funerary vessel.
A quoin, usually of stone, with a concave rebate at one corner forming the surface against which the rounded edge of a canal lock gate turns, making a kind of hinge.
A graving tool used for engraving objects. Prehistoric versions are usually made of flint or other stone, later versions usually of metal.
A cross found in a market place.
Sedimentary rock consisting mainly of calcium carbonate. Varying in grain size, colour and hardness, quarried and used throughout the country.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
A smooth bore weapon usually for firing shot as opposed to bullets.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A place, often including a BAKERY, where sweetmeats and pastries are sold.

The name given by the Allies during the Second World War to the German motor torpedo boat. E Boats carried two torpedo tubes and anti aircraft guns. They had a maximum speed of 39 knots and were considered superior to their Allied counterparts.
A by-product created during the manufacture of a tool.
A render with small washed stones added as aggregate. Popular in the early 20th century.
A castle erected without permission, ie. without a royal licence to crenellate.
A system of stones or wooden obstacles placed close together to impede the advance of enemy forces. Do not use for HILLFORT sites.
An area used for crushing mineral ore or stone. Often includes mechanically powered ore crushers.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
Former grade pending relisting. Approximately equivalent to Locally Listed.
A room or group of rooms for healing the sick. Where it is a monument use the Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A site where concrete and concrete products are manufactured from a mixture of cement and aggregate.
A type of cotton cloth of a pale yellow colour.
A building or room within a granary used to dry grain. Often consisting of an oven with a refractory-brick drying floor above, on which the grain was placed.
Loss of a vessel due to bombardment from ship, shore or submarine. For Aircraft use SHOT DOWN.

Geologically sandstone consists of particles of quartz naturally cemented together by either silica, calcium or iron. It is this geological composition that accounts for the varying colours and grain sizes found in the many building sandstones.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.
A ring, often metal, which is used to be thrown as part of a game.
Use for structural objects within or connected to a place of worship, eg font. For structures, use a monuments thesaurus.
A representation of the crucifixion of Christ or related scenes as a sculpture in a churchyard, etc.
Objects used or associated with the movement of goods or people.

A built structure, generally below ground, designed for the interment of several burials over a period of time. Usually constructed with a door or sealed entrance to allow reopening for further burials.

A cathedral in which the chapter was composed of canons who lived in their own houses and were not governed by a monastic rule. Nine such cathedrals existed in England between the 11th and 16th centuries.
A piece of material worn as a band around the arm.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
A graduated length of material used for measuring distances.
A mill used to dress ore by means of a jigging machine.

A hole in a wall in which cross timbers, known as putlogs, were placed to allow scaffolding to be erected. Putlog holes are often left unfilled and are often the only evidence for the use of scaffolding.
A site where scientific and technical instruments such as microscopes are assembled.
A special school to train personnel for employment in Air Traffic Control and operation duties.
A short timber connecting a cruck's timber, or blade, to a wall plate.
The ground immediately surrounding a place, particularly a religious building.
Includes interim, research, specialist reports on a specific topic.
A roofed structure, open on one side, usually attached to a building, providing a seating area and its occupants with an uninterrupted exterior view.
A building where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.
A feature which forms part of a building and has a specific functional usage or decorative form.
An aeroplane with the capability to land at sea, the underside of its fuselage shaped like the hull of a sea-going vessel and designed to make contact with the water.
A simple instrument where two pieces of material are manipulated to knock together.
A tree-lined way or approach where the trees have been cut into various forms and shapes.
A mixture of lime or more recently cement with sand and water used for bonding stones or bricks.
64 Type DFW55373 projector sites arranged in and 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
Molluscs found in fresh or brackish water habitats.
The fruit or seed of a cereal plant such as wheat, corn etc.
The remains of the shell of an oyster.
Use for vessels registered in Ukraine
A component of reciprocating engines - the moving component that is contained by a cylinder.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
An open area used for drying products manufactured using an industrial process.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
A room or suite of rooms used as dwellings, eg. in private houses, hotels or tenement houses.
A steam engine, often used in the 18th century, which drove a pump to return water back to a waterwheel so that it could be used over and over again.
A building used as the headquarters for the Home Guard during the Second World War.
The interpretation of visualisations derived from Airborne Laser Scanning, or LiDAR, data usually resulting in the identification of archaeological features and landscapes.
A chapel within a parish church or other religious building for use by the lord of the manor and his family
A soft, grey to white coloured, sandstone formed during the Cretaceous period, whose sand grains are cemented together with lime.
A book in which visitors to a property, monument or exhibition record their thoughts and impressions on their experience.

Capturing visible spectrum photographs or images of monument features or character using still or motion cameras from an aircraft or other airborne vehicle or apparatus. Covers both digital and film-based cameras.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.

The capture of imagery using an orbiting satellite. The type of imagery is very varied including visible light photography, infrared and multi spectral photography as well as imagery derived from radar and lidar data.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of candles.
Collective name for a series of rocks (granite, syenite, porphry and slate) found in the Charnwood Forest of Leicestershire. Index with specific stone type where given.
A stall where eels, either raw or cooked, are sold.
A set of steps or a framework of bars and steps for crossing over a fence or wall.
A hand operated mechanism used to raise and move water, liquids, compressed gases etc.
Scissor like tool, usually larger than scissors, used for cutting, pruning or trimming.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
A piece of cloth or plastic worn especially by babies to protect clothes while eating.
A building housing a board organized to protect the interests of commerce.
A building containing soft play equipment for children.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.
A decoy fire positioned close to a legitimate target which would be lit in the event of an incendiary attack in the hope that subsequent bombs would be drawn to the area of the decoy.
A mullion of square section set diagonally.
A large bath used for Jewish ritual ceremonies.
A mill in which barytes concentrates were ground to fine white powder, normally by use of flat millstones similar to those of a corn mill.
A place where processed wood is sold.
A case in which a pipe would be held to protect it.
An indicator of the extent of an area of land.
Dummy construction in the form of a battery used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
A building housing an engine. Use specific type where known.
A place of worship for members of the Methodist Reform Church. This group was the result of a secession from the Methodists in 1849. They remained until joining with the Wesleyan Association in 1857.
Late nineteenth and early twentieth century warship armed with guns and torpedoes.
The earliest subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.
Sites, building, structures & features associated with the supply & drainage of water & the disposal of sewage and waste water. Includes bodies of water, waterways & associated ancillary structures.

A Dutch barge-like sailing vessel whose shallow draught enables it to navigate in shallow water not accessible by other vessels. Used for fishing or carriage of cargo in the 19th century this type of vessel was adapted for use as a type of leisure craft.
A stoppered bottle, for serving drinks.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A semi-circular or pointed vault uninterrupted by cross vaults, the ceiling bearing a resemblence to a tunnel or the inside of a barrel.
A drinking vessel with a handle.

A site consisting of, usually two, sub-circular enclosures linked by a linear ditch running tangentially to the enclosure boundaries. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period in the Wessex region.
A type of factory building, often single-storey, designed so that windows incorporated into the vertical faces of its saw-tooth roof can allow the maximum amount of natural light into its interior.
A Classical convex moulding, often decorated with egg-and-dart or similar motifs.

A musket where a wheel on the lock is wound back and when the trigger is pulled the wheel moves dragging pieces of iron pyrites over the lock tocreate sparks and set powder in the pan off and so firing the main charge.
Technique using electromagnetic fields to map subsurface electrical conductivity anomalies. Can be used as a high-sensitivity metal detector.
A purpose-built factory for more than one occupier (eg. for several different workshops).
A dish comprising three or more lobes, usually equally spaced. There may be one or more animal or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Chimney used on an industrial or commercial site.
A workshop used for the small-scale production of leather goods.
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.
A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.

Archaeological excavation is a structured investigation with defined research objectives which normally takes place as a condition of planning permission.  It will involve the investigation and recording of an area of archaeological interest including the recovery of artefacts and environmental evidence.  Once on-site works have been completed a 'post-excavation assessment' will be prepared followed by an appropriate level of further analysis, publication and archiving.
External decorative plasterwork often incised or modelled with ornamental patterns. Usually applied to timber-framed houses, especially during 16th and 17th centuries.
Use wider site type where known. Only use term where no other part of original building survives.
A type of Ionic diagonal capital where all four sides are the same and with therefore eight volutes.
A workshop or factory where bells are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A figure, representation or image, which is itself regarded as sacred.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the engineering industry.
Purpose built workers' accommodation comprising single rooms with communal eating and washing facilities. Usually for short stay accommodation only.
Religious establishment, founded in Somerset, where free love was practised.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
A centre attached to a prison where families and friends can visit with the inmates.
A small vessel with a cabin as an integral part of its construction.
A site where iron ore is extracted.
A large jug or pitcher with a wide mouth.
A truss of slighter construction between principal trusses in an elaborate roof.
A small type of seat, usually without a back, set on legs.
A portable stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 3527/43.
A chimney placed at an angle with the walls so that there is an obtuse angle with each wall.
Hard, often coloured, can be transparent. Found on its own as crystals and veins but also as a major constituent of all three geological rock types.
Use for cargoes of live animals only.
The commonest type of roof with sloping sides meeting at a ridge and with a gable at each end.
An object used to pick the teeth with.

A complex of buildings, often within an enclosure, housing a pre-Benedictine Reform secular religious community. Now commonly used to describe the main church within such a complex, which over time attained higher status.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.
Metal alloy with lead as the principal component.
A net used in fishing to catch or land fish.

The measuring of annual tree-ring growth shown by most tree species in temperated regions. Regional chronoliges are required to date any particular piece of wood, the longest of which, for Germany, works for the present to approximately 14,000 yrs ago.
An appliance that produces light by means of a liquid fuel and a wick.
A factory where aircraft engines are assembled.
A Norman keep, in the form of a circular or polygonal enclosure surrounded by a wall.
The residence of an admiral of a port.
Use for vessels registered in the Czech Republic. See also Czechoslovakian (for vessels registered between 1918-1992)
A roughly hemispherical mound constructed primarily of stones, normally containing or covering one or more human burials. The mound may be surrounded and partly retained by a low stone kerb.

A structure, often sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Sub RSGs were introduced between the RSGs and local authorities to allow the RSGs to focus on strategic direction.
A microlith retouched to a thomboid shape. (Source: SARC)
A dome shaped structure, with an aperture open to the sky, used to house a telescope.
The limit to an area as defined on a map or by a marker of some form, eg. BOUNDARY WALL. Use specific type where known.
An oval window placed with its long axis horizontal. The term is often applied to similar round windows.
A place of worship specifically for mariners and their families.
A building used to dry teazle heads in. Teazles were used to raise the nap on cloth in teazle shops.
A tower or turret in which bells are hung.
A farm or group of buildings where Silkworms are bred. The Silkworm when changing into a pupa spins a cocoon made of silken filaments, these are then unwound and used to manufacture silk thread.
An excavation used as a means of concealment, protection or both.
The earliest subdivision of the Mesolithic, or Middle Stone Age.
A flexible holder for a bladed tool or weapon.
A building in which a judicial court is held.
A sailing vessel, generally with three masts, square rigged on the fore and main mast.
A Swiss-styled house, usually with steeply pitched and projecting roof.
A building for the crushing of stones and minerals.
Usually a row of bushes or small trees planted closely together to form a boundary between pieces of land or at the sides of a road.
A factory manufacturing personal hygiene and beauty products
A room or group of rooms usually below the ground level and usually under a building, often used for storing fuel, provisions or wines.
A large room within a school or college used and appropriately furnished for the sitting of examinations by students..

A small prefabricated, reinforced concrete structure manufactured by Messrs Orlit Ltd for the Royal Observer Corps.  The first were ordered in 1951, most were redundant by 1955, a few remained in use in eastern England until 1965.

A solid concrete or stone base on which a machine (often an engine and therefore called the engine bed, forming part of an engine house) was mounted to power an industrial process. Dates from the 19th century.
A building in which apparatus measuring the amount of water supplied/used is housed.
A porch in front of the solid wall of a cloister.
A place where injured or endangered animals are kept and looked after.
A missile base armed with the Bristol Bloodhound surface-to-air missile. Bloodhounds were deployed to defend the launch sites of Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
An old ship hull used as a base for lifting tackle.
A seed or fruit with a hard shell, often edible or used to produce oils.
Iron coated in zinc, giving good protection against weathering.
Groupings of assets with a clear visual design or historic relationship.
Place where food or money was handed out to the poor.
A device with a handle and cutting edge to help remove skin from vegetables and fruit.
Thinner and narrower than a horse shoe these are also rarer as donkeys tend to be shod less often than horses.
A frame to a structure formed by precast concrete beams placed in pairs.
A building, usually part of a complex, where medical treatment and hospital facilities are provided.
A building in a quarry consisting of a series of loading bays in which stone is loaded onto wagons.
London Parks and Gardens Trust Site Reference
A site with accommodation buildings and ancillary facilities for Royal Air Force personnel.
Monument existing as an upstanding earthwork, ditch or artificial watercourse, or as a low stone built feature not covered by the other categories.
An establishment providing medical or surgical treatment for the ill or wounded. Use narrower term where possible.
The element or elements that make up the different parts of a structural plan.
A pair of uprights supporting a crosspiece. Often very decorative, fire dogs were probably used as a spit or to hold pots over the fire.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of clay.
Steps found at a landing point.
A capital which is circular and has several mouldings but no foliage.
Development relating civic and municipal buildings.

A high status building of the medieval period, consisting of a hall and attached room at first floor level with rooms below possibly for storage or living accommodation for a lower status family. The first floor was accessed by an external staircase.

A brick-built building with four windows on the north-facing wall with a pitched roof and with a dormer roof light on both sides, intended for drying, storing and packing parachutes.The 2355/25 was the first design for a purpose-built parachute store.
An axe with a cutting edge and a hammer head.
A place of worship for members of the Romanian Orthodox Church, the national church of Romania.
A waterwheel in which the incoming water is directed onto the periphery below the top of the wheel.
A large, flattish basket used in winnowing the chaff from the grain.
Mark 3 or the third variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
Scissor like object used for cutting, clipping, shearing etc.
A loose piece of clothing about hip length worn over other clothes, not usually tucked in at the waist.
Naturally occuring substances eg. coal and salt, obtained by mining.
A container used to hold and or pour out liquid in honour of a deity.
A stick for agitating milk in a butter churn.

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.

The hobby of using a metal detector to hunt for buried coins or artefacts; alternatively the use of a metal detector to locate metal artefacts on an archaeological excavation that otherwise would go unnoticed.
A chamfer that has been hollowed out to form a concave shape. This is also known as a chamfret.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.
A cross, erected on a highway or in an open place, at which monks and others used to preach.
A weight used for the measurement of wool.
A pit for the reception of night-soil and refuse.
A framed canopy suspended above the dais or high table at the upper end of a hall.
A steam whistle or siren used for signalling purposes.
A path or road for pedestrians, laid or beaten in with stones or other materials.
A 20th century feature found in public parks and seaside resorts. The face of the clock is planted with low-growing flowers and plants, while the moving hands are covered with small foliage.
A stone on which flax stems were beaten with wooden mallets, a process known as beetling.
Salts or organic derivatives of phosphoric acid, especially compounds of Calcium or Iron found in cereals and minerals.
A container used to hold an offering.

Stonemason's name for granite found lying upon the moorland surface, as opposed to having been quarried, in the West Country and the Lake District. Used, as found, since prehistoric times, in later years was often dressed and shaped.
A factory where glue is produced.
A sculpted cross, or a cross incised into stone or trees, to mark a parish boundary.
A post, made of wood, metal or other material, erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons such as measurement, calibration etc.
A place where trams are maintained and refitted, etc.
A workshop for testing guns, incorporating louvred sheds to serve as firing ranges.
A pictoral depiction of an area of landscape.
Enlargement of the floor area of an existing building.
A short, horizontal brace set between a tiebeam and a wall plate to strengthen the structure.
A garment hook having a flat plate, often decorated, with two or more holes for attachment and a hooked projection. The term is often used for early Medieval examples.
A stone used to instruct a coachman to take an extra trace horse to assist on roads of a steep gradient.
A hard, lustrous metallic element obtained from various ores, including sphalerite, and used in roofing, alloys and for galvanizing iron.
Musical instruments by how the sound is produced by the instrument.

One of two or three bands on a classical architrave, each projecting slightly beyiond the one below, often separated by enriched mouldings. Also a vertical band or board, such as that over a shop front on which its name is painted.
A farm on the estate of a manor.

A technique utilised in maritime recording; a remote operated vehicle (ROV) is a tethered underwater robot. ROVs have been used to locate and inspect a number of historic shipwrecks in depths beyond the reach of human divers.
A small disc or flat ring of metal, wood or leather.
An object used to create a blast of air.
A bowl with no noticeable base angle, so that the walls and base form a continuous rounded curve (Source: MPRG)

Composed of loose uncombed lengths of harvested wheat which are formed into bundles for laying. Distinctive appearance with both ears and butts visible on the surface traditionally using hazel spars which hold the straw in place.

Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
A grotto decorated with shells, sometimes a room in a house, sometimes a detached building.
A small, sharp bladed knife for sharpening pens, originally sheathed, now the blades fold.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and equipment to and from the surface of a mine.
A medical container for collecting urine for study.

Sites, buildings, structures, features and areas of land associated with cultivation, the rearing of livestock, gathering, hunting & fishing. Includes farm based processing of foodstuffs & storage of agricultural produce.
Calcium sulphate used as a fertilizer and for making plaster of Paris.
A room within a school, private house or institution used for lessons.
A waterwheel where the inflow of water strikes the paddles, or floatboards, below the axis of the wheel.
A command centre used to co-ordinate information received from Royal Observer Corps observation and monitoring posts.
Cards, often printed with forms, for the recording and sorting of information in a structured manner.
The edible seed of the palm tree.
A representation in the round of a living being, allegorical personage, eminent person or animal, etc, sculptured, moulded or cast in marble, metal, plaster, etc.
A horizontal member of a wall frame between posts or studs, also the horizontal member in panelling, a panelled door or a window.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.
An area of a building or complex, such as a workhouse or hospital, for isolating new residents before admission into main building, used to prevent spread of disease
A bowl used to wash in.
A pit where calcium oxide (Quicklime) has been hydrated to produce calcium hydroxide, known as slaked lime.
A shaped rod which passed through a hole in the door and was used to raise a latch or to slide a bolt.
Platform or structure used for viewing performances.
A well with an unusually high mineral content that combined with extensive periods of evaporation may give objects a stony exterior. Once believed to have been caused by magic or witchcraft.
A vessel used as a platform for flying a barrage balloon from.
A works or factory principally engaged in the manufacture of dynamite
A purpose built apparatus for the testing of helicopters.
A device to extract juice, usually from fruit.
A fishing boat using nets which are free to move with the tides and currents.
Residences of religious people and members of the clergy.
Chests connected with the burial of a body.
A compact steam engine of moderate power in which the steam cylinder was placed vertically on a table with the crosshead and guides mounted immediately above.
The remains of a vessel which has either sunk or suffered structural damage to the extent where it can no longer function.
A furnace for the manufacture of glass. Includes glass cones, open hearth and oil-fired furnaces.
A tank or pond containing a layer of sand etc, for filtering large quantities of liquid.
An artificially raised level of ground.
Data stored in a format that is meant to be manipulated and read in one or more software systems.
A room where meals, particularly breakfast are partaken.
An instrument of torture used to compress one or both thumbs.
A searchlight battery, which points out to sea, used to locate enemy shipping
A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to wooden structures or objects by the comparative study of the growth rings in trees and aged wood.
A mould in which an axehead is cast.
An engine used for directly winding up coal from deep mines, dating from the 18th century.
A civil vessel disguised as a warship.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground,  intended to be used by the regional government as an air raid shelter in the event of a nuclear attack.
A specially marked ground used by children for the game of hopscotch.
An Alternative Action report is generated for a site where scheduling has been considered but not recommended.
A staff to support a lame or legless person.
A specialist hospital where water treatment is given to patients suffering from muscular-skeletal complaints, etc.
A security device attached to objects.
One of a pair of straight or curved members set at an angle on the tie-beam and framed into a principal rafter, often supporting a purlin.
A mechanism within a windmill, attached to the striking rod, allowing the opening and closing of the shutters or vanes of patent sails.
A commercial bakery or bread factory. If domestic use BAKEHOUSE.

A landscape which has been specifically designed or modified. Often indicated by proven below ground stratigraphy, revealed by deliberate investigation including geophysical survey, or other surface monuments or structures.
A place of worship for members of the Serbian Orthodox Church, the national church of Serbia.

A tower situated above the rampart walkway and in between the angle towers along a defensive structure, such as a castle wall. They were used as lookout towers, roofed strongpoints or platforms from which missiles could be discharged or artillery fired.
A factory where paper is made. Use with power type where known.

A type of large permanent military aircraft hangar with a curved steel frame and storage annexes on its side used in World War II. It was intended for storage purposes on Aircraft Storage Unit stations.
A building used to house calves.
Development related to schools, colleges and universities.
A building or room used for the exhibition of upholstery for sale.
A container used to assist in cooling water.
A container used as a  lavatory.
Hard wood, reddish-brown in colour with a fine-grain often used in the manufacture of furniture.
Armour made up segmentally, usually of bands of material.
A machine for combing out wool, cleaning out extraneous matter and short fibres and laying the combed long fibres more or less parallel to each other as required for Worsted spinning.
A specialist hospital treating patients with chest disorders and diseases, can be pre sanatoria.
Development or changes to infrastructure including below ground services, sewage plants, drainage works
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
A timber set on the back of a cruck blade to carry a purlin.
A garden of regular, linear or geometrical design, often associated with the traditional Italian, French and Dutch styles.
A building where samples of corn were sold or auctioned during the early to mid 19th century. When not in use, between market days, the buildings were used as public halls.
A fitting of unknown function. Use more specific type where known.
A building, site or structure associated with the hunting of animals.
A craft which is equipped for and performs hydrographic surveys.

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
The impost, or point at which a vault rests upon its support, and from which it seems to spring. Hence the term describes the bottom stone of a vault, which lies on the impost.
A ball of chalk found on Neolithic sites.
A public house where no alcohol is sold.
Room, usually part of another building, for storing and preparing roots and other animal feed.
An inlet in the banks of a navigable river, often lined with brick and gated, into which boats can be drawn for repair etc.
A chest made of stone, wood or lead, used to enclose a dead body.
An area or space within a building.
A site, building or factory where seawater is used in the production of salt.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
A purpose built quay for supplying ships with fuel.
A building in which a supply of arms, ammunition and provisions for an army is stored.
A candlestick in which a simple socket is set in the centre of a drip tray or saucer. There may be a vertical loop handle linking the socket to the rim of the saucer. (Source: MPRG)
A lightweight prefabricated structure of corrugated galvanized steel having a semicircular cross section. The design was based on the Nissen hut developed by the British during the First World War.
Use for vessels registered in Iceland.
An object on which thread or yarn is wound or hooked.

A square pillbox with walls up to 48in thick, designed to emplace a 2 pounder anti-tank gun. A large opening in the back allowed the gun to be wheeled into position at the large embrasure in the front wall. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A machine, powered by steam, gas, electricity or other energy source, which produces energy of movement. Use for stationary industrial engines rather than transport use.
A carving, often a bust or full-length figure, originally found above a ship's cutwater. Use as an external feature only.
A semi-permanent ahed designed to Air Ministry specification 1136/27 as a quick and cheap hangar for stations overseas
A pile of rough stones and soil used for the growing of ferns and other plants.
An area of land enclosed by two parallel ditches. Use with specific shaped enclosure where known.
A chapel situated within the demesnes of a manor. Can be a separate building or an integral part of a manor house.
A projection left on a stone block to allow it to be hoisted into position.

A steel aircraft hangar evolved from the German "Lamellendach", a segmental roof design of the 1920s using a diamond shaped web of pressed steel producing a hangar with a shallow curving profile. Used for both military and civil purposes.
A building housing one end of an underwater telegraph cable.
A garden building, usually in the Gothic or classical style. The term can be applied to many types of garden building with an interior space in which to stand or sit. Use specific type where known.
A type of staple used to hold two object together.
A site for the sale or hire of agricultural machinery.
A storehouse in 16th and 17th century houses.
A steam engine working at a fixed location.
A small, often weatherboarded, roadside house in which cab drivers could rest and take refreshments. Late 19th century onwards.
Fine grained, whitish, granular variety of Gypsum. Suitable for carving.
That portion of the Atlantic Ocean which stretches from the Equator in the north to Antarctica.
An interment of unburnt, articulated human remains. Use specific type where known.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of patients with cancer or related illnesses.
Combined physical and mental health difficulties or conditions.
A site or building where silver was processed and/or worked and fashioned into objects.
A weapon featuring a single or double edged head attached to a wooden shaft.
Use for the remains of any part of a reptile.
Use for vessels registered in Egypt.
A measure for liquid, usually for a quarter of a pint.
An area for the testing of guided missiles.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
A room set aside within a building where social and other functions such as parties, presentations and meetings can be held.
An arch at the liturgical east of the nave, carrying a gabled wall above, separating nave from chancel.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.
A tall wooden pole used to support telegraph wires.
An area off the coast where ships anchor.
A manually produced image for illustration or record purposes.
A floating, fixed marker used to indicate to a navigator a sea area to approach or avoid.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.

A dating technique for the founding of individual populations based on the assumption of steady rates of mutation in mitochondrial DNA. Sometimes used to produce dates for stratigraphic layers containing fossil specimens of populations.
A beaker adapted by having a pedestal base. The upper part of the pedestal is solid and may be thrown as an integral part of the vessel, or added as a separate element.(Source: MPRG)
A gutter running behind a parapet wall, the water channelled by it being discharged from holes in the wall.
A building or site conducting research into communication techniques for use in the Royal Navy.
A building, usually in a rural setting, with a range of facilities for the use of members.
The field or area of ground on which a battle or skirmish was fought.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the front and rear elevations of the building.

Blocks of concrete with four protruding arms so that, whichever way up the caltrop is placed, one arm will always point upward. Used in imitation of the iron caltrops thrown on the ground to impede cavalry.
A store for undressed meat, usually for keeping grouse, partridge, pheasant or rabbit in a cool environment.

A map-based understanding of coastal and marine historic character; its GIS and linked texts extend Historic Landscape Characterisation principles to give a common framework of baseline information for the sustainable management of change from land to sea
A building used by visitors at a health resort.
Excavation of new basement serving  an existing building.
An industrial site or building where the machinery is powered by a steam engine.
Carved stones used for marking a grave.
A cup offered as a prize in a contest.

Ammunition from any period found to have been expended (cannonballs, shells, bullets) which may indicate the possible site of a battle or action on land or at sea. Index where appropriate with Battlefield Debris as a Monument Type.
A structure, usually or concrete or sandbags, in which a machine gun was emplaced.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.
A structure consisting of a box or platform for carrying goods or passengers from one level to another. Use specific type where known.
An unofficial, usually local, substitute for coinage, which could be exchanged directly for goods or services in certain areas or with specified retailers.
A bar used to increase the force being brought to bear in order to move an object.
A building used to smoke fish or meat.
