A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear disorders and diseases.
An object for touching or pricking an animal's sides to increase control of it, usually used with horses.
A school built and/or supported by voluntary contributions.
The residence of a bridge keeper.
A steam engine in which the cylinder, crosshead and crankshaft lie in a horizontal line, as opposed to vertical designs.
A machine used for weighing objects.

A type of flanged lid where the lower flange is partly cut away to leave two projections or lugs, which can be fitted into corresponding cut-outs in the rim of the vessel beneath and secure the lid when it is rotated. (Source: MPRG)
A small anti submarine escort vessel built in World War II
A small cold water bath, often known as a natatio when part of a Roman bath complex.
A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.
A building or large scale site for the manufacture and/or storage of weapons, ammunition and equipment.
An indoor court where the ancient and complex sport of real tennis is played, eg. the court at Hampton Court Palace.

Permian limestones which have had their chemical composition naturally altered with the calcium content being replaced by magnesium. Fine grained and varying from yellow/brown to cream in colour, although they weather to a dark grey.
A temporary earthwork or fortification constructed by forces laying siege to a castle or town, etc.
A barn used to store hops.
A metal receptacle used for burning coals, charcoal etc to provide heat.
A site, usually including fuel tanks, pipe works and control buildings, where flaming petroleum was intended to be used as a weapon against a hostile invasion.
A mechanized gate or barrier at a level crossing used to prevent road vehicles crossing a railway line when a train is approaching.
A small pierced disc which glitters, used as ornamentation on clothing
A building or site used to assess the mechanical state of a vehicle.
A material made of felted fibres bonded by bitumen. Often used as a roofing material.
Pasture to which animals were driven for grazing, with associated temporary huts for domestic or agricultural use.
A tract of land with trees, sometimes acting as a boundary or barrier, usually smaller and less wild than a forest.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
A site containing one or more artillery pieces and/or rocket launchers for firing at enemy aircraft.
A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of sawdust concrete panels. Produced by Maycrete Ltd during WWII.
A cylinder containing a piston by which fluid can be ejected or sucked in.
Block of flats incorporating broad, street-width balconies to give access to dwellings and connect to other blocks.
The systematic collection of samples from a defined study area analysed for phosphate content. Elevated concentrations of phosphate are a generalised signature of human activity.
A crane fixed to a quay, used for the unloading of ships cargoes.
A racing track, often within a permanent stadium, for racing dogs, usually greyhounds and whippets.
A single decked cargo vessel carrying the majority of its cargo on deck.
A shallow pond containing salt water and used for the manufacture of salt through the evaporation process. For metal vessels associated with the DIRECT BOILING and SLEECHING SALT WORKS use SALT PAN.

A long narrow rectangular earthwork enclosure of Neolithic date, usually defined by a bank and ditch and presumed to be of ceremonial function. Known examples range in length from less than 100m to c.10km.
A prison site for the containment of servicemen captured in war.
A shaft sunk into the ground to reach the water level.
A site where small electrical goods such as radios, lamps and heaters are manufactured.
Use for vessels registered in Australia.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.
A display or depiction of authorised armorial bearings, such as the elements of a coat of arms, livery and personal badges and flags, mottoes etc..
A room, usually lined with wood panels, that is heated to a hot and steamy temperature using a small stove and intended to be used for relaxation and therapeutic purposes.
Use for vessels registered in Panama. Often used as a flag of convenience.
Originally built as a family house. Converted into flats during the 19th or 20th century.
A stringed musical instrument, usually played with a bow.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
The bony outgrowths found on the heads of mammals used for display or combat used for a variety of purposes.
An area of land, often enclosed, used for cultivation or the grazing of livestock.
A public ground with facilities for games and other activities.
Short vertical timbers which go from the rafters to the inner plate on a thick wall.
A windbrace that bypasses one purlin to be jointed into the next  purlin or principal.
A flat, and usually level area of mown and cultivated grass, attached to a house.
Access for survey was not available at the time of the survey visit.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted.
An archaeological unit of soil in a horizontal plane which may seal features or be cut through by other features.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34 but with slight design modifications as detailed in drawing number 1960/34.
Railway constructed specifically for the movement of coal around the pithead of a coal mine.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
A small private chapel in a church or house, either attached or in a separate building.
An alcoholic spirit distilled from sugar products, especially molasses.
A defensive cattle enclosure added to fortified towers.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A widening in a canal to allow boats to turn around.
An extractive pit or pits, usually 2.5m square by 2m deep dug to extract tin ore in areas where streamworking is not possible. Usually dug along a vein rather than across it.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A tool used to provide grip and mechanical advantage in applying torque to tighten or loosen objects such as nuts and bolts.

Collective name for, in a true geological sense, a metamorphosed limestone, eg. Carrara marble, and, in the British sense any decorative stone that will take a polish, eg. Purbeck marble. In the latter's case index with specific stone type where given.
The part of a house frequented by servants when not performing their duties.
A light, ductile metal, used in the manufacture of aircraft etc.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
A light, ornamental building or structure situated close to the sea.
Any vessel designed for speed or endurance racing.
A round bottomed container to be held in the palm of the hand.
An internal combustion turbine engine powered by diesel, in use during WWII, for example.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings and yards (regular or loose courtyard in their form) are sited alongside a routeway.
The address as identified in a statutory document. This may be the same as or different to the Primary address
Use only for natural features mistakenly assumed to be archaeological or natural features with archaeological significance.

A purpose-built facility providing an area for wheeled sports, such as skateboarding, skating and BMX cycling, equipped with ramps and other structures and obstacles for the performance of tricks and manoeuvres.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
Use for deposits formed in lakes or ponds.
An area of hardstanding to allow movement of farm transport in all weathers.
An area of land enclosed by one or several boundary ditches. Double index with a term to indicate the shape of the enclosure where known.
A bowl adapted by having a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
An arch which is formed by keystones but is flat like a lintel
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
Decorative ornamentation of a formalized lily.
The architectural element made of brick, tile, stone or certain woods which surrounds a fireplace to provide aesthetic and safety benefits.
A ditch which is not continuous but instead is made up of segments which may vary in length and width.
A small, steel shelter designed for use as a firewatchers post during an air raid.
Land use involving no operations likely to be damaging to archaeological remains.
A commercial building used primarily as a trading place for wool merchants.
Hut for use at Level Crossings that were not adjacent to Signal Boxes.
The loss of a craft due to structural or engine failure. In the case of loss resulting from the malfunction of navigational or operational apparatus, use INSTRUMENT FAILURE.
A structure, partly underground, for the preservation of ice for use during warmer weather.
Durable artificial stone consisting of china clay, sand and finely ground stoneware cast from moulds and fired in a kiln. Commonly used for architectural ornament and facings.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around four sides of an open cattle yard.
A room or building occupied by a person employed to keep accounts of workers' hours of labour.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
A toilet or toilets for public use.
Transport vessel hired for the enforced removal of convicts to penal colonies abroad(e.g. Virginia, Australia), or for their return to Britain.
A semi metal, poisonous element used in a variety of industrial processes and in some medicinal preparations.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
A plastic covered tunnel designed to protect vulnerable plants from the weather and allow vegetables to be grown out of season
A disc >4mm with a central perforation.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a polygon and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A training school where ballet is taught.
A college where subjects relating to trade and commerce are taught.
A laundry attached to a hospital.
A series of flat-topped structures, usually made of stone or wood, used to facilitate a person's movement from one level to another.
A part of a building or complex where administrative duties are undertaken.
A room in a church where vestments and sacred vessels are stored.
A fereter or repository for relics or any building containing such a repository, or any place or structure where worship is offered or devotions are paid to a saint or deity.
A container in which  dice are shaken and from which dice are thrown.
Products derived from the carcasses or hides of animals. Includes bone and ivory products, blubber and grease but not meat.
A vessel, usually a merchant vessel, altered to resemble a warship or another vessel.
Materials used to equip and fit out a ship. Includes masts, spars, rigging etc. Use only where evidence is less specific, otherwise use most relevant term.
A building housing washing facilities and toilets. The term occurs mainly in a military context.
A cereal, yellow in colour, the grains of which are embedded in a core known as the cob.
The external face or elevation of a building, especially the principal front.
A type of bridge which completely encloses the traffic using it.
A large piece of material used on a bed for sleeping on or under.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land commemorating an historical event, person or animal.
A non-metallic element, yellow in colour, used in a variety of processes.

An investigative method using an infrared camera to detect temperature differences in the ground. The thermal camera does not record the actual temperature of the object in question. Instead the camera records the infrared radiation emitted by the object.
A tool with a sharp, concave edge for shaping wood, stone or metal.
A vessel equipped with sealed tanks for transporting sewage and dumping it in deep water.
A mug with more-or-less straight side which flare out from the rim to the wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A composite instrument in which air is forced through one or more drones and chanter from an inflated bag or bladder.
Metal shaped blade that flares out to a curved cutting edge, with a side loop to further assist hafting.
A building used for the education of, and as a residence for, chantry priests.
Works where yarn is prepared prior to spinning.
Waste material or dross separated from metals during smelting or refining.
A jug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile form rim to base, which are roughly equal in diameter. (Source: MPRG)
A building associated with the legal administration of a forest, eg. Forest of Dean.
An object originally created to communicate a particular personal belief, achievement, status or membership. It includes articles of adornment or clothing worn primarily for their symbolism.
A raw material determined by its form or a finished product material characterised by its end shape or form. See MATERIAL <BY FORM> Class List for narrow terms.
A simple, one-piece Bow Brooch with a spring of four coils, sometimes  less, its chord tucked beneath its head and variations to bow and catchplate. Dating from the first century AD.
Fish eggs, e.g. from cod or, for example, caviar.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows a circular course, but is not regularly laid out.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a naval dockyard.
Use broader site type where known
A small pair of shears with crossed blades, usually used for pruning.
An electricity-producing power station fired by oil.
Model village built as a holiday resort.
An ancilliary building or structure associated with a military base. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.

A flour milling machine which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a �sudden death� process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
A type of jug decorated with applied figures in the form of knights in armour. (Source: MPRG)
A geometrical planting of trees in the form of the number 5 as represented on a dice.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, and later used to direct air traffic. Use more specific type where known.
Cloth or leather covering for the leg or ankle.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.
A structure used for the storage of coal.
A small cargo boat found on the River Severn in England, with a mast which could be taken down to allow the boat to pass under low bridges.
Building used for field studies and outdoor pursuits in the countryside and in an urban context.

A jar adapted by the addition of a pierced bunghole just above the base. The hole can be simply a hole in the wall of the vessel or made through a circular knob or disc of clay. There may be one or two vertical loop handles. (Source: MPRG)
The official residence of the chief officer of the municipal corporation of a city or borough in England.
A monument visible as a trace on marine survey equipment
A wooden panel, mounted on the wall of a church, bearing the Achievement of Arms of an individual whose funeral has taken place there.
A short timber connecting a cruck blade to a wall above the point at which the blade diverges from it.
A site where methane gas, released by coal mining, is collected and processed.
A structure, or building, forming a supplementary and subsidiary part of a main complex.
A miniature railway on which targets can be placed to provide moving targets on a firing range.

Any notification, update or amendment relating to the scheduling of a monument. Usually includes description and a map showing the limit of the scheduling. It confers a statutory status and receipt is an acknowledgement of the scheduling.
A container, in the form of an urn, for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A residence of two or three monks of the Gilbertine order dependent on an English mother house.
A place where people recovering from illnesses or accidents are helped to recover their physical and/or mental capabilities.
A tower used as a watch tower by the coastguard. Often, though not always, built as part of a Coastguard Station.
A building or a room for accounts.
A site incorporating all of the production processes for the manufacture of plaster.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of spaced post- holes which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A site and associated buildings used by the military for various purposes. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.

Monument whose existence is indicated by the discovery of isolated artefacts or an artefact scatter. Eg a scatter of roofing tiles indicating the presence of a building. Use narrow terms where circumstances of discovery are known.
A block in the position of a tiebeam.
An partly-worked millstone that is still to be finished.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 1762/39.
A dark outbuilding or cellar with internal recesses for overwintering skeps of bees.
Includes some structures that are not strictly buildings. Use a more specific term where possible.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 14383/40.
A triangular or wedge-shaped timber cocking-piece attached to the upper face of a rafter near its foot  in order to reduce the slope above the eaves. Such eaves are referred to as being sprocketed.
A short timber set across the top of a wall to take the foot of a rafter and an ashlar piece.

A subsidiary enclosure externally attached to an enclosure of known or unknown date and function. The annexe is generally smaller than, and secondary to, the main enclosure. Use more specific site type where known. Do not use for Roman military sites.
A site or building where barrage balloons are manufactured. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
A container designed to be difficult to get into or out of, thus ensuring the safety of objects inside the container.

A system of defensive works such as anti-tank obstacles, ditches and pillboxes, designed to stop the advance of an enemy. Defence lines were constructed across and around strategic areas of ground and sites such as industrial towns.

Areas of past and current land improvement, involving operations capable of disturbing the archaeology, e.g. land drainage, land reclaimation, cultivation including areas of ridge and furrow but not Celtic Fields.
Originally used to describe very strong, often thick, rope made of metal or hemp. Now can be used for protective flexible tubing encasing wires such as telephone wire.
Fine art depiction in oil, watercolour or other media on wood panels, canvas or paper
A ground used for the performance testing of motor vehicles, for example prototype vehicles.
A type of drying house, usually circular with a conical roof.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Order of Tiron.

Limestone formed during the Devonian period, and found predominantly between the Exe and Tamar rivers in Devon. Varying in colour from black/grey to pink/white it was often polished to imitate, and be used as, marble.
A prepared area used for the game of netball.
An elevated table or podium on which to place or sacrifice offerings to the deities.
A flake of stone struck from the core where the length is less than twice the width.
Deciduous wood from the native elm tree, commonly used for framing or cladding of lesser timber framed structures due to its poorer weathering qualities as compared to oak.
A tool, usually metal, with roughened surfaces in the form of very small teeth.
A factory manufacturing bearings, including ball bearings for use in precision equipment.
The class or material that a photograph is produced upon. [AAT] Use a specific term or terms as appropriate.
A room or space with an arched ceiling or roof, the depth of which exceeds its span.
Ketch or yawl rigged vessel with a large mizzen sail used in the west country.
Refers to the abandonment of a vessel at sea due to its becoming unseaworthy.  Do not use for vessels abandoned having run aground. For aircraft use DITCHED.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
An establishment open at night for refreshment and entertainment.
Written communication, generally in the form of letters.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of electricity.

A camp providing accommodation for members of the Canadian Forestry Corps along with facilities such as saw mills for the sawing and squaring of timber to create pit props, shoring, crates etc for the war effort.
A three dimensional representation of a figure, whether animal or human, produced by carving, casting sculpting or similar.
An aircraft hangar designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers usually erected on aircraft factory sites rather than operational airfields.
A site or building used for the storage and maintenance of both land and sea vehicles and from which terrestrial or maritime operations could be carried out.
Temporary settlement relating to the construction of railways, viaducts, dams, etc.
Owned or used by another Government Dept, administered by DOE
A loft over a stable or barn used for storing hay.
A tool used to reduce the diameter of metal rods. Consists of a pair of semicylindrical surfaces.
A horizontal timber positioned at the bottom of a framed wall into which posts and studs are tenoned.
A tent especially one made of bark, rushes or skins spread over a set of arched poles that are lashed together.
A small outer courtyard, or service-yard.
A buttress attached to a corner of a structure, seeming to be a continuation of one of the walls.
The heat-resistant wall, or sometimes decorative cast iron panel, at the back of a fireplace.
A metal pin with two arms which is passed through a hole and held in place by the springing apart of the arms.

A place of worship for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers. The Religious Society of Friends is a denomination founded by George Fox in c.1650 who believed in passivist principles and a rejection of the sacrament.
A stick inscribed with a prayer or prayers for use in praying.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of standing stones, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A purlin that is joined to the back of a principal rafter.
Soft, white, porous sedimentary rock, a form of limestone composed of the mineral calcite.
A pit used to trap game. Often originally covered and consealed, and sometimes with sharpened stakes in the base.
A purpose-built triangulation point used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac monks.

A room in the house of a Justice of the Peace in which cases were heard. Houses after 1848 contained these for prestige purposes since the practice of hearing cases at home was made illegal at that date.
Long alignment of cairns lying between two large cairns; first recognized as a site type on Sourton Tor, Dartmoor.
A building or site used for the exercise and training of military personnel.
A flag or military symbolic representation on a pole.
A building, or room within a brewery, where beer or cider undergoes fermentation in vats or tuns.
A laithe with an attached house.
Lenses worn in a frame designed to improve or protect the vision of the wearer.
Cargo vessel or warship captured by a warship or privateer of a hostile nation in time of war, usually taken into that nation�s mercantile, privateering or naval service.
A maze used for the act of penitence.
Any small rigged warship below the sailing classification of frigate.
Traditionally, pieces of unleavened cake or bread usually small in size and dry, crisp and hard.
A calcareous, hard substance, the external skeleton of marine polyps, used in the manufacture of jewellery.
A structure, part of a structure or area consisting of plain masonry.
The foremost church within a parish.
Cut or uncut stones, usually intended to be set into jewellery, and including precious gems, e.g. diamonds, sapphires, or semi-precious materials, e.g. quartz, agate, amber.
A prototype semi-underground silo based launch system specifically designed to hold and fire the Blue Streak Missile. The silo was constructed at RAF Spadeadam in c1959 and abandoned in April 1960.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
Unpublished written work such as manuscripts, dissertations etc. not disseminated to the public.
A craft used to retrieve torpedoes after practice firings.
A share or portion of land, allotted to a person, often used for growing, vegetables, fruit, etc.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
Use for vessels registered in the Republic of Ireland (Eire).
A device inserted in the ear canal to protect the wearer from loud noises or the intrusion of water, foreign bodies, dust or excessive wind.
A window with a single mullion and a single transom.
A pit used to bury a large number of people who have died, or been killed, either as a result of warfare, epidemics or natural disasters.
A stopper made of cork used to prevent liquid escaping from a container.

A list of buildings of special architectural or historic interest. This list confers a statutory level of protection status to the buildings contained within it and usually includes a description of each building.
A concrete which is either aerated or made from lightweight aggregate.
A mug with roughly vertical body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A screen used to decorate or protect an opening.
In the Classical Orders, the horizontal assembly of architrave, frieze and cornice carried upon columns and pilasters.
A site where household rubbish and other waste products can be disposed of. May take the form of a pit, rubbish tip, landfill site or incineration plant.

A place of worship for members of the United Reformed Church, a group formed in 1972 by the amalgamation of most of the Congregational Churches in England and Wales with the Presbyterian Church in England.
1/12000 of a foot or 25.4 μm. Also known as mil
A factory where musical instruments are manufactured.
A rigid holder for a bladed weapon.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
A cube of material used to make up a mosaic.
An arch built into a wall above another arch or lintel to relieve it of some of the weight of the structure above.
A form of Neolithic long barrow comprising an oval, rather than rectangular or trapezoidal mound.
A shop that sells men's clothes, either off the peg, bespoke or both.
A set of marks found on the wall of a building, thought to be a form of sundial.
A series of links joined together to form something that is flexible and strong. Usually metal, chains have a variety of uses but usually involve joining one item to another.
A doubled rafter, separated by cleats, spacers or distance pieces.
An aircraft hangar designed to be moved from site to site as necessary.
A pin worn to hold two or more pieces of material together, often when being worn as clothing.
Purpose built or modified structure or building used for scenery in a television program.
A garden containing trees or shrubs pruned and trained into various geometric, zoomorphic or fantastic shapes.
A supply of water used to keep canals that were vulnerable to water shortage topped up.
A depot for the transfer of town refuse to river barges before transportation to the REFUSE DEPOT.
A musical instrument producing sound from a membrane.
Purpose built or modified structure used for scenery in a film.
A pier of brick, masonry, etc, to which the hinges of a gate are attached.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A garden with real or supposed Swiss features, including buildings and plantings.
A hospital department, open 24 hours a day, for the immediate reception and treatment of emergency cases.
A room for storing and maintaining the equipment used in riding, eg saddles, bridles, reins etc.
A circular stylised ornament, essentially a patera with floral enrichment, associated with classical architecture and occurring on the soffits of coffers, and as the fleuron of the Corinthian abacus.

A poorly understood Neolithic monument comprising a very long, narrow earthen mound. They may be of single-phase construction, or represent the addition of a linear extension to the bank of an existing Long Barrow.
A capital which is decorated with stylized leaves similar to small volutes.
Storage medium for information (text, images, files etc) in an encoded digital format.
A ceiling beam aligned with the length of a building.
Any of the plants of the grass family, Graminae, cultivated for their edible seeds, especially corn, wheat etc.
Manmade feature to contain water for the purpose of floating miniature boats in it. Different to BOATING LAKE as lake can be naturally occuring park feature and can be used for full sized boats.
Objects forming fragments or parts of a building's fabric, structures and associated services, eg drain pipes. Where an object is a fixture or fitting use the separate class.
A mine in which access is gained by a straight entrance driven on a constant downward slope. Use with product(s) extracted and MINE where known, eg. COAL MINE.
A shopping complex, usually indoors, comprised of a number of separate retail outlets surrounding an open space. Often on more than one level.
A separate compartment for livestock in which they are free to move about.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of wine and cider.
A road vehicle designed to carry many passengers.
A building providing lodgings for police constables.
A town for citizens of Roman or Latin status with a constitution governed by charter, which if possessing only Latin rights could be promoted to the status of a colonia.
A quadrangle or courtyard, often grassed or planted, surrounded by cloisters
A mirror designed to be held by hand.

Light detection and ranging is a type of aircraft based remote sensing which records reflected laser pulses. The data can be used to produce very accurate digital elevation models. For ground-based work use LASER SCANNING SURVEY.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
A structure, into which a cart can be drawn, to enable it to be loaded from above.
A large wheel, often of timber construction, rotated by the walking action of people or animals placed within it usually to provide a power source for another machine or device.
A burial ground for military personnel.
A stone, situated alongside a road, providing directions to travellers.
A type of dagger, usually used by civilians in the medieval period, with a H shaped hilt.
A comb made up of riveting together sections between connecting plates.
An archaeological unit of soil in a horizontal plane which may seal features or be cut through by other features.
Guild Of The Holy Cross Chapel
A chain used to inhibit a prisoner's freedom.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal

Style of early Bronze Age pot found widely in north-western Europe with a deep, largely plain, outwardly flared body above which is sharp carination, usually decorated and sometimes with an applied cordon, and an inwardly angled neck.
The powdery residue of burnt bones.
Debris resulting from the manufacture of tools and other artifacts from bone.
An entrance large enough for carriages and vehicles leading through a building or wall into an inner courtyard.

A system of excavation, developed by Mortimer Wheeler, whereby a site was uncovered by means of a grid of square trenches with baulks between them to aid the recording of the stratification of all four sides of each trench.
Remains of any part of a hazel (Corylus avellana L.) nut.
A container for the storage and/or transport of food and/or liquid.
Publication on a specific topic, or limited scope of subject matter. Complete in itself, though may form part of a series.
A chapel for the use of travellers and pilgrims.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a short tubular spout applied just below the rim.
A container for loose gun powder. Sometimes with a regulator to release enough powder for one shot.
A small, usually hinged, box made of copper alloy which protected a seal.
Ornamentation fixed to a horse's harness.
A building housing a fan used for the ventilation of mines
Powder produced by grinding cacao beans, used as the main ingredient for the drink Cocoa.
A building where clothes are washed.
Pieces of undressed stone, waste fragments of stone or fragments of slate.
A roof design, common to weaving sheds, featuring a sawtooth profile with unequal slopes forming each ridge and  lights on its northern side.
Unenclosed wasteland, forest and pasture used in common by the community.
A piece of sculpture usually representing the head, shoulders and breast of a person.
Any vehicle/craft used for transportation on water.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canons.
A water mill where the waterwheel directly drives a vertical shaft with grindstones on.
Record of an individual context (ie layer or feature) from an archaeological excavation.
A cleansing or separating machine used in a corn mill for removing smut from grain before it is ground.

A lid with a distinct flange, projecting upwards, horizontally or downwards, and an integral knob. Complex examples can include a simple locking device: lugs on the lower flange can be twisted into matching cut-outs in the rim to lock it. (Source: MPRG)
A bridge used for carrying liquids, usually water, although sometimes oil, in a pipeline over a river. Mid 19th century onwards.
Including ground in current use for burials and legally consecrated ground, e.g. graveyard, chapel-ground etc.
An inward radial-flow reaction turbine developed by James Thomson.
A means of transportation where cars, chairs or cabins are carried above the ground by means of one or more cables suspended between towers or pylons.
A case in which a comb was carried.
A room equipped for the care of babies and young children.

A building, often with underground rooms, used to receive all reports of aircraft locations, to assimilate and assess this information in order to provide the most accurate possible picture to the Operations Room of a fighter or bomber Group.

Transport vessel used for the repatriation of wounded troops, particularly during the First World War. Loosely described as "hospital ships", these ships were distinct from hospital ships proper by being defensively armed.
A cluster of piles for mooring a vessel.
An area within a hospital concerned with the care and medical treatment of expectant mothers.
A site, building or factory used for the production of salt.
A workshop forming part of a domestic dwelling.
A structured set of data taken from a larger work to assist in location of particular subject matter.
A man-made trough or valley through a hill, carrying at its base a railway.
A recess within a wall or room.
A building adjoining a cricket pitch with facilities for players and spectators.

A tunnel built alongside a canal tunnel to enable a horse to be unhitched and led through the hillside to meet the barge when it emerged from the tunnel. Mainly built prior to the development of the towpath tunnel.
Weapons including portable firearms and large artillery pieces.
Military weapon with long shaft and bill style head. For agricultural style bills use bill hook.
A bungalow joined to another to form one building.
A vessel used to produce butter from milk through agitation.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
Sites and buildings used in the coordination of the defence of the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.
A screen of wood or stone, used to divide the nave from the choir.
A site or building associated with active or passive defence of the landing ground and buildings of an airfield.
A man-made ridge to carry a railway across a declivity or area subject to flooding.
For example tumors, leukemia, bone/ breast/ colon/ prostate cancer, Hodgings Lymphoma/ Disease, oral/ throat cancer, melanoma, ovarian and pancreatic cancer and other related illnesses.
Engineering workshop housing specialized machinery such as lathes, presses, etc., for making machines.

Collective name for, in a true geological sense, a metamorphosed limestone, eg. Carrara marble, and, in the British sense any decorative stone that will take a polish, eg. Purbeck marble. In the latter's case index with specific stone type where given
A crane, usually used in engineering workshops, that can be moved from place to place, often by means of rails.
A sculpture on top of a tomb etc.
A spire, or spirelet surmounting a roof, especially over the crossing of a French Gothic Cathedral.
A pair of tongs used for placing coals onto a fire.
A tube, cyclinder or similar casing enclosing the mechanism of a pump.
Sites and structures used for the transportation of goods and people under roads and rivers, or through hills, etc.
The limit line of a parish.
A building used to prepare and store dry food such as hay and straw for the feeding of cattle.
A cutting blade with handle used for food preparation and consumption.
A building housing a boiler, often connected to a steam engine house.
An indoor or outdoor market where butter was sold.
A building, usually housing electrical or electronic equipment, used for gathering and disseminating information. Use specific type where known.
A lime kiln in which coal is burnt, as distinct from a flame-free kiln in which wood or peat is used.
A tunnel built to allow internees (in a camp, prison etc.) to escape.
A container made of interwoven strips of pliable materials, such as cane or reed, often carried by a handle.
WW2 LAA battery consisting of two or four 40m guns or Bofors guns. Associated structures included tented accommodation, ammunition shelters, a 100 gallon water tank, latrines, wash-house and kitchen.

Analytical Earthwork Surveys are generally undertaken to; promote the understanding and appreciation of archaeological sites and landscapes; to establish proper curatorial advice; to generate appropriate Conservation and Management Plans and; to assess rates of determination and threats to the heritage asset.
A designated area, usually sited at a strategic crossroads, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to act as a rallying point for defenders.
A building, usually open to the public, containing a number of areas for bathing. In the case of such a complex containing baths for swimming, also index with INDOOR or OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL.
A mill whose machinery is driven by water.
A fishing spear with two heads to grip fish between.
A building where people could bathe in salt water. Salt water was believed to have medicinal properties.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
Item in a format suitable for normal reading or viewing, without a computer or other device.  For digital files or disks use MACHINE READABLE STORAGE MEDIUM or specific terms.

A type of temporary military hutting used throughout WWII constructed of brick in 'stretcher bond' 4.5 inches thick with a light steel truss roof usually covered with corrugated asbestos sheeting. Used for accommodation, as gyms, training huts etc.
A place of worship at the site of a mortuary.
A substance secreted by some plants which hardens upon drying but is soluble in water.

Use where an entire, wrecked or incapacitated, craft has been recovered or salvaged, possibly leaving debris or other evidence of its presence at the wreck or crash site. If part of the wreck remains on the seabed use PARTIALLY RECOVERED.
A wheeled device supporting a windmill's fantail that moves around a trackway thus turning the windmill into the wind.
A prison for the confinement of people who owe money.
A central area within a building.
A covered ambulatory, usually arcaded, arranged around three or four sides of a quadrangle in a monastic or collegiate establishment.
Hydrocarbon secretion of a tree or bush, either naturally exuded or deliberately tapped from the tree, valued for its varied uses in chemicals and perfumery.

A form of bronze axehead of middle or late Bronze Age date in which narrow, high flanges on both faces are hammered over to enclose the axe haft. Some types feature a side loop to further assist hafting.
A school design consisting of single-storey buildings with classrooms entered from a verandah.
A section of a window between mullions; thus for example a three-light window.
A mobile crane usually found on a marine or inland quay.
A tool to apply material to the seams of a ship.
An instrument used to compress a substance into a smoking pipe.
Objects used or associated with religious, ritual or funerary activities.
A building used for the safe storage and public display of jewellery, eg. the Jewel House at the Tower of London.
Any part of a maritime vessel. Use more specific term where known.
A pair of common rafters with a collar.
A joint with a loose tenon morticed into two touching pieces of timber
Residential area built to house athletes and their coaches at the Olympic Games. The buildings are generally reused as public housing after the contest.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
An abbey or priory of Grandmontine monks.
The flesh obtained from pigs eaten as food.

Circular or sub-circular enclosure defined by a bank and (usually internal) ditch, with one or two (rarely more) entrances. Of ceremonial/ritual function, they contain a variety of internal features including timber or stone circles.
A roof consisting of a series of rafters and arch braces set closely together to give the appearance of a continuous, uninterrupted arch or curved plate.
A silicate mineral used since the Bronze Age as gemstones and abrasives. Found in many colours including red, orange, yellow, green, purple, brown, blue, black, pink and colourless.
A hospital where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness. Medical facilities for treatment are also available.
A horn used in hunting to give signals.
A device patented in 1733 for speeding up the weaving of cloth.
Line used with hooks attached to it in order to catch fish.
A place of worship for followers of the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion, a Calvinistic Methodist sect founded in the 1740s by Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon.
A patented design of twin-cylinder, inverted vertical steam engine, which can be started irrespective of the position of the crank.
Material consisting of fragments of stone, sand, gravel, slag etc. used in the manufacture of concrete.
A multi-level structure designed to simulate tall buildings to allow firefighters to practice firefighting and rescue techniques
A vault with a ceiling or undersurface subdivided by ribs into bays or webs.
The SI derived unit of specific volume.
A plan type of a hall with two wings and a central porch.
A hard sharp point used to cut a design into metal.

A high status, walled, Roman burial ground containing cremations and/or inhumations in mausolea, tombs, barrows, coffins or cists. Dating from the late 1st to the 4th Century AD. DO NOT USE for cemeteries of later dates which are walled.
Groundwork to provide a designed landscape e.g. to provide visual or sound barriers including slope profiling and earth moving.
Vegetable matter decomposed in water and partially carbonized to form bogs, whence slabs are cut out to use as fuel.
A decorative garden, often landscaped, laid out with intricate flower beds and hedges, and often containing ornate sculptures, fountains and garden ornaments.
A pole with a blade used for rowing or steering a boat by leverage against the water.

Used to identify and measure various sediment layers that exist below the seabed. A sound source emits a signal vertically downwards and a receiver monitors the return signal that has been reflected off the seafloor and sub seabed sediment layers.
Concrete or steel pontoons that supported the Whale piers. They were moored in position using wires attsched to Kite anchors.
A building appropriated by a school for the purpose of teaching pupils.
Photographic transparency on nitrate base material.
A viscous, bituminous pitch which can be used for surfacing roads.
A cutting tool where the plane of the blade is at right angles to the shaft.
First Rate Ship Of The Line
A workshop, associated with a tannery, in which the fleece is removed from the skin prior to the tanning process.
A gripping tool consisting of two hinged arms, usually with serrated jaws.
A steam-powered machine used for raising ore or water from a mine.

Series of rooms in a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term in Monument Type Thesaurus if it is a freestanding building.
A tool used to sharpen another tool or object.
A site in which one or more searchlights were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
An object fashioned in the image of a penis.
A flat surface designed to hold objects. For a set of shelves use shelving.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
Waste flakes and cores produced in the manufacture of stone implements.
To mark the end of a turnpike road.
An iron frame placed over a coffin or at the entrance to a grave to act as a deterrent against resurrectionists.
A small house, usually on the estate of a country house, forming part of a widow's dower and intended as her residence.
A military side-opening aircraft hangar originally designed for seaplanes and used RNAS bases from 1916. Steel framed with asbestos or corrugated iron cladding.
A bayonet designed to plug into the muzzle of a musket or rifle.

A two-storey, all-concrete construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A concrete parapet all around the roof differentiates it from 5845/39.
A tool used in etching which is the use of acid to breakdown parts of a metal plate in order to create an image.
An object which when hot is used to smooth fabric.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance of a tomb.
A long room for recreation, often on an upper floor.
Mark 2 or the second variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A factory manufacturing insulation material for electrical cables.
Any by-product which cannot be reused.
A roof in which pairs of rafters are fixed to the ridge piece and the wall plates without any collars or tiebeams.
A bead used to create a space or interval within a necklace.
A raised structure from which a priest can preach.
A plain, narrow moulding or area, sometimes projecting, separating two decorated mouldings or features such as the vertical grooves on a fluted column.
A mine designed specifically to be dropped from an aircraft, often into the sea.
A building used by the church to promote Christianity through lectures, study, etc.
A mechanism, either automated or consisting of winches and pulleys, that raises sacks of grain on ropes or chains from one floor of a mill to another, usually through one or a series of trap doors.

A small dispersal WWII military aircraft hangar featuring an "A" shaped steel frame clad with corrugated iron; end doors were supported by outriggers when open.Typically used on aircraft storage units or satellite landing grounds. Variations in size.
One of a building's horizontal divisions, being the space between two floors, or a floor and the roof structure.
A military dining room where members of the armed forces eat and take recreation.
A furnace used for the refining of precious metals. eg. the separation of silver from argentiferous lead.
A semi-circular window, often decorated and with its glazing bars radiating like the ribs of an opened fan, set above a door.
An improved water frame spinning machine which differed from the water frame in mechanical details, being larger and operating at a much faster speed.
A rock-like deposit consisting largely of calcium carbonate, formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate out of calcium-rich water bodies such as springs.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.
A large, usually metal, container used for the storage of liquid fuels.

A conglomerate rock comprising well rounded flint pebbles in a very hard matrix of fine pale coloured sand, bound together by hard natural silica cement. The pebbles are usually coloured ochre or red and have black rims.

Clothes which are distinctive in cut, colour and fabric and worn by members of the armed forces, emergency services or civilian organizations to help to distinguish their members form other organizations.
A vessel lost due to aerial bombardment.
Factual information conveyed orally to a recipient.  Where this has been transcribed, use an appropriate term from the TEXT hierarchy.
The principal room in early houses, which occupies the entire height of the building.
A bed of low-growing foliage plants, all of an even height, arranged in patterns that resemble a carpet both in the intricacy of their design and in the uniformity of surface.
A place on which a fire is made.
A spiked stick, the spiked tip frequently of metal, used to urge livestock forward.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
Buildings and structures associated with good health and recreation.
A room or part of a church where the vestments, vessels and records are kept.
Cloth that has been woven in fixed lengths for sale.

A jar with a profile that flares outwards from base to rim, but usually with a constriction at the neck. Squat examples, with a height less than the minimum diameter, could be classified as bowls. (Source: MPRG)
Coastal area above high water levele. Specify in Description using: sand, sand dune, shingle etc.
A toy in the image of a human being.
A small latrine or toilet, usually built into the thickness of the wall of a castle or great house, with the waste dropping into a cess pit or straight to the outside.
A dense, high strength, low absorption brick of uniform size, employed predominantly in industrial structures such as railway viaducts.
A principal member in a cruck truss.
A mechanism through which crude coal gas is passed to remove any impurities eg Ammonia and Sulphur.
Objects concerned with marriage and weddings.
A specific type of hand held  hollowed wooden clapper, known in Europe from medieval times onwards.
A moulded ring around a shaft.

A type of tower mill, either with turbine-type sails able to take wind from any direction, or with sails working with shrouds to direct wind from one direction. The sails directly drove millstones set beneath them.
The part of the wall that supports a pitched roof at the end of the roof.
A room in which board and table games are usually played.
A pond used as a water supply for the operation of a furnace or blast furnace.
A bayonet designed to fit over the muzzle of a musket or rifle, allowing the gun still to be fired.
An area of land, usually on a slope, which has been built up to provide a flat surface for the cultivation of crops.
Baths containing water impregnated with mineral substances in which patients bathe for medicinal purposes.
An area within a hospital where patients with contagious diseases are isolated from the rest of the hospital.
A site where clay is mined from the ground.
An aeroplane featuring three wings, or planes, placed one above the other either side of its fuselage.
Room in a building or complex in which the master of an establishment, such as a workhouse or a school, is accommodated.
An object used to mark each mile and to indicate distances to locations.
A foreshore structure to prevent barges from sinking in the river mud. Made by placing chalk on fascines of brushwood, which is in some cases retained by a timber revetement.
A level crossing designed to allow the passage of aircraft to and from a runway which has a railway or road running through it.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 17658/40.
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.

A farmstead with multiple yards which are grouped together and regularly arranged (other than the defined E, F, H, T or Z plans). The yards may relate to one or more buildings or ranges which may be of either loose courtyard or regular courtyard form.
A plot of earth used for the raising of plants.
A brick made of clay which is difficult to fuse, used in boilers and fireplaces.
A weapon with a sharp edge or point.
A joint in which both timbers are reduced in thickness.

A spatially discrete scatter of mixed artefactual material found on the ground, seabed or riverbed which may have been deposited over time rather than resulting from one particular event. Index particular types where appropriate.
A transverse ceiling beam set below wall-plate level in order to increase head room within the roof space; it carries knee principals, or the struts or braces of an interrupted tiebeam truss.
Open yard for keeping cattle in during winter. Used from the mid-14th century in drier, Eastern, arable counties.
A site where peat (vegetable matter decomposed in water and partly carbonised), used for fuel, is cut.
A plucked string instrument of a specific medieval / early post medieval type.
Stiff hairs used in the manufacture of brushes.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.
Use for vessels registered in Slovenia.

A jar-shaped vessel with pierced apertures or cut-out on an open or closed pedestal base. Herbs, spices or scented woods would be placed in the pot and a burning coal placed underneath to warm the herbs so they would release their scent.
A garden in which a variety of plants are grown to encourage butterflies.
Two masted ship with fore and aft sails and two or more masts.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55414.
Mud walled building found on the Solway Plain.
An 18th century hand-operated machine capable of spinning several yarns at once, invented in circa 1767.
An enclosure used for baiting bulls.
A plan in which a four-sided figure has all its angles at right angles and its opposite sides equal and parallel.
A tiebeam whose central section is omitted to increase head room; its inner ends are held by a slip-braces or struts rising from a dropped tiebeam and can be used in end frames.
A churchyard or memorial cross set on a long shaft.
A hook from which a lamp could be hung.
A controlled point with warning lights and gates or barriers where a road crosses a railway line.
Metal used primarily for roofing and ornamental purposes, being lighter and stronger than lead.
An ore containing a high proportion of manganese.
A device on an airfield for securing aircrafts when parked outside in order to prevent major movement due to the weather or other conditions.
A written work issued at regular intervals and numbered consecutively.
Iron, usually unworked, in the form of bars.
An object in which a candle is put in order to provide light.
Fossilized animal dung, often ground into powder and used as fertilizer.

Originally an area planted with evergreens or winter-flowering plants for winter display, they can also be large glasshouses built for public entertainment where the original purpose of displaying plants has either disappeared or been minimalised.
A building or site from which a watch can be kept to prevent the illegal import/export of goods.
A figurative representation used in divination.
A place where jockeys are accomodated.
Fine grained, brown/yellow to dark grey coloured cretaceous sandstone. It is a particularly good freestone and was often used for ashlar finishes.
The deliberate deposit of a body in the ground, usually located in a special area set aside for the purpose of burial, such as a graveyard or cemetery.
Letter A2 - No need to consult
Urban road or open space with typical activity, traffic and pedestrians. Double indexing may be appropriate with e.g. TRADE AND COMMERCE or CONSTRUCTION.
An object made of sponge used to wash or clean with.
A small explosive device, usually hand thrown.
Large submarine intended to operate with a surface fleet at sea.
A building used for meetings and other events by Scouts Associations.
A rope, clog or fetter used to limit the movement of animals through the tying of two or more feet together.
A planned programme of investigation conducted within a defined area aimed at identifying and surveying previously unrecorded sites and checking the condition of known sites.
A twin cylinder compound steam engine introduced in the 1870's which combined a horizontal and vertical configuration in the same machine.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
A tall, usually steel, structure used to receive and transmit radio telegraphy signals.
An upright member supporting a coping or handrail in a balustrade or staircase.

A stone axe in which the surface is fully covered by negative removals. Core axes may be made on flakes and have part of the flake's original surface but this cannot be part of the edge otherwise use FLAKED AXE. (Source: SARC)
A toy designed to exercise the ingenuity.

A device in which a large quantity of low pressure water is made to pump a small proportion of itself to a greater height than its source or to a higher pressure; achieved by using the pressure rise resulting from suddenly interrupting the flow
Drinks containing alcohol, an intoxicating substance found in fermented or distilled liquids.
A mill used for the sizing and drying of warp threads before they were wound onto warp beams as part of the power-weaving process.
A hospital where people would pay a subscription in order to recieve treatment when ill.
A place of worship for members of the United Methodists Church, a group formed in 1907 by the amalgamation of the United Methodist Free Church, the Methodist New Connection and the Bible Christians.
An often ornate building housing the source of an ornamental cascade, eg. Chatsworth House.
A nineteenth century plan where two or four wings of a house are constructed at an angle to the core, usually at approximately 45 degrees to the wall of the core building.
A shaped flint used in flintlocks to create the spark to fire the gun.
One of the allotropes of carbon, commonly used in pencils.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
A machine for hoisting or moving heavy weights, consisting of a spar or boom set up obliquely, with its head steadied by guys, and furnished with suitable tackle and purchases.
Metalwork attaching or attached to a harness.
Paper currency. Bank notes may be of any denomination or value and of any nationality.
A small two masted craft, with oars as well as sails.
Residue resulting from the presence of sewage. While you can have a cesspit, it contains sewage not cess.
Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.
A cemetery containing more than one burial type eg cremations and inhumations.
A non-profit making restaurant administered by a Local Food Committee which provided customers with good quality and wholesome food which could be purchased without ration coupons.
A clip for marking or holding down pages in a book.
A jar with vertical concave body walls. (Source: MPRG)
Craft used to maintain, supply or assist larger vessels whilst in harbour.
A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.
A pit alignment accompanied by a linear bank (or banks) running parallel and adjacent to the line(s) of pits.
A factory or complex of buildings where creosote oil is produced. Creosote oil is distilled from coal tar and used as a wood preservative.
A building situated within the estate of a manor or country house.
A piece of material worn over the head and or shoulders.
A building used for the daily administration of that branch of the RAF dealing with training pilots.
A portable object of stone, bone, metal or other material featuring a deliberately engraved or incised design.
A large cauldron used in the making of a preservative from the bark of spruce, fir or other conifers. The preservative was used to treat nets, sails and other fishing gear.
A nunnery of nuns belonging to the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
Use for vessels registered in Hungary.
The characteristics of a sailing vessel where her type is determined by her masts and sails.
Programmes of investigation which assess and record the condition of heritage assets.
A fertilizer derived from nitrogen; also known as nitrate of ammonia.
A garden featrue where several allees radiate from a single point (usually the house). French for 'Goose Foot'
A place where calcite is extracted using both quarrying and deeper mining techniques. Calcite/limestone is used for making glass, paper, photography, statues, building, and animal food.
A radio station set up to broadcast signals aimed at 'bending' or altering German navigation transmissions.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
A series of panels, usually of wood, combined to line a room.
An area of ground indicating the site of a horse or man-powered winding mechanism.
Ash and partially fused residues from a coal fired furnace or fire.
A road which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.
A stone which bears an inscription commemorating an event or person.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
Machinery, e.g. drive wheels, used in powering and excavating mines, i.e. mines for the extraction of minerals such as coal, lead or tin.
Includes processing and manufacturing of all forms of wood.
An area of flattened or compacted ground used for charcoal burning.
A room containing one or more thrones.
A type of GARDEN HOUSE, usually in the form of an open-fronted shelter with seat.
An area of ground on which anti tank guns can be placed for testing purposes and to practice firing at targets.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.
An ornament for the ear, usually clipped to the lobe or fastened through a hole pierced in the lobe.

Judged as irreparable or no longer seaworthy following a wrecking incident (from which the vessel may have been recovered) or a difficult voyage: a term with legal force indicating that the vessel is unfit for service.

A building which has been moved from its original site either through active human intervention or natural processes such as erosion. For structures or objects such as gravestones use MOVED STRUCTURE.

Imported Roman brooch with a wide, highly arched flat backed bow, one end rolled forward onto the head to form a hinge for the the pin. Named for the head inscription assumed to be a maker's name. Dated to first half of 1st entury AD.
A pedestal terminating in a head or bust of Hermes or some other deity.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
A vessel used to maintain supply or assist larger vessels. Use more specific term.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Carthusian order.
A building or part of a building used specifically to store items of hardware and ironmongery.
An area for the testing of rockets and guided missiles. Includes all structures associated with both the firing and testing of rockets and missiles.
The Medieval period or Middle Ages begins with the Norman invasion and ends with the dissolution of the monasteries.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
Traditional term for any fine to medium grained igneous rock, containing large crystal fragments.
A decoy site designed to simulate a burning urban area during a bombing raid in order to lure enemy bombers away from legitimate targets.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of foodstuffs.
A place where gold ore is extracted.
The unsystematic study of ground surfaces and collection of visible archaeological material.
A place where dead animals are buried.
Hard, transparent, often coloured mineral. Can be found on its own as crystals and veins but also as a major constituent of rocks such as granite. Often used decoratively.

A light timber framed building usually with brick panels which rests on a timber frame with jacking points; should ground subsidence occur the structure could be jacked to a level position. Usually found in the Cheshire Salt Field.
A grooved block placed in series, alternating with the metopes, in a Doric frieze.
A tool for holding or compressing objects together.
A level space in a garden occupied by ornamental flower beds.
A staff used for ceremonial purposes, often highly decorated.
The vertical face of a step.
Horizontal tunnel opening from the surface used for haulage or access to a mine. It can also be used for drainage.
A building specifically built to house life saving apparatus used when conditions prevented the lifeboat from deploying.

A two-piece Bow Brooch dating from the early to mid-first century AD in Britain, originating in Gaul. Featuring a wide flat reeded bow, this and the Thistle Brroch were the first to conceal the spring mechanism with a cylindrical or semi-cylindrical hood.

A large, circular, reinforced-concrete tank supported on concrete staging built to Air Ministry drawing number 1178/25 and designed to hold 30,000 gallons of water. The height of the tower varied according to local site requirements.
An official residence of a bishop used during the summer months.
A vessel used to carry essential supplies, such as food and armaments, to naval ships in order to keep them replenished whilst on patrol. Use more specific term.
A factory for the manufacture of rocket motors, both for civil and military use.
A building in which an organization or society is instituted to promote literature through lectures, study and research, etc.

Composite substance of plaster formed by gypsum, sand and lime and coloured with pigments, fixed under heat and highly polished. Used to imitate marble and popular in the 17th and 18th centuries for architectural features.

A conglomerate rock comprising well rounded flint pebbles in a very hard matrix of fine pale coloured sand, bound together by hard natural silica cement. The pebbles are usually coloured ochre or red and have black rims.
Flat bottomed vessel used for loading colliers in the north east, similar to a lighter.
A water pump situated at the side of a road or track for use by travellers and their animals.
An enclosure of stakes driven into the ground, sometimes for defensive purposes.
A timber screen, often richly decorated, placed in front of a chancel to support a rood loft.
A series of recessed, ornamental panels decorating a ceiling.
A sacred area of a building or a consecrated piece of land.
A plan of a building which consists of two or more cells where the chimney is placed on the axis of the building between two rooms and midway between the lateral walls.
Stone composed mainly of calcium carbonate, used as a building material and in the production of cement.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
Written communiques, often of a military or governmental nature, requiring fast delivery.
A street lamp in which the light is produced by the burning of coal gas. More recently natural gas has been used.
Any factory used for the manufacture of textiles.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a river where boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods and passengers.
A binder combined with various aggregates which sets and holds together into a mass which then hardens and gains strength.
A three panelled altar decoration that can be closed.
A small craft of wickerwork covered with waterproof material.
Pieces of material, usually decorated, used as standards, for signalling or for decoration. Often used as a symbol of a particular nation eg. the Union Flag of Great Britain.
An object that carries the weft in a loom without the need to be passed from hand to hand. The thread is wound into the shuttle and can be used in hand or machine looms

A mound of fire-cracked stones, normally accompanied by a trough or pit which may have been lined with wood, stone or clay. Assumed to be locations where heated stones were used to boil water primarily for cooking purposes.
A channel or pipe providing water to a canal or other body of water.
The premises of a coal merchant where coal and other kinds of solid fuel can be bought.
A device allowing a variable amount of air through in a single direction which varies the note produced.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
A joint in which one timber is reduced in thickness.

A designated area within a town or village with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to threaten the flanks of an enemy force which had broken through a stop line.
A house which has been altered to increase its defensive characteristics.
A place of worship for followers of the Methodist New Connexion, a movement founded in 1791 when Alexander Kilham led the first group to split from the Methodists.
An instrument for holding back a part of a body eg an organ.
A strip of material, leather etc used to hold two sides of an object together.
A symbol with secular signifigance, particularly implying authority.
A wall built to give shelter to sheep.

Any structural component, usually of wood, which is believed to have derived from a vessel. Double index with the appropriate type of structural component eg. BEAM or if known the original term from the MARITIME FIXTURES AND FITTINGS thesaurus.
A general term given to all horizontal timbers laid on walls or posts in order to support other timbers.
A funnel-like container from which grain or other material is fed to a grinding mechanism below.
The horizontal timber running the length of a roof and positioned at its apex.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the boundary follows an irregular curving course.
A glass-house or hot-house constructed for the cultivation of a grapevine.

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
An opening or shrine, usually containing a statue, framed by a pair of pilasters or columns supporting an entablature and pediment.
An artificial watercourse for the conveyance of water.
Horse powered ore crusher, consisting of a stone wheel running over a circular iron or stone bed.
A light weight umbrella used as a sun shade.

A significant historical association of local or national note, including links to important
local figures, may enhance the significance of a heritage asset. Blue Plaque and
similar schemes may be relevant. Social and communal interest may be regarded
as a sub-set of historic interest but has special value in local listing. As noted in the
PPG: ‘Heritage assets … can also provide meaning for communities derived from their
collective experience of a place and can symbolise wider values such as faith and
cultural identity’. It therefore relates to places perceived as a source of local identity,
distinctiveness, social interaction and coherence, contributing to the ‘collective
memory’ of a place.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
A movable bridge that swings or rotates around a central pier, or one that is pivoted only at one end, to provide a passageway for navigation.
A trough or gutter for conveying liquids such as water or molten metal. It can be cut in the surface or formed of wood or other materials.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A building providing lodgings for members of the police force.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.
Small discreet rural settlements which do not provide the commercial, legal or ecclesiastical services typically found within medieval urban areas.
A large ship's boat powered by oars and or an engine.
The point or block from which an arch or vault starts. The block generally has a horizontal base and sloped top.
A wing in a workhouse to accommodate vagrants overnight.
A light, buoyant material obtained from the cork oak. Cork is used in floats and as stoppers for bottles.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Hospitallers for administrative purposes on their estates.
A small round dish on which a drinking vessel is set.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A fortified building or site with purpose built emplacements for artillery pieces.
An Egyptian container for holding the entrails of a mummy.
The SI derived unit of luminance.
A lamp designed to be hung rather than to stand.
A form of frying pan, usually medieval.
Craft intended for recreation and not intended for any commercial use.

An archaeological field evaluation involves exploratory fieldwork to determine if significant remains are present on a site and if so to define their character, extent, quality and preservation.  Field evaluation may involve one or more techniques depending on the nature of the site and its archaeological potential.  It will normally include excavation of trial trenches.   A field evaluation report will usually be used to inform a planning decision (pre-determination evaluation) but can also be required by condition to refine a mitigation strategy after permission has been granted.
Any activities, that have a physical impact upon the archaeological resource where the purpose is not primarily archaeological research.
A vessel for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A small semi circular scraper current in the Bronze Age.
A three-storey RNAS control tower, incorporating meteorological office on the ground floor and an air watch office on the second floor.
A floating structure consisting of two walls standing on pontoon tanks, the latter of which can be flooded to receive a vessel and then pumped out until the pontoon deck and the ship are dry.
A roof constructed of horizontal tiebeams and curved trusses.
The engine housed within the fuselage of an aircraft that powers its flight.
A place of worship for Methodists, a movement founded by John Wesley. Following his death in 1791 there were many secessions.
A passage between two rooms in a house or leading from the door to the hall.
Use for large remains such as fruit, seeds, plant parts, buds etc.
An establishment used to serve ice cream to the general public.
A grave or sepulchre enlosed or covered by a memorial.
A site or building used to co-ordinate Air-Sea Rescue operations.
A sculptural or decorative representation of a human figure. Includes mythical and fantastical figures such as Cupid, Atlas etc.
Programmes of research or investigation which seek to identify the significance of a heritage asset, often to inform proposals for change
A workshop used for completing the shape of a product or part by turning on a lathe or wheel.
A building where the study and practice of preparing, preserving, compounding and dispensing drugs is performed.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers in Southern Area (Taunton Line).
A building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit in. Use more specific type where possible.
A bit for an auger to scoop out material.
A plan in which entry is directly into a room without being situated opposite a fireplace.
Characteristic waste flakes struck off in the manufacture of adzes.
An obstacle on a golf course constituting a hazard. Usually taking the form of a sand trap or dirt mound.
