A mechanical device consisting of a system of signal lights operating in sequence, placed at road intersections and pedestrian crossings to regulate traffic.
Durable wood from the cedar tree.
The forms of armour used to protect various parts of the body.
Small cargo vessel used for short coastal voyages carrying a variety of cargoes.
An unsocketed earthenware or porous concrete pipe laid end to end unjointed so as to drain the ground.
Goods, including machinery, manufactured from iron.
The corner upright bar of a polygonal sash.

Headquarters buildings on military airfields for administrative purposes housing offices, lecture rooms and in some cases a library and a meteorological office. On smaller airfields it is called Station Offices. Abbreviation SQH.

A preliminary assessment of a building or structure, often carried out as pre-application work, including an archive assessment, a general description of the structure, photographs and an annotated ground plan.
A detached external pier by which an arch or vault is prevented from spreading.
A cereal used to make spirits, beer and coarse bread.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal horns.

The rarest of the recognized types of round barrow, consisting of a flat, wide circular mound, which may be surrounded by a ditch. They occur widely across southern England with a marked concentration in East and West Sussex.
A place of burial for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers.
Term used to indicate the basic unit of accommodation in the plan of a building. It does not necessarily relate to the structural divisions within a building.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
A factory for the production of missiles
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
A container holding a set quantity used specifically for measuring grains or cereal.
An enclosure for pigs that includes a covered pen and yard.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the drainage and/or ventilation of mines.
A wooden commode containing earth, which was used to cover and absorb human waste. An alternative, and rival, to the water closet.
Shallow draft vessel used to carry ammunition.

A mill used for the production of mortar; a combination of sand, lime and water, used to make the joints between courses of bricks in buildings. In more recent times cement has replaced lime to create a quicker drying mortar.
The building attached to a cathedral or collegiate church where the dean, prebendaries or monks and canons met for the transaction of business.
A pilotless aircraft armed with explosives and fuelled to stall over its intended target.

The NPPF defines the setting of a heritage asset as ‘the surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent is not fixed and may change as the asset and it surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to appreciate that significance or may be neutral’. An assessment of the contribution made by setting towards the significance of the affected heritage asset should be undertaken as part of a Heritage Statement and used to inform planning decisions. It uses existing baseline information such as views and surrounding spaces to assess the current setting of a heritage asset and how the proposed development would affect that setting.
The wood of the evergreen coniferous tree characterized by single needle-like leaves and errect cones.

An operations room, built to drawing number 3395/40, to control the lighting arrays of the 'T' type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. It was semi-sunken for added protection and then covered in earth
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the retrieval, refining, processing and storage of petroleum oil.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.
A hard aromatic seed, obtained from the fruit of an East Indian evergreen tree and used as a spice.

A structure to which a net filled with mail bags is attached. Situated next to railway lines, it allows mail to be collected by a train without it stopping, the bag being 'caught' by the train as it passed. Can also be used to 'catch' mail.
A light anti aircraft position, usually open-walled and built of concrete, brick or sandbags used to emplace one or more machine guns mounted on pintels.
Collective name for any stone that has become impregnated with iron oxide. Index with specific stone type where given.
A room in which servants slept.
The residence of a person employed in the textile industry.
A club founded to provide education, relaxation, and recreation for working men.
Observations made by an archaeologist or architectural historian as the result of a field visit to a site or monument.
A road or street covered with small, rounded cobble stones.
An earth based plaster the mixture of which may contain clay, dung, straw, lime putty, sand or horsehair.
A house or range of buildings where domestic dogs and cats can be kept for a period.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
Lime plaster, consisting of lime and sand, is the oldest type of render. Applied externally to walls or onto laths for infill panels and usually limewashed.
A college associated with, or forming part of, a university.
The use of oxygen (O) isotope ratios in ice or ocean sediment cores to date global environmental change.
A place of burial. Use more specific type where known.
Data suitable for processing using database management software.

The common design of steam engine, where steam enters the cylinder at one end, and after it has pushed the piston to the other end, its direction of flow is reversed as the piston returns, the steam leaving  the cylinder through the exhaust ports.
A container, usually rectangular and having a removable or hinged lid.
A wing joined to the main body of the building with the roof at right angles to the main roof.
A park for the use of the public for entertainment and relaxation.
A garden surrounded by a substantial wall.
Objects used to transmit a definite message through a visual non written means, includes stamps and matrices to create these.
An arch which has a larger radius on the front face of a wall than on the back.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.
A covered shopping street, sometimes with galleries, dating from the late 18th/early 19th century.

An object which serves as a vessel. This class includes containers for which the function is either specific or unknown. Where the function is known, the term is also included within another class, eg churn.
A metal or wooden framework suspended within an opening in an external wall, fence, hedge etc, to allow ingress or egress.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
Small fragments of wood or bark.
A machine for combing the fibres of cotton, worsted, flax etc to remove short fibres, clean out extraneous matter, and lay the fibres more or less parallel to each other.
A building where artefacts, scientific specimens, antiquities and similar objects of interest could be examined through microscopes by members of the public.
Defined as exactly 0.9144 metres by the International yard and pound agreement of 1959

A glass sphere in a metal frame standing on a small pillar. A card is placed behind the sphere which focuses any sunlight, marking the card and thus indicating how many hours of sunlight there was on that day.
Purpose-built structure with thick walls used to store clay before transportation.
A small tool with a shovel blade and a pick blade set at right angles to the handle.
A steam engine working an underground cable haulage system in a late 19th century coal mine.
A fountain decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A principal rafter below a hip rafter that supports the ends of purlins under a hip.
An underground room or building with an arched roof, often used as a burial chamber. Use wider site type where known.
A simple wind-driven machine used for a variety of purposes.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the smelting of metals.
A large Mediterranean cargo or transport vessel of the 15th to 17th century, usually less than 400 tons.
A purlin that is joined to a principal rafter by a tenon joint.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
A ceramic made from clay and fired in a kiln or oven. This term has been used interchangeably with EARTHENWARE and with TERRACOTTA
The limit line of a county.
A treasury, often the bursar's room in a college or university.
A door with a planked outer face and spaced horizontal members such as battens or ledges on the inner face.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
An excavation open to the sky, caused by the extraction of coal, stone or similar. Use with product type where known.
A double-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich. Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
The residence of the head or president of a chapter, or community of religious persons.
Small fishing craft used mainly for fishing, cutter or ketch rigged.
Protective covering for personal defence, objects designed to kill, injure or overwhelm an opponent or quarry, and ancillary equipment.
People who leave their native country to settle in another, often for financial or religious reasons.

Used to record resources dating to, and associated with, the Second World War. For other types of resource not directly associated with the war, (such as houses, built during this period) use MID 20TH CENTURY.
A moulding on the neck of a column.

Used to record resources dating to, and associated with, the First World War. For other types of resources dating to, but not directly associated with, the war (such as houses, built during this period) use: Early 20th Century.
A maritime fitting for spacing rigging elements and preventing entanglement.
Bone like material which grows in a branch-like fashion on the heads of male deer and reindeers in general.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
A factory used to make packaging equipment.
A telescope which is mounted so as to allow the observation of only those objects in the sky which are passing over a local meridian, an event known as transit.
A balance engine used to replenish the water levels of a river by transferring water from a reservoir or other supply.
A law court exercising summary criminal jurisdiction, preliminary hearings and some civil jurisdiction. Formally established by name following legislation of 1949.
A barrier which rotates on an axis and is usually so arranged as to allow a person to pass through  an opening only in one direction.
Evidence of past environmental conditions, eg insect, seed, pollen remains
In use for small scale horticulture.
Refurbishment of waterways including canals and canalised river channels and associated buildings and structures.
A column at the corner of a structure.
A bowl for the washing of hands, often in a religious institution.
A sharp blade used for shaving.
A school established by a charity.
Narrow ridges representing the surviving surface traces of later prehistoric cultivation.
A structure consisting of a large plastic pipe attached to a high tower and sloping down to a swimming pool. Water flows down the inside allowing people to slide down into the pool below.
The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.
An object belonging to, used by, or related exclusively to one person and normally carried or kept privately by that person.
A vessel used in 'dry cupping' to form a vacuum over an area of skin.
A pad of cloth or fur for keeping the ears warm.
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.

A stone wall, often of considerable length, built to divide an area of land. Most occur as part of extensive walled field systems. This is a regional term specific to Dartmoor and should not be used in other parts of the country.
A structural member that supports a purlin and is also a common rafter.
A decorative clasp to fix sleeve cuffs together.
A tap inserted into a barrel to allow liquid to be drawn from it.
A farmstead where the working buildings are arranged around a yard.
Transparent, hard substance made by fusing soda-silica which solidifies from a molten state.
A settlement where previous house sites are now unoccupied, but often visible as earthworks, crop or soil marks.
A field covered with herbage for the grazing of livestock.
A sepulchral monument erected to commemorate a person or persons buried elsewhere.
A building containing a number of areas for bathing, some of which are naturally heated by thermal springs.
A vertical member standing without support.
An establishment used for the manufacture of jacquards and dobbys, which are textile loom components that control the weaving of complicated or figured patterns.
A strut which is part of a pair which support the collar and are supported by the tiebeam.
A hole or opening in a ship's hull to allow light and air to enter the vessel, or to aim a weapon through.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
A clear liquid that forms oceans, rivers etc.
A bottle for the storage and transportation of milk.
Type of survey involving the drilling of deep and narrow shafts in the ground used to describe deposits, understand stratigraphy and collect cores amples.
Metal, usually gold and silver, in the form of ingots prior to being minted into coinage.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
Listed Building Certificate of Lawfulness proposed
A friary belonging to the Franciscan order. Includes houses of both Friars Minor and Friars Observant or Capuchins.
A metal spike for fixing one object to another.
A large barn used to store the tithe (a tenth part of the annual produce of agriculture etc.) which was paid by the tenants of ecclesiastical lands.
Areas and spaces within a monument or site.
A light covering for the foot, usually worn indoors.
A muzzle loaded explosive projectile fired from a mortar. Typically they are short range and low velocity with a high arcing trajectory.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye and ear disorders and diseases.
A tunnel running under a river or through a hill along which vehicles may travel.
A building used to store coal.
Southern hemisphere (not in mean summer intertropical convergence zone); note this is prepended with the last 300 years of SHCal13
A microlith retouched to a trapezium shape. (Source: SARC)
An axehead of flint or other stone commonly used for Neolithic types.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A separate functional unit of a hospital not necessarily on the same site.
A building, structure or landscape created to commemorate a person or event.
Cylindrical, self-propelled missiles which travel underwater and explode on impact.
An educational establishment primarily for children aged 16-18 years old but can provide education for more mature students.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 18441/40.
A place where the creative arts are taught to students.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.

An aircraft designed to land on water. They can be divided into 2 types: Flying boats (designed with a hull allowing the aircraft to land directly on water) and Floatplanes (where the undercarriage was replaced by fixed floats).
A room or building where clothing and other fabrics are washed, mangled, steamed and ironed.
A building, usually associated with a hospital, where doctors live. Include blocks of self-contained flats.
A chain, band or cord, often bearing beads, pearls, jewels etc worn around the neck.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
A stall where animals are kept individually.

A type of warehouse found in naval victualling yards, used for the storage of rum, a ration of which was given on a daily basis to members of the Royal Navy, up until the 1980s, when this practice ceased.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.
A school founded by the British and Foreign Society to provide non-denominational education. Usually built and supported by voluntary contributions.
Building used for the display of inscription panels and memorials to those buried in the underlying catacomb.

A prefabricated structure of standard lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed in 1940 for use as barrack accommodation.
A building where sugar is stored.
A rectilinear ritual enclosure of Iron Age date
A grave which has been formed by cutting into the bedrock of a site.
An aircraft lost due to offensive action. Includes air-to-air and ground-to-air combat. For Vessels use GUN ACTION.
A fuel derived by dry distillation from coal.
Remains of the wood seeds of fruits such as apples, pears, grapes or citrus.
The premises of a builders merchant where building materials such as stone, cement, bricks, tiles and timber could be bought.
A tube for conveying the voice from one room or building to another.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, used to indicate the limit of an area or piece of land.
A room intended to contain a bath and often other toilet facilities.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and maintenance of railways and rolling stock.
A multihulled craft consisting of two hulls, or vakas, which are usually joined together by a frame or other structure, formed of akas. Catamarans can be sail or engine powered.
A small, industrially manufactured, air raid shelter, designed to be used inside buildings and to provide cover for nightwatchmen or firewatchers remaining on site during air raids.
A mutiple role hangar for aircraft and general storage, manufactured in the USA as a kit for on-site assembly  during WWII and post-war. It comprises a steel box frame and a canvas covering.

A short-term storage centre of goods or special parts to facilitate the rapid processing of orders and supply of goods to customers; unlike a warehouse, the emphasis is on the moving of goods rather than on a long-term storage.
A site, building or factory where geologically-derived brine is used for the production of salt.
One of a set of windows placed vertically and linked either decoratively or by aprons extending to the lintel below.
A textile-weaving factory housing powerlooms; commonly a one-storeyed shed with wide, north-light roof carried on iron columns.
A beaker with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A channel or pipeline that feeds water to a waterwheel.
An area on post-war military airfields for parking aircraft on quick reaction alert to allow immediate access to the runway. Abbreviation ORP.
Large open hearth furnace often located inside a brick cone for use in steelmaking.
A room that serves as a combined living-room, kitchen and workshop.
A weight hung on a piece of string or twine used to show the vertical.
A horizontal, moulded band, usually projecting, running across a wall, often indicating the position of a building's interior floor.
A cylinder of fur or cloth into which the hands are placed to keep warm.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a railway. Use more specific type where known

A hinged plate of brass, iron or wood inboard of a ship's scuttle or porthole which can be lowered and secured with a butterfly nut to prevent damage to glass in heavy weather or mask internal light from enemy vessels.
An object originally created to be worn on the human body or on clothing for ornamentation rather than for protection or as a body covering.
A place used to clean the fleece of sheep before shearing. This could be a watercourse temporarily dammed in order to wash sheep.
British 'M' class submarine modified to carry and launch a small sea plane.
Alloys of iron which have great strength, malleability and which are able to be tempered to different degrees of hardness. Used for the manufacturwe of tools, machinery etc.
An object which encloses a light source but allows light out through holes, glass etc.
Use with other minerals extracted and MINE where relevant, eg. ZINC MINE.

A pedestal lamp with a drip-tray below the bowl. There may be a vertical loop handle linking bowl and drip-tray. Some variants have a more enclosed bowl form with a small tubular spout projecting from the bowl. (Source: MPRG)
Microscopic animal remains. Use more specific term if known.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A plain area situated between the top of the shaft and the capital of a Renaissance Tuscan or Doric Order column.
A large tent which can be used as accommodation for parties and exhibitions.
A flexible, transparent sheet of film bearing a number of reduced images.

A shelter for doves or pigeons, often containing nesting boxes, either free-standing or built into other structures (barns, towers etc.). If a dedicated,  free-standing structure, index with MONUMENT TYPE: DOVECOTE.
Originally, a house of higher social status in a town or port, often with a storage cellar.
Use for vessels believed to come from Africa but where the precise nationality is not known.
A place of meeting and worship for followers of the Church Army, a body of trained lay evangelists devoted to evangelism and social work.

A hydrated aluminium phosphate mineral sometimes used as a semi-precious stone, and for carvings and ornamental use. Named after Variscia, the historical name of the Vogtland in Germany. Mainly green in colour.
A vessel or aircraft lost due to an accidental explosion.  Do not use for losses caused by deliberate action.
A vertical or inclined excavation giving access to an underground mine.
A decorative moulding shaped to resemble a length of cable or twisted rope.
A mould in which bullets or musket balls are cast.
A bay window, supported by corbelling, cills or brackets, projecting from an upper storey of a building.
A place where weapons are kept.
National Heritage List for England List Entry Number
A storehouse associated with rope manufacture (eg. in naval dockyards).
A narrow strip of fine material, used for trimming or tying.
The second subdivision of the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age. Characterized by the fine flake tools of the Mousterian tradition and economically by a hunter gatherer society.
The third and latest subdivision of the Iron Age.
A window either in the shape of a four leaf clover or circular with four foils enclosed.
A machine gun post designed by James Ruck constructed from hollow blocks and prefabricated concrete sheeting with loopholes allowing for a garrison of eight.
Large cargo vessel specially built and equipped for handling large quantities of ore.
Circular spoil heap surrounding a wide central depression, the entrance to a mine shaft.
Sulphates, used in medicine and to colour inks.
A plsce were herbal beers are brewed.
A room in which food is prepared.

Wooden rods or stakes which can be interlaced with twigs or branches to make walls or fences, or more commonly, to form the basis of panels in traditional timber framed buildings which are then covered with daub.
A residential home for adults with learning difficulties and/or physical disabilities.
A place of worship for Christadelphians, a fundamentalist sect founded in America in the late 1840s who rejected the trinity and awaited the second coming of Christ.
An outline of the circumstances to be addressed, with an indication of the scope of work which will be required (English term)
The rigging mast of a sailing ship erected as a monument. Used for naval displays.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
A group of, usually three, standing stones forming a square with an open side and often found with a stone circle.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
An outer garment worn on the legs.
A geophysical technique for imaging subsurface structures in cross section from electrical measurements made at the surface, or by electrodes in one or more boreholes.

A propulsion system for ships which need a maximum speed that is considerably faster than their cruise speed, particularly warships. It consists of diesel engines for cruising and gas turbines for high-speed transits.
Previously arable, usually part of Countryside Stewardship Scheme.
A container for holding water that has been blessed by a priest and is used for symbolic rituals of purification.
An outbuilding containing brewing equipment, as opposed to a large commercial BREWERY. Often found in conjunction with public houses, country houses etc.
A post box mounted on a lamp post.

A stone faced earth bank, usually with a concave batter, and with the base the same width as its height and the top half the width of the base.  Vegetation usually grows out of the top.  Found mainly in Cornwall, but also elsewhere in the Atlantic Arc.

A large type of military repair hangar mainly used on WWII bomber bases, constructed using steel stanchions and clad in corrugated iron. B 1 hangars were part of a series of prefabricated buildings intended to supplement existing hangars on bases.
A hollow moulding, often enriched, similar to a scotia or cavetto, used in Gothic jambs and cornices.
A structural member that supports a purlin. Use PRINCIPAL RAFTER where the principal is also a common rafter.
Originally a room in a house where a family would gather, usually in the evening, to sit and read, write, sew, play music etc. This term has become commonly used as an alternative to living room.
A workshop or factory unit where small or light goods are manufacture without the need for large-scale industrial machinery.
A layer of impervious material, such as lead or bitumen, usually placed between a wall and a roofline to exclude water.Impervious material to exclude water.
Walls composed of clay, earth, straw, lime and sand, mixed with water. Constructed without shutters in layers upon a stone or brick plinth and usually covered with protective limewash.
A report detailing the results of an archaeological evaluation
An item designed to be played with by children.
A cage specifically designed to hold insects.
A small hand operated rotary drill used by dentists.
A stringed instrument with a fingerboard which has frets on it.
Engagement between any combination of warship, privateer, or commercial vessel in a time of war but not itself a battle. Such skirmishes may precede or follow naval battles.
A string of beads used to aid the memory in reciting a set of devotions.
Shaped material used for covering buildings, usually as a roofing material though can be used on walls or floors. Often of fired clay they can be of other materials particularly stone.
Fish which has been preserved by drying.
Sites used for the manufacture of chemicals used as the basis for complex chemical processes or products.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier consists of several straight or near straight sections.
A building or room used for the storage of pottery moulds.
A building, within a gas works, housing a gas purifier.
Written copy of recorded interviews collected to illustrate history from personal experiences.
A metal counter used in calculation of financial sums but not itself directly exchangeable for coins, goods or services.
A picture or pattern produced by either by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours or by painting directly onto a wall.
A vault or crypt under a church or chapel. Use wider site type where known.
A house consisting of a public hall with private living accommodation attached. Built from the medieval period onwards.
A subsidiary tower or projection attached to the front of a keep containing access to its first floor entrance.
A pipe designed to act as a drain or within a drain.
A large container or reservoir for liquids or gases.
An office which administers the affairs of the church.
A stone/cobble/boulder with worn/smooth wear traces left by grinding/polishing axes/adzes.
Traditional roof covering consisting of materials such as reed, straw or heather layered and fastened together onto roof to form a run off to prevent water penetration.
A place where cars and other road vehicles may be parked and left.
A post set up, to which offenders were tied to be whipped.

Dark and dense hardwood timber which may be sourced from various species of true ebony from southern Asia and Africa, but the name may also be given to dark hardwoods from elsewhere, e.g. the Americas.

A communication system in which cylindrical containers are propelled through a network of tubes either by compressed air or partial vacuum. They are used for transporting solid objects, as opposed to conventional pipelines, which transport fluids.

A place of worship for Wesleyan Methodists. This was the original Methodist church from which the other denominations seceded. In 1932 they joined the United Methodists and the Primitive Methodists to form the Methodist church.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
A building which houses the administrative functions of a local authority.
A workshop used for the decoration of fired pottery or ceramics. Usually part of a larger complex.
A building equipped with instruments and a flight simulator used to teach members of bomber crews how to correctly identify targets for bombing.
An area of land which has been drained or cleared for habitation and/or cultivation.

An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to co-ordinate information collected by the outstations for relaying to headquarters.
A series of long, raised ridges separated by ditches used to prepare the ground for arable cultivation. This was a technique, characteristic of the medieval period.
Intervention into the archaeological resource intended to gather information about past ecologies and economies, formation processes, and to retrieve material for scientific dating purposes.
Artificial mound of earth, turf and/or stone, normally constructed to contain or conceal burials. Use specific type where known.
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.
A strut with a reflecting counterpart that forms the letter A on either side of a king post.
A garden where yew and other coniferous trees are grown.
A long vertical pillar usually of stone used as a structural support in buildings often artistically sculpted or shaped.
A hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to send information to the control station for relaying to headquarters.

A system of fortifications constructed along a national frontier to contain the local population, as well as keep out undesirable raiders eg. Offa's Dyke. Use with more specific monument type where known.

A prefabricated structure consisting of trough shaped asbestos sheets bolted together to form a seven sided building in section with end walls of rendered brick. Manufactured from 1942 by the Universal Asbestos Company for use as airfield accommodation.
A dish with straight or convex sides that turn inwards, forming an acute basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A structure extending into the sea for the purpose of preventing further movement of washed up sand and shingle.

A jug form which usually has a short, narrow neck and rim and an applied spout. The spout is usually tubular and free standing, or attached to the rim/neck, rising from just above the high shoulder or girth. (Source: MPRG)
Spice from the bark of an East Indian tree
Northern hemisphere mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal13
A bridge on which dwellings or commercial premises have been built.

A type of military aircraft hangar of the Cold War, hardened and therefore protected against the effects of nuclear weapons. It comprises a semi-circular structure built of corrugated-steel supporting a reinforced-concrete skin. Three NATO designs.
An adjustable, horizontal beam, supporting the vertical stone spindle in a water or windmill, which allows the gap between the grinding stones to be varied.
A small bag or pouch for carrying money, especially coins.
A stone screen, usually found in a monastic or collegiate church, that separates the choir from the nave.
Systematically positioned hole, or holes, utilised in all studies that aim to sample the nature of the topsoil and subsurface deposits.
A plug for closing the neck of a container.
Visual and descriptive record of a building, usually interior and exterior. Equivalent to Historic England Level 2.
A capital warship, often steam driven, heavily armoured with armament of large calibre guns deployed in turrets.
Stone used as a building material which has been finished, or dressed, before use.
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
A metal bar to strengthen the heel and or sole of a piece of footwear.
Bomb series based on growth season
A timber frame placed in the bell chamber of a church tower or belfry designed to hold the bells.
The arrangement of straps used to control an animal and/or to attach the animal to a vehicle.
An ancilliary building, usually to provide gas for lighting a particular building (eg. railway stations, factories, etc) as opposed to public GAS WORKS.
A carved, convex block, often richly decorated, at the intersections of vault-ribs, beam-junctions or terminations of mouldings.
A protective covering to a drain.
The most common form of joint between two timbers meeting at right angles or at an oblique angle, the mortice being a socket cut in one timber to receive the tenon projection of the other.

Hemispherical mound surrounded by a ditch (or occasionally two or more concentric ditches), often accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank. Mound and ditch may sometimes be separated by a berm. Use specific type where known.
A room in which a judge sits to hear cases and undertake other official proceedings which are not of a sufficient importance to be brought into court.
Specialist hospital treating patients with physical disabilities.
Loose fibres obtained by unpicking old ropes. Mainly used to caulk seams in wooden vessels.
A manor or estate owned and run by an order of knights and governed by a preceptor.
A piece of machinery for lifting stone, or containers loaded with stone, from a quarry.
A flake or blade with retouch along one or more edges.
Lantern slide developed using a wet process.
Works for the extrusion of aluminium and for creating aluminium products.
Waste matter, usually liquid in form, consisting of the contents of sewers and cesspits.
A truss in which two pairs of arch braces form a continuous curve from the wall-heads or below to meet  in the centre of the collar.
A tool for splitting and chopping.
Fine cotton fabric of a delicate weave.
Use for the remains of any part of a bird.
A covered area of ground attached to a building.
A hearth constructed specifically for the manufacture of pitch.
A structure providing protection against the weather at tram stops.
Excludes terms specific to MARINE CONSTRUCTION SITE.
A metallic element often used in alloys and historically used in pottery and glass-making, paints, enamelling, and in cosmetics and medicine. Often derived from its sulphite ore, stibnite.
Buildings designed for the accommodation of large numbers of people, rather than single families, etc.
A building, room or area, often within or attached to a church or other building, serving as a place of  worship. Where a monument, use the Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A large free-standing arch erected to commemorate a triumph or victory.
Oared sailing vessel developed in the 15th century, the larger English version with secondary oars coming into use in the 16th century. Not to be confused with GALEAS.
A buttress that is set slightly away from a corner. Usually one of a pair.
A box or cupboard enclosing the fuses for the electrical circuits within a building.
A prepared area, traditionally grass, where tennis is played.
A burial ground for followers of the Jewish faith.

A concrete structure, based on drawing number (11008/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was considered less vulnerable than the (3329/41).
One of several stones used to raise a farm building, such as a granary, above the ground surface.

A sailmaker's thimble used in the sewing of canvas, consisting of a flat thimble in a canvas or leather strip with a thumb hole. The whole is worn across the palm of the hand, which gives it its name.
Loss due to action of self propelled submerged missile.

The upper parts of walls carried on arcades or colonnades in the nave, choir or transepts of a church or hall, rising higher than the lean-to roofs of the aisles and pierced with windows to allow light to penetrate.
The hair from the coat of goats and sheep, made into yarn and used in the manufacture of woollen cloth.
Crystalline allotropic form of carbon used in pencils, as a lubricant etc.
A building containing a number of single roomed cells used for detaining prisoners.
An iron bar or rod running through the core of a windmill's windshaft that causes the opening and shutting of the vanes on patent sails.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War. The U Boat carried 12 mines but was otherwise unarmed with no deck gun or torpedo tubes.
A house used to accommodate camels, often found at a zoo or wildlife park.
A hospital where elderly people receive medical treatment, but not overnight accommodation.
An area of land used for camping. Often includes facilities for washing, catering and entertainment.
An axe designed and weighted to be thrown.
A temporary fence of boards, often enclosing a building on which posters and bills are attached.
A classroom constructed from prefabricated sections.
A structure or building, often within a secluded area of a garden, where people could go for quiet reflection.
A metal or stone plate or tablet, usually inscribed, set into a wall, pedestal, floor etc., often serving as a memorial.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a railway yard or sidings and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
A building used for public Christian worship. Use more specific type where known.
A tool used to produce designs in plaster on the outside of buildings.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.
An area within a large fireplace where it is possible to sit.
Large piston used to operate lifting bridges, lock gates, etc.
A covering of metal, stone or pottery set on a chimney breast above a fire to prevent smoke entering the room and instead directing it up the chimney.
A place in which brewing and sometimes baking took place.
Component. Use wider site type where known.
A magnetic metal found abundantly in certain ores and widely used for the manufacture of tools, machinery etc. Iron is also a chief component of  steel.
Fourth Rate Ship Of The Line
A semi-automatic loom developed  in Lancashire. Although it is self-acting, it has to be stopped to recharge empty shuttles.
A beam the end of which is fixed beyond the upright it passes through.
A mixture of coals that have been formed into briquettes or blocks. This fuel took its name from the fact that it was under patent in the late nineteenth century.
Use for vessels registered in Turkey or the Ottoman Empire.
A three masted fully rigged warship armed with 24 to 38 guns on a single gundeck.
A railway used for the conveyance of coal and other minerals.
A frame set with teeth used to drag over ploughed fields to break down the earth clods etc.
A whole male figure used in place of a column to support an entablature.
A garden, often geometrical in layout, or area for the cultivation of roses.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.
An area of hardstanding on which ammunition is stored.
Large wooden hammer beams pounding cloth in a fulling solution.
Hard, unglazed, brown, versatile earthenware which can be used as a tile or moulded into statuary.
A monastery governed by a prior or prioress. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, FRIARY, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A cairn erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
A piece of strengthened material worn projecting over the forehead and eyes to provide shade for the eyes.
A building plan in the shape of a cross.
The second subdivision of the Iron Age.
Traditionally a place where meat and fish were sold.
Machines for automatically feeding fuel onto the fire of steam boilers and other furnace plant, introduced at the beginning of the 19th century.
A room in a school devoted to the formal instruction of pupils.
A burial ground for followers of the Islamic faith.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes.

A row of houses linked at first floor level by an open continuous gallery which runs through the front of the buildings. Access to the gallery was gained by flights of steps. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A bridle joint which is invisible from all sides of the timber.
A metal disc before it is stamped to become a coin.
A small metal bar for the cleaning of dirty footwear before entering a house, etc.
A stone used to cover a grave.
A building housing filters for sewage. Usually associated with a sewage pumping station.
An animal skin prepared as a writing or painting surface.
A purpose built indoor cricket facility for training and playing matches
A cantilevered block projecting from the face of a wall and supporting a structure such as a parapet, beam or arch.

Lightweight building block traditionally made with coke breeze from gas works combined with sand and cement. Use this term generally to denote a light, modern concrete building block with man made characteristics.
A small, defensive settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling and ancillary buildings, surrounded by a palisade.
A moulding that projects from a wall above an exterior opening and is shaped to channel rainwater away from it.
A house of friars of the order of St Dominic. Also known as Friars Preachers or 'Black Friars'.
A mixed house of Augustinian nuns, canonesses and canons.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the enactment and enforcement of public law.
A site which has produced evidence of in situ production of items derived from antler.
A garden designed to provide living material for the study of botany and horticulture.
Grinding mill for producing dyes and pigments from natural materials.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
A brace extending from a vertical to a higher horizontal timber.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
A very high chimney, though more often a chimney stack containing only one flue.
Letter D3 - Condition historic building recording
A map generally produced manually to indicate main features of an area quickly, for example to assist location of a particular place.
A trench in the form of a flattened 'W' with a flat concrete roof covered in turf, supported on concrete pillars. The name derives from the resemblance to a child's drawing of a seagull in flight.
A hospital department concerned with the reconstruction or repair of parts of the human body using transferred tissue, either in the treatment of injury or for cosmetic reasons.
A chamber built into a wall in a defensive structure.
Objects denoting membership and/or authority. Including objects associated with ceremonial rites or symbolising secular power.
A hospital for convalescents or consumptives.
A building used as headquarters by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A crude shelter for persons engaged in the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
A wheel rotated by the treading of persons or animals to power machinery to raise water, etc.
Full Shielded Self Propelled Mounting System
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote science through lectures, research, etc.
A group of cairns in close proximity which are predominantly funerary or ritual in nature.
A fence that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.
The round seeds of the plant Pisum sativum which grow in pods and are eaten as a vegetable.
A blank for a knife that has not been hammered out.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a single handle
A site occupied by people who have no legal right to the land or buildings on it.
Shelter on military airfield to provide night time accommodation for airmen during WWII.
An instrument in the form of a pair of pincers used to grip and pull objects, usually used in surgery.
Metal hoops used to hold the staves of barrels in position.
A place where soup and food is available to the homeless.

A northern term for water reservoirs at steam powered industrial sites that are part of the steam raising plant and are used for recirculating condenser cooling water. The lodge had to be large enough to supply the condenser with cool water for a day.
Use for recording the names of vessels or sites that have since been identified correctly.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
A projection which can be used to lift or suspend an object, often used as a handle.
A position or place that allows a wide or favourable overall view of a scene or situation.
The part of the bridle that fits around the horses head.
Internal combustion engine powered by diesel fuel.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of the explosive bellite.
Hair taken from animals and used in a variety of manufacturing processes.
A small vessel used to carry supplies and personnel to lighthouses.
A site, including hangars, moorings and ancillary buildings, used for the storage, maintenance, take off and landing of airships.
Cubicles for housing rams, resembling pigsties with their own yard but slightly larger.
A subsurface detection method performed by striking the ground with a heavy wooden mallet or a lead-filled container on a long handle.
A small works used for the production of agricultural tools such as hay rakes.
A stone used to crush objects.
A bridge with two or more decks allowing it to carry various modes of transport at the same time.
An area in a town where traffic is prohibited, often containing shops.
A mound or structure on which an archery, musketry or artillery target is erected. Use specific type where known.
A form of entrance closed by a gate.
A pen, often circular and stone-walled, for rounding up livestock.

The investigation of heritage assets along thematic lines, usually to inform the production of a thematic study. Such studies bring specialist insights to bear on the particular area of study, but may not address other aspects of the site's significance.
A roof made up of common and principal rafters.
A building where threads of different qualities and colours are mixed together.
An ore, such as stibnite, containing a high proportion of antimony.
Wool, textile, or synthetic floor covering material.
An estate or manor of a subordinate community of the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem. Includes the mother house, the Priory of St. John, Clerkenwell.
Armour designed to protect the chest, sometimes permanently attached to a backplate.

The measurement of a surface, either in elevation or plan, determined from measurements derived from two or more photographic images taken from different positions; this allows three dimensional viewing of the surface to be mapped.
An area of ground on which a house is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a house.
A tool for perforating or stamping, used in conjunction with a hammer.
Gold fashioned into coins for use as currency.
A car park on the roof of a building.
The weight attached to a spindle used for handspinning.
An odourless, tasteless powder obtained from cereals and potatoes, used for stiffening fabric.
A classical order in which the columns or pilasters are applied to a wall.
A place where architectural ornaments such as stone vases and urns are manufactured.
A strung object used to produce sound usually from a string instrument eg a violin bow.

Aircraft as cargo carried whole or crated ready for assembly on arrival at the destination port. Do not use where the vessel is an aircraft carrier and the aircraft is carried as part of the vessel's armament.

Collective term for the Burlington (Silurian period) and Borrowdale (Ordovician period) groups of slates from the Lake District and parts of Cumbria, Lancashire. Hard, fine grained metamorphic rock, varying in colour from green/olive to black/blue black.
An establishment in which prostitution is practiced.
An abbey or priory of Carthusian monks.
Natural inorganic substance possessing a definite chemical composition in a crystalline form. See MINERAL Class Listnfor narrow terms.
A chain used to inhibit a slave's freedom.
Persons captured in land or naval engagements either being transported to prison out of their native country, sent for exchange, or being returned home.
A strong vehicle with four wheels for carrying loads, usually horse or ox drawn.
A report detailing the results of a field survey. Usually restricted to a survey of a small or specific area or site.
A place where goods and merchandise are temporarily stored before being transported to or from somewhere by road.
A barge fitted with a large tank in its hull for carried liquid cargoes.
A bag containing food hung around a horse's head.
A site used for the production and/or working of glass.
A facility for the kitting out and induction of recruits before being sent on for training.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.

A post-excavation assessment often follows the completion of any archaeological fieldwork and comprises a formal review phase, where results are assessed according to their significance and potential to further understanding of the historic environment. As part of this assessment phase the work needed to complete any further study or analysis and how it will be disseminated is identified.
A place where boats are built and stored.
Conglomerate consisting of rounded flint pebbles held together in a natural silica and sand cement.
An air raid shelter, designed to be placed in the garden. Made from prefabricated components, they were often semi-sunken and the structure then covered with soil for added protection.
Equipment used to scrape and smooth objects.
An establishment used for the custody of money received from, or on behalf, of its customers.
A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
A vessel which has been deliberately scuttled using explosive charges.
A hammerstone but with broad groove worked around much or all of centre to enable fixing to a handle; usually associated with mining/metalworking.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
A college where the applied sciences and the mechanical arts are taught.
A light, ornamental building or structure built to incorporate, or in association with, a mineral spring.
A machine for mechanically separating the grain from the straw and husks.
An enclosed observation tower, usually made of brick or concrete and raised on four legs, associated with WW2 bombing ranges.
A lead seal marking newly woven cloth which served as a quality control method in medieval and post medieval periods.
Bay-leaf shaped decorative ornamentation, usually adorning mouldings or friezes, often depicted in a garland arrangement.
An establishment from which food is distributed to the public during wartime or similar states of emergency.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
A truss with paired vertical posts set on the tie-beam and supporting collar purlins or plates.
A hydraulic engine patented in 1830 comprising a large specially shaped cast-iron outer casing enclosing a close-fitting but separate solid globe.
A printer's workshop in the newspaper/publishing industries.
The powdery residue left after the combustion of substances, especially wood and paper.
A building, or group of buildings, deliberately designed for rhinos.
A fortified Roman site, usually under 1 hectare in area, strategically situated, housing small military patrols, often defended by a rampart, one or two ditches and a gate.
A ring, flange or short piece of pipe, made of iron, clay or other materials, used to join and seal two sections of water pipe.
A drawn representation of an archaeological 'find' or other cultural object.
A way, path or road through a cutting.
Airborne survey to discover, record and monitor archaeological sites and other heritage assets. Sites will usually be recorded by aerial photography.
Metal used primarily for roofing and ornamental purposes, being lighter and stronger than lead.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of rugby.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34. It became the standard design for watch offices with a large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
A piece of armour designed to protect the arm or a part of the arm.
Fortified wine produced on the island of Madeira.
A projecting part of a building that overhangs the wall below it.
An object made to hurl a spear further and faster than possible by hand.
A pillbox which has been modified from a standard Directorate of Fortifications and Works design. Double index with specific type where known.
A dwelling, located at the entrance, or gates, to an estate or park, etc.
Armour used to protect a horse.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A screen separating the choir from other parts of the church.
An open market where cloth and other textiles can be traded.
A small square or lozenge-shaped pane of glass as used in a leaded light.
Fairground attraction designed to create optical illusions to give a sense of unbalance and unease.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of crucibles.
A group of buildings where consumer goods, such as small machines and electrical components, are manufactured.
The upper part of the classical entablature. Also a moulded projection crowning a door, wall, window etc.
A crane which is driven by a petrol or diesel engine and travels on either crawler tracks or rubber tyres.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for bears, including shelter. For bear baiting enclosures use BEAR PIT.
A mechanical device, used in a corn mill, that sieves and grades flour or meal and separates oversized particles.
A room in a monastery from which alms were distributed; or the residence of an almoner.
A stone grooved on one face thought to have been used to straighten and smooth arrow shafts.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
Animal skin that has been hardened or treated by a tanning process.
Miner's term for fine grained, often light grey/fawn coloured porphyritic rocks. Commonly found in Devon and Cornwall.
The collection of information relating to the location, distribution and organisation of past humna activities involving field or site-based investigation of a certain geographic area.
A hut used for the accommodation of members of the armed forces.
A flat band carrying a motto.
An abbey or priory of Dominican nuns.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by sleds.
Clothing worn specifically for formalised dancing.
A container used as a lavatory by bedridden people.
A room, within a building or institution, equipped for conducting scientific experiments or research.
An intrusive feature cut for the purpose of containing a cremation burial within it.
A circular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the form of cylinders usually 2 feet across x 2 feet 6 inches or 3 feet high. Cylinders were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
Designating or pertaining to hard, brittle substances produced by strong heating of clay.
Use for vessels registered in Slovakia. See also Czechoslovakian (for vessels registered between 1918-1992)
A place where boats are stored.
A place of worship for the believers of spiritualism: The belief that the spirits of the dead can somehow manifest themselves and speak with the living.
A structure used for the transmission and interception of radio signals. Usually composed of a number of different elements such as aerials, receiving equipment and supporting pylons.
A building constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
A bell worn by an animal, eg sheep, goats, cows and hawks, to inform the owner of the animal's position.
A precious metal characterised by its yellow colour and resistance to tarnishing.
A building or workshop where fine furniture, often veneered, is made.
A pipe in which a substance is smoked.
A type of windlass for drawing up ore.
A building or series of rooms specially designed for the recording and transmission of live or taped television programmes.
Cut human hair, usually intended for wig-making.
An object which supports or is attached to a blind.
A bowl adapted by the addition of one or more handles. The handles may be vertical or horizontal loops, or straight, or may comprise vertical or horizontal lugs. (Source: MPRG)
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
A heating apparatus in which coals or embers are placed in the pedestal or base below a container in which food or liquid could be held and kept warm.
An object used in the preparation of a body following death. It was used to plug the orifices of the body.
A temporary, usually roofed, wooden structure placed on the ramparts or walls of a castle to improve the defenders field of fire along the length of a wall.
The fruit of certain varieties of the plant Capsicum Annum eaten as vegetables.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used as accommodation for the armed forces and, during WWII, as emergency housing for bombed out civilians. Also used for storage.
A plant community which includes low shrubs e.g. heathers, bilberry, gorse also the presence of bracken.
Smoke generators (also known as smoke pots) were used to create a smoke screen to provide defensive cover for strategic targets
A platform, usually in concrete, on which radar equipment was mounted to assist the targetting of artillery guns. The platform is often the only evidence surviving in the landscape.
A high pole, painted with spiral stripes of different colours and decked with flowers, erected on an open space, often the village green, for merrymakers to dance around on May Day.
A photographic frame of developed black and white film from which a positive print can be produced.
A building or buildings used for the production of whistles.

A type of goose pen with stone-clad compartments, built into the base of a Cornish hedge near the periphery of a farmstead. Aspect is often towards entrance track or driveway since geese were used in similar role to guard dogs. Particular to Cornwall.
A pit or emplacement surrounding a concrete pedestal, or 'thimble', which was used to mount a spigot mortar. Deployed by the Home Guard during WWII as an anti invasion measure.
A gauge for measuring the volume of water flowing from a river to machinery using the water for motive power??
An alloy, principally of copper or tin, but which may also include zinc and/or lead.
A framework, often made of steel,  supporting a crane or similar structure, or for supporting a platform or stage.

An acoustic method which involves the creation of a shock wave through the ground. By recording the time interval between the initial shock and the reflected or refracted shock waves it is possible to define subsurface deposits.
A covering for the arm, usually attached to or part of another garment.
A slope, usually with rails, along which a vehicle can be moved between two relatively flat stretches of railway, or by which a boat can be transferred from one level of waterway to another.
A container with a perforated bottom through which material is shaken or poured.
A works used for the production of copperas, a green iron sulphate which is used as a fixative in the dyeing process.
An entablature of the Tuscan Order consisting of a plain architrave, frieze and cornice without decoration or enrichments..
A small spherical bell for fastening onto the leg of a hawk.
A specific type of early medieval pin. Do not use in instances where a pin has become detached from the brooch.
A narrow timber board or moulding lining the base of an interior wall as a finish between it and and the floor.
A long much indented leaf usually curled over at the tip which is a standard form of foliage in classical decoration.
Sheets of iron or steel coated with tin.
A flake or blade tool with more than one notch on its edge.
A container, usually square or rectangular, used in metal processing for separating metals one from another, usually silver from gold.
A pool of water and associated ancillary buildings designed to accommodate sea lions.
Landing craft designed for carrying military vehicles and used for beach landings and as a ferry.
A head cover which can be attached to a piece of outerwear, eg a coat, or can be separate.

6 Type DFW 55373s placed in a 3X2 rectangular plan. Each projector was separated by 31-34m. Hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each projector, but ammunition stored outside the perimeter.
Use only for the historic region of North America. For modern places use NORTH CAROLINA or SOUTH CAROLINA.
Road or paving material combining crushed stone, rolled and mixed with bitumen type mixer.
Diesel engined submarine designed for long ocean voyages in search of enemy shipping.
A receptacle used as a home for bees, traditionally made of thick straw work in the shape of a dome,but sometimes made of wood.
An instrument for gauging the amount of rain which has fallen over a stated period.
A machine, usually contained in a building called a flour mill which reduces grain into constituent parts or �streams�  which include flour. For a Flour Mill buliding use FLOUR MILL in Monument Type.
A large division of a building which lies across, and at right angles to, its main axis, such as the arms either side of the crossing in a cruciform church.
A building in which textile rags are sorted according to fibre types.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A rotating circular platform operated by machinery to turn a steam locomotive around.
The hard material, consisting mainly of calcium compounds, which makes up the skeleton of vertebrates. Used for ornaments or ground for use in the manufacture of bone china.
A building on a railway system housing levers used to regulate trains on the tracks using signals and to change the points to enable a train to transfer from one track to another.
Heavy caterpillar tractors fitted with broad blades to the front for moving or levelling earth and obstacles.
A building used to manufacture Producer Gas. Producer Gas is a mix of gases formed by passing compressed air through hot coke.
Grassland fertilized by allowing floodwater to cover it in winter.

A prefabricated structure consisting of sectional timber framed units that were bolted together. The structure was clad with weatherboarding and had a felted roof. They were used as temporary accommodation on airfields. Also see 'Type A'
Seeds of any of the various related plants of the leguminous plant Vicia faba.
A building used as a headquarters and reporting centre for an Army, Navy or Air Force Group.
Flat-bottomed barge with shallow draft adapted for carrying bulk cargoes among the shoals of the Thames Estuary; usually spritsail-rigged, though other rigs were permissible.
Any vehicle for transportation on land.
A garden designed in the style of the elaborate gardens of the Renaissance, eg. formal, geometrical layouts of lawn and paths, stone steps, balustrades and statuary and fountains.
An enclosed compartment within a building intended for a purpose other than as a thoroughfare.
A pen for holding sheep waiting to be washed.
A sailing vessel defined by a combination of such factors as hull design, locality and rig.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of meat.
A steel framed transportable hangar similar in construction to Type T2 but about half the size. Designed in 1941 and 1942.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
Thin round flexible disc with magnetic surfaces for storing and retrieving data. [AAT]
A three-dimensional decorative ornamentation composed of a series of Vs forming a zigzag.
A passageway or lane between buildings.
An ornamental foliation in panels or tracery so called because it is arranged around five intervals, known as foils or cusps, that describe the outlines of five leaves or petals.
Paper, often decorated with a printed pattern, painted or embossed design, and usually provided in rolls and used to line the interior walls of a building for decorative purposes.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
Three-dimensional artwork usually created out of stone, e.g. marble; metal, e.g. bronze; ceramics, e.g. terracotta, or other suitable materials.
A point where water issues naturally from the rock or soil onto the ground or into a body of surface water.
A frame shaped to fit around the neck and shoulders of a person for carrying buckets. Usually made of wood.
A building used for the care of the sick. Only to be used where part of a complex, eg. a workhouse. In such cases use with appropriate monument type.
The hull of a dismantled ship used as a prison.
Remains of the animal group characterized by having jointed limbs and segmented bodies, including woodlice, spiders, insects etc. Note, crustaceans have been included in this category.
Buoyant, light material obtained from the cork tree.
Loss of a vessel due to running aground and subsequently refloating before final loss.
A small stem powered warship with its hull protected by iron plates. Used to bombard targets onshore, especially in the Crimean War.
A container used for holding or serving food, especially an open shallow container.
A wall connecting two pavilions, bastions, towers etc..
A mole or pier-like structure situated at the entrance of a harbour, or running out into a lake or the sea, usually used for the landing of craft.
A platform, sometimes floating, for the landing of passengers and goods from vessels.
A cultivated plantation of watercress, usually situated near springs or small running streams.
Full access to interior and exterior of buildings or structures.
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
A hollow or rectangular block which acts as a flue allowing the passage of gases or heat.
An accounts office, especially within an industrial or commercial complex.
Container with arched handle used for carrying liquids, foodstuffs etc.
Two masted vessel with a square rig on both masts.

A mill which ground clinker in the cement production process. During cement production a mixture of lime and clay is burnt which forms a clinker which is then ground into powder. When mixed with water it solidifies to hard cement.
A cairn featuring a mound of small diameter (normally less than 6m), which is surrounded by a kerb of stones which are considerably taller than the mound.
A small opening built into a stone wall or hedge to allow small animals through.
A site where millstones have been cut to shape and/or fabricated from smaller pieces of stone.
Saxon rectangular burial chamber comprising a large sunken 'room' lined with wood. 6th and 7th century AD.
A pattern used to create a consistent shape for an object, often hollow and reusable.
A staircase normally used by servants and tradesmen.
A gaming piece for the Viking game of Hnefatafl.
Ornamental band or chain worn around the arm or wrist.
Place where ships and boats are dismantled.
Garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of the deceased are scattered or buried.
A stationary hoisting machine consisting of a rotating drum around which a cable, rope or chain is attached.
Powder mixed with water and applied as a paste for binding stones and bricks or for forming floors, walls etc.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.

A musket fired by use of a flintlock. A gunflint is held in the lock which on pulling the trigger pushes back the pan cover creating sparks which set off the powder in the pan causing a flame to go through and set off the charge in the barrel.
An area of common grassland in a village used for grazing cattle, recreational purposes, etc.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.
A large strong case or box used to contain objects for storage or transport.
A rudimentary roofed building found in school playgrounds, open at the side. Used as a shelter from bad weather.
A capital of the Tuscan Order featuring a square abacus.
A piece of wood scored across with notches for the items of an account and then split into halves of which each party kept one.
A site equipped for passive or active defence against an airborne enemy assault.
A substantial house in a town or the country (particularly associated with medieval London). Use more specific monument types where known.
A building used for services by a nonconformist protestant sect, especially by Quakers and Presbyterians.
An obsolete vessel used as a weapons target.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
A column joined to another by a band or ring.

A flask holding gunpowder used to prime a firearm, ie to provide a small quantity of gunpowder to be put in the pan which would be lit to set off  the main charge in the barrel. The powder would often be a finer grade than that used for the charge.
Remains of the endocarp (stone) of a member of the genus Prunus which includes sloes, plums, cherries, apricots and peaches.
Small ocean going vessel fitted with loading doors in the bow. Used for ferrying tanks or other fighting vehicles to beach landings.

Historic building recording is an investigation to establish the character, history, dating, form and development of a historic building or structure which normally takes place as a condition of planning permission before any alteration or demolition takes place. The outcome will be an archive and a report which may be published.

A patented manmade rock invented by James Pulham and Son of Broxbourne. Pulhamite was used to join natural rocks together or crafted to simulate natural stone features. It is an artificial form of sandstone.
An area of several rooms in a medieval house or building. Probably for domestic use.
A multi-purpose commercial building, used primarily as a trading place for merchants, but also incorporating shops, public offices, guildhalls, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of screws.
A sharp pointed nail with a large flat head.
A gun emplacment which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55503
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
An outdoor trail that has keep fit equipment with supporting information plaques intermittently positioned along its route
A fragment of the body of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
Workshop for placing handles on mugs, teapots, etc.
A flag or object depicting a symbolic representation carried as part of a religious ceremony.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the Air Ministry. Usually found on or near airfields.
A shallow artificial pond, usually found on the coast, in which sea water is allowed to evaporate leaving behind the salt.
Use for vessels registered in Georgia.
An area of shallow linear cuts made by the removal of turf for fuel or building material.
A building or structure where electricity is generated.
A shaped stone, which could be hand held, used in combination with a saddle quern to grind or rub grain.
A machine for spinning cotton yarn.
A wheel, usually steam driven, used for raising water by means of buckets attached to its circumference.
A horizontal tunnel dug specifically for draining, for example, a mine.
Hard, durable, dark grey stone, the purest native form of silica, which can either be used decoratively or as a main material. Predominantly found in East Anglia and the South East.
The space in which a door is placed, allowing passage through.
A soft, marshy garden, often peat-based where water- and peat-loving plants are grown.
A swimmin pool restricted to the use of men only.
A town laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
Structure used for viewing deer hunt.
A pond storing water to supply a HAMMER POND.

A vault composed of concave cones, inverted and overlaid with ribs that rise from the springing of the vault and diverge equally in different directions, producing an effect like the ribs of an opened fan.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of steam power.
A school that is directly funded by central government (specifically, the Department for Education) and independent of direct control by local government in England.
A building where pins are manufactured.
A granular, crystalline, hard rock often used as a building material.

Monument visible as a mark in standing crops or parchmarks, but where no subsurface deposits have been proven eg by excavation or other ground disturbance, in which case SUB SURFACE DEPOSIT should be used.
Name given to a vessel of the East India Company. Usually large, well built and magnificently decorated.
A device to limit the amount of liquid coming from a pipe or hole.
Fish of the family Clupeidae, common to the North Atlantic. They are caught for food.
A scaled drawing based on measurements taken from life.
A wayside inn for livestock traders.
A darkened room or workshop used by photographers to process prints from glass plates or photographic film.
A vessel consisting of three small pots joined, often on a hollow ring, at the base.
The SI derived unit for the refractive index.
Field or area of ground where washed new cloth is stretched out to dry.
A ship of the line mounting between 64 and 80 guns typically built with two gun decks.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
A tower in a semaphore communication system. Often a three-storey building on a hill in line-of-sight, signal towers provided working and living space, usually for two crewmen with their families.
A former ground surface buried beneath an earthwork or other sequence of deposits. (includes palaeosoils, turf lines)
A quarry for the extraction of Serpentine, a major metamorphic mineral which is easily polished and easily carved. A major variety, lizardite, is found in Cornwall.
Defined as species introduced after the last glaciation, e.g. sycamore, sweet chestnut, etc. Specify in Description whether currently managed, neglected, unmanaged or management not determined.
Cargoes transported in sacks or bags, usually wheat, corn, flour, fruit, or coal. To be used only where the cargo is said to be "sacks" or "bags" of goods. Use specific term where known.
A duct or channel for hot air to travel through.

A stand by set house similar to 13244/41 and designed to drawing number 16302/41 and comprising of 4 rooms; a fuel storage room, a transformer chamber, a switchgear chamber and the main engine room with 3 diesel engines.
