A vessel, usually made of stone, which contains the consecrated water for baptism. Use a broader monument type if possible.
An administrative building used by the official in charge of a dock or harbour.
A camp used to accommodate members of the Womens Land Army who undertook essential agricultural work during the Second World War.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.

A vessel composed of three or more equally spaced lobes and usually, a waisted or pedestal base. The handles are vertical loops, generally of strap form. There may be two opposed handles, or one per lobe junction. (Source: MPRG)
An external structure used to sit on.
A piece of fabric with a design, used as an emblem for military or naval purposes, signalling, decoration, display, propaganda etc.
A small warship built to operate close to the shore or in river estuaries. Used for shore bombardment and patrol duties.
A garden created within woodland where imported species such as camellias, magnolias and rhododendrons are grown.
An ornamental green stone of the mineral nephrite.
A long outer garment reaching the ankles.

An enclosed structure, usually glass fronted, designed to contain, and facilitate the viewing of, objects or notices. May be built into the fabric of a room, affixed to an exterior or exterior wall or free standing.
A part of a building or structure that is an element of the construction.
The third and last subdivision of the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age; characterized by the development of projectile points made from bony materials and the development of fine blade flint tools.
A small projection designed to allow space for a bed.
A place where hats are made and sold.
A hard, igneous rock formed from the cooling of molten volcanic magma.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
A building occupied by the corps responsible for police and disciplinary duties in the armed forces.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of skin diseases.
Blocks of cast iron as it appears when first removed from the smelting furnace.
Mud, which has often been dredged from the beds of rivers.
A hospital block from where patients are discharged after an operation or other treatment.

The site of a deserted settlement in cases where there is evidence that it has deliberately been relocated in a single planned action, eg. to remove a settlement from an enclosed park, or to create a model community, as opposed to gradual abandonment.
The hall before a great hall.
A joint in which one timber is applied to the surface of the other.

A facility where natural gas is made smaller in volume, to facilitate its distribution through the National Transmission System. Term can also be used for a station, which recompresses the gas to the required pressure.
A free-standing building or a room used as a storage place for valuable objects.
A wing of a house used specifically for the storage of household materials and victuals.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
A round or polygonal building containing a wheel turned by an ox to provide power.

Any one of the cargo vessels of that name belonging to the different Baltic nations, in use from the mid 18th to the early 20th century. Usually ketch-rigged. Not to be confused with the oared GALEASS.
Manufacture and use of wood side products, ie. unprocessed wood rather than processed timber.
A float or pontoon supporting a flexible steel roadway as part of a Mulberry Harbour.
A roadblock, usually manned by the Home Guard, where the credentials of civilians and military personnel where checked before allowing them to proceed.

A late 17th - early 18th century house with a central chimney and fireplaces and a central door on the front; this door opened closely against the fireplaces, leaving a small lobby for access to the rooms.
An establishment where tea and other non-alcoholic refreshments and light meals are served.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of fistular and rectal disorders and diseases.
Fine grained, yellow/buff to grey/black coloured sedimentary rock.

A boat specifically designed for saving lives at sea, they can be either: a boat carried on a larger vessel for use in emergency evacuation of crew and passengers in the event of shipwreck or a boat built for the purpose of shore-to-sea rescue missions.
The subsoil traces of prehistoric cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of an ard to till the soil.
A metal safe built in to wall
An ancilliary workshop used for repairs, etc.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of three 10ft and two 12ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 10825/42.
A structure providing accommodation for poultry.

A floating pier, comprised of a floating pierhead (SPUD) and a roadway resting on pontoons (BEETLES). The pierhead and roadway were capable of rising and falling with the tide enabling unloading of troops and equipment to occur at any state of the tide.
An object used to fill up a hole.
A structure, often built undergound, used for defence and co-ordination of military activity.
A mark erected on or near danger or on shore as an aid to pilotage.
The SI derived unit of speed or velocity
Set of three seats for the clergy found in the chancel
A large structure, usually associated with power stations, in which hot water undergoes a process of cooling before being re-used .
A church attached to or founded by a college.
Hard, unglazed, brown, versatile earthenware which can be used as a tile or moulded into statuary. Used in a structural or semi-structural context as a moulded hollow block.
A dredger which can act as its own hopper and can thus transport the mud which it picks up to dump it at the desired place.
A large building or structure where coal is washed, sized and graded before being sold.
A small hut, dwelling or cave, usually in a secluded spot, in which a hermit lived. Hermits chose to live solitary lives often due to religious motives.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.
An ornamental decoration which projects from the surface it is part of.
A quarry for the extraction of Soapstone (also known as steatite or soaprock), a metamorphic rock largely composed of the mineral talc and rich in magnesium.
A large wooden structure built alongside the water's edge where ships may lie for unloading.

A hexagonal pillbox with an interanl anti-ricochet wall. The rear wall was lengthened to take two rifle loopholes in addition to the five light machine gun. Both 15in and 42in thick walls are common. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A horizontal member supporting the posts in a timber framed structure.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often part of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
A shallow tray or dish used for baking food.

A pit in which lye is used to clean hides/bones/etc. generally as part of the tanning process to remove excess fat, flesh, hair, etc. from the raw hide.  The residue from these pits formed a crude soap which could be used for various cleaning purposes.

A slender, cylindrical object. Use specific types of rod where possible. Where it is a rod of material which is part of a production process, eg a glass rod, use rod and enter the material in an object material field.
A dining hall, usually in a monastery or college.
A vault, often located under a chancel or chancel aisle, containing an altar and usually used for burial.
A site associated with the extraction, from the ground, of sand and gravel. Use more specific type where known.
Demasted old ship used as a floating prison.
A protected parachute store built with permanent brick cavity walls and a roof of reinforced concrete slabs in two heights separated by lantern lights.
Preceptory Of The Knights Of St Lazarus
Soft items used to make a bed ready to be slept upon.
Sites associated with the manufacture and engineering of vehicles.
A building, factory or works which was engaged in the manufacture of refining saltpetre. Often part of a gunpowder works.
A stone, usually found in a schoolyard, either built into a wall or forming part of a free standing structure, on which pencils can be sharpened. Although increasingly rare examples do survive.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.
A small timber fixed to a wall to support items such as cladding. Also a strip of timber fixed across two or more parallel boards to join them together or conceal their join.
A type of Red Wine from Bordeaux in France.
Reformatory established under the Inebriates Acts 1879-1900 for repeat alcohol related offenders
A tool used to twist fibres together to create yarn.
Houses specifically of monks, canons or religious men but not friars.
Solid masonry placed to counteract the lateral thrust of a vault or arch.
An object that has been cut off.

Reason	

The planning authority wishes to secure physical preservation of the site's archaeological interest in accordance with the NPPF.  

Condition	

No development shall take place until details of the final foundation design have been submitted by the applicant and approved in writing by the planning authority.  The development shall only take place in accordance with the approved details.
A path, or marked lane, designated for use by cyclists.
A small piece of metal or other material used to hold objects together.
A library which lends books (and sometimes other materials) to its members.
A sweet fluid substance, the nectar of flowers, gathered and worked up for food by insects such as bees.
A ship of the line mounting 100 guns or more on three gundecks.
The face within a pediment, as enclosed by the cornices, or the solid infill of an arch above an impost, sometimes embellished with sculptural or relief ornament.
People who have been convicted of criminal offences. Traditionally criminals, even those convicted of petty offences, were transported from Europe to penal colonies in the Americas and Australia.
The rotating top section of a tower or smock mill.
A piece of stone, usually shaped, of uncertain origin or use.
A space usually in front of a church entrance but can include the space surrounding a church.
A relatively small and heavily built vessel equipped with large engines. Used for towing ships at sea or manouevring them in tight spaces.
A place in which the artillery is encamped or collected together.
A type of coal preparation plant for the sizing, sorting and washing of coal.
The standard RFC power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 476/18 and comprising an engine room with a small workshop and driver's room.
The SI derived unit of volume.
An arch consisting of a segment of a circle connected to other segments with smaller radii.
A door, gate, doorway or gateway of grand or elaborate construction. Use specific type where possible.
A communal sleeping room in medieval houses for male servants.
A room in which food, usually meat, is kept.
Citrus fruit of a distinctive orange colour.
A room for detention and imprisonment within a prison.
A diagonally set modillion placed at a cornice's external corner.
A small yard attached to the rear of a house or other building.
A grass, used in paper making, native to Spain and North Africa.
Used for the island of Jamaica which gained independence from Britain in 1958.
A system of petrol burners, pipework and pump houses on an airfield used to 'burn' away fog so that aircraft may take off and land safely.
A vessel with a type of rigging where the main driving sails are fixed to yards which lie square to the mast.
Buildings, sites or structures used for the manufacture of linen and/or flax.
Ore containing a high proportion of sulphur.
A decorative feature in the form of small pyramids in a continuous line.
A road, sometimes raised as a causeway, which serves as an approach road to a building or bridge.
Cargo vessel specially constructed to carry bulk items such as grain. Does not include liquid cargoes.
A wheel with a series of teeth on its outside which interlock with similar teeth on another cogwheel to receive or give motion.
A building housing an engine, usually with an attendant boiler house and chimney. Used for winding from a pit.
A component of a salt works housing iron pans where the brine was evaporated above a furnace and flue. Such houses were lightly built in order to allow the heat and steam to escape.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
A market consisting of stalls erected in the street and selling a variety of goods.
A portable beehive, often made of straw.
From 1822, any vessel in the service of HM Coastguard, principally deployed on Customs and Revenue duties, i.e. anti-smuggling operations. Superseded the Preventive Service Vessel.
An open balcony or gallery extending along the outside of a building, providing principal rooms with shade by means of a roof or canopy supported by posts or light columns.
A jug with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body, a pronounced inward-sloping shoulder and a marked neck/body angle. (Source: MPRG)
An instrument in which strings are vibrated by an internal wheel cranked by a handle.
A box used for storage or shipping.
Oil derived from palms, used for a variety of purposes.
A structure consecrated for devotional purposes.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.
A container, usually glass, used for storing medicinal substances.
An hydraulically powered machine that tips coal into railway wagons, usually situated at a pithead.
Use for vessels believed to come from Asia but where the precise nationality is not known.
A short squat gun or cannon used to test the strength of coarser blasting powders. Mainly 18th-19th centuries.
A vault whose bay is divided by diagonal and transverse ribs into six compartments or cells.
Fine to coarse grained, cream to green/grey coloured oolitic limestone. Quarried since Roman times, it is one of Britain's best building stones, hence its use throughout the country.
A site used for the manufacture of gunpowder.
A structure consisting of a large, metal framework holding a skyward facing dish. Used for transmitting and receiving signals which are relayed by satellite.
A bag or case stuffed or padded, designed to be slept on.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A circular ornament worn on the head.
Deposits formed by the mass downward movement of surface deposits over underlying frozen ground under periglacial conditions.
A collection of objects deliberately grouped together and hidden.
A glass-like compound first made in ancient Egypt. It involves coating a core material of powdered quartz with a vitreous alkaline glaze. Also the name given to a tin-glazed earthenware.
A plan of a structure which has eight sides.
A building plan where space is unconstrained by partitions.
A subsidiary form of preceptory provided with a chapel. Use specific type where known.
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, followed by boiling of the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE

A subrectangular earthen enclosure defined by a ditch, usually with an internal bank, assumed to have been used for the primary exposure or burial of human remains in the Neolithic period prior to secondary burial elsewhere.
Equipment used on or with water craft.
A wall-mounted moulding defining the upper edge of the dado, intended to protect the wall's surface from damage caused by chairs being pushed against it.
A grand staircase where the lower flight splits into two upper flights.
A jug with a body profile resembling two cones joined together at their widest points, producing a distinct carination. (Source: MPRG)
Medium grained, intrusive, black or dark green coloured, igneous rock.
A public recreational complex centred around an open-air swimming pool. Use SWIMMING POOL as a component of LIDO.
A capital at the corner of a colonade or portico in the Ionic Order in which the volutes are splayed outwards at 45 degrees.
A joint consisting of a projecting tongue fitting into an open housing in a scarf joint or the apex of a rafter.
An ornamental chain, worn around the ankle.

A six oared rowing boat which originated in Cornwall in the 18th century. Originally used as a pilot vessel, useage adapted to include cargo vessel and lifeboat. Today gigs are used in sporting events.
A communal room or building attached to flats.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an H-shaped plan, commonly with cattle housing to two or more cattle yards.
A house built using experimental building techniques and materials.
A yellowish, tarnish-resistant precious metal used to make jewellery and coins.
A farmstead where the buildings and yards are loosely arranged, with no focal yard. Use more specific type where known.
Equine mammal used primarily as a beast of burden.
A spiked, iron plate fixed to a boot for climbing on ice.
A building used in the Second World War to co-ordinate action against enemy air raids.
A manufacturing complex where the hides of animals are turned into leather, consisting of buildings for fleecing and drying, as well as treatment pits.
A canopy suspended, or on pillars, over a throne or altar.
Mark 1 or the first production variation of an aircraft.
A timber, horse-powered device consisting of a large, rotating drum around which a rope would be wound, hoisting material from a quarry pit, mine shaft etc..
A site where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.
A precious metal of lustrous white colour with great malleability and ductility.
A three dimensional representation of an object, person or animal.
A group of buildings, or part of a works, housing apparatus used in the process of distilling.
The residence of a well keeper.
A dam which can be raised or lowered to regulate the flow of water.
Northern hemisphere mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal04
A core part of a town or city that has or had a particular set of characteristics; for example an area of high status residences or an area where a particular industry/trade was centred.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
A horizontal timber that joins the collars of a series of roof trusses.
A shallow, usually circular, dish on which food is served or eaten from.
The residence of a marsh keeper.
A vertical timber set on a collar or tie-beam extending to the apex of a pitched roof.
A tube for the transport of liquids and gases eg for drainage purposes.
A pendant in the shape of a cross.
An object of Bronze Age date, usually of gold, with an unknown function.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
A vessel for the storage and transport of wine.
A base of the Roman Doric order with a torus, an astragal and a fillet.
Limestone formed during the Jurassic period. Provides many widely used building stones.
Prefabricated small building that is designed and built to be movable rather than permanently located.
A site, including buildings and hardstandings, used for the storage and distribution of ammunition.
Planting of a substantial number of trees e.g. as a commercial crop. For small scale planting use: planting scheme.
The term scrub includes invasive woodland characterised by the presence of birch, willow, alder, ash, sycamore, conifers as low trees, with shrubs.
A building or site used as a storage and distribution centre.
Generally understood to mean aircraft whose normal loaded weight is less than 2750kg (6060 lb).
Use more specific term where known.

Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.
A small island, especially within a river.
An inclined wooden trough which channels grain evenly from the feed hopper into the eye of the stones in a corn mill.
A sedimantary rock composed of fine grained clay particles. Flaky mudstone is called shale.
World War II naval support vessel usually converted from a mercantile or other warship type and used for the distillation of water by both the Royal Navy and the American Navy.
Maritime monument identified as a ferrous object lying on the sea bed detected using marine surveying equipment that detects localised anomalies in the Earth's magnetic field.
A piece of furniture with one or more doors concealing storage space.
An open space or covered building in which cattle, goods, etc, are displayed for sale.
A building or site for the manufacture of livestock fodder.
A living thing that is not an animal. Use for unspecified plants only. Use a more specific type where known.
A general term for the weatherproof coat on the external walls of a building.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
Containers identified by the form they take rather than by function.
Solid bars made from pure zinc.
A spoil heap consisting mainly of slag, pieces of refuse material separated from a metal during the smelting process.
A flat surface supported by legs used for many purposes.
A hanging frame with branches which act as candle holders or to which lights are attached.
A room for washing and cleaning linen.
A sailing frigate mounting 32 to 44 guns with the main battery on a single deck.
A decorative piece descending vertically from the bottom of a newel on a staircase, or from the junction of barge boards  at the apex of a gable.
Part of an instrument that is used to modify or limit the sound of a note.
Fairground attraction containing a number of ghoulish displays designed to scare visitors.
A vessel used for carrying mines between warships and supply depots.
A window with three openings, the central light being arched and wider than those flanking it.
A large pillbox-like structure, often L-shaped or angular, with numerous loopholes used as a defensive position.

A piece of metal or wood, or other material used in the manufacture of an item, intended for further fabrication and therefore representing an unfinished object. Usually relates to objects manufactured in quantity such as coins, knives etc.

An educational institution, introduced in the 1960s. Distinguished from universities by traditionally training technicians in business, industry and commerce for an immediate local area, and offering more part-time classes, etc.
A construction trench dug to receive a line of posts for a wall, with associated packing.
Tile nailed externally to a wall and usually laid in mortar designed to present a brick-like appearance.
A crane powered by a treadwheel and used for lifting and lowering, dating from the Roman period. Also used in later periods to assist on building sites, at mines and in ports.
An instrument for measuring the angular distance of objects, and particularly used for navigation by noting the position of the stars.
Holders for one or more candles, usually of metal or pewter.
A small, double-handled bowl with horizontal loop handles decorated with a cockerel motif. (Source: MPRG)
A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
Information encoded in a defined structure (for example, lists, tables, and databases), intended to be useful for direct machine processing. [DC] For manual data use index, gazetteer etc.
A purpose-built trench used to test chemical warfare weapons.

Monument whose existence is inferred from the traces of architectural features. Eg include shadow marks on building walls or beams, pillars, floors incorporated into a later structure, suggesting the existence of an earlier building.
A beam that is part of a frame in a wall.
A window where the sash is hung vertically and the window opens outwards or inwards.
A fortified site in which a gun, mortar or cannon is positioned.
City and port on the Mediterranean coast.
A gulley in the form of a circle for holding vertical posts in the walls of iron age round houses.
A longitudinal timber set on top of a timber frame, brick or masonry wall on which roof-trusses or rafters rest.
Change in land use that might have archaeological implications.
A knife designed to be used for pruning plants.

A power source deriving its energy from solid fuel, which is used to boil water in an almost closed vessel, producing steam which moves one or more pistons in tight fitting cylinders, the energy being transmitted by a piston rod to a diversity of devices
A report on the archaeology of an area, based primarily on existing records and resources.
A curfew with straight sides flaring outwards from the top. (Source: MPRG)
A brush or perforated ball on a handle used to sprinkle holy water.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, used for the storage of military vehicles.
A school run by a Christian church.
A boat fashioned out of a section of tree trunk.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
A fortified wall surrounding a town or city.
A box to contain the dowry which is a gift or endowment given to or on behalf of the wife.
A small building built over the end of a water conduit or spring.
An instrument where vibrating air is confined by a tube. Use narrower terms where known.
Thin flexible sheets made from the pulp of wood or other fibrous matter.
A large building, situated at a railway terminus, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from a railway.
Construction blocks manufactured using clay which is then fired or sun dried.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of charcoal.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.
A concave glass dish used to hold material for observation or experimentation; so named for its resemblance to the disc covering the face of a watch.
The oil rich seed of the plant Bracchus napus.

A core used to produce flakes from a single plain platform. The base of the core, or 'keel', is often formed by alternate removal from a process resembling cresting. Often one end has a relatively unmodified section. (Source: SARC)
A hollow instrument containing material that produces sound when shaken.
Measurements or factual information which may occur in a manual catalogue system or database.
A pit or enclosed area used for cockfighting.
A building or wing of a large house in which the servants would live and carry out some of their duties.
Use for the construction style of the armour, eg plate armour.
An underwater technique that records bathymetric (depth) data by generating point depths in a line directly beneath the transducer mounted on a vessel as it progresses along the acquisition line.
Use for coastal cliffs; for inland features use OTHER 9.
A wide mouthed container, usually cylindrical without handles.
A workshop or factory where the barrels of cannon are cast.
A high status Iron Age grave in which a two or four wheeled vehicle accompanies a frequently richly furnished inhumation burial. A barrow may overlie the grave.
An independent school for children up to the age of 11 or 13 in which pupils are prepared for entry into a public school.
A building or compound housing a permanent establishment of members of a religious organization to do missionary work.

A loom developed by Joseph Jacquard in 1801 which used a series of punched cards to control the movement of the warp threads thereby allowing complex patterns to be created without the intervention of the weaver

A mineral crystal of thin, tough fibres which can be woven. Used for high temperature insulation or as reinforcement in asbestos cement building board and corrugated roofing. If used to imitate slate, use artificial slate also.
Steel in the form of rails eg. for use in the construction of railways.
An isolation hospital for infectious diseases and leprosy, sometimes known as a Pest House; commonly situated on the edge of a town.
Use for craft powered by an engine which provides propulsion by expelling reaction mass, such as jet and rocket engines.
The junction of two timbers at right angles, with chamfers or mouldings meeting on a diagonal line, where one timber is cut to fit around the chamfer or moulding of the other timber.
A mechanical device, used in a corn mill, that separates bran from meal to produce a whiter flour.
A building housing an economizer, a machine designed to preheat water for boilers.
A tomb with a raised canopy over it.
A marked path along which aircraft taxi to or from a parking area, runway, etc.
A dish adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A stone, terracotta, wooden or metal receptacle used to grow flowers in.
A vertical piece of wood fixed on corners of walls to help the fixing of plaster and to protect against damage to the plaster.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two linked ranges to create an L-shape. They can comprise a barn and an attached shelter shed to a cattle yard or an interlinked cattle housing and fodder range.
A small room or building containing a lavatory and, in more recent times, washing facilities.
Survey using photographic or other recording equipment mounted on or used from either an aircraft or other airborne vehicle or a maritime vessel/submersible craft.
A one or two storey reinforced concrete structure, usually associated with two T shaped radio masts. Term is specific to army anti-aircraft control centres operational between 1950-55.
A structure used to dry turf on. Turves were used as a fuel and as a roofing material.

The period once referred to as the Old Stone Age. It is defined by the practice of hunting and gathering and the use of chipped flint tools. This period is usually divided up into the Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic.

A large, movable barrier, usually an iron or wooden grating with pointed bars along its bottom edge, with its sides set in vertical grooves above a castle's gateway enabling it to be dropped to bar entry.
A long barrelled firearm. The barrel is spirally grooved on the interior, which gives the bullet a spinning motion leading to greater accuracy over a longer range.
A pillar, rod, pin, or plate of a sundial, showing time by its shadow.
A cross connected to a reliquary or containing a relic itself.

The side compartment of a building, usually a church, hall or barn, separated from the main body of the building by an arcade; or a passage allowing access to rows of seats in an auditorium or church.
A small, single storey building used as the Pilots' room on fighter stations and as the watch office on bomber stations.
A place of meeting and worship for Exclusive Brethren, an exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
Hard, coarse grained, calcareous sandstone, coloured by iron oxide. Quarried in the Guildford and Godalming area of the South East.
A building, site or container used to store the bones of the dead after they have been removed from graves to allow new burials.
A watchtower used to guard prisons, camps or other facilities.
A tool used to impart heat in order to fuse two or more metal surfaces together.
Inshore craft used for carrying troops and military equipment used either for beach landings or as a ferry. Use specific type where known.
A building, or part of a building, used to house doves and pigeons, usually placed at a height above the ground, with openings and provision inside for roosting and breeding.
An item that cannot be identified. Use more specific term, if possible.
A workshop for combining flax or hemp as a preparatory stage of rope making.

An establishment originally providing terminals to allow the public to access the internet, usually for a fee. They originally provided snacks and drinks to customers although now this is not always the case.
A part of a musical instrument played by the feet.
A shop selling ironmonger's goods, household tools and utensils.
Site or building constructed or adapted for indoor and/or outdoor leisure and sport activities, for example archery, team-building and "outward-bound" activities based on military training.
A long tapered flexible pole used with a fishing line and usually with a fishing reel.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A coastal site producing salt by dissolving rocksalt or other impure salt in seawater, then boiling the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
The cured flesh of a pig.
Lightweight, strong metal with good corrosive resistance, normally used as an alloy.
A Mark 6B aircraft which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A wall containing apertures to allow a weapon to be fired through it.
A form of whip or lash, often used for self mortification.
A pair of cannon balls joined by a solid bar.
The first standardized design for a building for the duty pilot. It took the form of a small bungalow with a bay window on the front elevation.
A building containing a range of processes for cleaning and processing metallic ores.
A tall, hollow pipe, usually cast-iron, resembling a lamp-post. Used to ventilate sewer systems.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
Pertaining to or deriving from a living organism. See ANIMAL Class list for narrow terms.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A military storage aircraft hangar designed in 1937. It has a curved profile and is constructed from steel ribs supporting a concrete skin. The roof is covered with earth and turf.
A mill used for the processing of tin ore by crazing, stamping or smelting.
Deliberate collision with another vessel in order to inflict damage.
A decorative moulding featuring a repeating star-like motif carved in relief.
Thin, rectangular tiles, usually made of wood, used for roofing.
A rod to lift the odd numbered warp threads to enable the weft to be passed through.
Glass to control or reduce the effects of the sun, includes both reflective and absorpative types of glass.
An enclosure where the boundary consists of a line of discrete pits, as opposed to a continuous ditch. Use with a term that describes the shape of the monument.
An underground cell, or group of cells, used for imprisonment.
Dress designed to be worn for theatrical purposes.
A window which has its head beam decorated with elements of tracery.
A band of material worn around the neck, waist or shoulder.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with tramway transport.
A hut 51ft long by 20ft wide used to dry, store and pack parachutes.Similar in design to the 2355/25, but constructed in timber instead of brick.
A ditch constructed to surround a town for defensive purposes.
A room where letters and parcels are sorted prior to dispatch
A model village built in association with a factory, mill, railway, or any other industrial complex; usually built by the employer.
Use for the remains of an egg whether from a bird, reptile or amphibian.
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.
A cord manufactured by twisting strands of material, such as flax, cotton, nylon etc., together to form a strong line.
A planned, self-contained, community incorporating green open spaces and containing housing, industrial and agricultural zones.
A crane used for moving coal during the refuelling of coal-powered vessels or locomotives.

An airfield building housing a turret gunnery trainer used to teach air gunners how to report the correct position of enemy aircraft by practising shooting against projected moving images of enemy aircraft displayed on a target screen (WWII).
A flat surface often with drawers used for working upon.

Remains of animals characterized as having bodies made up of annular segments, such as worms and leeches. Earthworm eggs and granule comonly occur. Bristle worms are found associated with marine molluscs.
A hand held tool for marking or graving.
A hand held device for mashing food, usually with a flat holed base attached to a handle.

A waterwheel where the incoming supply of water is introduced at the top of the wheel and drops onto the paddles, or buckets, of the wheel which rotates in the reverse direction to that of the incoming flow.
A building used to accommodate hippopotami.
A building or structure from which observation is kept of the approach of danger.
A hydraulic machine used to magnify the stroke of a hydraulic piston. The pulleys and chains of a crane or other device are attached to the jigger.
One or more ropes or straps attached to an animal's head to provide guidance and control.

A stone core with a conical form and a core platform which may or may not be prepared. Blades are removed around the circumference of the platform. The end of the core opposite the platform usually tapers to a point. (Source: SARC)
A ship used for treating patients or moving them between a battle zone and a safe area.
Photographic transparency on an acetate base material.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine designed to Air Ministry drawing number 12563/40.
The entrance to a building, apartment or any enclosure consisting of a movable barrier, usually lockable, of wood or other materials.
A garden where woodland and meadow flowers grow in an apparently natural way.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the extraction, processing & manufacture of finished goods. Includes structures associated with the supply, storage &/or transmission of power.
A Prehistoric monument type in South West England in which a natural boulder is surrounded by a man-made kerb of stones.
An iron rod with both ends sharpened and turned down, used for holding timbers together.
A site specializing in the manufacture of parts for the Aerospace industry.
The Middle Stone Age, falling between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic; marks the beginning of a move from a hunter gatherer society towards food producing society.
A sign used by the Air Raid Precautions network to assist in identifying vital equipment and resources in the event of an air raid or to aid movement during blackouts.
A specimen of material to represent the whole from which the sample was taken.
Scaffolding erected on a beach and in the surf so as to prevent hostile forces from landing.
A prepared piece of ground on which the game of Petanque is played.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A revolving stone used to sharpen or polish by grinding.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A mill manufacturing bobbins for the textile industry.
A bar fixed across a frame at an angle to stiffen it.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
An object designed to bring bad luck, divine wrath, disease etc upon the bearer or target of the curse.
A building, in a garden, park or open space, either housing a fountain or the machinery which powers one.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A specially prepared track used for fast motorcycle racing.
A tall, polygonal structure with ornamental roofs at each storey which is associated with Buddhist temples; the style was adapted for secular eyecatchers and pavilions in the 18th century in England.
Use for vessels registered in Estonia.
A building in which wool or cotton were beaten to clean and separate the fibres.
Manmade marks or earthworks which provide evidence for agricultural cultivation.
Current recorded information does not give the evidence for a monument, or the information is regarded as unreliable.
Building or structure housing a form of ore crushing device associated with tin mines.
A fine grained earth which becomes more plastic when water is added and can be moulded and dried to make bricks, tile, pottery, etc.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.
A small single storey structure with just one room containing a pyrotechnic cupboard and built of rendered brick with a flat reinforced concrete roof
The post at the centre of a winding staircase from which the steps radiate; or the post, supporting the handrail and string, at the angle of a square staircase.
A leather strap for sharpening a razor.
A military storage aircraft hangar built  in the late 1930s. It comprises a semicircular concrete structure with reinforced concrete columns, featuring a curved roof and straight walls.
A deep, rectangular or oval, straight-sided vessel with an everted, crenellated rim, used to hold either wax for dipping candles or molten sulphur for dipping matches. (Source: MPRG)
A tank found on hop farms in which creosote was held, heated from below by a fire with a chimney. The ends of hop poles were dipped in the tar to prevent rotting in soil.
Two buttresses which meet at a right angle at the corner of the structure they are supporting.
A building equipped with facilities for bathing, and occasionally public baths.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of less than 90 degrees.

Soil marks and other features of natural origin, including periglacial frost wedging, solifluction deposits, abandoned water courses, etc, recorded to avoid future confusion with features of human origin.
A device, usually wooden, or fabric on a timber frame, designed to catch, and be driven by, the wind in order to power a windmill. For maritime uses see the Thesaurus of Maritime Archaeology.
A piece of cloth worn around the loins.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
An open yard or place where timber is stacked or stored.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
A spike for separating the strands of a rope.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
A woven fabric used to trim clothes.

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of ammonal explosives.
A site or factory where waste slag from ironworking if further processed for use in manufacturing.
Used for measuring distances at sea. Until the adoption of the international definition of 1852 metres in 1970, the British nautical (Admiralty) mile was defined as 6080 feet.
A curfew with a rounded profile merging into a rounded top, with no discernible angle. (Source: MPRG)
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
A house for storing or drying saddles.
A place used for the milking of cows.
A room where organizations and associations meet for the undertaking of presentations and consultation.
A wooden or metal object used to provide a rhythm by striking another object.
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna
A structure, building or site housing equipment for transmitting radio or television signals.
A pontoon element of a Mulberry Harbour that sits between the Spud Pontoons that allow oit to rise and fall with the tide.
A small light vessel with a schooner rig often used for fishing.

Class of elements and alloys that are characteristically lustrous,ductile, fusible and malleable. These are extracted from ore minerals originally existing in nature and processed before becoming a recognisable metal. See METAL Class List for narrow terms
A free school for poor children.
A steam powered winding gear used at a colliery or other mine.
Even grained, poorly fossiliferous, light brown/cream coloured, oolitic limestone. Quarried in the Bath area.
A site where copper or copper based alloys are produced by smelting copper ore.
A tool used to impart an image, impression or mark onto a surface.
A tablet with a handle fitted to the back of it.
A place where appropriate acts, rites and ceremonies are performed to honour or revere a supernatural being, power or holy entity. Use specific type where known.
An often stately and ornate entrance to a canal tunnel.
A road or pathway raised above surrounding low, wet or uneven ground.
A layer of remains left by a single culture, from which the culture can be dated or identified.

Simple organisms, mostly single celled, that move by means of two flagella (complex cellular projections). Most live as marine plankton, but some occur in fresh water. Members of the Kingdom Protista.
Manmade constructions used to prevent water flooding the surrounding area. Often taking the form of a bank or wall but may be more elaborate e.g. the Thames Barrier.
Deposits formed as the result of the action of ice masses during glacial periods.
A bridge whose deck is directly supported from pylons by straight cables without vertical suspenders.
Use for vessels registered in Scotland.
A hinged, sliding or rolling door placed over a window's exterior or interior.
Food, usually hay or straw, kept for the feeding of animals.
An instrument made by inserting a stick through a membrane stretched over a hollow vessel then played by rubbing the stick.
Use for the function that the armour is intended for, eg parades, field use, decorative etc.
Any brooch with the pin sprung or hinged at one end and the catchplate at the other end of a curved or flat bow. Can be one or two piece construction.
Use for the remains of any part of a plant.
The opening at the base of a chimney stack.
A tertiary vault rib, usually employed for decorative purposes, that links one intersection of the main ribs to another.
A building or group of buildings containing equipment capable of transmitting and receiving radio signals. Use BROADCASTING RADIO STATION for broadcasting establishments e.g. BBC Radio stations.
A ship designed specifically for the carriage of liquid cargoes, particularly oil.

A factory or group of buildings engaged in the manufacture of acetone. A variety of processes may be used to manufacture acetone including the use of destructive distallation of wood and fermentation technology.
Deliberate interment of a complete, or substantially complete, animal. Use the object type thesaurus term ANIMAL REMAINS where skeleton is fragmentary.
German city spanning the river Rhine.
A barge with a lugsail rig commonly found on the River Thames in the late 19th century. Also a general term applied to the family of Deal luggers.
A building which has been altered to increase its defensive characteristics. Use more specific term where known.
A large structure, found at sports stadiums, from where television or radio broadcasts are made of the sporting events.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
A tower used to store grain in.
Rammed earth or clay of a low moisture content used to make floors or walls, or found between shuttering.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
An enclosed chair for carrying a person, usually carried by two people.
A room set aside for the purpose of reading, such as in a library or a club.
A loft for the storage of hay.
A mill used to process raw timber.

Geologically sandstone consists of particles of quartz naturally cemented together by either silica, calcium or iron. It is this geological composition that accounts for the varying colours and grain sizes found in the many building sandstones.
A small dye works, often associated with a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
Glass fragments collected for re-melting. This includes not only worked fragments, but pieces broken from blowing irons and pontils, (moyles). All periods from the Roman onwards.
A small brick structure attached to a house for keeping fish prior to cooking.
A decorative moulding in the form of a chain.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A usually shallow cut linear feature often used for drainage.
A seat of state, often highly decorative, used by monarchs, bishops, etc.
A waterwheel where the inflow of water strikes the paddles or floatboards well below the axis of the wheel, ie. the water more or less passes under it.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached to both ends forming an H shape.
Canvas or similar fabric used for the manufacture of sails.
Articles, particularly drinking vessels, manufactured from glass.
Machinery for lifting pieces of stone or loaded trucks out of a quarry.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of military personnel and/or their families.
A simple, flat or nearly flat lid. In ceramic forms, often made by rolling out clay rather than by throwing on a wheel. (Source: MPRG)
A collection of dwelling-houses and other buildings, usually larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town with a simpler organisation and administration than the latter.
A building or settlement enclosure with a thick drystone wall, generally circular or oval in plan, usually sited in an elevated position.
One of only three 'true' British marbles, pale green and white in colour.
Large, moulded, unburnt blocks of clay type soil laid in a similar way to brick, but bedded in lime and clay 'mortar'. The walls produced are characteristically thinner than those of cob and pise.
Old ship with a hull stripped to the water line and used as a platform for mounting the sheers used to lift masts into and out of sailing ships.
A round container, open and wide at the top with sides sloping inwards toward the bottom.
A long narrow spoon used to remove cosmetics or medicines from narrow necked containers.
A large bolt or arrow fired from a ballista.
An holistic approach to landscape, using GIS, which maps diversity of landscape character as a means to managing future change in ways that are appropriate and sustainable.
A barn which is constructed with a timber framework; between the members are panels which are infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brickwork, stone or other materials.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of earth or stone. Use more specific type where known.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A pathway, not necessarily designed as such, beaten down by the feet of travellers.
An object which contains or is inscribed with spells against disease, witchcraft etc, or providing luck to the wearer.
A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
An area of agriculturally used land, which is divided into small, elongated, rectangular fields running parallel to each other.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A military base normally between 20 and 30 acres in size, containing legionary and auxiliary battle units, which served as stores depots and winter quarters during campaigns.
Early form of powered hammer, usually wooden, used primarily in the iron industry.
An arch of the Tuscan Order.
Use with wider site type where known.
An abbey or priory of Savigniac monks. Order merged with Cistercians c1147.
Fine grained earth which becomes more plastic when water is added. Mainly used in the manufacture of bricks, pottery and other ceramics.
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.
Use where the motive power behind the turbine is unknown. Use  DIesel Turbine Engine or Steam Turbine Engine where appropriate
A stone commemorating a person or event.
A building or site where lead is obtained from ore.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group founded in Manchester who broke away from the Methodists in 1806.
A barge with a spritsail rig commonly found on the River Thames.
An open grating of wrought iron, bronze or wood, forming a screen to a door, window or other opening, or used as a divider.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice bombing.
An often stately or ornate entrance to a railway tunnel.
Optical and/or navigational instruments with powerful lenses for observing remote objects or used in astronomy.
A mechanism used to turn a trolleybus around.
A demasted ship used exclusively for the storage of grain.
A coke-filled tower used for the dissolving and neutralising of acid produced by alkali-making processes.
Dating to or characteristic of the reigns of any of the first four kings of Great Britain called George.
A device with a sharpened surface used to grate objects such, as vegetables or cheese, into smaller pieces.

Nowadays a hospital block where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical and surgical treatment. Formerly a place where psychiatric patients were primarily segregated from other patients in a hospital.

A site where a cable was fired into the air, with parachutes attached to either end, to present an aerial obstruction to bring down, through contact, fouling and general drag, or obstruct the passage of an aircraft. Usually found as one of a group.
Includes all trees, flowers, vegetables etc. and any products manufactured from them.
A workshop or factory where statues are made by casting molten material into moulds.
A series of concentric mouldings decorating the curved face of an arch.
Photographic image produced using an ink-jet printer.
A golf course, clubhouse and ancilliary buildings.
A deposit that has been burnt and not subsequently disturbed. Refer to Archaeological Science thesaurus for terminology relating to those redeposited from their original location.
A construction material made by the firing or baking of clay.
An object assumed to be to pick limpets out of their shells.
A building or set of rooms where a newspaper is compiled and produced, before being printed. May include facilities for printing.
A long shafted weapon with a head that can be edged and/or pointed.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Reform Union, a movement formed in 1859 by those members of the Methodist Reform Church who did not join the Wesleyan Association.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A pillbox with walls that have been thickened to protect against shells. Double index with specific type where known.
A lid with a shallow conical profile and an integral knob. (Source: MPRG)
The blue dyestuff prepared from the leaves of the plant Isatis tinctoria, and sometimes used to discribe the plant itself.  Later superseded by indigo.
A type of bridge which was designed for temporary use and then capable of being moved to another site. Use for temporary bridges which have remained in situ since erection.
A power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 207/17 and comprising four rooms; a driver's room, workshop and store, battery room and engine room containing 2 generator sets.
A place where sails are manufactured.
Machinery including tractors, ploughs, harrows etc, which are used on farms.
A door adorned with panels, usually arranged in pairs.
Fine grained, buff, brown to green coloured Cretaceous sandstone. Quarried at various locations in Sussex. Not to be confused with Sussex marble which is a cretaceous limestone.
A private room or parlour usually at the same level as the hall.

A circular pillbox, usually consisting of a concrete pipe with a timber and corrugated iron roof, surrounded and covered by earth and sandbags. Built to a design by Norcon Ltd, a company dealing in concrete pipes.
A vehicle containing a couch shut in by curtains and carried by men or beasts of burden.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.
A shop where fish and chips are sold.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of radio valves or similar electronic components.
A shortened common rafter that runs between ridge and a valley rafter, or between eaves and a hip rafter.

A flour mill which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a ï¿½sudden deathï¿½ process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
French warship broadly equivalent to the English 4th to 6th Rates, with as few as 4 to as many as 50 guns.
A paddle blade, typically of wood, from a horizontal or vertical mill wheel.
A place of meeting and worship for Open Brethren, a non exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
An unlit, highly visible and distinctive feature on the coast that can be used by mariners for navigation during daylight only.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
Soft, medium grained, green/grey coloured, highly calcareous, cretaceous sandstone. Mined (more frequently than quarried) since pre-Norman times from the Reigate area of Surrey.
A table of months and days in the year.
A building or structure used for the storage of sugar.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached at one end, forming a T shape.

A coin which has been struck in relief on one side, usually the obverse side face down on the anvil die, and incuse on the other side, due to a previously struck coin sticking to the upper or punch die.
An abbey or priory belonging to the Tironian order.
A room set aside for the initial treatment of injuries sustained for example in public amenities such as lidos.

Use for any soil or sediment. Sediments consist of mineral and/or organic material deposited by any process involving natural or human agencies. Soils are discrete bodies of altered mineral material (either sediment or in situ rock remains).

A place of worship for Bible Christians, a group who split from the Wesleyan Methodists to form their own church in the South West of England. They were amalgamated into the United Methodist Church in 1907.
Monument whose presence is inferred by discovery of unstratified artefacts, for instance in plough soil.
A supported, roof structure covering all, or part, of a railway platform.
Use for an aircraft propelled by a jet engine, which provides forward thrust by pulling in air, heating and compressing it, then expelling it along with exhaust gases.
A weight attached to a fishing line in order to help it sink towards the bottom.
The area of a town or city, such as a harbour or dockyard, alongside a body of water.
An early form of powered forging hammer, featuring a cast-iron hammer head fixed to a pivoted wooden arm, introduced circa 1500 and used primarily in the iron industry.
A jar whose profile resembles two truncated cones joined together at the widest point, forming a carination at the centre of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)
Programmes of research that seek to identify the archaeological and/or architectural significance of a site or landscape.
A training establishment for gunnery personnel.
A building in which cordite paste is blended with the solvent acetone and Vaseline to form a cordite dough.
A two pronged spear for catching eels.
A vehicle on runners for carrying loads or passengers, especially over snow. Could be drawn by horses, dogs, reindeer and/or pushed or pulled by people.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
A small monastery or nunnery of the Augustinian order dependent on a larger mother house.
A stone or boulder which lies lengthways on the ground and may be used as a table, altar etc. Use only for isolated stones.
An establishment providing care for the terminally ill.
A positive colour image on film which can be projected onto a screen when light is shone through it.
A small cup for holding a boiled egg upright while it is being eaten.
An area of a building functioning as a hospital.
A 19th century ore processing works which processed the waste material from a mine.

A multipurpose hut constructed from stone and turf, covering a square or polygonal plan. It has drystone walls and a slightly corbelled roof, usually topped with slabs. Can be either free-standing or embedded in a Cornish hedge. Particular to Cornwall.

A rectangular arena, rounded at one end designed for chariot racing. The racetrack circled a central barrier (spina) constructed between two turning posts (metae). The only known example found in Britain, so far, is in Colchester.
A planked or battened door, with large nails or pegs with projecting heads keeping it intact.
An automatic power loom invented by James H Northrop in 1894.
A large, fortified permanent Roman military base, made of timber and stone, surrounded by a rampart and ditches.
Uncultivated land lying alongside a thoroughfare.
A window that is lower than others in the chancel side wall.
The dried leaves of the plants, Nicotiana tabacum or Nicotiana rustica, which are smoked (in pipes, cigars or cigarettes), chewed or taken as snuff for their relaxing properties.
A receptacle used as a home for bees, traditionally made of thick straw-work in the shape of a dome, but sometimes made of wood.
A body of water placed in such a way as to reflect a building or landscape feature.
Part of a piece of jewellery.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a farm. Use more specific type where known.

The intrinsic design and aesthetic value of an asset relating to local and/or national
styles, materials, construction and craft techniques, or any other distinctive
characteristics.
Beaches used for the departure of troops and equipment for the D-day landings.
A joint with a notch cut into its invisible inner face.
A small house built out of rough logs.
A small pond, usually circular and serving as a feature at the centre of a walled garden, used for the purpose of filling watering cans.
Use for a craft powered by an internal combustion engine powered by petrol fuel.

A structure used to show the time of day by means of the sun shining on a 'gnomon', the shadow of which falls on the surface of the dial which is marked with a diagram showing the hours. Can be freestanding, usually on a pillar, or fixed to a building.
The mid third of the 20th Century.
An impression made in soft ground by a passing animal or human. The soft ground may have subsequently hardened.
A small earthenware container used for liquids.
A native hardwood of the Beech family with hard and durable characteristics which traditionally made it appropriate for structural work.
A water feature intended to play a trick on a visitor by drenching them unexpectedly. The device would be triggered by the visitors foot or remotely. Italian for 'water jokes'.
A building in which railway wagons can unload local goods.
Medium to coarse grained metamorphic rock, colour being determined by its dominant mineral. Often used for floor and wall cladding.
An arch where vertical piers raise the springing line.
An object designed to float in water and to support a net.
Polished stone balls interpreted as ritual objects in the Scottish Iron Age.
A rod used to create repousee work on metal vessels. The rod is Z shaped.
Any member that connects two bodies, such as the sloping sides of a roof, to prevent them pulling apart.
A piece of metal, usually in the form of a disc, struck or cast with an inscription or device to commemorate an event, or awarded as a mark of distinction.
The solid, upright part of a battlement separating the openings, or crenelles.
Construction of a new pipeline and associated works.
A room specifically used for the display of furniture and other related materials
A small doll controlled by the operators hand either directly or with strings.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mortar shell.

A term for any vessel powered principally by sail and oars, or oars alone, used especially for war. As a broad term it may refer to Roman galleys, or more specifically to an Anglo-Saxon or Norse warship of the Viking Age.
A room intended for the pursuit of recreational activities.
Movable joint attached to fixtures and fittings to enable opening and closure of eg a door.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A garden with one or more platforms with walks, often on different levels, usually close to the house.
Objects associated with the care and use of animals.
A room for the storage of food and drink.
A transportable hangar designed by A & J Main of Glasgow.
Small scale enterprise producing bricks but not at the same site as the extraction of clay.
A precious or semi precious stone used within jewellery.
Dairy produce obtained by churning cream and used in cookery as a source of fat.
A ceiling that is curved or vaulted, sometimes employed to give a space the appearance of a vault.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
A spheroid produced predominantly by birds, though also produced by some animals, which encases the young creature providing a place for it to develop.
Any form of fastener used to fasten clothing together.
A detached, sometimes monolithic vertical structural element usually circular, square or polygonal bearing an ornate eight-voluted Ionic Capital.
Dried or partially dried plums eaten as fruit.
Term for ore store/ore hopper, used particularly in Yorkshire and Derbyshire.
A hospital where Air Force personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A device with two flat plates and a mechanism used to force the plates together, to  help solidify milk products in cheese making.
Equipment and parts used in the manufacture of railway tracks, locomotives and rolling stock.
An appendage worn on the front of breeches.
A building or room in which wood is stored.
A pen to separate the boar from the other pigs.
A school in which students are taught according to the beliefs of the muslim faith.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
A track of two parallel ruts deliberately cut in the ground or living rock for the guidance of two-wheeled carts when the way was obscured by darkness or water.
A place where osiers (willows) are grown for basket-making.
A horizontal member connecting rafters or cruck blades at a point between their feet and the apex of the roof.
The rear part of a Roman fort, where  barrack accommodation, stables and stores were situated. Use with wider site type where known.
An area of prepared ground on which a sport is played. Use more specific type where known.
A pit in the ground from where minerals are dug.
Generic name for the hard, white/cream coloured, freshwater limestone. Quarried on the Isle of Wight.
A large room with fixed seating, often including audio-visual facilites, in which lectures are given.
A mill which contains machinery for separating grain from the chaff.
A non residential building providing recreational, social and other facilities, especially for the elderly and those with special needs.
An aisled timber or masonry hall, serving as the chief administrative public meeting centre and law courts for a Roman town. Usually located alongside the forum.
A long piece of timber, thicker than a board.
A truss with braces crossing and fixed to each other, thus tying a pair of rafters together.
An offshoot of the Wesleyan movement founded in 1838 by John Banyard at Rochford, Essex. In 1956 it changed name to the Union of Evangelical Churches. There are 17 chapels in Essex and London.

The extraction of samples from selected features on a site to identify a characteristic magnetic response from sediments derived from the features in order to predict the response that similar features would produce. Also used to prospect for sites.
An early Medieval commemorative monument in the form of a stone which has been inscribed with symbols.

Ditches interrupted by wide, regular causeways. Each section of ditch is about 30-40m long, and each causeway is 10-15m wide. In some cases, a network of fields has been created. Found mainly in the South East of England.

Name given to a workhouse after 1929. The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished Poor Law Unions and Guardians, and control passed to public assistance authorities run by county boroughs and county councils. Lasted until 1948 when poor laws were repealed.
A maritime monument where the hull of a vessel is mostly in one piece, with large pieces of the superstructure intact.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the shape of a round bottomed cone usually 2 feet 6 inches across x 2 feet 9 inches high. Buoys were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
A building used by a group of people who meet socially to participate in activities, usually related to a particular interest or occupation.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
Describes a Classical interior, exterior or facade without pilasters or columns.
A war trumpet, usually Iron Age.
Hard, fine grained, blue/grey coloured sandstone. Quarried in South Wales and the Bristol area and commonly used, throughout the country, as a stone roofing material (stone slate).
A separate hospital building, or block of an asylum, where new arrivals were segregated from old inmates for a defined period. This system was developed from the mid-19th century onwards.

A supermarket for American military personnel, the National Guard and the Reserves and their immediate family, usually sited on a military installation throughout the world. Use term only in conjunction with an American military base.
A short blade set at an angle in a slot between two handles.
A piece of pointed wood, usually to be driven into the ground.
Refurbishment of an existing building, without extension to the floor area. Does not include extensions - use Building extension
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
An undefined structure used in the training of people in a certain skill.
Vessels of various types used specifically for providing an initial training in seamanship.
A recording of voice, music or other sounds.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
A form of floating, moveable pier designed for use in open water.
A special type of barn, lacking a threshing floor, usually with open walls, intended for the dry and well ventilated storage of hay only.
A large room or building at a school used for assembly and other activities.
A circle of wooden stakes or stake holes in the ground.
An object used to preserve fish by immersing the fish in smoke.
A joist that has its end resting in a recess in a transverse beam.
Large board used for covering the internal surfaces of a building, ie. floors, walls and ceilings. Some forms can be used as external cladding.
A group or complex of fields which appear to form a coherent whole. Use more specific type where known.
A storehouse for ore, often found in conjunction with a BLAST FURNACE.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
A movable bridge lifted at one end by chains or ropes either to stop traffic passing over it or to let traffic pass under it.
An abbey or a priory of Cistercian nuns.
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, without any boiling stage
Compact, grey/green/brown/white-speckled coloured igneous rock, peculiar to Cornwall. It is easy to carve and readily takes a polish, hence its similarity to British marbles.
A base of the Tuscan Order, featuring a square plinth supporting a large torus with a fillet above.
A site used for the extraction of peat.
A wall structure built to direct a current into the desired channel in a harbour, river etc.
The residence of a cloth cutter.
A Muslim temple or place of worship.
A slab which can be decorated, shaped, hollow etc. Used for a variety of purposes in construction.
A firing step from which standing defenders could fire over the crest of a high parapet.
An instrument for establishing the horizontal line of sight and used in surveying. It usually has an eyepiece and an air bubble in a glass tube or dome.
For example Binge eating, Anorexia Nervosa and Bullemia.
An office for the administration of town or country estates.
A pedestrianized shopping street, or a more complex arrangement of shopping 'squares' and walkways.
A conspicuous ornament usually a feather or of horse hair worn attached to headwear.
A drawing, often made in the field as the basis for later work, or to quickly convey important information.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
Use for vessels believed to come from Australasia but where the precise nationality is not known.
A freestanding pole, stake etc often used to support a superstructure.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of glass.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
An unidentified feature on the seabed recorded by fishermen as an obstruction to trawling.
A tunnel through which a tramway runs.
An enclosed, defensible passageway, equipped with gun ports, extending into or traversing a dry ditch.
A staircase, circular in plan, that winds around a central newel.
A covered trench, often in a zig zag form, made for the purpose of approaching a beseiged place under fire of the garrison.
Large keyboard, percussion instruments in which strings are struck by hammers to produce notes.
The primary mechanism within an engine or device that transmits motion, especially rotary motion, to  wheels, cogs, turntables etc.
A fine white clay used specifically for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes and for whitening leather.
Only use for sites considered for designation but not ultimately listed or scheduled.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
Northern quarryman's name for any fine grained, dark grey/black to green coloured igneous rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
A tug equipped with water tanks and pumps for fighting fires at sea or on the shore line.
Goods, particularly cloth and garments, manufactured from wool.
A thin, rectangular panel, sometimes enriched with sculptural relief, placed between the triglyphs in a Doric Order frieze.
A standardized rectangular steel container used for the transportation of goods by road rail and sea.
A building, sometimes polygonal in plan, attached to a cathedral, church, abbey etc. and used for the assembly of chapter or brethren, often to address official business.
American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.
Engine driving a continuous wire rope for the haulage of tubs in a mine and at the heapstead.
Heart failure and various heart conditions.
A notional line of resistance defined by anti tank obstacles, pillboxes and gun emplacements.
A sailing ship with a sufficient numerically large gun armament to stand in the line of battle.
A stick used to bring down curses.
The outer curve of an arch or vault.
A building used primarily for the performing of plays.
A room or rooms containing fitness equipment such as running machines and weights.
A vessel designed to operate below the surface of the sea.

A jar adapted by the addition of one straight handle, attached to either rim or body, and usually with a lip at right angles to the handle. The body is generally rounded, with a short neck and an everted rim. (Source: MPRG)
A service building to a country house, farm, etc, used for baking. If commercial premises use BAKERY.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Bridgettine order.
A vessel composed of three or more separate compartments, joined together and pierced to allow liquid to flow from one to another. There may be one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A magnetic tape used to record moving images and sound. Use for both cassette and reel tapes.
An aisle divided into chapels. This term is sometimes applied to the screens dividing the aisle, or the chapels themselves.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which scientific experiments are carried out.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
A bracelet holding charms or being itself a charm.
A gap which allows air to circulate.
A heated iron used to label, burn or mark animals, slaves, criminals etc.
A place where money is coined under public authority.
A complex of buildings producing power derived from nuclear energy.
Block for the treatment of separate diseases.
Use for miniaturized monument type. Index with actual monument type where possible.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of foot disorders and diseases.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.
A stone heated in a fire then dropped into a liquid to heat it.
A resource whose content is primarily words for reading. For example - books, letters, dissertations, poems, newspapers, articles, archives of mailing lists. [DC]
A place of worship for Particular Baptists, a Calvinistic Baptist denomination who believe in predestination.
An object that commemorates an animal, person, location or event.
A chemical fertilizer made by treating powdered phosphate rock with sulphuric acid.
A building housing a steam driven ventilation fan used in mines
A flexible pipe, usually fixed to a pump or tap, for the conveying of water.
