A plan of a feature or small area generally done in the field to quickly record the main features.
An edging of stone forming the kerb of a path.
A club where predominantly rhythm and blues style music is played, analagous to a jazz club.
A slope, usually with rails, along which a vehicle can be moved between two relatively flat stretches of railway.
A building housing court rooms and associated offices and cells, in which the Quarter Sessions were held.
A style of construction following an established set of criteria, based around the conventional use of a type of column.
A house, the inhabitant of which keeps an official register e.g. a registrar's house near a cemetery would keep an official record of deaths and burials.
A pool of water, and ancillary buildings, designed to accommodate penguins.
An inhumation, usually Roman, which has been covered by tiles to form a tent-like structure over the body; the apex is covered by ridge tiles.
A thin flat board or plate usually with a raised edge on which things can be carried.
A soft, porous, white to light grey coloured limestone.
Ground and crushed bones used as a fertilizer.

An area of managed countryside designated for visitors to enjoy recreations, such as walking specified parks and trails, in a rural environment. Often provides public facilities such as parking, toilets, cafes and visitor information.
A large container with lip and handle usually for milk.
A tool used for splitting straw. The straw splitter would be pushed down the hollow shaft of a piece of straw to produce six flat lengths of straw ready for plaiting. Used in straw hat making.
A mill or works where needles were manufactured.
Traditionally 3 miles. No longer an official unit in any nation.
A building or structure in which bricks are made.
A container packed with explosives, with a detonator triggered by contact or a timer,  for the purpose of destroying enemy craft, personnel etc.
A small building housing a valve which controls the flow within a water regulation system.
A farm building erected in the 18th and 19th century which were architect-designed rather than built in the local vernacular style.
A hospital which primarily cares for patients injured in accidents.
Medium hard, green/black coloured. Found in many igneous and metamorphic rocks.
A long building with a louvred roof in which silver is refined using the Pattinson Process, which had been developed in the 1830s.
A building containing a small stone cylindrical furnace, eg. used for tin smelting in Cornwall.
A hard, compact, unprocessed, fibrous cellulose substance. The roots, trunks and branches of trees and shrubs consist of this tissue.
A stone edging on a footway dividing it from a carriageway.
A fine grained earth which becomes more plastic when water is added and can be moulded and dried to make bricks, tile, pottery, etc.

A settlement consisting of several hut circles, either grouped together or dispersed. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Use specific forms where supported by the available evidence. For isolated hut circles use HUT CIRCLE.
A large shallow bowl for letting liquids stand.

A steam engine in which the spent steam leaving the cylinder passes to a condenser instead of being exhausted to the atmosphere. The condenser creates a partial vacuum which increases the pressure drop across the engine, so raising its efficiency.
A monument featuring an artificial circular shallow depression surrounded by a bank which runs around the rim of the depression.
A group of buildings in which local sewage is filtered and purified in large rectangular or circular tanks.

A hole in the ground which has been created by driving or hammering an upright stake into the ground. As a feature of some archaeological sites they may often represent the only surviving evidence for the former presence of an above-ground structure.
Power station using domestic refuse as its principal fuel.
A shelter, sometimes camouflaged, for the observation of birds and animals at close quarters.
A garden building, octagonal in plan, designed in the style of a classical temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A house in a terrace built on top of another, with access at high and low level to either side.
A flat oval or circular ornamental feature decorated in relief, often with flutes or floral motifs.
An instrument for writing or drawing, which usually consists of a thin rod of graphite surrounded by a wooden cylinder.
A building or room for the distribution of medicines, eg. in a hospital or clinic.
Products, such as cheese and butter, manufactured from milk.
A boundary post for the payment of tax or duty.
A receptacle for the storage of water.
A brick built railway signal box, usually with a reinforced correct roof, designed to minimize the effects of blast damage from aerial bombardment and thus protect the signalling equipment.
A tower, consisting of one or several testing shafts, for testing lifts and for training personnel.

Standard dwelling of the non-ruling classes of Japan until the mid twentieth century. Minkas are timber-framed houses with mud-plastered panels and thatched roofs. The design varies from region to region. Minkas served as home as well as workplace.
Solid bars made from pure Copper metal.

A building, with adjacent open areas, in which buses are maintained, usually having an extensive area free from upright columns or stanchions to permit overnight storage, repair bays, stores and an office.
A flatbed lorry with a concrete defensive position fitted on the back enabling the "pillbox" to be driven to where it was most needed in the event of an airborne force landing on the airfield.
A cupboard set into the eastern wall of a synagogue, facing Jerusalem. The Torah scrolls are kept in the Ark.
A grooved ring holding a gem or semi-precious stone.
A site where Celestine or Celestite (a SrSO4), originally used in sugar beet refinement, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A place where scrap metal is collected.
A plan in which the building is two rooms deep but has no central corridor.
A wooden framework with holes for the feet, and occassionally hands, in which the offender was restrained.
Buildings associated with the extaction of uranium from its pitchblende or copper ores.
A window in the form of a three-leafed clover.
A charcoal fired shaft furnace used for the direct reduction of iron ore to produce wrought iron.
A grain grinding mill in which the meal is ground into flour between revolving metal rolls.
A form of Neolithic burial monument comprising a large circular stone or earthen mound, with a low and narrow entrance passage leading to a wider and higher stone built chamber.
A school where the applied sciences and the mechanical arts are taught.
A mill for grinding ochre for the paint making process.
A small building housing a lavatory.
A fence or barrier made of metal or wooden rails.
A distribution of artefacts indicating the presence, or former presence, of a monument.
A pair of cannon balls joined by a chain.
An inclined course on top of a projecting sill, cornice etc., designed to throw off rainwater.
A hand held utensil with two or more prongs to hold food.
A scale or index of a sextant, astrolabe or similar instrument.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.

For example, spinal tumor, stroke, Alzheimers, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Cerebral Palsy, Chronic Fatigue, Dementia, Distal Muscular Dystrophy, Huntingtons Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, Narcolepsy and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.

A well or spring, possessing religious or otherwise ritualistic significance, around which a structure, such as a niche, wall or shelter, has been constructed. In the case of the water source being a natural spring, double-index with SPRING.
Headgear for a horse, usually consisting of a series of buckled straps and a mouthpiece, bridle bit, by which the horse is controlled.
A running track used for athletic practice and competition.

A distinctive form of terrace found in the northeast consisting of a long, two storey terrace indistinguishable from a conventional house externally, save that each unit has two front doors, one leading to a separate dwelling or dwellings upstairs.
People who are considered to be the property of someone else and who are bound to obedience.
A short timber set on top of two cruck blades.
A mould in which a sword is cast.
A place where ambulances are serviced and maintained.
A market appointed for the sale of wool.
A combination of obstructions, used either to stop enemy forces or force them off the road.
An often ornate wrought-iron bracket used to hang lamps outside public houses, shops, hotels and restaurants, etc.
Rock containing a high proportion of calcium phosphate.

Privateer operating under government licence to act against enemy merchant shipping. The term is closely associated with North African privateers which operated off the Barbary coast prior to the mid-1800's.

A monument previously consisting of a built structure, but which has been demolished, such that only a ground plan and foundations or similar are thought to remain. Where all below ground traces have also been removed use DESTROYED MONUMENT.
A jar with one or more lips added on the outside of the vessel wall over a hole pierced through the wall. The lips do not usually rise above rim level. (Source: MPRG)
Algae usually found as a silica skeleton. They obtain their food by photosynthesis and are used in ecological reconstruction.
A building or building complex where municipal offices and other public buildings are situated.
A joint which has a splay interrupted by a step
Photographic print on glass, using a wet process.
A building in which moist guncotton is dried by warm air for use in nitroglycerine manufacture.
A cable, usually erected between posts, used to prevent the landing or hostile aircraft.
A small hinged opening within a large door.
An instrument, usually consisting of a disc and pointer, formerly used to make astronomical measurements, especially of the altitudes of celestial bodies and as an aid in navigation.
Use for 'constructive total loss' (CTL) or where a vessel is abandoned because she is beyond repair or has become so after abandonment, which may include acts of vandalism.
An open lamp which was filled with oil then a wick floated on the oil.
A hall licensed for musical performances, singing, dancing and other entertainments, exclusive of dramatic performance.
Sites and structures associated with pedestrian transport.
An underground bomb-proof structure used as a command centre for military operations.
A machine used for the purification of water, usually for drinking purposes.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.
An open sided building known to have been used for sheltering cattle.
A room frequently in a military building where sentries guard and protect the premises.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
Headwear where a band of material is wound around a cap.
A public building where regular dances were held.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
A site where jet is extracted from the surface of the ground.
A pointed projectile fired from a crossbow designed to injure or kill a given target.
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on an English mother house.
An object used to catch fish. The line is tied in the middle of the fish gorge which then lodges in the throat after the fish has swallowed it.
A building with shelves and/or stands for skeps or wooden hives, and flight holes through the walls for bees.
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases etc. and powered by a steam engine.

Any activity, undertaken by professional archaeologists or experienced amateurs, that has a physical impact, actual or potential, upon the archaeological resource, substituting the physical resource with recorded information.

An establishment used for the manufacture of reeds and healds, which are components of a textile loom with related functions, in that they move and control the threads, and similar wire-based construction.
A chapel that radiates from an apsidal end of a cathedral or church.
The residences of people associated with the sea.
Tool used in dentistry either for examination or surgery.
A post to which the offender is tied to be whipped.
A plain four walled court used to play the game of racquets on.
A factory where tapestries were manufactured.
Fine earthenware with raised patterns of coloured decoration in the form of an enamel or coloured opaque glaze. Use for decorative wall facings.
Documents written on sheets of paper or similar, collected together and bound between protective covers.
The third and latest subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.
Former grade pending relisting. Approximately equivalent to Grade II*.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific late 1950's to early 1970's.
A circular band, usually metal, worn on the finger for ornamentation.
In the glass industry this is bench-like structure within the melting-furnace on which crucibles are placed.
A civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
A building where official archives are kept for public inspection.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
In which a range of conifers may be planted e.g. spruce, larch, pine.
Large inshore craft with a retractable loading ramp in the bow. Used to carry tanks ashore for a beach landing or as a tank ferry.
Photographic negative developed on waxed paper.
A protected building used for the storage of explosives and other pyrotechnic equipment and designed to Air Ministry drawing number 2647/37.
A licenced establishment where wine and other alcoholic drinks are sold for drinking on the premises.
An item used in caring for the body for appearance and cleanliness.
Any type of jug with decoration representing the form of a human face or figure. The shape of the vessel often forms the outline of the human face or figure. (Source: MPRG)
An arch whose height is equal to its span.
A small store building at a railway station for the storage of equipment and other stores associated with the railway.
Wooden panelling, especially interior wall panelling that rises only to dado height.
Large warship with no armour and a high speed. Used for reconnaisance and raids on enemy merchant shipping.

Roman bow brooch, dating from the third to fifth centuries AD, with a P-shaped profile and a characteristic crossbar, often adorned with knobs at its end and on the head. Shown in contemporary illustrations as being worn by high ranking males.
A place where canal boats are built and maintained.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cluniac order dependent on an English mother house.
Single masted east coast trading vessel, ketch rigged or single masted.
A metal container for liquids and foodstuffs, often sealed.
A small building housing pilot's and locker rooms with flight offices and a watch office. The only known example was built at Tangmere.
A railway yard with associated buildings used for the maintenance and storage of locomotive engines and rolling stock.

An astonomical instrument, and navigational aid, in the form of one eighth of a circle and used to measure the angular altitude of heavenly bodies. Invented in 1731 and used into the 19th Century, it was superceded by the sextant.
A waste product from smelting metal.
A small building used as a shelter by a constable of the watch responsible for patrolling the streets at night to safeguard life and property.

Controlled investigation, recording and removal of archaeological deposits in targeted areas in order to answer specific questions relating to a particular archaeological site or landscape. Usually undertaken by university departments or amateur groups.
A small container for holding oil, vinegar, salt etc for use at the table.
A form of limonite, found in wet ground, from which iron can be extracted.
A fort with projecting bastions, which came into use from the 16th century onwards.
A sewer or irrigation channel designed to avoid blockage.
Formerly a scheduled monument now descheduled
A building or structure with a six-sided plan.
A group of coins deliberately deposited together.

A jar with a single handle attached to the rim edge and looped over the top of the vessel. There may be a lip. Profiles can vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A tool used in making wooden hurdles.
A centre providing emotional and practical support to those living with life-threatening illnesses.
Plain, white, cotton cloth often unbleached.
A large store for the temporary accommodation of goods awaiting transportation to or from the sea.
A mounting or fitting attached to a chariot.
A vessel with equipment for processing dead marine life whilst still at sea.
A military depot where horses were taken and trained for service in the army.
In timber framed buildings this is the division of a wall into narrow panels by vertical studs.
A container used with an alembic as part of the distilling process.
A functioning clock designed to serve also as an ornamental feature or sculpture.
Anglo-Saxon two-piece bow brooch, dating from the 8th to 9th centuries AD, so named for the distinctive bow shaped like the arching body of a caterpillar.
An apartment or suite of rooms usually occupying the top floor of a building.
A garden maintained for the study and cultivation of plants for medicinal purposes.
Multicellular marine alga, which grows on the seashore, in salt marshes, in brackish water or submerged in the ocean.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
Hard, fissile sandstone which weathers to a dark brown colour. Mainly used as a stone roofing material (stone slate) throughout Sussex and Surrey.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.
A building in which goods were kept prior to being cleared by customs officers.
An administrative building used to organize and co-ordinate the activities of members of the armed forces.
American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
A cornice along the sloping edge of a pediment or gable.
A type of back to back house built on a hillside, of four storeys and with entrances at different levels.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic occupation site, excluding occupations of caves and rock shelters. Evidence for occupation may include traces of hearths and other structures.
A wall between two towers or pavilions, usually surrounding a building, and often forming a major part of the defences.
A holding on a smaller-scale than an ordinary farm.
A floating structure designed to resist the force of waves.

An upright, or originally upright, stone featuring a hole which is often large enough in diameter for a person to pass through, eg. Men an Tol, Cornwall. Do not use for perforated portable stone artefacts.
A piece of cloth worn over the head.
A site used for the functional testing of aircraft and their components.
The remains of any part of any animal. Use specific term where possible.
A type of retort used for distillation.
The class term, use more specific terms.
Use for vessels registered in Switzerland.
A small, walled fortlet, situated every Roman mile along the length of Hadrian's Wall to defend a gateway allowing the passage of people and as a garrison to accommodate patrol troops.
A factory making flame retardant materials.
A staff with a fork at one end which would be used to hold a lighted slow match which was used to fire a canon.
A current valid alternative address. For example may be used to record a second address for a site or building which fronts on to 2 streets.
A collective name for the pans and fire bars used in the making of salt through evaporation.
An object which has been rejected eg due to being misshapen, spoilt etc.
A vessel containing equipment for reducing the magnetic structure of a ship's hull making it immune to magnetic mines.
A diagram or drawing made by projection onto a horizontal plane, often of a building.

A temporary structure used for the firing of bricks or tiles. Unfired bricks or tiles were stacked upon a layer of fuel (usually wood) and then surrounded by a wall of old bricks and covered by a layer of mud or clay. The clamp was then fired.

The British designation for any German submarine built for military purposes. U-Boat is an anglicization of the German U-Boot, an abbreviation for Unterseeboot (Undersea Boat). In German U-Boot refers to any submarine.
A structure used for music, dance, ceremonial or civic events.
Site used for the maintenance of aircraft.
A plan in which the front entrance opens into a lobby opposite to an axial chimney stack.
A framed fireplace hood built on a bressumer and extending from one outer wall to the other or to a spere.
A site where copper ore is extracted directly from the surface of the ground.
Use for vessels registered in Sweden.

Survey using a magnetometer, a device capable of detecting variations in magnetic susceptibility between topsoils, subsoils and rocks, can also be used in a maritime context to detect variations in the magnetic field of seabed sediments.
An initial synthesis of the data collected from an excavation.
Development of new commercial premises including shops, offices, banks etc.
Circular or almond-shaped halo surrounding the figure of Christ, the Virgin or a saint.
A cutting, bank or block positioned against the wall of a trench, fort, parapet etc. to allow riflemen to shoot over the crest of the wall or parapet from a standing position.

A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which concrete panels were slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation during WWII to be resistant to bomb blasts & used for military accommodation, child nurseries and clinics etc.

A small notebook formed from two tablets usually made of wood, bone, ivory or metal. They were given as commemorative gift by a consul on his installation and often decorated with the image of the consul.
An area of the northern Indian Ocean bordered by India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Accommodation for the warrener(s) usually located within the boundary of the Rabbit Warren. They also provided a place to store nets, traps and other necessary equipment.
A mechanical testing machine used to carry out pioneering tests on various materials, particularly cast-iron beams, to determine practical data on their strength and other properties.
A buttress set away from the structure it supports, joined to it by an arch.
A garden building usually in a secluded spot, resembling a hermit's dwelling and built as a resting place, retreat or viewing point.
Curved, interlocking roof tile of S-shaped section usually made of clay or concrete.
Parts which make up a vehicle.
An enamelled plate brooch, dating from the second and third centuries AD, depicting an animal often with religious significance, such as hares, birds, fish and horses, sometimes with rider.
In the glass industry, a flat block of stone (idealy marble), cast iron, or a ceramic material, on which cylinder glass is flattened. Medieval and Post Medieval.
A portable beehive, often made of straw.
One or more coils of barbed wire intended to impede the advance of hostile troops.
The smallest piece of timber (2-5cms) across used in building, employed on rafters to support the roof covering or in a partition as a base for plaster or external render and wall covering.
The passage, area, lobby, room or vestibule into which a building's main entrance opens.
Right angled triangular plate for determining, measuring or setting out set angles.
A long graduated staff used in surveying to help measure distance or height.
A two-storey watch office similar in design to drawing number 1959/34 but constructed completely from concrete. A large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
Buildings and structures associated with the production, processing and storage of coal gas.
A drawing used to convey information about the arrangement and size of features in a defined location under study.
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.
A low, wide, circular ring or bank of stones surrounding an open, roughly circular area which is (or was initially) free of cairn material. The inner and outer faces of the bank may be kerbed.
A slate tablet, often framed in wood, for writing purposes. Use a materials thesaurus to record the material type slate.
Limestone formed during the Jurassic period. Composed of ooliths, literally small rock particles with the appearance of fish roe.

A distinctive form of jar being a flat-based, straight-sided or slightly rounded jar with two opposed, upright, rounded, tongue-shaped lugs raised from above the rim and bridged by added, internal struts used to suspend the pot over a fire. (Source: MPRG)
A board marked up to play a game upon.
Solid bars made from pure iron.
A container used to hold, store, examine or create medicinal substances such as ointments, medicines, drugs, pills, tablets etc.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of timber products.
An inclined timber used to support and provide rigidity to roofs, partitions etc.
A tall pole topped with a bell used to summon the workforce to their place of work.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.
A sloping timber in a staircase holding the ends of treads and risers.

Sites, buildings, structures and features used for permanent, seasonal or temporary accommodation/habitation & related ancillary buildings. Includes commercial, military and religious sites used for residential purposes as well as industrial workplaces.
A written description of the structure including archive assessment supported by drawn and photographic evidence including a ground plan.
A bridge for carrying a road or railway over another.
A fan used to create an air current to separate grain from chaff.
The large main axle on which a waterwheel, which turns the shaft, and a pitwheel are mounted.
A decoy site designed to simulate the flarepath lighting of permanent RAF stations, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.
A drinking vessel with two or more handles.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
Cornish miner's term for slates formed during the Carboniferous and Devonian periods.
An attic workshop for textile manufacture, usually weaving.
An outbuilding used for the storage and maintenance of horse-drawn carriages.
The main administrative building and headquarters of a regiment
Potassium Carbonate obtained from the ashes of burnt plant matter and used as a fertilizer.
A hard level roadway or other surface from which aircraft take off and land.
A series of columns in a straight line supporting an entablature with no openings or glazing.
A battery mounted in the flank of a bastion from which flanking fire is directed across a curtain wall.
A building or site for watching specific military activities or the movement of enemy forces, etc.
Loss due to action of free floating or tethered explosive device set to explode on contact with or in proximity to a vessel.
Character and / or management not determined.
A hard, bone-like material obtained from animal teeth.
A large metal pylon structure used to tether airships.
A pit where domestic waste material is deposited.
A site used for all the processes associated with the manufacture of roof, floor or decorative tiles.
An observation post, usually well concealed, intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organisation), in the event of an invasion, to watch enemy movements without being seen.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
Manmade constructions used to prevent rivers breaking their banks and flooding the surrounding area with water. Often taking the form of a bank or wall.
An object used to prick holes on each side of a manuscript page to mark the postion of the horizontal lines.
A factory used for processing raw materials. Use more specific mill type where known. See also TEXTILE MILL, for more narrow terms.
A building where radium is used in the treatment of cancer.
A picture or pattern produced by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours. May be in the form of a floor.
An upright framing member, or mullion, that separates two panels, such as in a panelled door or a window.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land associated with sport, leisure & entertainment. Includes sports grounds, hunting forests, cinemas, theatres etc.
A small tool for boring holes with a cross handle and a screw tip.

The interpretation of information on aerial photographs usually resulting in the production of maps and records of archaeological sites and landscapes. Many aerial photographs may be consulted for a single analytical survey.
A small box or chest for valuables, especially jewels.
A path across a road marked with black and white stripes where pedestrians may cross.

A pistol fired by use of a flintlock.A gunflint is held in the lock which on pulling the trigger pushes back the pan cover creating sparks which set off the powder in the pan causing a flame to go through and set off the charge in the barrel.
A projection used to clip clothing together.
Pipes manufactured from copper used for a variety of purposes, especially plumbing.
Register of Parks and Gardens Legacy Number
Tropical giant grass with hollow stem used structurally or as a covering material.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
Use for vessels registered in Italy.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.
A bowl specifically used for shaving.
A pipe through which water is conducted.
A collective term embracing a church tower's entire structure, including its spire.
A freestanding structure commemorating nations, actions, soldiers and/or civilians that served or died as a result of conflict.
A pebble or small cobble with a small circular depression in one or both faces. The depressions, if on both faces, are usually directly opposite. These items may be unfinished pebble hammers.
A complete cross-frame from ground level to ridge in a box-framed building.

A bowl with a straight handle projecting horizontally or diagonally upwards from the rim, particularly or completely hollow, but not opening into the vessel. A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
An enclosed encampment, often featuring temporary or semi-permanent structures, used for the detention of prisoners of war, refugees or other civilians detained on political or social grounds.
A section of stone or brickwork employed in a timber-framed building to fill the spaces between uprights or studs.
A hut, usually containing lead pans, in which salt water is boiled to produce salt.
A structure for producing power through a rotary motion achieved by the weight of men or animals treading on a succession of moving steps or a belt that forms a kind of continuous path.
An often ornately decorated theatre for the performance of opera.
A vessel used for transporting passengers or goods.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.

Roman, mid-1st century AD two-piece Bow Brooch, derived from the Colchester Brooch, with a winged, transverse head  protecting a spring mechanism held by a rear facing hook over the chord, its profile evoking a leaping dolphin.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A room within a building, such as a shop or leisure complex,sometimes equipped with cubicles or screens to allow a degree of privacy, where clothing can be tried on or changed.
A roof with a slope of less than ten degrees to the horizontal.
A drinking vessel, made of glass, designed expressly to be used for the consumption of wine.
Usually made of iron, this bound the end of an axle and was perforated to allow a linch pin to pass through the axle and keep the wheel in place.
Use for the remains of any part of an amphibian.
A sole held onto the foot by straps or thongs.
A system of long, continuous banks and/or ditches dividing land into well defined areas. Possibly used for controlling livestock

An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to recieve coded information from the out-stations in the surrounding area for relaying to headquarters via direct phone line.
A beacon used for coastal navigation. Many date from the Medieval period.
A projection from the bottom of a church stall designed to provide some support for a person standing in long services.
A room or small building kept at low temperatures for the storage of perishable items, particularly food.
An educational building where examinations are held.
A jug with an evenly rounded profile and a discernible basal angle; the maximum diameter is near the mid point and in the upper half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)
A blunt headed instrument used for striking objects.
A house occupied by an employee of a waterworks. Usually found in association with a pumping station or waterworks.
A building in which the buying of raw cotton and finished goods took place.
The part of a rib or arch visible below the general surface of the vault.

A group of four houses in quadruplex form within a single block, of approximately square plan and set in a spacious garden. Such houses were usually provided for supervisory or skilled workers within a textile factory.
A factory manufacturing electrical equipment, such as engines, transformers and generators for use in industry.

A building temporarily requistioned for use as a hospital. Auxiliary hospitals treated the less seriously wounded and were less strict than military hospitals although they remained under military control.
Southern hemisphere; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of SHCal04
A building used to coordinate civil defence in times of war. Can also be utilized as aid centres in times of national emergency.

An artificial aperture from which water springs. The water supply usually came from a lake or reservoir higher up in order to ensure the necessary flow and pressure. More recently fountains have been powered by pumps.
An arched half-rib applied to the lateral wall surface in a vaulted bay, its function, rather than structural, being to complete the pattern of the vault's main ribs.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
A disc capable of holding more data than a conventional CD or CD-Rom. Commonly used as storage medium for film and interactive products.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A garage for the storage and maintenance of motor vehicles, such as ambluances and fire engines, used for civil defence purposes.
A classical order with an Attic base and fluted column. The cornice has dentils and the capital volutes.
An ornamental moulding whose curved, segmented form resembles that of a scallop shell.
Broad term for all types of animated or live action images.
Sites, buildings and structures for the defence of the coastline from sea and air invasion.
Earthworks of uncertain date and purpose, consisting of cross-shaped banks sometimes with an accompanying ditch. Their distribution is largely confined to North Yorkshire.
A vessel or aircraft lost at sea, cause unknown.
A rafter set diagonally where two sloping rooves meet.

A central tower with a single-storey wing either side. The tower contained the watch office on the ground floor, observation room on the second with each wing containing an office for the Chief Flying Instructor or the officer commanding and their aides.
An outward radial flow reaction water turbine.
A building used for the shelter and protection of deer, especially in winter.
A building or site where the carcasses of whales were butchered and rendered into by products such as oil, fenk and whalebone.
A pavement walkway for pedestrian use, often raised above the level of a road or path.
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.
Small engineering works specialising in the production of items such as ploughs and threshing machinery.
Hard, coarse grained, green to pink coloured igneous rock. Commonly used as a polished cladding.
A light, sometimes ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation, used for entertainment or shelter. Use specific type where known.
The remains of living organisms preserved in stone over a long time period. This may be the internal or external moulds of, usually, the hard parts of an organism (shells, bones, etc.).
A polygonal or circular stone forming part of the shaft of a column.
A small narrow rectilinear enclosure with high hedges boundaries for the cultivation and shelter of flowers, particularly Daffodils and Narcissi.

A large shallow pan, usually metal, in which seawater or brine is evaporated for the extraction of salt. The name is also often applied to the exterior pits or ponds used for the same purpose (see Thesaurus of Monument Types).
Man made structure, usually sub-terranean, built to contain water for the purpose of immersion of people for sport and leisure.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a plantation.
The excrement of seabirds and bats used as a fertilizer.
The rectangular pit in which the lower part of a waterwheel revolves.
A large, circular hollow, often with a platform and seating built into the sides, used for preaching.
A row of buildings built during different periods, as opposed to a TERRACE.
A flat, horizontal piece of  timber or masonry projecting  from or recessed into a wall to hold objects.
A building used for the storage of fish.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, set up on a road, canal or railway to mark the miles from or to a place.
A rescue tug equipped to care for survivors from torpedoed vessels and also available for towing to port ships damaged by enemy action.
Structures used for the lifting or hoisting of goods, machinery, vehicles, people and livestock.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using hovercraft services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and materials to and from the surface of a mine.

Fish which have been caught and kept alive. Fish were kept alive on ships in earlier centuries to ensure they reached their destination as fresh as possible. In more recent times exotic fish have been kept alive to sell as pets.
A free-standing structure, in the form of a cross (+), symbolizing the structure on which Jesus Christ was crucified and sacred to the Christian faith. Use specific type where known.
A continuous row of WEALDEN HOUSES.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
Various seaweeds which are burnt to obtain the salts contained in their ashes, which are used in the manufacture of soap and glass.
The largest boat belonging to a sailing vessel, and usually the means of escape from a sinking ship; powered by oars.

A maritime coring technique which penetrates the ground due to the force of gravity. Since the speed of penetration is the same as the sampling speed, it barely disrupts the sedimentary layers. A cable attached to the ship is used to recover the core.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of interlacing ribbons or cords, usually in an intricate pattern.
A car park, on two or more levels.
The residence of the supervisor of an inclined plane.
A stylised, leafy decorative feature reminiscent of, and sometimes referred to as, honeysuckle

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, some examples have steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
Former grade pending relisting. Approximately equivalent to Grade II.
Thin rods or threads of metal formed by rolling or wire-drawing and used for a variety of purposes including electrical circuitry.
The rural residence of a country gentleman.
A broad design of sword used for cutting and slashing.
A building housing the stand-by generator set and associated equipment which could supply electricity to all essential services in the event of a power cut.
A recess or chamber near the altar which holds a relic. A feature of medieval churches.
Light material used to cover the face or head.
Change of use for an existing building.
A covering for the foot not enclosing the ankle.
A shed for storing fishing bait.
A room, furnished with tables and chairs, where meals and refreshments are served and consumed.
A building in which the lay sisters resided. Lay sisters were not nuns and as such weren't bound by any vows. They could leave the convent and even marry if they wished.
A ring fixed to a vehicle through which the reins were passed.
A knife with a hinged blade which folds into a slot in the handle.
A building housing a beam engine.
A mill in which oilcloth (a heavy cotton or linen cloth with a linseed oil coating) was produced.
A pipe or channel for conveying water or other liquids.
A pattern cut out in wood or metal to help shape something accurately or to reproduce shapes.
An apparatus used for the process of condensing: the conversion of vapour into a liquid.
A written journal, often of a personal nature.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the disposal of domestic and industrial waste.
A building or room used for small scale manufacture. Use more specific term where possible.
A flexible container with an opening at one end.
A garment covering from the waist to the knees, similar to trousers but stop at the knees.
A building plan in which the rooms are symmetrically placed.
A building housing an electric powered mine ventilation fan.
An end scraper which has a retouched end that is concave in form. (Source: SARC)
A cruck, forming the main upright of a wall but whose blades are truncated by a transverse member.
The residence of a prison governor.
The limit line of an area pertaining to a medieval manor.
A machine tool similar in general appearance  to a shaping machine but in which the head or ram carrying the cutting tool moves in a vertical plane.
A flat based stone used in conjunction with a grinding stone
20th century plant for separating minerals using variations in water-repellent properties under controlled chemical conditions. Survives as ruins of buildings or tanks.

As this proposal affects a scheduled monument I have drawn it to the attention of our Inspector of Ancient Monuments who should be contacted for further advice.  Scheduled monuments are legally protected under the ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act 1979.  Proposed works require scheduled monument consent in addition to planning permission.
A place where a ship lies at a wharf. Use specific type where known.
A place of residence and worship for Anglican monks.
Visual and descriptive record of a building, drawing on the full range of sources and including consideration of significance. Equivalent to Historic England Level 4.
An end scraper that has a retouched end which is convex in form. (Source: SARC)
Large storage structure for powdered cement.
Intended for personal decoration, objects made of precious, semi-precious or imitation metals and gemstones.

A structure comprising of two walls of stone or wood with nets or fish traps attached. Located in coastal waters, on shelving coastlines or in river estuaries they form large enclosures with a V or L shaped plan. The narrow point on the seaward side.
A site where machine tools, machines designed to remove surplus material from a work piece by accurately guided cutting tools, are manufactured.
A joint with each timber ending in a cut slanted across its length.
The vertical lining of a doorway, window or other opening.
A long pointed weapon used to catch fish by stabbing.
A small, narrow boat with pointed ends propelled by paddling.
A prepared core from which a single flake or blade has been produced. The technique was primarily used in the Palaeolithic and Neolithic.
The premises of a police officer for a parish or township who was appointed to act as a conservator of the peace within the district.
A small hemispherical or flared bowl with a solid pointed base or spike. May include a wick lip at the rim and one or two pierced lugs for suspension. (Source: MPRG)
A side-opening steel framed shed. A smaller version of the SEAPLANE SHED (TYPE F) they were built from 1916 on RNAS seaplane bases
A piece of land used for the cultivation of hops.
A light made by dipping a rush in grease.
A small room communicating with one or more apartments.
A hall in which public assemblies and meetings can be held.
A watch office with additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store.
A place where people can recover from illnesses or health problems through controlled eating and programmes of exercise, etc.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
The front piece of horse armour.
Non-pavilion type of attached ward block.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
A box with a perforated top used for perfume.

Controlled investigation, recording and removal of archaeological deposits according to the principles of strategraphic excavation. The size of an open area can range from holes to examine pile foundations to extensive trenches of 100 square meters.
The measurement of trapped electrons by exposure to high-frequency electromagnetic radiation. A useful technique for dating tooth enamel, shells, coral and calcite form 5,000-1,000,000 years old.
A furnace or oven for burning, baking or drying. Use specific type where known.
A sleeping apartment usually containing a number of beds and sometimes partitioned into cubicles.A room for sleeping in, usually for a number of beds.
A thin, flat rectangular piece of slate, or  similar material, used as a roofing tile.
A kiln used to calcine the component parts of cement to remove excess water and other ingredients.
Flat, rectangular piece of material, traditionally of wood but now of any material, used in the construction industries.
A cemetery comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels.
A furnace in which the flame is turned back over the substance to be heated.
An object in the sea bed recorded on the Hydrographic Office plot of objects snagged by nets during trawling.
A workshop for the manufacture of clothing, eg. tailor's workshop.
Paper products intended for note-taking or correspondence, e.g. blank notebooks, diaries, writing paper, postcards
The structure at the top of a draw well.
A peg or upright object which is the target of a ball in skittles.
A stone or brick used on a corner to reinforce it and also as decoration.
A container designed to assist in cooling foodstuffs or liquids. Use specific type where known.
Proposal of or alteration to an existing planting scheme. Includes limited tree planting.
A market building, pre-19th century, incorporating other function rooms, eg. theatres, courtrooms, schoolrooms.
A hard, translucent variety of jade which is rarer than the other varieties of nephrite as a result considered to be the best and very desirable.
A type of cushion capital with the lunette on each face cut into a series of truncated cones to form a scallop shell-like decoration.
A small container for an aromatic substance, eg perfume.
A body of still water often artificially formed for a specific purpose. Use specifc type where known.
A propulsion system for ships using a combination of steam turbines and gas turbines to power the shafts.
The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
The debris resulting from metal working processes.
A building where patients or inmates of a hospital or workhouse were disinfected and their clothes washed or burnt to prevent the spread of infectious diseases or other ailments.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious woman or nun, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
Use for completed, accuarately surveyed maps
Ornate or patterned decoration, carved into or moulded from plaster.
A building or area within a brewery where barrels of ale are stored.
A pin used to hold hair in place.
A vessel used for carrying cargoes, fitted with defensive weapons. Use with specific type and form where known.
A spandrel that is sunk below the surface of the arch.
A gate or valve that controls the flow of water from a reservoir, harbour, etc..
A camp kitchen, usually associated with the military.
A hidden dungeon entered through a trap door from the room above it. Also a similarly concealed pit into which prisoners would be cast.
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
Sites used for the production of drugs and other medical products.
A building containing a weighing machine for weighing goods; sometimes found in markets, ports, etc.
A lid resembling an inverted dish with a flat top and an integral or added knob or loop handle. (Source: MPRG)

A large steelframed military aircraft hangar designed in 1939, intended for aircraft maintenance on operational stations. It includes side annexes for workshops and offices, provided with a large number of windows. The annexes are of brick or concrete.
Operations in excess of 25 cms. If possible state depth in Description.
Development of golf course, including works on associated buildings and facilities.
A flanking tower, or projection from the main walls of a defensive work from which a garrison can defend the ground in front or on the flank.
A pointed tool used to pierce holes, usually in textiles.

A signalling structure used on WWII airfields, comprising a concrete square base with a kerbed border into which concrete signal symbols could be placed to advise pilots in the air of current airfield state e.g. directions of landing and airfield circuit.
A substance designed to emit a sweet smell.
An enclosure for the containment of a bull.
Urn with a heavy rim or collar which may be vertical or slightly inverted. This may carry incised or impressed decoration, particularly herring-bone, encircling lines, hurdling or chevron decoration.
Smooth rendering applied to the exterior of buildings which may be incised to suggest coursed masonry. Made of lime and sand or brick dust, and more recently, cement.
A long handled heavy hammer used by two hands.
A building in which people are held in a state of imprisonment or confinement as punishment. Usually associated with military and political offenders.
A room used for storing food.
A tool used in making pottery.
Iron Age or Roman coastal site producing salt by boiling of seawater in fired clay pans, resulting in characteristic mounds of 'BRIQUETAGE' (see Archaeological Objects Thesaurus).
A vertical structure used to draw off smoke from a fire.
A designed for the carriage of livestock usually cattle or sheep.
A container used upon the altar.
A building used for the testing of aircraft and aircraft engines.

An underground structure from which operations covering the whole, or part, of the country could be directed in the event of a nuclear attack. Usually equipped with air filtration equipment and supplies for several months.
A concrete, concave wall 200 feet in length used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.

Roman, mid to late 1st century, hinged  Bow Brooch, related to the Aucissa Brooch, with side knobs on the upper bow, the curvature of which is confined to the brooch's top half, the lower half being straight. Frequently tinned to give a silver appearance.
One of only three 'true' British marbles, white in colour, predominantly used for sculptures and statues.
A reinforced concrete structure, often sited underground, used as a shelter from the threat of nuclear attack.
A building, administered by the Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, providing retail and leisure services to members of the armed forces.
A post, usually carrying a tiebeam, which forms part of a wall in a timber framed building.
The hard, close-grained wood of the Box or similar trees.
A component part of a treadmill crane, the shed is used to enclose the treadwheel.
A house or building where goods are made or prepared and displayed for sale and sold. Use more specific type where known.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A structure, usually of earth and concrete, and usually, although not always, subterranean, designed for protection against explosives.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of paper.
Land owned by the Duchy of Cornwall

An object such as an organ, display case or piece of furniture such as a pew, usually associated with a larger monument but which may be found in isolation. For example a war memorial roll of honour in its display case.
A surface formed by cutting off a square edge, usually at 45 degrees. Use more specific type where known.

A waterwheel in which the incoming water is directed onto the periphery at approximately the same level as the axle, the water being kept in contact with the floats, or buckets, by breastwork of masonry, timber or iron.
A room or building used as a store, usually for documents, works of art, books etc.
A vertical upright on either side of a door.
Any vessel propelled by sail or power and used for pleasure and not plying for hire.
A defensive construction situated in the sea, designed to protect the land from seabourne attack. The term applies mainly to those monuments built from around 1860 onwards.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A temporary airfield in use during the build-up to D-Day. They consisted of a natural earth or grass surface reinforced with wire mesh.

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber.  Produced by De Havilland.
A deliberately made missile fired from a sling.
The hot room in a Roman baths.
A building, or buildings, providing accommodation for an infantry regiment.
The entrance to a road tunnel, sometimes of a grand construction.
A joint in which the end of one timber is shaped to fit around the moulding on another.
The equivalent of a colonnade but using pilasters.
An artificial, sometimes temporary, platform on which helicopters can take off and land.
A specialist hospital where medical and surgical dental treatment takes place.
A staircase, usually leading from a dormitory, used by monks to enter the transept of a monastic church.
A complex of buildings with the purpose of providing and storing food and drink supplies (esp. for the navy).
An instrument for breaking open hard shelled nuts.
Equipment used to bore a hole in a solid object through the use of a twisting, drilling action.
Use for vessels registered in Croatia.
A barrier, usually of wood or chain, stretched across the entrance to a harbour, port or anchorage, to control entry and/or limit the effect of the weather on the wave action.
A site where unprocessed wood is used to manufacture goods.
A wheel driven by wind or steam for the lifting of water.
Garden or open-air enclosure, usually connected to commercial premises, where tea and other refreshments are served to the public.
Prayer hall at burial ground, especially a small walk-in memorial devoted to a deceased Hasidic rabbi.

Use for a craft where a type of steam engine where the steam is first expanded in a high-pressure cylinder, then having given up heat and losing pressure, it exhausts directly into one or more larger volume low-pressure cylinders.
An establishment serving coffee and other refreshments and inexpensive foods. Between the 17th and 18th centuries they were also meeting places for political discussions.

An extra processing unit which can be used in conjunction with single beam echo sounders to determine the roughness and hardness of the seafloor. Mainly used for marine biology, but has been used in archaeology.
A room to withdraw to from the dining room.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A crane that is fixed to a quay and used for the loading and unloading of cargo.
A long seat for reclining on.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
A malleable, ductile ferromagnetic metal widely used for structural and decorative purposes.
A section of a psychiatric hospital or psychiatric ward set aside for children and/or adolescents with mental illness.
A ship designed or modified to carry large numbers of mines and be able to lay them as a minefield.
A female figure used instead of a column, usually supporting an entablature.
A building in which raw pottery is finished by dipping it in glaze.
A flexible armour designed to protect the torso.
A short bay, usually in a hall, commonly as a smoke bay or for a cross-entry.
Monument thought to be archaeological or historical but proved to be natural.
A government employment agency for those out of work offering advice on jobs, training and retraining.
A hospital department for the medical and surgical treatment of teeth disorders.
A building in which the fibres of new woollen cloth were raised by brushing with teazle heads.
A crane located on a quayside used for the loading and unloading of goods and materials to and from vessels.
Bases of this order are often referred to as spira and have a double astragal in the middle.
A large discharge pipe with a valve for drawing water from a water main. Used to help extinguish fires.
An arch made up of part of a circle, the centre of which is below its springing line.
A bone or antler point with rows of barbs, usually on one side only.
A pit or tank containing chemicals for the preserving of animal hide.
An object that contains bones. Use a monuments thesaurus where this is a site type.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
An artificial fall of water often taking the form of a water staircase.
A place or building where animals can be washed. Often in the form of a pool with a walled funnel-like structure enabling animals to be guided into the pool.
The edible product of a plant, usually consisting of the seed and its sweet, juicy envelope.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
Site associated with the testing of nuclear material or its containers.
The site of the formal burial of cremated bone, sometimes 'urned' in a vessel or casket of glass, wood or, more commonly, ceramic.
A tower serving as a reservoir to deliver water at a required point.
A partition or wall behind an altar, often separating the choir and altar from the ambulatory and east chapel.
A booth, shed or stall erected at the side of a road, canal, bridge or gate where a toll must be paid.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of spirits.
Blocks carved out of granite and used as a building material.
A building where masts are made and stored.
A style of dressing including all the clothes, accessories etc worn at one time, as in a particular country or period.
An object used in tablet weaving to control the shed.
A garden which consists of rocks and rock-loving plants that require little water.
A building used for the testing of weapons for quality, accuracy and explosive power.
Goods, usually foodstuffs, preserved in glass bottles, jars, etc. Examples are bottled fruit, pickled onions, jam, honey.
A stone or boulder which has been deliberately set upright in the ground. Use only for isolated stones. Otherwise use specific type where known.
The recording of a surface, or surfaces, using scanning technologies, to create a 3D model of the target structure/object.
A chapel, often attached to or screened off inside a church, endowed for the celebration of masses principally for the repose of the founder?s soul.
A junction whereby two members or elements of an artificial structure or mechanism are joined or fitted together, whether rigidly or hinged.
An object used in lighting a fire, lamp, oven, candle etc.
The third and latest subdivision of the Bronze Age.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the explosive Gelignite.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.

Rectangular slabs of concrete with a sloping top usually with sides of 5 feet by 3 feet and 3 feet high which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
An approximately circular or oval setting of spaced, usually freestanding, upright stones. More than one circle may be present, arranged concentrically.
A jug with straight vertical sides and roughly equal rim and base diameters. (Source: MPRG)
The establishment of an undertaker who is responsible for the management of the ceremony connected with the burial or cremation of a dead body.
Accessories used in furnishing and embellishing a building or structure.
A stone missile fired from a ballista, larger in diameter than ballista shot.
A room intended to contain a bed.
A building housing the brakes for an incline railway or tramway.
A round, oval or rectangular straight-sided dish, divided into two or more units or compartments of varying sizes by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)
Outer casing of an explosive cartridge fired from a cannon or mortar.
Used where an existing building is designated as the residence of an official.
Optical discs on which programs, data, or music are digitally encoded for a laser beam to scan, decode and transmit to a playback system, computer monitor or television set. [AAT]
A room used for sleeping or resting in. Use more specific term.
The impost, or point at which a vault rests upon its support, and from which it seems to spring. Hence the term describes the bottom stone of a vault, which lies on the impost.
A thin piece of metal which when struck vibrates to produce a sound, can be used in pairs.
A place where pheasants are reared and kept.
Specify in Description using: hedge, fence, wall etc.
19th century school administered by a school board.
A priory dependent on a foreign mother house. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
A material made from extremely fine fibres of glass and is used as a reinforcing agent for many polymer products.
A free standing small turf and timber fortlet, situated every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A pipe designed for smoking opium.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A grain, obtained from the grass Oryza sativa, eaten as a staple in many parts of the world.
A wall with niches in a CREMATORIUM to display the urns containing ashes. Use only when related to funerary site.

Systematic recording of building facades that produces a seamless mosaic of digital images by identifying control points and defining limits to each image. The rectified mosaic can then be introduced into a CAD environment.

A jar adapted by the addition of three or more vertical loop handles. They may be equally spaced, or confined to one section of the circumference. Profile vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A stone on which plague victims placed vinegar-disinfected money to pay for food left for them by the townspeople.

An engine or prime mover, in which a mixture of air and fuel is ignited inside a closed cylinder, and the resulting explosion drives a piston to the opposite end of the cylinder, its movement turning a crankshaft via suitable mechanical parts.
Area feature visible as an earthwork or cropmark with no known function.
A gable supporting a roof, placed at right-angles to the main part of the roof.

An information gathering exercise to facilitate an understanding of the potential environmental impact of a development proposal; includes the collation of specialist reports from a variety of disciplines.
A building used for the finishing, drying and storage of lace.
A container for the storage and or use of cosmetics.
A school in which elementary subjects are taught to young children.
A forest killed by rising sea-level. Nowadays only tree stumps survive.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A multi-purpose, two-storey barn, built on a hillside with entrances at both levels to a first floor threshing barn and ground floor animal housing.
A temporary support placed under a vault or arch to support them during construction.
A vessel used to carry a pilot to a ship.
A soil, which may be buried or exposed, that has developed in a past landscape.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templars
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of urinary disorders and diseases.
A twisted fibre which is immersed in wax, grease or oil except for one end which is lit.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of kidney disorders and diseases.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
A roof truss used for small spans with a saw-tooth overall shape braced by vertical and diagonal members.

Part of the WWII air defence radar system, whereby in 1939 a chain of radar stations were established along the south and east coast of Britain. The equipment was based upon apparatus developed for ionospheric research.
A Romano-British brooch type, appearing at the end of the first century AD and developing during the second, characterized by a flat plate to which the pin and catchplate are attached at the back.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, one example has steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
A pit containing the waste product form iron working.
A plan in which the chimney stack backs onto the cross passage between a building's two entrances.
A very small spoon used to provide liquid to mix with ink on an ink stone.
The remains of a shell of a mussel.
Non-specific building type associated with an airfield.
A tower with one or more horizontal platforms extending out over deep water for use in diving competitions.
A mobile crane which floats on water.
Data storage device in disc form that uses lasers to write and access data; can store data in analog or digital form. [AAT]
Partly subterranean operations rooms for the lighting arrays of the various types of bombing decoys in use during the Second World War.
Photographic image produced on transparent medium suitable for use in projection equipment. Use specific term where known.
A long, low-rise building consisting of rows of attached individual suites of rooms used for overnight accommodation by motorists.

Reason	

The planning authority wishes to protect archaeological remains during development works.  

Condition	

No development shall commence until details of  fencing, signage and other control measures to protect archaeological remains in-situ have been submitted by the applicant and approved by the planning authority.  The approved programme must be implemented in accordance with the approved details and maintained for the duration of operational works.
Fruit native to the countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea.
Conglomerate consisting of rounded flint pebbles held together in a natural silica and sand cement.
A section of a hospital specializing in the treatment of patients with serious mental disorders.
Refers to art, whether carving or painting, applied to free -standing stones or cave walls.
An entablature with a plain architrave or principal beam over which are the frieze and cornice.
A field or piece of ground used for the playing of games and other activities.
A wholly or partially underground chamber, often beneath a chancel, equipped for religious services and usually containing tombs.
A barge with a crane or sheer legs used for moving and maintaining mooring buoys.

High speed craft developed in the 20th Century which employ a wing-like structure mounted on struts below the hull which lift the vessel above the water line during forward motion, reducing drag and increasing speed.
Buildings, structures and sites for the detection of encroaching enemy forces.
A privately-funded home for the care of the elderly.
Daily record of events or appointments.
A piece of bone used for divination.
An area where birds are protected and bred.
A length of straight, curved or angled earthwork or cropmark of uncertain date or function.
An uncrystallized syrup, produced as part of the sugar refining process. Used as a food additive and in the production of rum.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.

A long, thin cane of glass made by layering glass of various colours in a mould and pulling the soft glass until the cane was of the desired thickness. When cut and viewed in section the cane has a mosaic like appearance.
A library for use of the public.
The part of a road intended for vehicular traffic.
A large, high-ceilinged room, usually in a great house or palace, serving as a principal reception room; also a room used by the public for a specific purpose; or a drawing room in a house.
A building used as the command centre of a military operation.
A single-storey structure, usually situated against the exterior of a walled garden's south facing wall, used for storage and often accomodation.
A glasshouse used for the cultivation of tropical plants.
Sandy, light brown (cream to golden) coloured limestone, easily worked and readily available.

Carboniferous sandstone varying in grain size from coarse to fine and in colour from white, yellow, pink to brown. When only Gritstone is mentioned, unless otherwise specified, assume it to be Gritstone (Sandstone), as this is the more common usage.
Residence for retired people, often in the form of an apartment complex, differing from a nursing home as the residents live independently.
A purpose-built or adapted structure intended as a headquarters for an air raid precautions warden.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
An early thermosetting plastic commonly used for its properties of electrical insulation.
A tool used to cut or split wood.
Mark 5 or the fifth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
An accessory vessel to a cremation.
Canal docks where the freeboard of a boat was marked. By placing increasing ton weights at 4 points around the boat, its displacement could be marked for toll purposes.

Sites used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for sites associated with military installations. For non-military sites use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
An initially worked quern that is still to be finished.

An apparatus, featuring an ascending and descending platform or compartment, for carrying people or objects from one level or floor to another. This term can include the shaft or well in which such an apparatus operates.
A building, usually part of a hospital complex, in which contaminated clothes, bedding and utensils are disinfected.
Mascarene Islands, Africa; dependent territory as a departement of France.
A natural or artificial elevation of earth or stones, such as the earth heaped upon a grave. Use more specific type where known.
A temporary fieldwork, usually a few feet in height, constructed for defence against enemy forces.
an instrument or tool used for medical purposes.
An earthen bank that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A defensive position, often constructed from sandbags, designed to protect a group of infantry.
A thick heavy weapon used to strike the opponent.
The middle section, between the architrave and the cornice, of an entablature.
An establishment where people get their hair dressed and cut.
A dark, viscous liquid, obtained from the ground, which is refined for use as a fuel for motor vehicles and in generators to produce light and heat, and as a solvent.
Wood which is used as fuel for fires.
A photographic slide of a colour (polychromatic) image.

A jug that incorporates a practical joke or conundrum into its construction. A combination of cut-outs in the body and hollow handles and tubes render conventional use impossible. The puzzle being to work out how to empty it. (Source: MPRG)
A machine used for the loading and unloading of grain to and from a warehouse
The space occupied by or left where a post has been.
A plan of a house where the buildings are around at least three sides of a quadrilateral courtyard.
A box in which letters are deposited on delivery.
A building used specifically for testing the boilers of railway engines, both hydraulically and with live steam.
A reservoir or tank used to hold a supply of water for fire-fighting purposes in the event of the main supply being damaged or cut off.
17th/18th century lightly armed privateer, usually either a 'Dunkirker' or Dutch.
An aerial photograph taken at an angle other than 90 degrees to a feature in the landscape.
A room in which domestic appliances and facilities for cleaning are stored.
A light, usually encased and mounted upon brackets, often used outdoors.  It may be powered by gas, electricity or house a candle.
A structure indicated by the presence of post holes and of uncertain interpretation.
Casing for electrical connections: an enclosed and protected box inside which electrical circuits are interconnected or branched for distribution.
One of a number of tiles cemented together to form pillars supporting the floor above a hypocaust.
An heraldic design depicting armorial bearings.
A structure used for the production of hydraulic power. A head of water was raised at the top of the tower by means of pumps. Used for powering machinery.
A workshop or foundry where iron articles are made by casting molten material into moulds.
A written work issued in parts, with the intention of creating a completed sequence.
Hard, durable, dark grey stone, the purest native form of silica, which can either be used decoratively or as a main material. Predominantly found in East Anglia and the South East.
A cross erected within a town, usually funded by the inhabitants.
A vessel which runs aground and does not get off.

A place of worship and meeting hall for members of the Salvation Army, an evangelical sect founded by William Booth in Nottingham in 1865 and derived from Wesleyan Methodism. They rejected the sacraments and adopted a quasi-military rhetoric and style.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
A vertical partition used to separate one area from another.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G..  Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
A small fast warship powered by diesel or petrol engines. Built during World War II for coastal patrol work and anti shipping missions close in shore
A high speed, single acting compound steam engine with centrally placed piston valves controlling the distribution of steam.
A schedule of work in sufficient detail for it to be quantifiable, implemented and monitored.
A type of foundation in the form of a post sunk into the ground to support a building platform.
A colonnade all around the exterior of a building or an interior space such as a courtyard.
A capital warship lightly armoured but with the same gun armament and stem turbine propulsion as a DREADNOUGHT BATTLESHIP.
All vessels, use more specific type where known.
Personal apparatus for telling the time, worn either as jewellery or purely functional in nature, usually on the wrist or as a suspended fob.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A pillar housing a transformer to convert AC electricity supply, for use by electrified transport systems or for domestic purposes.
A camping place set aside for the use of caravans.

Structural elements (parts of hull etc.) or fixtures and fittings (masts, etc.) lost during a naval engagement without incurring the actual loss of a ship. May also be used as a monument type for expended ammunition (e.g. shells, cannonballs).
A container for ointments or perfume.
A hard, white, fine-grained substance forming the main part of the tusks of elephants, walruses, hippos and narwhals.
A horizontal beam over an opening to support a wall.
