A protected parachute store similar in design to the 6351/37 except constructed wholly from reinforced concrete.
A wooden framework with holes for the head and hands, in which the offender stood.
An area in a church, sometimes defined by screens, containing a shrine. Also a shrine, usually portable, containing religious relics.
Fishing smack specialised both for working shoal water and for trawling for shrimp, predominantly in and around Morecambe Bay.
A mill for shredding cloth, for use in flock paper, etc.
A pool and ancilliary buildings used for the housing of dolphins.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by wagons on rails on a road.
A scraper with retouch at right angles to the bulb of percussion.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Templars for administrative purposes on their estates.
A water pond in which lilies are grown.
A floating bridge, generally temporary, whose decks are supported on low flat-bottomed or hollow floats.
The second subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.
People who serve as members of an army.
A building, or part of a building, for the milling and pressing of cider apples to produce cider (or pears for perry) and for storing the drink in barrels.
A marker of some form used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.

A pit lined with the bony cores of animal horns. Thought to date from the 17th/18th centuries and believed to have been used in the tanning industry although some may have been used for casting cannon.
An apparatus for weighing, usually consists of a beam on a pivot with a means of supporting the object to be weighed on one side and weights on the other.
Buildings, engineering constructions and machinery, used for the purpose of supplying a town, etc, with water distributed through pipes.
A prefabricated structure of a light timber frame with external weather boarded walls and a timber felt covered roof. They were used as barrack blocks during WWII. Manufactured by Magnet Limited.
A mooring, usually consisting of a concrete plinth, to which a barrage balloon was attached.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
A pillow-shaped, flat topped rectangular mound often surrounded by a shallow ditch used to farm rabbits.
Space used for storage in the roof.
A supporting structure for drilling machinery used in the extraction of or prospecting for mineral oils.
A building with an aisle on one side only.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group who were formed in Staffordshire and influenced by American evangelical ideas and who left the Methodists in 1811.
Also known as a half-beam engine, named for the characteristic nodding action of the overhead beam which is supposed  to resemble the action of the rear legs of the grasshopper.
A factory or works principally engaged in the refining or manufacture of TNT.
A pit or tank where the chemicals used in tanning are washed from the animal hides.
A storage facility used for the accommodation and dispersal of vehicles. Often used by the military and emergency services.
A pit which shows evidence for having been used for cooking. Often contains charcoal, burnt bone fragments etc.
Draining of waterlogged coastal or river margin land to provide building or agricultural land.
The principal Anglican church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with railway transport.
Decorative ornamentation consisting of alternating bead shapes with small, elliptical forms resembling reels
A vessel which has been dismantled for the purpose of removal from the shore after stranding.
A structure providing protection from the elements to passengers waiting to board a ferry service at a dock, riverside, harbour or quay.

A technique that measures the amount of time it takes pulses of  electromagnetic energy sent into the ground, from a transmitter, to reflect back from the interfaces between layers and other subsurface features in order to produce a subsurface profile.
The edge of a roof that hangs over the wall.
Metal used primarily for roof coverings and window fittings. It is easy to work, can be worked cold and does not rust which makes it suitable for holding or repelling water.
A building associated with funerary rites and burials.

Court where sessions were held periodically in each county in England, for the purpose of administering civil and criminal justice. Presided over by itinerant judges acting under certain special commissions. Abolished 1971 and in 1972 replaced by Crown C.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
Site where steel is produced from molten pig iron using a Bessemer Converter, a development from the cementation and crucible steel-making techniques .
A ravine formed by using water to reveal or exploit a vein.
Dating to the reign of Elizabeth 1st of England.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.
A structure which can be an area within a building, a separate building within a complex or a detached architectural component of a building
Small vessel built or adapted to lay and recover anti submarine nets in harbours and anchorages.
A dock or basin, often inland, used for mooring yachts and other small pleasure craft.
Tableware manufactured from any kind of ceramic and either carried as an export cargo or for the benefit of crew and/or passengers on board ship.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cistercian order.
The residence of a teacher, often on the site of a school.
A flour milling machine using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.
A unifacially worked early stone tool.
A building or group of buildings, often surrounded by a system of fortifications, used as a residential and training site by members of an armed force.
A container in which the Sacrament is carried.
A container for the storage of tobacco.
Instruments used within geometry, geometrical drawing and navigational mapping.
A brittle silvery metallic element used in the manufacture of many alloys.
A place where refreshments or meals may be obtained.

A purple or violet variety of quartz often used in jewelry. Amethyst is a semi-precious stone which owes its violet colour to irridation, iron impurities, and the presence of  trace elements, which result in complex crystal lattice substitutions.
A device to hold and rotate food against a heat source during cooking.
A platform or other structure for the use of a band of musicians.
A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.
A small brush used fro cleaning teeth.
A mug with straight sides flaring outwards from the base towards the rim. (Source: MPRG)
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in textile making.
A structure, often movable, used as a platform for the display of a traders goods in a market.
Hard, transparent, often coloured mineral. Can be found on its own as crystals and veins but also as a major constituent of rocks such as granite. Often used decoratively.
A small vessel propelled on water by an engine, oars or sails.
A plan form of a structure or building.
A machine used in a mill to remove bran scales and flour from grits or middlings.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
Roofing material consisting of stems or stalks of wheat, rye, oats or barley separated from grain and laid flat in 'yealms' which form an overlapping surface which sheds water.
For the storage and recharging of battery-powered miners lamps.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
An apparatus for weighing people, animals or things.
A building used for the storage and distribution of civilian respirators and Air Raid Precautions equipment.
A type of engine house creating power by means of compressed air, typically associated with collieries where it is used for raising coal.

Any boat used to transfer crew from shore to an offlying vessel. May also carry the catch from a fishing boat to shore. Used as special boats by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution for conveying crew from the beach to a moored lifeboat.
A furnace where metal is manufactured from ore.
A short stabbing weapon, designed to be fixed to the muzzle of a musket or rifle, even in some cases to pistols. Some were designed to be used both fixed to long guns and independent of them.
An object worn, or carried, to cover the face.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on an English mother house.
A site where clay is both extracted and fired to produce bricks.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
A conical or flat-topped tip of waste discarded from a mine or similar site.
Buildings and structures associated with the acquisition of electronic signals for the purpose of intelligence gathering.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.
Man made structure to contain tidal waters, often part of a LIDO, bathing or swimming complex at the sea edge.
An establishment with automatic washing machines available for public use.
A type of slender support carried on a corbel.
A mine from which potash is obtained. Potash is a deposit of potassium carbonate: the only example of a potash mine in the country is at Boulby in Cleveland.
Outdoor site for domestic washing, etc.
Equipment used to grip an object.
A ridged roof that slopes on all four sides.
A massive hammer of wood, stone or iron.
A cruck which is set in solid masonry above floor level but stretching a long way down the wall.
A steam engine with a horizontal beam connecting the piston and crank.
A steeple in which the spire resembles a crown.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
A metal reinforcer worn on the sole or heel of a boot.
A protective structure, often made of sandbags with reinforcement, designed to protect aircraft at airfields from enemy attack.
A pier used to raise a structure or building above ground floor level so that there is open space beneath the structure
A staircase where the vertical members are placed at the ends of flights to support the strings, handrails, trimmers and bearers.
The flat slab at the top of a capital.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the sale, exchange &/or storage of goods or services. Includes commercially operated catering establishments & lodging premises.

An offshore station, equipped with a fixed electronic radio navigation and positioning system such as Hyperfix. The transmission principle are pulsed and phase comparisons systems. Superceded by Global Positioning System in 1994.
A block, usually of iron, upon which objects are shaped and hammered eg in smithing.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A hollow ball for containing aromatic substances eg perfume.
A mixed-flow reaction water turbine, developed in the USA in 1840 by James Bichino Francis, in which water enters the runner radially and leaves axially.
The taking of samples at regular intervals from the surface of a study area in order to retrieve information on the different chemical elements present.
A refuse heap of discarded shells.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used for storage and as workshops, cinemas etc during WWII. Designed at Romney House, London by the Directorate of Fortifications & Works.
The official residence of a dean.
A type of bridge which has machinery and movable elements, eg. to allow vessels to pass.
An automata or water device which surprises the unwary onlooker with water. A feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
An oil obtained by the distillation of wood and used as a solvent and paint thinner and in some medical preparations.
A small structure comprising of a 'shelf' of wood or metal sitting on pillars and erected for the benefit of porters to allow them to rest their burdens.
Zinc, now mainly used for smelted zinc but has been used to include zinc ores.
A fine net worn over the hair.
A building where advice, counselling and medical treatment is available.
Fine-grained, non-humified, organic mud formed under water. Principally composed of plant material, typically of faecal origin.
A tunnel used to test scale model propellers and hulls to consider the impact of caviation on wake, propulsion, vibration and noise.
The top stone of an arch which holds it all in place.
A small room off a bedroom, usually in eighteenth century houses, in which a person would have their wig powdered.
A tower built to display a large clock.
A method of floor construction in which sections of joists run at right-angles to one another.
An educational institution for the training of teachers.
Originally a fence against which trees and shrubs were grown. Later used to describe a row of trees and shrubs forming a hedge clipped into a green wall.
A round barrow featuring a low, wide mound surrounded by a ditch which may be accompanied by an external bank.
A projecting starched frill worn around the neck, especially 16th century.
Pleated skirt, usua;;y of a tartan material, worn by men and women.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice shooting by aerial, seaborne or land mounted weapons.
A curved structural span which is supported at the sides or ends. May vary in shape from the horizontal flat arch through semicircular and semielliptical forms.
A large store where wool is stored.
A nonconformist church for the followers of Edward Irving.
Seaside structure, usually consisting of a manmade retaining wall that keeps a relatively large area of the tidal water partitioned off for controlled boating or swimming.
A long slim candle used for igniting objects.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
Limestones formed during the Carboniferous period. Many are cut, polished and used as marble.
A vessel for carrying a cargo of coal in bulk.
A pan with a perforated bottom for straining or rinsing food.
A hopper for the storage of ash.
The residence of an employee with the duty of maintaining a section of a railway or road.
Includes worsted and other wool-related textiles.
A ward in a workhouse for vagrants
A factory or works engaged in the manufacture of the explosive guncotton. They may be found as separate factories or form part of a cordite factory.
A hut, usually built as part of a complex on a military base or airfield and used for the recreation of military personnel.

A sheet or board made from a mixture of thin strips of wood and cement which are bound together through compression within a mould. Woodwool slabs are used for roof or wall cladding, providing fire resistance, and heat and sound insulation.
A flat, level area of ground within a garden. Often raised and accessed by steps.
An open area, often paved or cobbled, surrounded by buildings and accessible to the public.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
Dairy produce formed from the curds of milk, coagulated by rennet and pressed into a solid mass.
A building for the storage and processing of grain crops and for housing straw, farm equipment and occasionally livestock and their fodder. Use more specific type where known.
A fatty substance derived from the fat of animals used in cooking.
An instrument for measuring magnetic forces, especially the strength of terrestrial magnetism.
A cylindrical device using ceramic or metallic balls to grind materials like ores, chemicals, ceramic raw materials and paints
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A building or site used by the armed forces for the storage and issuing of military stores and materials.
A building used to dry wool in.
A building, site or structure associated with various racing sports.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
A place where sheep are washed in a chemical bath to control  the parasites of sheep. To conserve the poisonous chemicals the bath is usually small and are not allowed to enter any watercourse.
A small pin or stud worn in the lapel, often decorative.
A bent piece of metal or bone, often with a barb, which is tied to a line and used to catch fish.
A ventilating fan house with an expanding chimney.
Scenes of snowfall or lying snow.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
An item used to fasten a cloak either to another garment or to itself.
A large container used for the process of cleansing and thickening cloth by beating and washing.

Cones of solid concrete usually 3 feet 6 inches in diameter x 2 feet high which, when placed in rows or groups were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
Parts which make up a maritime vessel.
A bank formed at the end of a field by soil which, loosened by the plough, gradually moves down slope through a combination of gravity and erosion.

A site, usually with docks and control buildings, used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military vessels or the administration of the Royal Navy. May also include accommodation buildings for personnel.
A sign, situated near a road or bridge, indicating a toll.
A soft, heavy, malleable metal, often obtained from the mineral galena. Traditionally used in the construction industry for roofing and plumbing.
Residential development, including housing, flats, tower blocks etc. For single houses use: building construction
Area in a brewery used for the production of beer by the Burton Union method.
A device for removing the core from fruit.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cluniac order.
A small moulding on the top of the architrave in the Doric order.
A building used for meetings and worship by a religious community trying to propogate its faith in an area.
An object made up of a wick surrounded by wax or tallow which burns slowly to provide light.
Purpose-built lodgings for assize court judges. Early 19th century.
A window divided into lights by mullions.

A building that houses material that can be used to facilitate the study of a site, landscape or an historical event/period. Such centres are often found in close proximity to the sites and/or landscapes that they seek to encourage the study of.
A roof consisting of trusses that have a pair of brackets supporting the hammer posts that in turn support the rafters.
Objects used for looking after hair.
A storage container designed to contain corn.
The object used to make impressions in wax as seals.
An enclosure or niche in a library or cloister used for study.
A concrete marker placed to indicate the direction of a target on a bombing range to aircraft.
Steel which has been formed into sheets.
The space between the high altar and the east wall or chapel in a large church, and often the area west of a Monks' choir.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.

A small bowl on a pedestal base above a drip-tray or saucer. It may have a wick lip at the rim. May have pierced lugs projecting form the rim for suspension of a handle, spout or vertical loop handle linking bowl and saucer. (Source: MPRG)
Objects which cannot be assigned to any one particular class, or the function of which is unknown.
A factory making baize for snooker and gaming tables.
Use for vessels registered in New Zealand.
The piece of stone or flint remaining after blades have been produced.
A very long trough laid between the rails of a railway track to allow a suitably equiped steam engine to scoop up water whilst in motion.
A building housing material used to explain the significance of a site or landscape to the public e. g. an archaeological site or nature reserve.
A building or room where railway tickets may be bought and administrative duties associated with a railway are conducted.
A watch office designed for bomber satellite station comprising a long, temporary brick hut with a watch office, operations room and crew briefing room.
A boarding or day school for children who had committed minor crimes or who lived in circumstances where they were likely to commit crime.
A site where guns, mortars or searchlights are mounted. Use specific type where known.
A club or cafe where popular music is played for dancing.

Technically a quick setting hydraulic cement or lime,but term has been adapted to denote cement made from burning lumps of marl found in London clay,a technique adopted for C19th building work. Name not intended to denote a relationship with Roman period
By-product or waste, resulting from an industrial process.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with water transport.
A bit which scoops out material.
A hiding place for stores, often underground, used by smugglers.
A building from which the firing of torpedoes can be controlled and evaluated.
A pier where passsengers can embark and disembark and goods can be transferred to and from vessels.
An area within a building open to the public where light meals and drinks can be purchased and consumed.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
A building material used for coating walls and ceilings. Plaster can refer to gypsum plaster (also known as plaster of Paris), lime plaster, or cement plaster.
A building housing a Finnish-style steam bath.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
A place where sandstone is excavated.
A stone or metal post that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
A chalet designed in the Swiss style, eg. Kenwood, London.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
A weapon with a long shaft and a three pronged head.
A band of leather, cloth etc worn usually around the waist to support clothing, carry weapons, pouches, tools etc or as a decoration.
Curved, interlocking roof tile of S-shaped section usually made of clay or concrete.

A large hilltop or hillslope enclosure in South West England, located close to rock outcrops, and surrounded by one or more circuits of stone built walls. All are prehistoric; some are definitely Neolithic.
A tower which rises above the space at the intersection of the nave, chancel and transepts of a church. Usually pierced by windows to provide light directly to the area below.
A building where a stallion is kept.
Pertaining to or deriving from a living organism. See ANIMAL Class list for narrow terms.

Rocket projector site with a circular or octagonal concrete holdfast, 1.5m across, surrounded by a 4.6m radius octagonal concrete surround. Six such rocket projectors were arranged in a 3 x 2 grid. Personnel shelters placed midway between each site.
40mm gun emplacement created between 24th-26th June 1944 as part of the fourth deployment of Diver LAA guns to the Kentish Gun Belt. Each site had an extant searchlight battery.
A maritime monument where the fabric of a vessel has collapsed, leaving the hull structure flat on the sea bed but not widely dispersed.
A report detailing the results of an archaeological excavation.
A boundary marker for the payment of tax or duty.
A planned administrative capital for local government which provided amenities for the Roman and peregrine (non-Roman) inhabitants of the town.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance to a tomb.
A communal residence of secular vicars whose duties included the education of choristers attached to cathedrals and collegiate churches.
A shaped piece of wood that makes up a barrel, key etc.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.
A room to display various items of hardware and ironmongery.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A piece of stone or timber with a small cup shaped depression in its upper surface, set into the ground to fasten a door, gate, window etc to allow it to open and shut.
A very short brace between post and tiebeam, or post and wall plate.
An opening in a structure which is arched.
A site where artefacts are manufactured from jet.
A decorative piece connected to the altar.
The land mass comprising, the continents of North and Central America and South America. Use more specific type.
A hard silica rich rock, black or brown coloured, commonly found in nodular form.
Group of fresh water crustaceans which include the water fleas (Daphnia ssp.) the egg cases (ephippia) of which are found in archaeological deposits.
A thin masonry facing or cladding employed to conceal the surface or structure behind it.
Steam-powered torpedo boat developed in the early 20th century, and used in the First World War, a development of the torpedo boat destroyer, and distinct from the motor torpedo boat of WWII.
A specialist unit within a hospital complex. It may be a separate building or sometimes linked by a corridor or covered walkway to a main building.
A school where young children, usually under the age of seven, are taught.
Sites where controlled chemical reactions are employed to help manufacture domestic products.
A form of temporary horseshoe, of Roman date, used when unshod animals were brought onto metalled roads. Usually consists of flat plate, winged sides and hooked heel.
A beam that runs the width of a building.
A place where sand is extracted from surface workings.
A small support designed to help support a weight, such as that of a projecting member.
A large board, often attached to the side of a building, on which advertisements can be displayed. Use for external structures only.

Small, light, fast, all-purpose craft designed primarily for inland use. Generally flat-bottomed, often with rocker; sharp bow, sharp or transom stern, lapstrake or carvel planking. Propelled by oars, sails or motor. Used for fishing and leisure.
An engine, introduced in Germany 1748 for use in mines, worked by high pressure water.
An architrave surrounding a door, window or niche interrupted by large blocks of stone, and often by a massive keystone set under a pediment. Named after the architect James Gibbs (1682-1754).
A Mark 2A aircraft which has undergone slight modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 10cm or less. They were highly accurate radars and gave better sea level coverage than the earlier Chain Home Low stations.
A building housing a winching mechanism.
A board on the lower edge of a sloping roof which protects the top of the external wall.
Block, often made of concrete, to secure smaller maritime craft. Many were made during the Second Wold War to secure craft which were to be used in the D-Day landings.
A pit filled with rubble, etc., into which rain or waste water flows in order to disperse into the surrounding soil.
Animals and products made from the carcasses and hides of dead animals.
A building over a well housing machinery for raising the water. Often consisting of a DONKEY WHEEL or HORSE GIN.
A metallic substance made by combining two or more elements at least one of which is a metal. Use more specific terms where known.

Management Plans help pull together an understanding of significance to evidence the conservation and management of heritage assets. From this informed basis, plans are then used to develop programmes of repair, restoration or to draw up proposals for change. Management Plans should be structured to meet the needs of the specific property/site and designed to be used for every day reference by staff managing the site. Management Plans not only pull together and analyse the history of a site or landscape, they can also be an important record in their own right.
An engine house used to pump water to the top of an ACCUMULATOR TOWER.
A building used for broadcasting radio programmes for public entertainment. Often includes recording studios, transmitters and offices. Use RADIO STATION for non-broadcasting uses eg. Military.
Part of a church in front of the choir and usually enclosed by tombs, screens etc.
A machine for applying protective size to yarn intended for warp
A fitting specifically functioning as the strengthener and support for the end of a strap of leather or fabric.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
In churches a niche, or shelf, within or beside a piscina, or a table for the sacramental elements and vessels. (Source: Pevsner Glossary)
A pipe, usually of reinforced concrete or metal, which delivers pressurized water from a dam to hydraulic turbines.
A slender and elegant base usually of Attic type with two tori, two scotiae and two astragals.
A bridge that incorporates a span that moves upwards vertically to provide a passageway for navigation.
A type of textile mill found in Lancashire in the 19th century. Small businesses paid the owner rent for space for their machines, and power from the mill engine or waterwheel.
A structure used to dry peat on.
A stone-lined pit in which seaweed was burnt. The calcined ashes were used in the manufacture of soap and glass, amongst other things.
A raised platform or stage for public speaking or conducting an orchestra. Also a platform for supporting cameras during filming.

A type of stoneware jug dating to the 16th and 17th centuries, popularly known as a Bellarmine jug, shaped in the figure of a bearded man. They were produced in the Cologne region, particularly Frechen.
Specify in Description using: path, road, track, bridge, lay-by etc.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A box crane which uses hydraulic power
A small gateway cut through the curtain wall or its flanking towers. Used primarily as an outlet for counter-attacking forces.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.
A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.
A projecting spout to throw water from a gutter away from the wall, frequently decorated with grotesque figures to spew out evil away from the House of God.
A building or site deemed to be importance locally. Local listing status is a planning consideration.
A wig, toupee or section of extra hair designed to replace or enhance the wearer's real hair giving greater quantity, bulk or length.
A factory where pencils are manufactured.
Remains of any part of a nut including the nutshell. The definition of nut as used here is any woody fruit or seed.
A mill for producing abravive papers and cloths such as glass paper or emery cloth.
An object which is propelled by force away from a launcher, which can include from a human.
A device with a spirally twisted shaft, pointed end and handle for removing corks from bottles.

This is a pit used in the glass industry for the production of cylinder glass. The only surviving examle in England is at the Hartley Wood Glasworks, Sunderland. It is a feature of 19th century and later glassworks
A plan form in which pavilions lead off from a spiral corridor.
A small, heavy object used for keeping loose papers in place.
Use for vessels registered in Antigua.
A building or set of buildings and structures where power, especially electrical or mechanical, is generated. Use more specific type where known.
A building housing the acoustic detection equipment for a sound mirror
A priory of double order of Fontevrault nuns and brethren.
A working hospital, often near or associated with a university, where doctors and nurses are trained.
A large pit formed by, and for, the extraction of iron ore.

A type of military building associated with military airfields, where air crews were briefed for missions. The room could be a seperate building or part of an operations block and are built of varying types of temporary brick or nissen hut constructions.
An tool used to separate flax fibres from the wood and bark following retting.
An oval or circular decorative feature often bearing an illustration or portrait in light relief.
A straight rod, made of glass, plastic or other materials, used  to agitate or mix chemicals, pigments, beverages or other fluids or substances.
A flask with a rounded, almost spherical shape. (Source: MPRG)
Buildings and structures associated with the manufacture of rope.
A deep gutter, drain or sink.
A structure used for the housing and servicing of aircraft.
An apparatus for burning refuse to ashes.
A marker used in the playing of a game.
Narrow strips of wood used in the building industry.
A plant used for the manufacture of tubes and tubing, from wrought iron or steel.
A strong unbleached cloth manuifactured from hemp, flax or similarly coarse yarn. Used mainly in the manufacture of sails, tents and for painting on.
A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently low to be seen below low lying cloud. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a Low Light is usually accompanied by a HIGH LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
The part of an organ or similar instrument into which air is pushed then is emitted through the pipes.
A constructed space beneath the surface of the ground.
A portable indoor air raid shelter in the form of a steel topped table, often with wire meshing around the sides.
A signpost, usually placed at a juntion or crossroads, bearing a number of individual signs radiating outward from the post to indicate locations in several directions.
A town founded as an act of government by charter to house Roman or Latin citizens, usually retired legionaires who had been granted land within a territorium.
A drill where the bit is twisted by means of a bow with the string wound around the shaft of the drill.
An office at which the registration of marriages, births and deaths are recorded, and in which marriage ceremonies may take place.
A training college where workers can attend classes in vocational subjects. The classes are often day-release and sanctioned by the employer.
A mould used to cast coins.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or "navvys".
A piece of forest land converted into arable.
A place where silicate rock was extracted to be shaped for use as whetstones. Examples can be found in Derbyshire and the Blackdown Hills in Devon.
A works site making and/or maintaining drive belts for industrial power.
A bell mounted on an anchored vessel, buoy, headland, rock etc and rung as a warning to mariners in foggy weather.
A type of thermoplastic polymer which is versatile and cheap, often referred to as PVC. This includes plasticized PVC and unplasticized PVC (uPVC).
A bed raised above the level of the surrounding walks. A common feature of medieval and Renaissance gardens.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Augustinian order.
An oval or circular structure with seats rising in tiers around a central open space. Used for religious ceremonies, entertainment, training and armed combat contests.
Bleach works or bleach house for bleaching of textiles, etc.
A device used to lock another object.
A half or whole baluster applied to a wall or pedestal, thus described as engaged.
A building or room used for the repair and maintenance of machinery in a large complex, such as a hospital, school or factory.
A vault where the bay is divided by diagonal and transverse ribs into four cells or webs.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
Niche intended for pigeons or other birds to nest in, allowing the squabs and eggs to be harvested. Found inside specially built dovecotes and in the walls of other buildings.
A shaft, separate to the main working shaft, used to pump water out of the mine workings.
The heartwood of a leguminous tree from which an extract is obtained. The extract being used for dyeing.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
An indoor alley for playing bowls or skittles.
A purlin that rests against the lower surface of a principal rafter and is supported by a queen post, collar or raking strut.
A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.
A board, wall painting or other structure displaying advice, giving information or directions
A hydraulic machine used to drive a pillar crane.
An auger bit which creates its hole by drilling into the material.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A semaphore signalling tower on a railway.
Use for deposits formed in caves.
A crane with a projecting arm, usually one that can be raised and lowered.
The course or channel of a river or stream preserved as a geological feature.
An arch whose purpose is to arrest or prevent structural movement in a building.
Buildings and structures associated with signal communication.
The systematic survey and recording of graveyards and burial spaces recording the position of individual grave markers and the detail of any inscriptions.

A freelance boat used off the south and east coasts of England to provide passing ships with pilots, supplies, new anchors and other gear. Some helped sailing ships and barges get underway. Generally lug-rigged. Also used for fishing. Half decked.
A large board found at sporting events, erected so as to be seen by the spectators, on which the score of a game is kept.
A labyrinthine garden feature, common during the 16th and 17th centuries, created by cutting shallow pathways into deep lawns.
A vertical shaft, usually with an internal ladder, allowing access to a sewer or underground counduit for inspection and maintenance.
A plain stone course, sometimes projecting, above a cornice and counterbalancing the cantilevered sections of stone, or at the base of a building.
A chapel for followers of Benjamin Ingham after he left the Moravians prior to joining the Sandamanians.
A temporary kiln, in which the pots are stacked and baked in a pit underneath a bonfire.
A flexible container, usually leather, for the storage and transportation of wine.
An ore works at which gold was separated from the ore by the addition of mercury.
A school established by the National Society which was founded in 1811 to promote the education of the poor.
A place of worship and residence for followers of Buddha.
A chamber for heating or baking objects.
A termination, either in the form of a decorative feature or a right-angle applied to the end of the moulding, of a label, dripstone or string course.
One of the rolls forming the sides of an ionic capital, joining the volutes of the front and rear faces.
A room intended for, and usually equipped to aid, the performance of ablutions.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
The unarticulated remains of the body of a human being. If articulated use inhumation.
A communal wash area, sometimes a dedicated outbuilding, or facility, such as a basin or trough, used by monks.
A long shafted weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or as a missile.
A railway station or platform built specifically for the loading and unloading of goods.
A building containing mechanically powered ore crushers or rollers.
An archaeological component which cuts, overlies or abuts other features such as ditches, pits and building foundations.

A large communal room often occupying the full height of the building, used for functions such as meetings, entertainments etc. Traditionally found in medieval buildings but also found in later buildings emulating medieval architecture.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of stone. Includes preparation processes.
A structure for the storage of brine prior to processing, by evaporation, to extract salt.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.
An earthen mound, usually within an ornamental garden, on which a tree was planted.
Covering and accessories worn on the body.
A building containing celestial telescopes in which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
A loft, balcony or gallery, in a hall or church, for the use of musicians.
A wool combing machine for very fine wools.
A small body of water, either natural or artificial.
A strong, sweet fortified wine made in Portugal.
A purpose-built building with a brick tower constructed on one end, based on drawing number (9294/42). Used for the drying of parachutes.
Small crustaceans ranging in size from 0.2mm to 30mm and possessing a bivalve carapace or 'shell'.
A group of buildings, or part of a works, housing apparatus used in the process of fermentation.
A frame containing glass tiles or bricks set into a pavement to allow the lighting of basement areas.
A building containing a bier; a movable stand on which a corpse, often in a coffin, is placed prior to burial.
A decorative moulding in a diamond shape.
A brownish-red mineral commonly used as a semi-precious gemstone. A variety of the silica mineral chalcedony coloured by impurities of iron oxide.
Sites and buildings used for the storage or equipment, ordnance or vehicles. Use more specific term.
A decorative structure of wood stone or metal, incorporating a shelf, surrounding the opening of a fireplace.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
Mark 6 or the sixth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A stone on which a monarch traditionally sat during the coronation ceremony.
A matzevah from the Ashkenazi group of Jews descended from medieval Jewish communities of the Rhineland and Eastern Europe.  Characterised by upright headstones with Hebrew Inscriptions
A stud used for fastening an item usually used for clothing.
A hook with a spiked tang which allows it to be driven into a vertical surface.
Specify in Description using terms not included in the above

An instrument for determining, measuring or setting out right angles, usually consisting of two pieces or arms set at right angles to each other, but sometimes with the arms hinged or pivoted to measure any angle.
A building where jazz music is performed. Often situated in small venues to afford the intimacy of the musicians performing in close proximity to the audience.
A large, decorative garden ornament resembling a vase.
A building containing apparatus for the removal of large pieces of detritus from a water supply.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A thin, pointed implement used for sewing with a hole at the blunt end for threading the sewing material.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
A government office used for the collecting of excise tax/duty.
A translucent paper, which when laid over an existing image, permits the image to be seen and/or traced.
A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.
A path that is roofed over.
A mixture of paraffins distilled from petroleum and used as a fuel and solvent.
Wood which is soft or easily cut, particularly the wood of coniferous trees.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
A heated room within a monastery where monks could warm themselves.
A water point with a device to regulate the flow of water.
Recording of a complete broadcast radio programme.
Solid bars or ingots of silver.
A chapel where Roman Catholics worship.
Commercially manufactured sodium carbonate used in glass and soap making.
A room containing a toilet, water closet etc..
An S-shaped ornamental bracket with a greater height than projection.
A stone with a cross carved into the surface.
An area, often a village, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to stop the advance of an enemy force and to hold out for an agreed period of time.

Special concrete loading ramps nicknamed 'hards' had been constructed along river banks, beaches and inlets to enable organised embarkation onto various types of landing craft to take place, irrespective of tides.
Power generation by releasing stored water through a turbine driving a generator.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
An impulse water turbine comprising a wheel with hemispherical cups arranged around the circumference using high water pressure to revolve the wheel.
A rampart or other defensive entrenchment.

Condition	

No demolition or development shall take place until a written scheme of investigation (WSI) has been submitted to and approved by the local planning authority in writing.  For land that is included within the WSI, no demolition or development shall take place other than in accordance with the agreed WSI, which shall include the statement of significance and research objectives, and 
A.	The programme and methodology of site investigation and recording and the nomination of a competent person(s) or organisation to undertake the agreed works 
B.	Where appropriate, details of a programme for delivering related positive public benefits
C.	The programme for post-investigation assessment and subsequent analysis, publication & dissemination and deposition of resulting material. This part of the condition shall not be discharged until these elements have been fulfilled in accordance with the programme set out in the WSI

Informative	

The written scheme of investigation will need to be prepared and implemented by a suitably professionally accredited archaeological practice in accordance with Historic England’s Guidelines for Archaeological Projects in Greater London. This condition is exempt from deemed discharge under schedule 6 of The Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015.
Prehistoric structure consisting of three or more standing stones in close proximity to each other, forming an unroofed approximately rectangular structure open in one direction.
A burial monument, usually of Iron age date, comprising a small square ditched enclosure surrounding a central interment, which may also have been covered by a mound.
Marshal of the Royal Air Force
A tool used in the separation of fibres from the bark in flax working.
A fortified keep in the form of a tower, used as a last refuge or defence. If a component of a larger site, use KEEP.
A short timber linking two pieces of timber.
Decorative ornamentation of a flower or leaf.

A building, similar in style to a telephone exchange but smaller. They were used to compensate for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.
A musical instrument with a toothed cylinder.
Stonemason's term for any easily worked sedimentary rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
A group of related buildings, primarily with a domestic function, which is arranged along a principle axis such as a main road or routeway.
A rough shelter or dwelling, sometimes used to house cattle.
An object that is to become a padlock key. It has the correct shape but has yet to be cut to fit the lock.
A ship used for laying cables (often telephone cables) along the sea bed.

Condition

No demolition shall take place until a written scheme of historic building investigation (WSI) has been submitted to and approved by the local planning authority in writing.  For buildings that are included within the WSI, no demolition or development shall take place other than in accordance with the agreed WSI, which shall include the statement of significance and research objectives, and 
A. The programme and methodology of historic building investigation and recording and the nomination of a competent person(s) or organisation to undertake the agreed works 
B. The programme for post-investigation assessment and subsequent analysis, publication & dissemination and deposition of resulting material. This part of the condition shall not be discharged until these elements have been fulfilled in accordance with the programme set out in the WSI 

Informative	

The written scheme of investigation will need to be prepared and implemented by a suitably professionally accredited heritage practice in accordance with Historic England’s Guidelines for Archaeological Projects in Greater London.

Circular or near circular ditches, usually seen as cropmarks. Use the term where the function is unknown. Ring ditches may be the remains of ploughed out round barrows, round houses, or of modern features such as searchlight emplacements.
Man-made roofless edifice or construction which is intact or substantially intact, with significant survival of original features, even if no longer serving original intended function.
A building used by labourers who clean and pump the docks, and in general, assist shipwrights.
A small warship powered by petrol or diesel engines and armed with torpedo tubes and small guns. Used for coastal anti shipping patrols and warfare in coastal waters.
Any military base where the depot battalion of a regiment is based. Depot battalions maintain the stores and records of a regiment and train new recruits.
A building used to store fertilizers.
A church, sometimes circular in plan, founded by the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templar.
A body of water, building or structure found in a park or garden used as a water supply or ornament. Use more specific type where known.
A garden deliberately planted with white plants and shrubs.
A flight of stairs, situated on a building's exterior, extending to an upper storey.
A building or site used for naval communications.
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
Large semi-subterranean feature often packed with straw for the storage of potatoes and other root crops.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A mechanical structure, consisting of a roller or beam on supports, round which a rope or chain is wound, and used for various purposes, eg. raising a bucket from a well, etc.
A building used for fabricating balloon and airship envelopes.
A building or structure to house railway wagons.
A carved head of Iron Age or Roman date, with uncertain use.
A prepared area of cleared ground on which an aircraft could make an emergency landing.
Houses specifically for men and of chiefly mendicant religious orders. The status of priory is represented in several friaries. Use with PRIORY if required.
Building or structure covering a casting floor or pit.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic temporary site where there is evidence to suggest animal butchery. Evidence may include animal remains and a specialized tool assemblage.
Field survey undertaken to investigate land formation processes often carried out in association with, or in the vicinity of, an archaeological site, or as part of a wider landscape project.
An inclined timber running from a rafter to the inner face of a wall, forming a triangle.
A curved sword designed to cut with used by cavalry.
A mound in excess of 150 metres in diameter, of Late Neolithic date and presumed ritual function, eg. Silbury Hill.
A site associated with the large scale construction of buildings or items manufactured by the building industry.
The earliest subdivision of the Bronze Age.
A metal or ceramic cover for an open fire or hearth.
The process of transcribing the features on an aerial photograph onto a map or plan.
A weight used to sink a fishing net in water.

A building or tower used to communicate information to shipping or other stations using signals such as flags, fires or lights. Roman signal stations took the form of a stone tower surrounded by a ditched enclosure and were used to warn of Saxon raids.
The grains of various plants from which new plants grown.
An area of ground or water containing explosive mines.
Terms included here are for small scale agricultural production. See also FOOD AND DRINK INDUSTRY SITE grouping in INDUSTRIAL class.
A purpose built theatre with a central open yard, dating to the Elizabethan period. Famous examples include The Globe and the Swan.
A container for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
Aircraft hangars designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers to meet the requirement to repair damaged heavy bombers in situ on their airfields.
A night fighter station watch office based on the standard design dor Bomber Satellite Station watch offices
A place of worship for Unitarians, a movement which does not believe in the Trinity but only in the Unity of Christ. Christ was to them just an exalted human teacher.
A gun battery used to signal warnings to ships during bad weather.
A joint which has a splay with a short perpendicular section at each end.
A building in a military complex (eg. naval dockyard, castle, etc.) for preparing gunpowder.
A vehicle with two wheels for carrying loads.
A building used for the daily administration of the Royal Navy.

A stone core made on a large thick flake and characterized by a distinctive, unworked or slightly-shaped handle section. The platform is plain and microblades are detached mainly form the front section of the core. (Source: SARC)
A furnace used for the smelting or reheating of lead.
Man made shallow pool, usually made for children to play in rather than swim.
An enclosed area in front of a structure.
A badge, usually of lead alloy, distributed at various religious shrines of the medieval period and worn on clothing as proof of a pilgrimage and as a talisman.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.
Any building designed or adapted to accommodate trades and manufacturing activity. Use more specific site where known.
A house joined to another to form one building.
Small settlement with no ecclesiastical or lay administrative function.
A costrel with a narrow-mouth and two opposed handles or lugs on the shoulder.
An object to fasten, bind or join one item to another.

A capital with two rows of eight acanthus leaves rising above an astragal;from between the leaves of the upper row rise eight stalks,each surmounted by a calyx from which emerge volutes carryingthe corners of the concave sided abacus and central ornaments
A system of individually enclosed fields.
A sulphate of aluminium and potassium used in the dyeing process as a mordant to increase the intake of dye into a cloth.
A road or way for riding on horseback within a park or estate.
A building adjacent to a monastery where alms were distributed to the poor.
Living and working quarters for the cellarer who was in charge of provisions and the running of the cellar.
A key usually with a long stem with bit, stem and terminal in line.
A large room with fixed seating, designed for lectures.
A building in which potatoes can sprout and germinate.
A single line, or pair of roughly parallel lines, of pits set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes. The pits are not thought to have held posts.
A masonry or brickwork structure projecting above a roof and containing several flues.
A metal or pneumatic rubber rim to a wheel.

A floating breakwater in the form of a hollow cruciform tube 200 ft long by 25 ft high. Bombardons were designed to reduce the height of waves and formed the outer breakwater of the Mulberry harbours.
Hard, protective covering made largely of calcium salts secreted by soft bodied invertebrate animals.
A pump driven by steam power generated by solid fuels.
A set of clippers for finger or toe nails.
A site where weapons and/or explosives are tested experimentally, or are routinely tested as part of a manufacturing quality control process.

A large communal room often occupying the full height of the building, used for functions such as meetings, entertainments etc. Traditionally found in medieval buildings but also found in later buildings emulating medieval architecture.
Fast arterial road with separate carriageways limited to motor vehicles
A mine used for the extraction of any hard dark-coloured rock.
A metal binding or ring fastened around the top of a pile to stop splitting.
A row of balusters, usually made of stone, surmounted by a rail or coping.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
A panel of often decorated wrought-ironwork forming the arch between two gate-piers or standards or above a gate. Also used for an arched support for a lamp-holder between two standards.
A cluster of closely spaced barrows and related monuments (eg. ring ditches). Use with specific barrow-types where known.
The lower, horizontal surface of a room on which people walk. Can also mean a storey of a building.
A recreation ground with usually permanent structure. It usually contains rides such as ghost trains, helter skelter and roller coasters.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.
The final third of the 20th century.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.
A pit dug in the ground used to store meat, grain and other foodstuffs. A common feature of Iron Age farms.
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.
An object which supports or is attached to a curtain.
Used for holding water and washing hands, usually in the shape of an animal.
A building found at the site of a mine. Use specific type where known.
A school for pre-Infant school children, usually 3-5 years old.
A bottle used for the storage of medicine.
A large, level structure, usually of stone or timber, built alongside water to allow warships to moor for the loading and unloading of guns.
The SI derviced unit for wavenumber

Originally obtained by burning limestone to produce quicklime. Now a fine grey powder made from a mixture of limestone and clay used with water and sand to make mortar or with water, sand and aggregate to make concrete.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.
A body suspended so as to be free to swing, especially one regulating the work of a clock.
A decorative moulding depicting an animal or bird head, similar to a beak head moulding but with a shorter, cone-like tongue or beak overlapping the moulding set beneath it.
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
Hut along the coast, which provided shelter for lookouts known as "huers", who kept watch for the pilchard shoals that passed by the coast. Built of stone or wood. Particular common to Cornwall.

An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves and warehouses, where barges, narrow boats and other canal vessels can load and unload goods and supplies.
Tracked, armoured fighting vehicles designed for front-line combat.
Large field or yard used to lay fabrics out ready for bleaching.
Coal dust or slack, especially that of anthracite.
A deliberate miniaturised replica of an object.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote research.
A site where tanks and armoured fighting vehicles can be stored.

A prefabricated temporary structure made of lightweight timber framed panels clad externally with corrugated iron sheets. Used during WWII as officers quarters. Possibly manufactured by Boulton and Paul Limited.
An order in which the columns rise more than one storey in height from the ground or plinth.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of rugby is played.
The entrance to a tramway tunnel.
Establishments authorized to sell or allow the consumption of alcoholic liquors on their premises.
A room with apparatus for washing the hands and face, now often combined with a water closet.
A crane powered by a steam engine.
The plant, Allium sativum, whose bulb is used for culinary purposes.

A fairly regular system of small rectangular fields. Examples may date from the middle Bronze Age to the Roman period. The word 'Celtic' carries no chronological or cultural connotations in this context.

1st or 2nd century Bow Brooch derived from the Colchester. It typically has a pin hinged on a bar held in a cylindrical crossbar, the bow tapering and commonly decorated. Developed examples often have a headloop and enamelled panels.
Clothing, cloth and woven fabric manufactured from either natural or artificial fibres.
An educational establishment where dentistry is taught.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
The upper part of a column or pier.

A wide, shallow, straight-sided, circular DISH, with concentric divisions, formed by vertical partitions, or by concentric grooving around the base. The use is uncertain but the name implies it was designed to hold feed for domestic fowl. (Source: MPRG)
A building used for the daily administration of Civil Defence activities.
A road or way along a ridge of downs or low range of hills.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A temporary brick and timber watch office based on the all-timber 2423/39. Built after 1941 on many Operational Training Unit airfields the design was superseded by 8936/40.
A mine used for the extraction of uranium bearing ores.
A place where knitted fabrics and legware garments were manufactured.
Dutch galliot-rigged vessel used mostly for river trade in Holland but sometimes also for coasting or short sea-going voyages
A structure used to test the aerodynamics of aircraft or vehicles.
The top stone in a gable end.
A barracks including stables and associated buildings housing a cavalry regiment.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55415.
A purpose-built dwelling for the manager of a factory, works, textile mill, etc, often found within the complex itself.
A portable shelter, usually of fabric or leather.
A jar adapted by the addition of a single handle. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A defensive embankment with three or more ditches.
A colonnade where it is exposed to the air on two sides.
A type of small boat that was often carried, or towed by a larger vessel and used as a ship's boat. Dinghies can also be used recreationally as independent sailing vessels.
A fortified tower found at the angle of a castle wall.
A cheap eating and drinking establishment usually serving snacks and non-alcoholic drinks.
A site used for the butchery of animals.
An object marked or shaped by the pressure of another object upon its surface, whether by deliberate process or unintentionally.
A matzevah from the Sephardi group of Jews descended from medieval Jewish communities of the Iberian Peninsular and Northern Africa.  Characterised by flat slabs with Hebrew Inscriptions
A chamfer with a convex bead-like moulding projecting from the chamfer.
A machine for freeing the cotton from the plant.
Monument visible as a below ground man-made structure. Use for tunnels, mineworking, cellars, shelters.
A place of worship for Calvinistic Methodists, Welsh Methodists who split from the established church in 1811.
Purpose built area, incorporating water supply, for the cleaning of carriages, carts, etc.
A small, handled, open vessel, generally with a steep profile, designed to sit partially within a larger vessel and used to warm drinks. (Source: MPRG)

Controlled intrusive fieldwork which examines, records and interprets archaeological deposits, features and structures and, as appropriate, retrieves artefacts and ecofact remains within a specified underwater area.
An establishment dedicated to the study of theology and religious training.
A shelter for the storage of bicycles.
A settlement site enclosed within a timber palisade.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with the transmission & receiving of information. Includes signalling, broadcasting & telecommunications; does not include transport except where there is a specific connection with communication.
Open decked vessel used for sight seeing or pleasure voyages.
Area of land set aside and managed for the preservation of flora, fauna, their natural habitats and physical features.
A column whose shaft is interrupted by square blocks.
A flat, circular stone, usually made of sandstone, used in pairs for grinding corn and other meal.
A specialised form of crane, usually employed on a dockside, featuring a curving, solid jib.
A room where a monarch or similar would meet people, usually in a palace or similar building.

A curfew consisting of a half-bell shape with a raised flange around the cut-away side. A vertical loop handle joins the flange and body. The form is adapted for use against a wall and some are highly decorated. (Source: MPRG)
An 18th century garden building, designed in the form of a classical Doric temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
An urn containing a cremation burial.
A glasshouse used for growing pineapples.
Ore containing a high proportion of tin.
A sitting room fitted with large windows for the purpose of admitting the maximum amount of sunlight.
A principal that has a short, angled section, resembling a knee-joint, at one end.
A site or structure associated with the activities of the Royal Observer Corps. The Corps was reformed on 1 January 1947 and disbanded in 1991.
A large jug, usually rounded with a narrow neck, used for holding liquids.
A device for winding and casting a fishing line, consisting of a revolving spool with a handle attached to a fishing rod.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A place of worship for Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines which accept the Bible as the only source of faith.
A cylindrical, polygonal, or square element of brick, metal or terracotta fixed on top of a chimney stack to extend the flue and improve the extraction of smoke.

A prefabricated structure of cellular hollow plywood 'aero' beams and columns clad with timber framed units of flat asbestos facing sheets and a felt roof. Designed as airfield accommodation that could be reused as post WWII emergency housing.
An area of ground used for the testing of, and practicing with, weapons against fixed and moveable targets.
A tank within a salt works used for storing brine after is has been pumped from underground. The brine is then fed by gravity into the evaporating pans in the Pan House.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A heated room or building used to dry yarn after it has been washed.
A road surface made out of wooden blocks or planks. It was much used in English cities before 1940, but the cost of wooden blocks eventually made it uneconomical.
A shop where meat is sold. Often includes large cold stores for the refrigeration and storage of carcasses and a butchery where the carcass is cut up prior to sale.
Containers in which food and or drink is gathered or processed.
The area of a military base where engineering and maintenance functions are grouped.
A cloth or leather tunic, usually worn underneath metal armour, although sometimes worn by itself.
An open area, often paved or cobbled, surrounded by privately owned buildings and inaccessible to the public.

A decorative, repeating geometric pattern, utilizing motifs such as lozenges, leaves etc., applied to a wall or panel, or incorporated into brickwork by laying different coloured bricks in a series of squares, diamonds.
A small fast warship developed in the late nineteenth century. Armed principally with quick firing guns to destroy enemy torpedo boats.

A monument consisting of a built structure, but which has been demolished so that only a ground plan and foundations, or similar, are thought to remain. Where all below ground traces have also been removed use DESTROYED MONUMENT.
An instrument for taking measurements and describing circles, with two straight arms connected at one end by a movable joint.
A by-product created through a manufacturing process. This does not include the production of tools, for this use tool by product.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
Ornamentation worn specifically for formalised dancing.
A storey of lesser height than those above and below it.
A floor composed of small cubes (tesserae) of variously coloured materials (eg tile, stone, marble). In the Roman period, mosaics often depict a religious theme or symbol.
A vessel used as an ornament, often to hold flowers.
A commercial premises supplying ships with provisions.
A machine that presses apples to extract juice for the production of cider.
A type of kiln, usually built into banking, with a stone lining that was used to produce white coal which was used as fuel in the lead smelting process.
A building of varying designs intended for directing military aviation operations. Normally associated with military airfields.
A piece of land used to grow vegetables to be sold at markets.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.
A stone used to test how genuine an object is by rubbing the object against the stone, particularly used for testing gold and silver.
Second Rate Ship Of The Line
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A tomb designed in the form of a cist or stone box placed over a burial. Its outward form often reproduces the features of the classical sarcophagus or medieval effigy base.
A plate-steel water tower made with two compartments holding 30,000 gallons of water. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 20/40.
A monument erected as a permanent reminder of a military victory. The design usually includes images of the spoils of the battle.
A usually south-facing wall used for the cultivation of fruit plants.
The residence of a telegraph keeper, associated with a telegraph station.
Decorative ornamentation worn on the head.

A metal detector survey can take place as part of a wider survey of archaeological fieldwork programme. Projects that incorporate work on Areas of Archaeological Importance or Scheduled Monuments require Scheduled Monument Consent and/or a Section 42 licence. For a protected wreck site a Licence is also required.
A stable where horses are kept at livery, or are let out for hire.
Long stole worn by Anglican clergy during a service.
A building or site used by the armed forces for the storage and issuing of military stores and materials.
A cup with a marked change of angle in the body wall, generally at the point of maximum girth. (Source: MPRG)
A vertical stone mullion or shaft situated in the centre of a wide doorway to support its lintel or tympanum.

A classical ornamentation featuring foliage, fruits and, unlike Arabesque, human and animal figures, sometimes fantastic or mythological in nature. The term may have originated from the fact that many examples of such ornamentation were found in grottoes.
A raised lawn in a garden or park.
A free-standing house, not joined to another on either side.
A shady cavern built as a garden feature. In the 18th century it usually took the form of an artificial rocky cave or apartment decorated with stalactites and shells in a wild part of the grounds.
A large drainage channel used for improving the land.
A wedge shaped brick used to construct arches.
A stone used to instruct a coachman to unhitch a horse, previously taken on to help pull the coach up a steep gradient.
A site where clay is extracted from the surface of the ground.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
The outer layer of tissue on a tree or woody plant, often used in the dyeing and tanning industries.
A gun emplacement associated with a coastal battery.
A weapon which is a blade fixed to a long handle.
Objects used for the preparation of medicines or the diagnosis and treatment of ill health or disease.
A projecting structure in the roof of a mill containing a winch, allowing loads to be lifted clear of the building's wall and protecting the winch from the weather.

A register which including sites retaining any evidence of pre-1750 layouts; significant evidence of pre-1820 layouts; good examples of the best gardens from 1820 to 1880; are good examples of the best gardens laid out after 1880 but before 1970.
Mark 11 or the eleventh variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A pit over which a  corpse has been cremated on a pyre into which the remains and debris, and sometime grave goods, collapse and are buried. Generally confined to the Roman period.
One or more arches built across an angle between two walls to support a polygonal or circular structure.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
Rough, unhewn, undressed building stones with irregular faces, generally not laid in regular courses. Index with type of stone if specified.
An instrument used to measure the passing of time.
A pit used for the containment of clay whilst it is mixed to the right consistency for brickmaking.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A department devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.
A two post structure with cross beam for hanging criminals.
A photograph usually of a standing structure that has been manipulated to allow the creation of a measured drawing of the facade or elevation.
A broad class of drawing that is produced following precise conventions of scale and projection. [AAT]
A baluster, circular in plan, turned and cut on a lathe.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the metal industry.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.
A room for private work, reading etc.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Premonstratensian order.
An article laid over the floor or ground as a protcetive and or decorative covering.
A meeting room intended specifically for the use of a board of directors or governors of an organization or company..
An artificial channel for draining water or carrying it off.
Photographic colour print developed using wet process.
Use for deposits formed as a result of the modification of soils by humans for agricultural purposes.
Limestone formed during the Cretaceous period.
Southern hemisphere mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of SHCal13
A machine for beating out or separating grain from corn.

Heavy anti aircraft battery used from June 1944-May 1945 to combat the V-bomb threat. They are distinct from normal HAA batteries, being laid out in a V-shape, and early on were mainly for mobile 3.7-inch guns.
Weight used with any kind of balance.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
A shallow channel to collect rain water, attached to the eaves of a building.
Cattle fodder or fertilizer resulting from the extracting of oil from seeds.
A type of sword often used by infantry.
A small, finely-furnished room, traditionally where a lady could retire to be alone or entertain intimate friends.
A large building, situated by or near a canal, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from the canal.
A roof consisting entirely of common rafters, without the use of principals, in pairs but not connected by collar-beams.
A small or subordinate tower, normally forming part of a larger structure, housing a spiral or winding stair.
A small structure, often polygonal or circular, on top of a roof, dome, tower etc. featuring apertures to light or ventilate the building it adorns.
A kiln in which the prolonged heating or roasting of materials to drive off water, volatiles and sulphur so that they may be reduced to a powder, was performed.
Flexible, twisted fibres, joined together, for tying objects.
The process of investigating and recording historic buildings for the purposes of historical understanding.
The Captain of a vessel or aircraft
A term for a drinking vessel, although its use often implies a recognised quantity.
A piece of wax, lead, paper etc, with a stamped design, attached to a document as a guarantee of authenticity.
A hostel owned by a Christian association which provides cheap accommodation for young people.
A triangular piece of wood, usually of ebony, to which the lower ends of the strings of a musical instrument are fastened.

A metal, wooden or concrete box containing a telephone for use by the public, limited accommodation for use as a temporary cell, and a lamp on top that could be used to attract the attention of a passing patrol.
A specialist school for the teaching of deaf people.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
