A type of chain shot characterized by a number of chains attached to the main shot, causing maximum damage. Sometimes known as a Spider shot.
A rectangular sheet of roofing material created by a man made process (eg. asbestos cement slate) and made to look like, and used in the same way as, natural slate.
A garden maintained by, and for the benefit of, a community.
The use of ash and tephra deposits characteristic of single known-date volcanic eruptions to date stratigraphic sequences.
Use for vessels registered in Lithuania.

An enclosure defined by a single bank and entrance. They occur on every type of ground, although they favour sheltered, valley side locations. Smaller and usually less well defended than hillforts they are thought to be settlements of Iron Age date.
Decorative ornamentation of a key pattern
A canal tunnel built with one or more integral towpaths
A structure, usually sunk into the ground, for the purpose of allowing total bodily immersion as part of a baptismal ceremony.
An instrument for measuring or drawing angles, consisting of a quarter circle, graduated to 90 degrees, with a movable arm.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac nuns.
An instrument showing the direction of magnetic north and bearings from it.
A bridge whose deck is hung from above by large cables, chains or pinned iron or steel bars hanging from towers.
A round or polygonal building containing a HORSE ENGINE. Commonly found on farms next to the threshing barn, where it is used to power the machinery.
An industrial complex concerned with the manufacture of gas for domestic use from coal and oil.
A tool which combines two or more different types of tool.
In which the density of trees is significantly less marked than in woodland; if parkland is currently cultivated then classify land accordingly.
The top layer of earth consisting of humus and rock particles.
A building or range of buildings used to accommodate race horses.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.
Ground oats used as food, often in the form of porridge.

A small rectangular or sub circular area or areas bounded by an earthwork, ditch or similar boundary, where one side is formed by an existing linear boundary, forming a pattern reminiscent of clothes hanging from a washing line.
Infra Red Line Scan Aerial Photography
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
A place of worship for the followers of Buddha.
A building or site used for the manufacture, assembly and testing of weapons, explosives and associated military hardware.
A bridge made up of many relatively small members joined together in a series of interconnecting triangles.
Unspecified landscape feature. Use more specific type where known.
A depressed arch formed around three arcs: two struck from the springing line with one centrally placed arc struck from below it.
A counter from which beverages are served in a bar room.
An instrument consisting of a small lyre-shaped metal frame held between the teeth, with a steel tongue plucked with the finger.
A house in a line of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.

Any form of arms or ammunition whether from a formal organized military context or as a general cargo. Use specific terms - e.g. swords, bombs, where known; otherwise use this term primarily in contexts where the arms are unspecified or ancient.
A bitter beer brewed using charred or browned malt.

A site where a building once stood as identified by a level area of ground, often compacted or made from man-made materials. Use only where specific function is unknown, otherwise use more specific term.
A stone erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
Any non structural fitting on a vehicle.
Bricks capable of withstanding heat without burning. Used to line fireplaces, kilns etc.
Conglomerate consisting of nodules of calcium rich clay (marl). Used as a building stone from Roman times and as a key ingredient in Parker's Roman Cement, between 1796 and circa 1850.
A barracks comprising eight barrack blocks accessed via a central corridor. With four blocks on either side of the corridor the whole structure resembled a spider in plan.
Originally, the inner sanctuary of a Greek temple from where the oracle was delivered. Now used for any private chamber or sanctuary.
Decorative ornamentation consisting of alternating oval and V-shaped motifs, used to enrich ovolo mouldings.
A form of armour made up of overlapping squares of protective material.
An early steam engine using steam at atmospheric pressure. Chiefly employed in mine pumping. sometimes known as a vacuum engine.
The gate of a sluice which can be opened or shut to let out or retain the water.
Obstacles placed in open spaces and alongside roads designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy airborne forces.
A deep pit used for the burial of plague victims.
An area speciallly developed to accommodate commercial buildings.
A tool with an edged head and a wooden shaft, used for a variety of purposes.
A centre where treatment and rehabilitation training is given to patients recovering from injuries or accidents.
A building constructed from prefabricated sections. Use more specific type where known.
A textile building where the process of combing, a preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A bank or mound of earth used as a rampart or fortification.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of goods or merchandise. Use more specific type where known.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include  three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.

The nature and scope of further analysis should be included with the post-excavation assessment (PXA). All analysis must conform to that set out within the PXA and any variation must be confirmed by all relevant parties in writing. All techniques used must be demonstrably fit for the defined purpose(s), and comply with relevant legislation.
Use for vessels registered in Latvia.
A specially equipped ship designed to care for survivors of stricken vessels and offshore drilling platforms. These ships were often converted naval trawlers or minesweepers.
The black, lightweight and porous residue of partly burnt wood.
Instruments of psaltery and dulcimer type.
A lean-to or monopitched roof, or a projecting canopy over a door, window, or stair.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.

A place a worship situated at the end of, or built onto, the structure of a bridge. Often associated with bridge maintenance through the collection of donations, they may be endowed as a chantry for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.
A site, usually consisting of a bowling green and pavilion, frequented by lawn bowlers.
Any material consisting of glass filaments woven into textiles, paper or board.

A decorative feature of wood, plaster or carved masonry, often used in low relief on ceilings, panels or screens and resembling interlacing leather straps. Popular in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.
A roof featuring a covering of straw, reeds, rushes etc. used extensively during the medieval period but also popular in rural or rustic architecture.
A hall associated with a church, used for holding functions, meetings and for conducting parish business.
A hearth, normally placed clear of the walls, without a chimney stack or hood above.
A shop selling tea, butter, flour, sugar, spices, tinned foods and miscellaneous household stores.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A vessel fitted with a catapult for launching an aircraft.
A container used in the distilling process to catch the distilled liquid.
An internal combustion heat engine which uses gas as its fuel, and acts as a prime mover or power source for driving other machinery.
A crane whose winding mechanism was operated by hydraulic jiggers.
Medium grained, dark bluish-grey stone. Quarried mainly from the Rubislaw Quarry.
A building wherein silk worm cocoons are boiled to release the silk fibres.
A roof whose ends are partly gabled and partly sloped.
A shelter for the parson during the burial service.
A spiny evergreen shrub of the pea family which can be utilized as a roof covering in areas of its predominance, eg. heathland.
Appropriate for all assets, as judged against local characteristics.
A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.

A prefabricated cargo vessel produced in large numbers by North American shipyards during World War II to replace shipping losses caused by German submarines and replacing the earlier 'LIBERTY' ships.
The part of the chancel, between the altar rail and the eastern wall, containing the high altar.
A bridge supported by large beams or girders, originally of wood or iron, now usually of steel or reinforced concrete.
A water-powered forge or wire mill which manufactured metal wire combs for use in the textile industry.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
Book used to record information or impressions in the field, often as a preparation for more formal reporting at a later date.
National Mapping Programme Morph Number Sheet
Sites, buildings or stuctures associated with the entire process of salt production.
A building where people congregate to undertake sustained mental contemplation or religious or spiritual reflection.
An observation tower located on or near to a bombing range.

A four-storey RNAS control tower. The first floor contained offices for the commander flying and meteorological offices and the upper two floors, in the form of a central tower, provided offices for air traffic control.
A car adapted for ease of use by people with disabilities.
A cup with sides falring outwards from the base towards the rim, usually with a single handle.
A marine survey in which a multi-element transducer provides many (30-150) individual soundings of the water depth and echo strength for each ping.
An addition to the west end of a church which is similar to a porch or narthex but usually consists of a nave and aisles.
A diary used to record the events and activities during an excavation.
An earthwork used as a boundary marker.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on a foreign mother house.
Underground passage with storage chambers found in South West England.
A cover consisting of a plate for covering over or closing in a chamber or receptacle.
A pump used to transfer petrol from a storage tank into cars, lorries and other road vehicles.
Supplies including food, drink and equipment necessary for a journey.

Sites, buildings, structures & features categorized by their form rather than their function, where this has been deemed to be useful for retrieval purposes. Careful consideration will be given to the inclusion of new terms within this class.
Buildings, structures and sites for the training of military personnel.
An octagonal spire atop a square tower, the transition between structures effected by partially pyramidical masonry forms called broaches.
That area below low water level and inside territorial waters; the term maritime includes saline waters within tidal environments.
Ingress of water through damage or defects in the hull. Double-index with any cause, were known, e.g. COLLISION, and consequence, were known, e.g. BEACHED, FOUNDERED.
A band of cloth or other material worn around the head, not totally covering it.
A group of planted trees or shrubs, generally of uniform age and of a single species.
An open-sided building known to have been used for sheltering animals other than cattle.
Arlingham civil parish, River Severn, Gloucestershire
A site where petroleum is drawn.
A pure starch obtained from the tubers of the plant Maranta arundinacea used in cookery as a thickening agent.
Materials or substances, including petrol, firewood etc., used as a source of heat or power.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 4188/42.
A walkway on the top of a defensive wall, providing access to the parapets and towers.

A small, metal, crescent-shaped object, often highly decorated,  worn across the upper part of the chest by military personnel as a badge of rank and as a symbolic representation of the former piece of armour (see GORGET (ARMOUR).
A building, range of buildings or site, for the accommodation, rearing and/or treatment of animals, birds and fish, both wild and domestic.
Single lap regular shaped roof covering which can have one or more water channels. Typically made of clay or concrete. The name does not denote a relationship with the Roman period.
A precious metal, lustrous white in colour. Used for the manufacture of coins and other valuable items.
A conical container, usually made of earthenware, into which boiling sugar was poured and allowed to crystallize.
The contents of these documents do not confer any statutory designation on the monuments listed, they are purely advisory notifications for use within preserving the historic environment.

A cemetery of later prehistoric date comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels. The cemetery area is partly or wholly surrounded by an earthwork bank and/or ditch.
Use for vessel registered in Cyprus whether Greek or Turkish.
Oared fighting ship with ancillary sails.
A lancet arch designed in the composite style.
An object used to aid pouring a substance through a small opening.
A door made up of vertical planks on the outer face and horizontal planks on the inner face.
Refer to Inspector of Ancient Monuments
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
A dredger with a grab hung on ropes or chains giving it unlimited depth of excavation. they can lift solids or pieces of wreckages and can work close to ships or to a dock wall.

A maritime technique similar in theory to sub bottom profilers, however for 3D seismic surveys the receiver array is more complex involving multiple receivers so that a volume of sediment is studied rather than a single 2D line.
Views achieved from an aircraft or other high location.
A hotel where no alcohol is available.
A close fitting garment, usually stiffened by boning or similar and tightly laced to shape and support the wearer's figure.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the side elevations of the building.
Use for vessels registered in France.
A decorative garden ornament, usually of stone, in the form of a wide, shallow dish.
A missile fired from a sling.
Sandy, rough blue to green/grey coloured limestone. Quarried in Kent and widely used throughout the South East.
A shelter in a public park.
Missiles, such as cannon balls and musket balls, designed to be discharged from a gun or cannon using an explosive propellant.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A furnace used for melting metals for casting or for heating shot.

Sites, buildings, structures etc associated with the civil administration of settlements & enforcement of the laws of the land. Includes local & central government, settlements granted by the crown or ruling administration does not manorial settlements.
An area where builders keep building materials such as brick, stone, planks and cement.
A sound is a resource whose content is primarily intended to be rendered as audio. [DC] For example recorded speech, sounds or music.
A temporary hostel built for industrial or transport workers; for example, railway workers' hostels were provided for engine drivers.
A fast, armed vessel, small in size, often used for despatches and mail.
A light porous acid volcanic rock used for scouring and, in powdered form, as an abrasive and for polishing. Also used to make lightweight concrete.
A weapon which causes damage through exploding.
A small vessel used to carry fresh water to ships at anchor or in harbour.
A building used as a meeting place by a synod, an assembly of the clergy.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of football is played.
A container for the storing of substances.
A site used for the manufacture of leather products.

Double-handled storage jars characterised by a long neck and long body used as food and wine containers and for carrying such goods as cargo, found on shipwrecks from Classical antiquity (Greek/Roman).
An irregularly constructed, generally unstructured, mound of stones. Often, but not necessarily, circular. Normally a by product of field clearance for agricultural purposes.
A room within a building or complex, such as a workhouse, used for purifying objects with smoke.
A building or complex used for the temporary detention of people with no legal right to be in the UK who have refused to leave voluntarily.
A large defensive area that usually has to be crossed before entering the inner bailey of a castle.
A grotto or shrine dedicated to the nymphs, composed of fountains designed to imitate a natural grotto.
Use for vessels registered in Jersey, Guernsey or another of the other Channel Islands.
A ring shaped brooch, commonly Anglo-Saxon and medieval.
A case which holds and protects a mirror.
Citrus fruit of a distinctive yellow colour.
Fragments of metal broken up and set aside for reprocessing.

A service is a system that provides one or more functions of value to the end-user.  Examples include: a photocopying service, a banking service, an authentication service, inter-library loans, a Z39.50 or Web server. [DC]
A case designed to hold a fan.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of blasing or explosive gelatine.

A building used by the Royal Observer Corps as a headquarters and reporting centre. It may also fulfil an observation and nuclear fallout monitoring role. Use term to describe headquarters for plotting and monitoring nuclear fallout.
A modern building in which the load is carried by a metal girder framework and infilled with a light curtain wall.
A device for containing food whilst cooking it by the action of steam.
A hard, coarse grained, durable igneous rock. Can be used decoratively or as a main material. Found throughout the country.
A hangar used for the storage of barrage balloons.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A long and narrow hollow or trench dug in the ground, often used to carry water though it may be dry for much of the year.
Molluscs found in terrestrial habitats as opposed to fresh or brackish water.
An area within a hospital where patients receiving privately-funded medical and surgical treatment are accommodated. Often includes separate rooms.
Molluscs found in dry to damp habitats rather than fully aquatic or marine habitats. Use more specific term where known.
A long spear used on horseback.
Apparatus used for applying a mechanical force, or to perform a particular function. Use more specific type where known.
Thin sheets of material used for a variety of purposes such as writing on, painting on, or printing on.
A place where a product is given any finishing processes before being despatched to the user.
A place provided for leisure-time activities of young people.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of cotton
Timber or stone built structure, traces of which are found within some long and round barrows, in which human remains were interred prior to mound construction.
A large building used to store tea.
A decorative S-shaped moulding, usually placed at the top of a cornice, with  a concave lower half and a convex upper half.
A tower, normally forming part of a larger structure, housing a staircase.
Granular material consisting of small eroded fragments of rock or mineral grains, finer than gravel used as an ingredient in mortar and other traditional building materials.
A pit for the extraction of fullers earth (a hydrous silicate of alumina), which was used for cleansing, and finishing, cloth and wool.

A type of motorboat that provides accommodation for crew and passengers within the crafts cabin. Cabin Cruisers are usually between 25 feet and 45 feet long in length and are not to be confused with cruise ships which are substantially larger.
A tall, circular, polygonal or square structure rising from a roof, tower, turret etc., tapering to a slender point.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
A building at the entrance to an factory manufacturing explosives where a person was searched for matches, prior to entering the workplace.
A place of burial for members of the French Protestant Church.
A shrine often including representations of a god or gods or other holy relics which could be carried by worshippers whilst travelling.
A place of worship for Roman Catholics.
A key for winding a clockwork mechanism.
A place of accommodation at a college for staff and students.
Earthworks and buildings added around a bastion to enhance protection of the bastion.
A sitting room or lounge in a house intended mainly for use during the morning.

The Fi 103 is the more technical nomenclature for the Second World War German V1 flying bomb, produced by Fieseler. Multiple index together with Fieseler and flying bomb for maximum chance of retrieval for users.
A vessel with heating apparatus beneath it, for cooking or keeping food warm at the table.
A container for kohl, a powder usually made of antimony, used as eye shadow.
The openings between the upright blocks, or merlons, of a battlement.
Bag filled with soft stuffing used to support the body.
A pillbox in which the roof is detached from the walls and supported by a central pillar, thus leaving an embrasure allowing a 360 degree field of fire.

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
A board fixed at the gable end to purlins, often decorated.
A place of worship for followers of Hinduism.
A pronged iron hook used in cookery.
A tool with a curved blade and a short handle. The blade is on both sides of a line extended from the handle. If just on one side use reaping hook.

A transportable hangar designed by Callender Cable and Construction to Air Ministry drawing number 6633/37. A steel box-girder framework with corrugated iron cladding and canvas doors it had a clear door height of 25ft.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
Naturally occurring glacial rock fragments (diameter 64-256mm) larger than pebble and smaller than boulder.
Detached block comprising one or more storeys of wards.
A stone with the date on it, sometimes of an event, person etc.
A room that is underground or partially underground. Primarily used for storage.
A Vessel not designated under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986, which sank or stranded in military service during the 20th century, with resultant loss of life.
A factory used to make packaging.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons usually at a pithead.
A case for the transportation and protection of musical instruments.
An engine used for directly winding up coal from deep mines, first used in the 18th century.
A metal grid, usually iron, used to support pots over a fire.
Flint which has been burnt. It is not necessarily worked.
A round barrow featuring a small mound separated from a ditch of much greater diameter by a wide berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
Use for vessels registered in Finland.
a hard metal used in a lot of alloys.
Term applied to a pit trap itself and also a walled enclosure containing one or more pit traps.
A nail adapted so that the end of the nail can be turned over and driven back into the substance through which it has passed.
A site associated with Operation PLUTO (Pipe Line Under The Ocean) the operation to supply the allies with fuel following the invasion of Normandy.
Use where the presence or nature of a monument is inferred from placenames or placename elements.
Place for the cremation of animals.
A missile consisting of a number of weights joined together by cord. The bolas entangles the legs of a target causing it to fall.
A hard copy of digital data that has been printed onto paper.
A vessel for policing fishing grounds and fishing vessels.
A section of road that provides a passage beneath another road or railway.
A large self-service store selling foods and some household goods.
A site where fluorspar or fluoride of calcium, often used as a flux by copper-ore smelters, is extracted from an open cast mine.
Glass that has been coloured by fusing glass with a metallic oxide film or by burning pigment into the surface.

A factory used for the production of artificial limbs. They were often located within the precincts of a hospital, to enable fittings to take place and help the amputee to get used to wearing the limb.
A commercial building used for the production of detailed, often technical, drawings.
A telephone exchange housing one end of an underwater cable and used to send messages overseas.
The residence of a master shipwright.
An axe designed for fighting could be single or double headed and used with one or two hands. Where use is thought to be ceremonial multiple index with ceremonial object.
A port on the sea, rather than on river or estuary.
A decorative feature, usually Norman, in which fluting takes a spiral rather than vertical form.
A fragment of the rim of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
An open flat gound where the sport of shooting with bow and arrows is pursued. The ground can be equipped with targets mounted on butts and various fixed distance marker.
A burial vault built to contain the remains of members of a single family, household or dynasty.

A stone circle featuring four upright stones standing at the corners of an irregular quadrilateral. The monument may feature more than 4 stones, overall, but the corner stones are often the most prominent.

Desk-based assessment produces a report to inform planning decisions.   It uses existing information to identify the likely effects of the development on the significance of heritage assets, including considering the potential for new discoveries and effects on the setting of nearby assets.  An assessment may lead on to further evaluation and/or mitigation measures. All desk-based assessments should include a search of the Greater London Historic Environment Record.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of women and children.
A quern where one stone is rotated on another to grind grain.
A vessel used to carry away mud etc from a dredging machine and discharging it elsewhere.
Coiled metal used to give or limit motion.
Descriptive of inhabitants of, and cultural artefacts belonging to, Vietnam.
A room used primarily for storing food and drink.
Buildings used in the production of animal food.
A tool, possibly for cleaning mud from parts of a plough.
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.
A specialist veterinary hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of horses.
A mug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile from rim to base, which have roughly equal diameters. (Source: MPRG)
An 18th century garden building, designed in the style of a classical Ionic temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A farm where stallions and mares are kept for breeding.
Traditionally a dock where cambering, the bending of beams for shipbuilding, took place. Now used for a small dock.
German port of the western bank of the mouth of the River Weser.
A ring worn around the neck.
A cemetery comprising inhumations or cremations interred in stone cists.
A house of friars, originally hermits from Mount Carmel. Also known as ' white friars'.
A brace, running from a post to a principal, stiffening an interrupted tiebeam.
An object in the shape of an Egyptian dung beetle, used to symbolise the motive power of the sun. Use specific term where known.
A rib which spans a vault passing from springer to springer at right angles to the axis of the vault.
An Anglo-Saxon cruciform Long Brooch, often ornamented with knobs across and terminating its crossbar and head, and frequently with its foot shaped into a zoomorphic motif.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
The seal of a papal document
A facility used for the storage and distribution of fuel for transportation. Often associated with dockyards and railways.
A post to which ropes are attached to secure vessels at a landing place.
A small galley or Dutch trading vessel similar to a barge in construction.
A small window placed to cast light upon a fireplace.
A place of worship for members of a guild.
Fibres obtained from plants and used in the manufacture of ropes, sacking, canvas etc.
A complex of purpose-built or adapted buildings used for the maintenance, storage, assembly and control of sea mines and minefields.
A loft for the drying of thread or cloth.
A projection on which an object is fastened or which can pass through eyelets to fasten.
A place where wigs, hair-pieces and hair extensions are made and sold.
Remains of arthropods characterized as having a body divided into two segements and four pairs of legs, such as spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites.
A place of worship for members of the Seventh Day Adventists Church. This was formed in 1843 by followers believing in the imminent second coming of Christ.
Movable, usually functional, articles normally found in the home.
A purpose-built model village for the workers on a country house estate.
A machine used for drawing out and twisting together short fibres to make a yarn or thread. Use more specific term where known.
A buoy with a compartment into which shipwrecked mariners could climb to await rescue.
A grouping of retail warehouses and supermarkets with associated car parking.
Remains of Bryozoa, which are small animals, usually marine, that form colonies producing coral-like skeletons or jelly-like masses.
An emplacement mounting a small, portable electrically-powered searchlight.
An indented parapet consisting of raised parts, called merlons, separated by gaps, or crenelles.
An item used as part of a manicure.
A pond located at or near a swannery.
The place, hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
A site where barytes (barium sulphate) is mined. Barytes is also commonly worked from the waste tips of lead mines.
A spoon used to dispense communion wine.
A waterside building from which one could fish.
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
A technique which uses the measurement of decay in radioactive lead (Pb) isotopes to determine a date. Useful for sediments and lead-based paints between 1 and 400 years old.
Operations restricted to a depth of no more than 25 cms. If possible state depth in Description.
A workshop for the manufacturing of furniture.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a road across low-lying land or water.
A single storey building designed so that windows incorporated into the saw tooth roof catch the available light.
A building or room in which images of outside objects are projected on to a screen from a long-focus lens using natural light.
Auxiliary Unit Special Duties Zero Station
A shaft allowing access to an area. Often used as an additional escape route to the main shaft in a mine or as an air shaft.
A room for general daily use, usually in a family dwelling.
A rural school serving a number of villages, built in Cambridgeshire in the 1930s.
A strong, durable alloy of iron and carbon.

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
An engine that extracts thermal energy from pressurized steam, and converts it into rotary motion.

Monument visible, usually from the air, due to the fill of features being of a different colour than the surrounding subsoil. Soilmarks show up well in ploughed fields or areas where the topsoil has been stripped.  Term derived from AN32 Glossary
Any piece of timber that makes up the body of a maritime vessel, e.g. frame, decks, masts.

A crane consisting of a lattice girder carried on a lattice tower forming a T-shaped structure. A hoist is carried along the girder by a 'crab', enabling the crane to perform a variety of tasks eg loading/unloading of ships.
Animal skins which have been treated by tanning or similar.

Purpose-built structure, other than a bollard, to prevent vehicle or pedestrian access to a road or site, for example concrete blocks to obstruct vehicles accessing beaches on the north-east coast for illegal sea-coaling.
A raised step, usually made of concrete, on which supporters stand to watch a game of football.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
An engine powered by high pressure water, originally used in mine drainage.
A loft or gallery supported on a covered, vaulted structure and projecting over the rood screen proper, occassionally used by minstrels or singers.

A building, usually associated with, or found within the grounds of, a cemetery and used for the storage of coffins prior to burial. Reception houses were introduced as a result of concerns around the implcations for public health of C19 burial practices.
A stopping place on an underground railway system where passengers can board and disembark from a train.
A place where shale, a laminated clay or silt which has been compressed by the weight of the rocks over it, is extracted from the ground.
The process of investigating and recording historic buildings for the purposes of historical understanding.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A portable confining enclosure or framework.
A container holding items associated with the period of burial. Often buried to commemorate a certain event, such as the foundation of a building.
The cold room in a Roman baths.
An object used to stop a candle burning.
A mill for grinding corn. Use with power type where known.
A series of locks usually with short reaches between them allowing boats to travel up and down a steep incline.
A large, rectangular pillbox based on the FW3/28 with the addition of a small infantry chamber to one side of the main gun chamber.
A tool, featuring a straight, horizontal handle from which extends a metal hook halfway along its length, used by a shearman (one who shears sheep) in the handling of wool.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
A workshop containing machinery used to press textiles.
Equipment used primarily to cut, slice, chop etc, using an implement with one or more sharp edges.
A permanent Roman fort enclosed by a number of ditches and ramparts, used to house a garrison of auxiliaries.

A room where surgical operations are performed. Originally in the form of a room with a raised table surrounded by tiered seating from where students could watch an operation or disection be performed.

A maritime coring technique which uses vibration to facilitate ground penetration. With the force of gravity, and sometimes a piston, it can penetrate much deeper layers although the vibration provokes a slight mixing of the sediments.
Access to the site was limited e.g. to the perimeter of a large complex.
A column base featuring a hollow, concave - or scotia - moulding between two tori, which are projecting, convex mouldings.
An intricately designed garden in which ground coves, low shrubs or coloured earths are arranged in interlacing patterns resembling knots
An opaque, rigid sheath used to cover the penis. Not usually contraceptive and not for obvious visual display.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of a ball enclosed within petals.
A jug with a constriction between the upper and lower body sections. (Source: MPRG)
A moulding which is small, convex and circular.
Fine grained limestone, yellow or yellow/white in colour. Imported from France, mainly for ecclesiastical use.
Glass which has been coloured and decorated by painting.
A circular frame with a stretched membrane and small cymbals in the frame.
A detachable lock with hinged loop used for attachment operated by a key.
A building used to dry flax.
Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties
Use to record the names and parts of names of people and organizations.
The office of the body controlling a harbour and docks.
An enclosure or pen for confining geese.
A ship in government use, used to carry naval or military stores.
A specialised fitting for Roman armour. For a part of a garment use APRON.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.
A staff with a bent head used by a shepherd. For a crook used by a bishop use crozier.
A document or book written by hand.
A long shaft topped by an axe head. Differs from a battleaxe by the length of the shaft.
A hall, or main living-room in a medieval house, open to the roof.
An underskirt or dress with little shaping.
A place where meat and fruit, etc, is preserved by salting and/or drying.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of the essential logistical requirements of an armed force.
A file of computer information stored on a computer connected to the internet coded so that it can be accessed over the internet using browser software.
Equipment used primarily to bring percussive force onto an object.
A cross designed to be placed upon an altar.
Use for blocks in Emergency Medical Scheme hospitals (WWII).

A designation under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 that includes the remains of any aircraft which crashed, or any vessel designated (by name, not location) which sank or stranded, in military service after 4th August 1914.
An item used to join together clothing (includes footwear).
Obstacles such as scaffolding, barbed wire and concrete blocks or cylinders placed on a beach to impede the progress of enemy soldiers, vehicles or watercraft landing from the sea.
A glass vessel with a long tapering neck that is bent down. Used for distillation.
A seaside pier used as a promenade and amusement park.
A building or complex of buildings where cinematographic films are produced.
An engraved object which when struck imparts the image engraved onto the leather.
A small ornamental building in a garden, usually one-storeyed and consisting of one room. Use a more specific term where known.
A decorative ball usually used to ornament a bench end, canopy, gable, pinnacle or spire.
Shallow draft cargo vessel, often broad beamed and flat bottomed, powered by engine and or sail.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.

Bow Brooch derived from the Colchester type in the mid to late 1st and 2nd centuries AD. Typically the spring is held in a semi-cylindrical crossbar with closed ends and holding the axial bar and a hook or lug on the head to hold the chord.
A stone coffin embellished with sculpture.
Draught animals produced by mating asses and horses.
A stone or timber lined channel for conveying ore out of a working.
Forms of ride which are designed for entertainment.
An instrument played mainly by plucking the strings. Use narrower term where known.
A vessel which comes ashore and breaks up immediately due to severe weather.
A place of worship for Sandemanians, a movement founded by John Glass after his expulsion from the Church of Scotland in 1728. It was spread to England by his son-in-law, Robert Sandeman.
An outward projection from a defensive wall allowing the defenders to attack the flanks of any force attacking the wall.
A complex maze incorporating tall hedges. A popular feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
A concrete structure designed to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was only intended to be occupied during an attack.
An area partly or fully within the roof space of a building.
A flaky or spheroidal byproduct of the iron forging process, composed of either iron oxide or magnetite.
A slot, usually in a wall, into which a beam was placed.
A tall stack used to disperse foul air from the bottom of a mine.

Use when the vessel splits in two due to stresses on her frame where she lies unsupported either amidships or at the ends, typically after stranding, although this may also happen in similar conditions on the seabed after foundering.
A tank used for the storage of water, usually found as part of an institution like a workhouse or hospital complex
Use for vessels believed to come from North America but where the precise nationality is not known.
A court of criminal, and limited civil, jurisdiction in England and Wales. Established in 1972 to replace the Assize Court, following legislation in 1971.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
A piece of wood of square or rectangular section driven through a scarf joint to tighten it
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A large flake or blade blank thinned on both faces to form an approximate leaf shape. Precise function unknown.
A building or buildings where explosives are manufactured.
Buildings, structures and sites for regulating the flow of water.
Development of structures, dumps or other facilities on or above the seabed, below low water mark.
A place where people meet for entertainment, discussion or assembly. Use more specific type where known.
The area that contains the ambulatory, apse and chapels. Usually found in larger churches, monasteries and cathedrals.

Where appropriate, local planning authorities and the developer are advised to make investigative works open to and interpreted for the public and to include that as part of the WSI. Opportunities for public engagement, proportionate to the significance of the investigation, could, for example, include enabling participation in investigation, providing viewing platforms and interpretation panels, jointly designed open days in partnership with the local community, public talks and online forums as well as coverage in local media. Once analysed, the results and the knowledge gained may be communicated, in addition to formal publication and deposition of the archive, through displays, exhibitions and popular publications and might inform site design and public art.
A piece of ground, or a building, on which artillery may be fired at targets.
Flat bottomed, two-masted Dutch coastal vessel of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. Sometimes used as an English term for fluit, also a flat-bottomed vessel.
A Mark 5A aircraft which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
An aircraft with a single wing, or plane, either side of its fuselage.
Generic name for the fine grained, brown coloured carboniferous sandstone, quarried in the Leeds, Bradford and Halifax area.
A stud on the outside of a cruck blade and attached to it.
Buildings and structures associated with the processing and storage of natural gas.
A searchlight battery used to light a beach.
Building housing the machinery for the shredding and grinding of wood in running water and pressing of the resulting fibres into a pulp.
A building providing business premises to companies or individuals, sometimes for short periods, in exchange for a membership fee.
A musical instrument producing sound by air vibrating.
A machine used to raise and lower miners to and from the pit bottom.
A largely residential area on the outskirts of a town or city.
Pipes manufactured from concrete used in the construction industry for drainage etc.
An open pit from which coprolites or phosphatic nodules were extracted. Commonly found in the Fens and East Anglia coprolites were ground up and used as fertilizer.
A bowl with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A building providing dining facilities and recreation for commissioned officers.

A site used for the placing of an explosive, demolition charge. Many types of structures were prepared for demolition in the event of an invasion in order to cause the maximum disruption to the advance of hostile forces. Use more specifc type where known.

A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War. In addition to 18 mines, the U BOAT also carried 7 torpedoes in 3 tubes (2 bow/1 stern) and and 88mm or 105mm deck gun. A very successful design, UCIIs sank more than 1800 vessels.
A residential establishment for the care and accommodation of children and young people.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
Flat bottomed vessel used for coasting on the River Humber.
An alloy which is composed predominantly of tin (c.85-99 percent).
An inland settlement such as Runcorn, Ellesmere Port or Stourport, that combines docks and terminal facilities at the interface between land and canal transportation systems.
A container used to measure liquids.
A monument featuring a bank or mound constructed primarily of stone. Use specific type where known.
The tall, straight stalks or stems formed by plants found in the wetland areas, particularly The Fens. Used as a roofing material, the reed is laid with the ends forming the exposed covering surface.
An outbuilding where a horse-drawn carriage is kept.
A chamfer which does not extend the whole length of the surface it is ornamenting. The stop is the end of the feature and can be simple or ornamented.
A heat engine where an (internal) working fluid is heated by combustion of an external source, through the engine wall or a heat exchanger.
A large container used for washing the body.
A place of worship for members of the Russian Orthodox Church, the national church of Russia.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
A single seat with a back, sometimes also arms.
A brewery building where malt is mixed with hot water to form wort.

A structure, often found in 18th century landscape gardens, that demonstrates eccentricity or excess rather than practical purpose. They can take many forms - ruins, sham castles, towers, hermits' cells or grottoes.
A building providing accommodation, dining facilities and recreation for non commissioned officers.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious man or monk, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
Accommodation and facilities for aircrew away from the main RAF airfield.
A timber running obliquely across a series of common rafters.
A pad on which a post rests to support part of a structure.
Manufactured objects and devices used to apply a force to an object or perform a particular mechanical function.
Flats or houses first built by 19th century philanthropic societies as a model to encourage the development of approved working class housing.
Timber from trees of the genus Juglans, used for the manufacture of furniture
A covered area used for the drying of animal hides.
A purse, sometimes of bronze, usually worn on the forearm.
A settlement whose plan suggests the aggregation of several formerly distinct settlement nuclei into a single settlement.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A friary belonging to the Crutched Friars also known as Crosiers or Fratres.
A building used for the accommodation of sick and wounded members of the armed forces.

Thin layers of wood, bonded together to form a structural board. The grain of the adjacent layers lie across one another to give structural strength. Produced since mid 19th century for use in interior joinery, since 1930's for exterior use.
Softwood obtained from trees of the genus Pinus, often used for the manufacture of furniture.
Not to be used for indexing. Broad term used to assist retreival of all monuments where physical evidence is recorded.
Vessel fitted with broadcasting equipment and used for off-shore radio programme transmission.
The earliest subdivision of the Iron Age.
A building used for the decarburizing of pig iron to produce wrought iron.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the generation and transmission of power.
A carved stone female figure often found on castles and churches.
A form of volcanic glass with similar properties to FLINT and often used in the manufacture of sharp-edged tools.
Porous black residue of partly burnt wood, bones etc. used as fuel or, in the form of charcoal pencils, as a tool for drawing.

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.

A place of worship for the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem, a military order dedicated to the provision of hospitality for pilgrims, to the care of the sick and to the protection of the Holy Land.
A school in which the funds were raised through a system of shareholding whereby parents bought shares in the school and thus paid for their children's education.
A factory containing machinery for processing clay for the manufacture of bricks, tiles or pottery.
A container in which plants are grown.
A circle of spaced upright boulders emerging from a low, hemispherical, stony mound. The boulders may lean outwards due to pressure from the cairn material.
The hood used to completely cover a hawk's head.

Tools and equipment with a specific function and those for which a function cannot be assigned with any degree of certainty. Where the function is known, the term is also included under the relevant Class.
A specific German Stoneware form of rounded mug. (Source: MPRG)
The latest subdivision of the Mesolithic, or Middle Stone Age.

A form of cup which incorporates a joke or conundrum, where cut-outs or holes in the body make conventional use impossible. The puzzle is how to drink from it without getting wet; usually achieved by sucking through a hollow rim or handle. (Source: MPRG)

A building housing the permanent electricity generator supply for domestic use or small scale unspecified power generation on an airfield. Unlike stand by set houses, power houses had to cope with both essential and non-essential loads.
Aromatic vegetable substances, either in their natural form or ground, used to add flavour or scent to food.

Archaeological geophysical survey uses non-destructive techniques to detect the likely presence of archaeological features.  It is usually used as part of a field evaluation to inform a planning decision.  Geophysical survey is largely restricted to undisturbed greenfield sites and certain types of archaeological remains; but successful application of some geophysical methods to urban sites has increased in recent years.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.

The period of political and military opposition between the major Superpowers (USA and USSR) and their allies. Known as the Cold War as there were no direct military conflicts between the two main protagonists.
A plasterer's tool for smoothing the surface of plaster.

A prefabricated structure consisting of sectional timber framed units that were bolted together. The structure was clad with Canadian Cedar weatherboarding and had a roof of corrugated asbestos. They were used as temporary accommodation on airfields.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal bones.
A building or structural plan shaped like a T.
A large disc of stone revolving on an axis, used for grinding, sharpening and polishing.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for deer and other game.
A bowl for the ritual washing of hands.
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
Tools and equipment used for agricultural purposes.
A representation of a winged boy who represents Cupid or Love.
An area, with fixed defences, designed to act as a focal point for a defending force.
Term applied to both the pit trap itself, and the walled enclosure containing pit trap(s).
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.
A material in a granular form that is smaller than gravel and created by the erosion of rocks.
A weapon where an object is propelled away from its launcher by means of force. The launcher can be a weapon, eg a catapult, or a person. This term includes the projectiles themselves.
A walk or path lined with lime trees.
Use for vessels registered in Portugal.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.

The main office of a telegraph company containing rows of tables set with Morse sounders, keys, relays and pigeon holes from where MORSE coded messages were transmitted and received and telegrams dispatched.

A type of dish specifically designed to catch the juices from roasting meat. The dish may be oval, semi-circular, rectangular or wedge-shaped. Usually has one or two handles located on one long side and a lip at one or both short sides. (Source: MPRG)
Dried leaves from the plant Camellia sinensis, which is used to make a drink by infusing the leaves in boiling water.
Containers used for industrial or scientific purposes.
A chisel ended flaked axehead common in the Mesolithic.

A descriptive survey involving the systematic measurement and recording of the dimensions or features of a building. Where the survey is accompanied by systematic investigation and analysis, use Architectural Survey.
The outer boundary of an airfield.
Clothing designed to protect the wearer from physical hazards.

Condition	

No development shall commence until details of an appropriate programme of public engagement have been submitted by the applicant and approved by the planning authority.  The approved programme must be implemented in accordance with a timetable set out in the programme.

Composed of sand, stones or other aggregate and cement mixed with water which sets in a hard mass. The material is usually associated with modern building but was developed by Romans where cement was obtained from quicklime.
Woman's fur cape for the shoulders.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
A small bobbin used in lace making.
A building where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
An external wall cladding consisting of overlapping horizontal  boards.
A coastal gun/watch tower built as part of the anti-invasion defences during the Napoleonic Wars.
A pot for ink usually housed in a hole in a desk.

A dwarf shrub of the heath family used as an alternative to straw as a roof covering in moorland regions. Cut while in bloom and laid with the roots carefully entwined. The covering turns a characteristic black colour with age.
An area within a building used for the storage of cheese.
A slight structure built on an allotment for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, by the allotment holder.
A brace halved to the inside of studs, and so not visible from outside.
The principal Roman Catholic church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
Pieces of wood used to form the sides of barrels.
A place where vessels can land passengers and goods.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.
Amenity area development","Development of playing areas, sports facilities, parks, gardens and urban open spaces.
Short publication used to disseminate information about a particular project or organisation, issued on a regular basis.
Transportation, usually wheeled or tracked, used for the conveyance of goods or people.
An instrument designed to measure temperature.
An inclined ramp of earth, stone or brick used to deliver fuel to the firing hole of a kiln. Mediaeval and later.
A bridge, usually resting on a series of arches, carrying roadways or railways over low-lying areas.
A purpose built pit, usually below a gatehouse or barbican, into which the counterweight of a drawbridge could be lowered, thus enabling the bridge to be raised.
Flat stones used to create flat surfaces, e.g. pavements.
Use for a man-powered watercraft propelled by a paddle, such as logboats and canoes.
A window cut through a single slab of timber or stone.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
A structure for hanging criminals, often used to suspend criminals after execution, consisting of one upright post with an arm.
Works to remove industrial waste contamination or make safe shafts or other dangerous features on former industrial land to provide building or agricultural land.
An area of grass, marked out for use in the game of cricket.
Clothes, items of attire and ornament and objects for personal use by individuals, including toiletries.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
Building containing transformers to reduce the high voltage of the National Grid to the lower voltage of domestic supply.
Upright stones engraved on the edges with a Celtic script consisting of lines or notches.
Photographic negative on glass developed using a dry process.

A device, monogram or symbol usually carved on stone or woodwork near a buildingï¿½s entrance points, particularly doorways, windows and fireplaces, to protect inhabitants and visitors from witches and evil spirits.

A metal, often decorative, hinge constructed with a single large strap attached to the surface of the moving part wiht a loop in the end which fits over a pintle attached to the adjacent stationary frame.
A brush used to apply soap to the body when shaving.
A flat, circular plate, usually made of iron, on which food items are baked.
A track inlaid into a surface, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers and/or goods or raw materials.

The light emitted from sedimentary minerals or mineral inclusions in bricks when stimulated in the laboratory by infrared light. Used to date samples up to 250,000 years old; especially appropriate for geological sediments containing feldspars
Cement/water mix often used as covering. Use this for entries including slurrying and slurried.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
An inwards, radial flow reaction water turbine developed by Jean Victor Poncelet (1788-1867) in France in 1826.
An umbrella-shaped pavilion, Indian in origin, constructed over a funerary site. Can also refer to a funerary monument or cenotaph constructed in this style.
A rectangular multi-storey block of flats, greater in width than height.
A private fighting ship under a letter of marque or financed by subscribers, shareholders or individuals.
Sites and structures, often un-manned, intended to impede or confuse enemy forces.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of clothing.
A priory of Gilbertine double order of nuns and canons.
A road used primarily, but not exclusively, for the rapid transport of military vehicles, equipment and personnel.
A database stored on a computer linked to the internet, which can be queried and browsed by remote users using the internet.
A sawn piece of timber, thinner than a plank and often rectangular.
An enclosure used for the cultivation of fruit trees.
A support for an arch, lintel, beam etc.
An object which fastens cross ways.
An establishment where wagering and the placing of bets takes place.
Place for people who underwent regular blood letting.
A place from where rescue missions are co-ordinated and casualties treated after an accident, offensive action or disaster.
A place where abrasive mediums such as sand-paper and grinding wheels are manufactured.
The entire playing area and associated buildings upon which the game of cricket is played.
A board or slab, often with a thumb hole in it, used by an artist to hold and mix colours on.
A wide street, traditionally lined with trees.
A substance used to affect a human or animal by changing mental or physical states, particularly used in medicine.
A shed used for the maintenance and repair of aircraft.
A site where vinegar is manufactured from soured beer, wine or cider.
Barbed wire in the form of a coil which could be extended concertina-like to form a barrier to impede the movement of hostile troops.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
A complex of buildings and earthworks constructed for the storage of bombs and pyrotechnics.
A gun designed to be held in one hand. It has a short barrel length compared to long guns.
A building housing a whim, a machine worked by a horse, used for raising ores, etc, from a mine.
Ground-covering herbage, some varieties of which can be used, especially when dried and in large quantities, as a construction material.
64 Type DFW55373 single projector sites arranged in an 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
Roughly spherical, > 5 µm, soot particles produced from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels. Used as an indicator of industrialisation, and can also be used as a dating tool.
An arch, either pointed or round, which broadens above the springing line, creating a horseshoe shape.

A bronze axehead of earlier Bronze Age date the sides of which are raised, either by casting or hammering, to form flanges on both faces which aid hafting. Some types also feature a raised bar or stop between the flanges.
A chair fixed to the end of a plank which was pivoted to allow the incumbent of the chair to be ducked into water as a punishment.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.
The main vertical beam standing at the centre of a post mill carrying the bearing upon which the body of the mill rotates.

A Heritage Statement (also commonly referred to as a Statement of Significance) is normally required to support all development proposals for planning permission, listed building consent or scheduled monument consent, when the proposal directly affects a heritage asset or its setting. A Heritage Statement is an assessment of the significance of any heritage assets and/or their settings affected by a development, and of the potential impact of that development on their significance. It is an important practical tool to guide an applicant in developing their proposals.
A depiction of land, coastal or sea areas intended to aid navigation, usually using latitude and longitude co-ordinates.
Human beings. Use more specific type where known.
The residence of a ford keeper.
Shelly, gold/brown, coloured liassic limestone containing large quantities of crystalline calcite.
The meeting hall of a secular or ethical society.
A belt worn around the waist from which a sword is hung. Where worn over the shoulder use baldric.
A kitchen set up, specifically during World War Two, to serve food to members of the public, especially families whose homes had succumbed to enemy bombing.
A device used to trap or kill animals considered to be pests, eg. rats.
A tree named after a person or event associated with it, e.g. Byron's Oak at Newstead.
A slope, usually with rails, by which a boat can be transferred from one level of waterway to another.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.
An outline of the circumstances to be addressed, with an indication of the scope of work which will be required (Scottish term)
An establishment or works where the distilling of spirits is carried out.
A building or group of buildings designed for the breeding and rearing of animals, including fish and birds. Often include incubators and heated rooms.
An area of a barn, paved or boarded, on which corn was threshed by hand flailing. Use broader site type where known.
A building or complex, often associated with a historic site or place of interest, containing interpretation panels and information for visitors to the site or area.
A building from where marine operations are directed.
An establishment in which people, usually children, are taught.
A handled tool with a broad blade with slightly raised sides used for scooping or shovelling.
A room, usually in a hospital, in which a number of beds are located.
A system of lights to aid aircraft when landing at night. When viewed from above the runway lights form an outline of the runway.
A site where gypsum and anhydrate is mined.

A flint blade with negative impressions of removals on one side of the dorsal surface, creating a crest. These constitute part of a previously worked striking platfom or result from preparing the flaked surface on a core before detaching flakes or blades.
A head of water raised in a conduit system.
Usually a complex of buildings for the processing of raw materials. Use specific type where known.
A post, usually of iron or concrete, used to support a street lamp.
A structure providing protection against the weather at bus stops.
A room designed or suitable for dancing.
Materials selected and organised to be of use to teachers for use in education.
A pit used for the prolonged steeping of the flax plant in water to separate the fibres from the wood.
A rotating, domed, steel turret set over a circular pit used as a gun emplacement.
A steam engine from which the spent exhaust steam either passes out to the atmosphere and is lost, or in some cases is used as process steam in a factory.
A buttress shaped like an arch and springing from a pier in arched form to the wall.
An object which surrounds or makes up a keyhole.
A water-filled structure for experimental research.
A garden created to commemorate a person or event.
An arch formed around two arcs whose radii are each equal to the span of the arch.
Very light, depositional limestone formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate rich water (Tufa). The more dense and compact form, Travertine, is formed in a similar way.
An object decorated or otherwise marked by the use of a stamp; for example, a maker's stamp.
A machine for making paper in a continuous length.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55491.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of all types of wax.
A house for the keeper of a level crossing on a railway.
Large, brown, hard-shelled seeds of the palm tree Cocos nucifera, the flesh and liquid contained within the shell can be eaten.

A building within the gunpowder works complex. During the gunpowder production process, the mill cake was broken down, pressed and then corned. The remaining dust was removed from the corned powder by tumbling it in gauze-covered revolving cylinders.
The apse at the west end of the nave in a double-ended church.
A building associated with a spinning mill in which raw material is mechanically spun into yarn or thread.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
A building or structure in which processed cloth is dried.
A small-scale railway, often for the transportation of children at a place of recreation.
Construction works for the production of rigid or dirigible airships.
Coarse grained, dark coloured, igneous rock.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
Series of machines for mechanically slaking lime. 20th century.
Series of wire mesh screens used for grading lumps of coal according to size.
A building incorporating a model representation of the planetary system projected onto the ceiling.
The residence of a station master.
A hospital providing medical, surgical or psychiatric testing and treatment for patients with specific illnesses or injuries.
A bank which specializes in accepting savings deposits. Originally established to help the poor.
A long, narrow, rectangular plot of land used for the manufacture of rope. Usually walled, it may include small buildings and awnings at each end. Often attached to a warehouse.
A tubular orifice to assist in pouring.

A Roman Bow Brooch, dating from the later 1st and 2nd centuries often worn in pairs with a linking chain. Characterized by its distinctive head, sometimes enamelled, and resembling the mouth of a trumpet.
A type of large steel framed aircraft hangar introduced by the Royal Air Force in its Expansion Period with a number of designs between 1934 and 1939, to accomodate heavy bombers.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphate is extracted.
Development of new industrial premises including factories, warehousing etc.
The body of a church or chapel as opposed to galleries.
An upper story in a chapel, church or cathedral, situated above the aisle and below the clerestory, often arcaded and sometime called a Tribune.
A HORSE GIN used for domestic cider manufacture, especially on farms.
Animal skin that has been hardened or treated by a tanning process.
A room for temporary imprisonment and detention at a Police Station.
The grounds of an institution for higher education eg. a university, including the educational buildings, entertainment and sports facilities and student's halls of residence.
Engineering works dedicated solely to the manufacture and repair of boilers.
A member whose purpose is to keep two other members apart, so acting in a state of compression.

A twin-engined, multi-role aircraft built by Junkers. Originally designed as a medium bomber with the speed of a fighter, but its adaptability allowed it to fulfil the roles of night fighter, torpedo-bomber, anti-tank aircraft and photo-reconnaissance.
Fertile soil composed mainly of humus, sand and clay.
A mill used for the production of wadding, as opposed to yarn or cloth. Often associated with steam or water power.
A building used to house railway carriages.
A movable barrier, usually external, within an opening in a wall, fence, hedge or similar.
A flake that has had small flakes removed to blunt, sharpen, refine the outline or prepare the edge of the tool.
A fortress and dwelling, usually medieval in origin, and often consisting of a keep, curtain wall and towers etc.
A playing piece for the medieval game of table.
Any tree, shrub or herb of cellulose form, normally subsisting in soil and producing its food through photosynthesis.
A moveable section of  light fence, traditionally made from wattle and used for herding livestock, to separate land or to act as river bank revetments.

Single celled marine organisms. Some form calcareous tests (shells). They are used archaeologically to study the nature of marine environments or establish the presence of marine conditions or products (e.g. imported seaweed).
An apartment, usually with a north-light, used by artists.
A stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 1039/41.

In order to assess the impact that any development (including any ground works and archaeological mitigation) will have on the hydrology of a site the existing water environment at the site must be understood. This often involves looking beyond the red line of the site boundary to capture relevant aspects of river stream and drainage systems. Hydrology is a complex subject and the assessment should be carried out by a qualified specialist, usually part of the developer’s engineering team. The information gathered in a hydrological assessment is of use in identifying if the water pathways will change in a manner that could put waterlogged deposits at risk of drying out, it also informs the detailed design of foundations and a structures and in cases where preserving archaeological remains within/ under a new structure/ development it provides information on suitable redesign.
A decorative style on a block or band from which an arch springs.
An aircraft which has been forced to land on the sea in an emergency.
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
Workshop, as part of a gunpowder works complex, in which explosive is loaded into shells. Also used for expense magazine, where powder was stored between work processes.
A hard and lustrous metallic element, used for roofing, galvanising iron and a component of alloys such as brass.
A place of worship for members of the Greek Orthodox Church, the national church of Greece.
A usually large school providing courses for children of all abilities, between the ages of eleven and sixteen.
A long handled hook used for pulling a boat to a place eg another boat, or pushing off from a place.
The offices of a Government Department responsible for the administration of the country.
The horizontal surface of a step or stair.
The band or block from which the springing of an arch occurs.

A powerful machine comprising a pair of heated cylinders revolving inside a chamber, and used for converting raw rubber into a soft plastic mass by being 'chewed' between knives or teeth projecting from the cylinders.
The wall plate of the lower storey on which the joists of a jetty rest.
A factory where general hardware, fittings, items of ironmongery are produced.
Jet-propelled, pilotless aircraft carrying a one-ton explosive warhead. Also known as the Fieseler FI-103, the V1 was nicknamed the doodlebug, or buzz bomb.
A place where worship is offered or devotions are paid to a deity or saint.
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
A bowl comprising three or more equally spaced lobes. There may be one or more moulded animals or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Gun battery built specifically to mount short range weapons to defend a beach against an attempted landing.
A room where weapons and armour are stored.
A round barrow featuring a mound surrounded by a ditch, with no intervening berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external bank.
A large mounted gun, now disused and placed in a prominent position as a piece of street furniture or as a "feature".
A plot of earth used for the raising of flowers and shrubs.
An area of a building providing reading materials for the benefit of colliery workers.
A factory where food is preserved either by freezing, salting or pickling
A place for recreation with electronic game machines and gambling machines.

A machine for weaving cloth. A traditional loom comprises a framework with a horizontal back roller, the warp beam or warp roller, around which closely spaced warp threads have been wound parallel to each other, stretched horizontally onto a front roller.
A large bottle, generally protected by a basket or box, usually used for containing corrosive liquids, etc.
A coloured, glass-like substance (opaque or partially opaque) that is fused to the surface of metal or glass or pottery for decorative or protective purposes.

A device used to slow the fall of a person or an object from a great height. When open it consists of a large umberella like sheet with wires or ropes converging from the edge to a harness attached to the lower end.
Basic, black coloured, fine grained, igneous rock.
Factory for making Chenille a yarn produced by placing short lengths of yarn (the pile) between two core yarns (the core) these are then heated to set the pile in place.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a river, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A factory for the assembly of components. Usually associated with the manufacture of vehicles: cars, lorries, etc.
A housing for one or more bells, usually gabled or roofed.
A place of worship for followers of the Eastern Orthodox churches. This family of churches separated from the Western church in the 11th century and recognizes the Patriarch of Constantinople.
Storage tank for coal gas and possibly other types of gas .

A large rectangle roof tile with an upstand on one side, a roll in the centre and another roll on the other side, which fits over the upstand of the adjacent tile. The name does not denote a relationship with the Roman period.
A microlith retouched to a point, usually with oblique retouch. They are synonymous with 'obliquely blunted points' of the English Mesolithic. (Source: SARC)
An artificial pond or pool constructed for the purpose of watering  livestock, particularly in prehistory.
A gate used to seal the entrance to a dock to prevent water escaping from a wet dock or entering a dry dock.

An aerial photograph taken from directly above a feature in the landscape, suitable for mapping or survey purposes. For photographs taken from the air at an angle to the subject use OBLIQUE AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH.
Pictorial, painted or drawn material such as slides, drawings, photos, plans excluding cartographic.
A building where military officers are accommodated.
A clear area in a church covered by the transepts and crossing.
Hook used to support cloth on a tenter frame after fulling to dry the cloth.
A building or room, purpose built for the teaching, rehearsing and playing of music.
A hydraulic machine used to magnify the stroke of a hydraulic piston. The pulleys and chains of a crane or other device are attached to the jigger.
The point or tine of a fork.
A heavy, metallic element, which is liquid at room temperature. Used in thermometers and medicinal preparations.
A monastic enclave dependent on a mother house.
A transverse timber resembling a hammer beam but without a hammer post above, being braced to a principal or collar instead.
A short timber laid across the top of a masonry wall to carry a wall plate or the foot of a common rafter.
