A vessel, usually made of stone, which contains the consecrated water for baptism.
The entrance to a tunnel. Use more specific type where known.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A flat edged blade used in leatherworking
A building in which cattle are housed overnight, normally tethered in stalls.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
An building, often including recreational facilities, provided for the relaxation of serving Royal Air Force Personnel.
The under surface of an arch, lintel or projecting architectural feature.
A chapel within a parish church containing an altar and one or more tombs.
An object which has words inscribed, engraved carved or written upon it.

Soft, often white, but may be transparent. Dolomite can be found on its own, but may also occur as a replacement mineral found in some rocks, particularly limestone, formed after action by magnesium-rich fluids.
A mineral containing high quantities of Copper.
A frieze that has a convex section.
Geologist's term for any dark coloured, slightly metamorphosed igneous rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
Use with form of extraction where known. Also use MINE and other ores extracted where relevant, eg. SILVER MINE.
A central office dealing with financial accounts.
Workshop for the painting of vehicles, machines, etc.
A place of meeting and worship for Jehovahs Witnesses.
A stone used for sharpening edged tools, knives etc.
A plug to keep out dust, moisture etc.
A form of bone, which grows on the heads of members of the deer family and is shed annually. Antler can be used by man for a variety of purposes
A building used to aid in the drying of goods, for example, by means of flowing air.
Use for speculatively built 19th century "model dwellings", rather than those built by a philanthropic society.
A ring used to hold hair in place.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design number 454/43. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes
Clothes worn so that they are visible, usually but not always worn over other clothes.
A struck piece of flint or other stone where the length is at least twice the width.
Ignition from within rather than through external forces; frequently associated with cargoes of organic material such as manure, owing to an internal rise in temperature of the cargo itself.
A stone, slate, iron or wooden structure used to mark the site of a grave. Use only where evidence of the form is uncertain otherwise use more specific type.
A flattened glass sphere used to give linen a gloss.
A container for holding water in which to bathe.

A pit in a road or trackway covered with a grid, usually of metal poles (but can be of wood or stone) with sufficient space between the poles to prevent animals from crossing, without restricting access for vehicles and people.

The systematic study of ground surfaces and collection of visible archaeological material. Fieldwalking can be carried out as line-walking, grid collection and transect or quadrant sampling. Any material recovered is logged and stored by sample unit.
Water spraying tower for cooling coke after it emerges from the furnace.

An anti aircraft battery armed with 3 inch rockets with a ceiling of 22,000 feet. Both single and multiple launchers were designed. Single launchers being used to defend vulnerable points such as coastal batteries with multiple launchers defending town.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A large vessel, sometimes large enough to accomodate several gallons, often made of leather and richly decorated, for storing and serving liquor.
A tall, metal structure erected as a support for electric power cables.
A place of worship within the grounds of a cemetery.

A comprehensive written report drawing together the evidence from the recording programme, archive research and consideration of the historical and landscape context supported by measured plans and elevations and a thorough photographic survey.
Chronic kidney disease, diabetes, thyroid illnesses.
Weight on the end of a graduated line for measuring the depth of water.
A vessel for carrying messages between warships.
Development of more than one dwelling. Archived - Do Not Use
A metal stud hammered into the sole of footwear to provide grip.
A series of water or engine-driven crushing machines used in ore dressing.
Debris consisting of excess construction material used in the building of a nearby site or structure. If unsure of whether debris is from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
A playing area for the game of hockey. May be a grass or artificial surface.
Stone which has been crushed for use in the construction industry.
An inhumation burial in which the corpse is laid on a wooden bed, often surrounded by a collection of grave-goods. Anglo-Saxon rite of 7th century AD.

A type of clinker built wooden boat or ship held together with tendons of flexible wood such as roots and willow branches. Sewn boat construction techniques were used in many parts of the world prior to the development of metal fasteners.
An area of arable land with common rights after harvest or while fallow. Usually without internal divisions (hedges, walls or fences).

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.
An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
Position often screened by earth, stone or wood from which game is shot.
An electric fan used for the ventilation of mines.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the defence of the coastline from foreign invasion.
A seperate wing of a large house provide accommodation for guests.
A wooden bar sliding from a long channel at one side of a doorway into a socket in the other jamb so as to bar the door.
A mullion which divides a window with four or more lights and is larger than the mullions either side of it, often sharing the dimensions of the frame?s members.
A crane, usually used in engineering workshops that can be moved from place to place by means of overhead rails..
A non-vertical kiln where the shaft and burning zone is horizontal to the ground thereby allowing material to be fed in.
An alcoholic beverage distilled from grain or malt and usually flavoured with juniper berries.
A stone slab, raised on stone or wooden piers, used for the display of fresh fish. Usually found in market places.
A Roman wine cup with a shallow bowl and a circular foot.
A shaft designed to allow for the adequate circulation of air through a transport tunnel, for example.
A system of trenches dug by troops for practice purposes.
Entry to a hall through opposing doors with a partition screening the hall and forming a passageway.
A pier made up of several shafts against it. The shafts can be attached or detached.
A site showing some signs of occupation but evidence is insufficient to imply permanent settlement.
A flour mill using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.
A spirally grooved object used to join two or more materials together.
Fabric manufactured from fibrous materials, consolidated by heat and compression so that the fibres become matted together.
Characteristic waste flakes struck off in the production of axes.
A magistrates court sitting for the purpose of holding trials for children and young people. Replaced the juvenile court, following legislation, in 1991.
An indoor or outdoor market where fruit and vegetables are sold.
Romanesque overlapping  arcades, producing a series of pointed arches.
Any dome shaped metal bell struck either by an internal clapper or by a hammer.
A roughly square mound of stones which may also contain or conceal a burial.
A craft with two masts.It is usually cutter rigged on the foremast and has a small mizzen mast.
An observation post used by Air Raid Precautions wardens to watch for aircraft and bomb strikes.
An area including buildings dedicated to scientific research for commercial purposes. Often associated with, or operated by, a university or higher education institution.
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
The main body of a structure not including wings etc.
A mill, on two or more levels.
A drinking vessel, usually curved in shape, fashioned out of animal tusk or horn and sometimes with bands of decoration.
A chapel adjacent to, associated with or containing a well.
A malleable water repellant substance created by animals or as a coating to parts of plants.
A place where members of the British Legion meet.
Use for vessels registered in Northern Ireland.
The official residence of an abbot.
A large gearwheel which, together with a smaller gear called a pinion, connects two parrallel shafts and, in a corn mill, drives the stone nuts.
An establishment or building where the breeding and training of birds of prey takes place.
An English seventeenth century house plan consisting of a rectangular block two rooms deep, the rooms sometimes separated by a passage.
Structures erected on or near a public highway.
A metallic alloy of iron, carbon and silicon formed by casting in a mould.
An Italian cornice consisting of a bed moulding, a row of plain block corbels or modillions, and a corona or cornice.
A building containing machinery for operating sluices.
A gable with curved sides and an identifiable pediment.
A rafter of uniform size placed at regular intervals along the length of a roof.
A building or buildings where electronic components or devices are designed, developed, manufactured and assembled.
Trees planted in an ornamental circle. For earthwork surrounding trees use TREE ENCLOSURE RING.
Covering for the head, especially ornamental.
A counter balance designed to support the excess weight of a mineshaft's wooden beams.
A bow, fixed to a stock, with a mechanism to fire the bow.
A place of worship for followers of the Orthodox Catholic Church. Use only where the specific denomination is unknown.

Removal of samples from deposits, including archaeological contexts to recover information about past environments and economies, retrieve material for scientific dating and for the investigation of the deposits themselves e.g. formation processes.
An overshoe with a thick sole or set on an iron ring to raise the wearer's foot out of the mud and so protect normal shoes.
A stall where a cobbler mends shoes.
A dwelling-house with outbuildings and land assigned to its use.
An upright post set on a tiebeam or collar and used to support a ridge piece.
A garden consisting primarily of rocks and rock plants.
A small flake or blade with a series of notches along the edge.
The metal ornamental bedding and surround in which a gem or stone is mounted.
A jar for the storage of ointment.
A pavilion ward in a workhouse, used to accommodate inmates
Attachments that form part of the bridle.
A port, dock or harbour where ferries, hovercraft, ocean liners and cargo vessels can load and unload. May include road and/or rail terminals for transportation to the port.

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.
The SI derived unit of magnetic field strength.
The first third of the 20th century.
Specify in Description using: pond, lake, artificial lake, canal (if wet) etc.
A building or room used for holding, viewing, identifying or examining dead bodies prior to burial or cremation.
A place, hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
A friary of the Order of the Friar servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites. The Servite Fathers came to England in 1864.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.
A tool that produces a mark on an object through the application of percussive force through the stamp.
A piece of equipment fastened on an animal for carrying loads, including riders, or for assisting in traction.
A building or group of buildings situated close to the sea used by coastguards to enable them to monitor the coastline.
An obstruction, usually manmade, which is used to restrict or prevent access to a settlement, building or area of land. Use more specific type where known.
A refractory lined furnace in which an electric arc is struck between the electrode and the metal to be melted.
A pungent condiment manufactured from the dried berries of the plant Piper Nigrum. Use for cargoes of peppercorns or ground pepper.
An area, often consisting of widened streets or a town square, where booths and stalls may be erected for public sales.
An exterior, vertical pipe that carries rainwater from a roof's guttering, usually to a drain.
A room in which actions are checked, verified and approved.
A complex, comprising a workshop and a storage yard, used by a stonemason.
A cast iron hammer used for shingling iron or making heavy forgings.

A unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools within a covering structure.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of wine.
A hospital building of uncertain function. Use more specific type if known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within an earthen mound. Use more precise term where known.
A metal sphere, usually lead, fired from a musket. Often bound into a cartridge.
An exotic hardwood with great strength and durability.
A 'through' BACK TO BACK HOUSE - an interlocking L-shaped plan gave each house two street frontages, thus providing better lighting/ventilation.
An ornate version of an eight-voluted Ionic capital known as an angular capital or Scamozzi under which are added two tiers of acanthus leaves.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Association. This group split from the Methodists in 1836 and were separate until joining the Methodist Reform Church in 1857.
A house or centre used for meditation, contemplation and/or prayer.
The accurate survey and analytical depiction of earthworks and their relative chronological relationships by means of hachures and related symbols.
A hole dug to provide a firm base for an upright post, often with stone packing. Use broader monument type where known.
North of 40¡N; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal13
A circular arrangement of spaced stone uprights set within a high bank, often interrupted by a formal entrance gap.
An educational establishment where agricultural theory and practice is taught.
A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to materials or deposits using scientific methods such as Palaeomagnetism, Dendrochronology or Radiocarbon Dating.
Silver fashioned into coin for use as currency.
A cairn used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A group of electricity-producing windmills or wind turbines.
Two or more tablets of wood attached by a string or leather thong, with a raised border one side of which was filled with wax to write upon. Thin wooden tablets with ink writing are also known.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
The residence of a vicar, parson or rector.
A jar used to store medicines, drugs or the constituent parts of medicines and drugs.
Pens for housing cattle awaiting transportation.
Building or buildings used for the production of Gas Masks. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
Soft, loose-textured, woollen or man-made fabric.
A jar with an evenly rounded profile. (Source: MPRG)
A wall or masonry construction built for the purpose of retaining or supporting a bank of earth, wall, rampart etc.
A piece of furniture intended to hold drinks, side dishes etc.
A hard, black form of lignite that takes a brilliant polish. It is used in jewellery and for ornamentation.
Soft, very fine grained, dark coloured, sedimentary rock which splits easily.
A drill bit used in metal and wood working.
The stigmas of the crocus, Crocus sativus, used as a flavouring and for colouring food.
A circular flask with one or two flattened faces. (Source: MPRG)
A 16th century tower for observing tournaments, eg. at royal palaces.
3-D physical entity conveying information, e.g. a model, artefact or architectural feature.
An instrument for measuring height above sea level.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.
A building or room used for any type of engineering work. Use more specific type where known.
One of only three 'true' British marbles, green and white in colour, predominantly used in large public buildings.
A large bed surrounded by an earthwork and filled with composing vegetable matter and animal waste. This was used to produce Nitre, a constituent of gunpowder.
A school serving or supported by a parish. Usually teaching religious as well as conventional education.
A lift powered by an hydraulic system.
A Capital with a rolled up cushion-like form on either side creating distinctive volutes.
The pit in which human or animal remains are placed for interment,which may be either an inhumation or cremation.

A control tower constructed on RNAS stations by the Royal Marine Engineers. Built to a common ground floor plan they could be built with one, two or three storeys above this depending on the requirements of the station.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
A piece of animal bone roughly shaped with grooves in which pins are laid and held whilst being sharpened.
A roomspace within an abode which combines the specific functions of several of the more traditional roomspaces into a singular unified space.
A tool for extracting nails, tacks, pins etc from objects.
A freestanding staff upon which a flag is hung.
A garment worn from the waist down by women.
Monument with roof or walls intact or substantially intact, significant survival of original features, even if building no longer in use for original function.
A group of cairns occurring within close proximity to each other. Use for instances where the majority are clearance cairns. Also index specific types where known.
A beam which is half the width of a main beam, usually supporting joists.

A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of beer and other alcoholic drinks. Size may range from a single room such as a microbrewery in a public house to a complex of buildings including production line machinery for bottling.
A flat blade used to beat the weft against the newly woven cloth in weaving.
Debris derived from the demolition of buildings or other structures. If unsure of whether debris is resulting from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
A bridge in which one leaf may be retracted in a horizontal plane, passing on rollers over or under the adjacent fixed leaf.
A metal structure supporting high powered lights.
A style of decorative design consisting of intertwined, geommetrical patterns of leaves, branches, tendrils etc. Often defined as being devoid of human or animal figures.
An H-sectioned strip of lead used to hold panes of glass in position in stained-glass windows or other leaded lights.
Sites and structures for the transport of military personnel, vehicles and armaments.
The flue or channel that funnels smoke from a fire.
A waterwheel where water enters below the axle but above the bottom of the wheel.
A commonly coppiced wood from the genus Corylus.
A measure for liquid holding two pints which is a quarter of a gallon.
A group of buildings or rooms equipped with apparatus for scientific experiments or other research, testing and investigations.
The premises of an agricultural merchant where agricultural equipment, animal feed and fertilizers can be bought.
A small Anglo-Saxon cross-slab buried on the breast or beneath the head of a corpse.
A small protective fortification, such as an earthwork.
An oil-fuelled internal combustion engine, developed in the late 19th century, and usually made as a stationary, horizontal unit.
A building designed to house a lifeboat, usually with a stone ramp to launch the boat into the sea.
A military base used for training service personnel.
A place where gardening tools, plants, etc, are sold.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.
A circular concrete platform onto which aircraft would be taxied allowing the ground crew to calibrate, check and adjust the accuracy of the aircrafts compass, usually by rotating the platform.
Specify in Description using: private, public, formal etc.
The windlass used to wind rope around to raise and lower the bucket in a well.
A temporary castle built to house and protect troops beseiging another castle or town.
A comparatively thick, roughly  shaped piece of stone, usually square or rectangular, used to roof structures.
A building forming part of a colliery ventilation system exhausting stale air from shafts and headings.
A temporary kitchen set up in the field providing food for troops. Use with MILITARY CAMP if existence of this is known.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using ferry services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A works or factory where nitroglycerine is manufactured.

A platform projecting from the surface of a wall of a building carried on brackets, consoles or columns, usually placed before windows or openings, and protected by a railing or balustrade. It can also be a gallery in an auditorium.

A structure consisting of different cells equipped with instrument posts which supported finders. These provided range and bearing of the projected position of the target to guns emplaced in a nearby battery. Errected along the coast in the late 1870s.
Fragments of a structure, usually material that has been worked.
The fragmentary or substantial remains of a vehicle or aircraft. Where recovered from excavation double index with SUB SURFACE DEPOSIT.
A rotative beam steam engine patented in 1790.
An musical instrument where the strings are played by plucking or bowing. Use more specific term where known.
A small shallow cup used in assaying gold or silver.
A shallow draft vessel used to carry a crane.
A house with a range at the end of it, at right angles to the main range.
A building housing electrical or electronic equipment used for communicating over long distances. Use specific type where known.
A framed instrument, in which strings are plucked or hit, operated from a keyboard.
A prefabricated timber structure similar to Sectional hutting that was used by the Air Ministry for accommodation at airfields during WWII. Manufactured by Gerrard and Sons from 1939 to 1941.
An ornamental wand or rod carried as a symbol of authority
Place for the Home Guard to store equipment and amunition, either structural or subterranean during the defence of Britain.
A residence of two or three monks of the Augustinian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A mineral salt consisting of potassium chloride and mangensium sulphate, used as a fertilizer.
Any plants which are grown to be eaten. Includes parts of plants, especially roots and leaves.
A human-powered, pedal-driven, single-track vehicle, having two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other.
A vessel containing a religious oil or unguent.
A brace running from a vertical to a lower horizontal timber.
Visual record of a building, usually exterior only. Equivalent to Historic England Level 1.
Defences or an external wall surrounding a castle's motte or keep. Also a castle's outer court, or a court within a castle's walls.
A range marker allowing bombers to locate the bombing range.
A heated stone, brick or iron chamber used for drying corn.
An instrument with curved arms for measuring difficult or awkward shapes.
A burial ground for victims of the plague.
A holder for weapons, explosives and ammunition.
A place where stone is dressed or shaped for use in building, etc.
A succession of arches on shafts with no openings, attached to and used to enliven a wall.
A building combining a pigsty at ground level with a poultry house in a loft over.
A house in which a passage runs across the building, usually adjacent to a hall, between front and back entrance doors.
A garden house situated to provide a commanding view.
A type of carriage house, usually in a churchyard, for storing a hearse.
An object used to catch animals.
A gaming implement usually used in conjunction with a ball.
An enclosed piece of ground devoted to the cultivation of flowers, fruit or vegetables and/or recreational purposes. Use more specific type where known.
The official residence of an archbishop, eg. Lambeth Palace.
When a secondary mineral, use term for product type, eg. LEAD MINE.
A religious house governed by an abbot or abbess. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
Small, marine crustaceans are used as food.
A joint used to secure the end of a joist
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
A decorative container for serving cream.
A small warship mounting between 20 and 28 nine-pounder guns on a single deck.
Platform, usually stone-built, which holds the winding gear of a mine shaft.
The area at the end of an axle or shaft around which a wheel, bearing etc. pivots or rotates.
A sparkling, white wine traditionally from the Champagne region of France. Now used, loosely, to refer to any sparkling white wine.
A container in which substances are heated to high temperatures.
A housing, normally of triangular section, in a post to take the end of a prop, to hold the post upright during construction.
A purpose-built area of hard material of indeterminate use.
Any instrument for plucking or strumming a string eg a small piece of wood or plastic used to strum a guitar.

A room provided for the use of people waiting for a service, such as a train or bus service, or to see an individual such as a doctor or a dentist. When a dedicated structure, see Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A type of fairground or seaside amusement, often a permanent structure, where carriages travel at high speeds on an undulating track raised some distance from the ground.
A large, powerful, hand-drawn bow, usually 6 ft (1.8m) in length and traditionally made of wood.
A centre used by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A residential district planned as a unit.
A pilaster without base or capital.
A flattened rectangular version of a column of one of the classical orders.
A turret on the side of a house providing views across the surrounding countryside.
A series of billet mouldings forming a decorative band of small, regularly placed squared or rounded blocks.
A chapel attached to or founded by a college.

A sheet formed from wood which has been separated into its fibrous elements and reconstituted under pressure. The natural fibres produce resins which act as adhesive, but often additional adhesives are used.
An open grating of wrought iron, bronze, wood etc., forming a screen to a door, window or other opening, or used as a divider.
A room set aside within a club, hotel, large residence etc. for the benefit of guests or individuals who wish to smoke.
Ornamental wrought iron screen associated with gate lodges or entrance lodges.

A small underground chamber from where it was intended to monitor radioactive fallout in the event of nuclear attack.  The majority were built between 1956 and 1964, although construction continued into the early 1970s.
A coin-operated meter receiving fees for parking a vehicle in a street, and indicating time allowed.
A place where the popular gambling game of bingo is played.

Traditionally an amber-coloured globe lamp atop a tall black and white pole, acting as a signal to road users that there is a pedestrian crossing. Modern beacons may also include an outer ring of flashing LED lights.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.

Approximately circular or oval setting of spaced post holes indicating the former presence of a free-standing arrangement of upright timber posts. Often regarded as a wooden equivalent of the better known stone circles.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an F-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
Use for distinct structure on a large scale.
A thin slab of hard material, such as baked clay, shaped and used in quantity as a roofing material.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
A building used to shelter deer hunters.
A circular or oval window or panel. Also the circular opening at the top of a dome.

A relative dating technique for assessing bones from the same deposit. Often used to check for contemporaneity of bones selected for radiocarbon dating or to check for hoaxes such as the Piltdown Man.
Programmes of research or investigation involving the examination of primary documentary material to inform the understanding of heritage assets.
A large, manmade pool, usually lined with tiles, rubber or similar. Can be placed in the open air, eg. a LIDO, or built as part of a covered sports centre.
A factory where tobacco pipes made of clay are manufactured.
A projecting vertical window in the sloping roof of a house.
A place where social and other functions such as parties, presentations and meetings can be held.
A reinforced wall designed to reflect the blast from an explosion. Often found associated with powder magazines, pillboxes and air raid shelters.
An old ship converted for a variety of uses for which it is not required to move under its own power.
Hard, black, carbonized plant matter, usually found in seams below the earth's surface and used as a fuel and for the manufacture of gas.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
Any part of an aircraft. Use more specific term where known.
The residence or official premises of a consul, the official appointed by a state to protect its citizens and commercial interests in a foreign state.
Buildings and plant used for the refining of oil or the production of chemicals using oil.
Religious Society Of Friends Meeting House
A prepared slope on which rails are laid to enable early tramroads and railways to negotiate a steep gradient.

A site, complex or building which has been converted for use as the headquarters for the civilian authorities in the event of a nuclear attack or major natural disaster destroying the seat of government.
Deep ploughing to break up hard-pan or otherwise improve soil character in cultivated land.
Objects used for the preparation of food and drink,for cooking and consumption.
A structure, building or room within a building, used by a local authority for the continuance of local government in the event of a military or civil emergency.
Site of small scale industrial production often involving hand work and craft skills.
A flat-topped, often elongated, construction at which customers are served by staff in a commercial establishment such as a bank, shop, inn etc.
A hoisting mechanism powered by electricity.
A brass plaque, usually on the ground rather than a wall fixture, commemorating a person or event.
The position of a fire in a wood-fuelled furnace. All periods from the Iron Age  to the 17th century.
A factory where metal wire is manufactured.
Photographic print on self-developing photographic paper in a format developed by Polaroid in the 1970's
Use for vessels registered in Romania.
The main gearwheel in a water mill, sharing the same shaft as the exterior waterwheel but placed within the mill.
The residence and office of a chaplain.
A road block formed by placing rails or girders in an upright position in sockets in the road surface, forming a moveable barrier.
The horizontal assembly of architrave, frieze and cornice carried upon columns and pilasters in the Composite order; and so containing elements of the Ionic and Corinthian orders.
A school for instruction in the art of horsemanship.

A residence of two or three monks of the Savigniac order dependent on a foreign mother house. The order was originally founded by monks in Savigny, Normandy, in 1105 and first established in Britain in 1123 at Tulket, Preston.
A close fitting cap covering the sides, back and top of the head.
A long straight timber, halved across  other roof timbers, especially running from a wall post or aisle post across the tiebeam to the opposing rafter.
An ancilliary building within a larger works, as distinct from a SMELT MILL.
An aircraft maintenance workshop deriving from the use of  weather proofing varnish to aircraft canvas called "dope" in order to keep the canvas taut and airtight. From 1912 onwards.
An alignment of posts or postholes of unknown function
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on an English mother house.
An architectural ornament usually surmounting the apex of a gable, canopy or roof.
A report detailing the results of a study of the fabric of a standing building.
An open area within a bank where financial transactions take place.
A broad container, usually used for cooking.
A works producing gelatine from animal products for use as a culinary setting agent and in the photography, dyeing, brewing and glue industries. For explosives use GELATINE WORKS (EXPLOSIVE)
A beaker with a construction above the base to form a waisted profile. (Source: MPRG)
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the working buildings are carefully planned as linked ranges and are focused around one or more working yards. They often result from a single phase of building.
A pair of round edged tools like chisels to make a groove in iron.
A room set aside for the storage of goods or valuables. Use more specific term where known.
A building where miners could improve their knowledge by attending lectures and using the reading room facilities.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
The beans, or powder resulting from grinding the beans, of shrubs of the genus Coffea. The powder is used to make the drink Coffee.
The SI derived unit for current density.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A planned village or settlement, usually developed by a philanthropic industrialist , to house workers. Most include facilities for the education and betterment of the workers and their families.
A central point for the deposit, collection and recycling of waste materials.
Use for a watercraft powered by wind caught in an assemblage of cloth sails and masts.
A building used to accommodate donkeys.
A specialist hospital where the elderly receive medical treatment.
Use for a craft powered by an engine. Use also for cases where the precise engine type is not known.
HIstoric England Inspector of Ancient Monuments
A grave or sepulchre including a monument. Use specific type where known.
A small port town on the coast of northern Lolland.
An interment of human or animal remains. Use specific type where known. If component use with wider site type. Use FUNERARY SITE for optimum retrieval in searches.
Area of a garden for the cultivation of ferns.
A room in which music is performed.
A building where horses are rubbed down after training.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.

In fortification, a detached triangular outwork consisting of two battered faces forming a salient angle. Usually positioned in the ditch in front of a rampart and between two bastions. Term mainly for military architecture from 15th century and later.

Feature, typically a ship, boat, aircraft or vehicle, deliberately sunk for recreational and diver educational purposes in inland bodies of water used as dive centres, such as lakes and water-filled quarries, or offshore as artificial reefs.
An ornamental garden feature, sometimes with an associated bath house.
A building used as a control centre for the Air Raid Precautions network, responsible for issuing air raid warnings and coordinating fire and rescue services.
A stone or brick wall enclosing a park.
A clay tube with a small bowl at the end used for smoking tobacco.
The surface of a room which conceals overhead structural members.
A non perforated stone used as a hammer in making stone tools.
Hematological disorders such as chronic anemia, hemophilia and acute leukemia.
A circular toy which spins on a point.
A small roofed shelter for cattle without tethering point or stalls, but with a small yard attached. It is often detached from the main range of farm buildings.
A building, either purpose-built or modified, used for the co-ordination of the Fire Service.
A fitting incorporating a series of overlapping flaps providing ventilation or transmission of sound.
A small auxiliary engine to help start up a large steam engine - invented 1866.
A building housing machinery for crushing chalk for whiting. Whiting was used in toothpaste, paint, tablets, putty and other products.
A flat arch or lintel with quadrants on the corbels rising from the jambs.
A hulk or obsolete vessel filled with cement or similar material and scuttled to block an entrance to a port or anchorage, usually as a defensive measure.
A water-tight cover that closes and opening in a vessel's deck used for the ingress and egress of persons and cargo.
A stick used to beat a drum.
A platform on which corpses are placed and allowed to decompose in the open air, so as to leave only the bones for subsequent burial.
A gaming piece used specifically to play chess.
Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds. Can include small pre-Cranleigh institutions, eg: dispensaries with in-patients.
A hut provided as accommodation for hop pickers and may also be know as a Hop Pickers' Hut
Sheets of iron or steel bent into a series of ridges and hollows to give added strength and rigidity.
The residence of a canal worker.
A solid support of masonry to sustain vertical pressure and frequently each of the pillars from which an arch springs.
Open sided barn for the storage of wood produced by the periodic cutting of small trees.
A stone or brick wall either in, or enclosing, a garden.
An object constructed to allow birds to bathe in it.
A type of spearhead with a triangular blade bevelled at the edges and with a groove(s) following the outline.
A cast iron post similar to a lamp post, with revolving top to carry either coloured plates, or an oil lamp with coloured glass at night. Associated with canal or river navigation locks.
Substances, including acids, alkalis etc. obtained by or used in a chemical process.
A decorative S-shaped moulding, usually placed at the top of a cornice, with a convex lower half and a concave upper half.
An object used in washing or cleaning the body.
A marker of some form used to delineate a route, especially ones associated with pilgrimages.
A factory or works principally engaged in the production of a single base propellant, using nitrocellulose without the addition of nitroglycerine.
A vehicle or aircraft placed at the entrance to a site as a symbolic guardian.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of furniture or furniture related materials.
A building housing an electric powered ventilation fan for use in deep mine shafts
A craft on which is a machine for the loading and unloading of grain to and from a warehouse.
A commemorative monument to victims of the plague.
A jug with more or less straight sides that flare out from a narrow rim or neck to a wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A place where the science of historical and comparative language is taught.
A horn used to hold loose gun powder for recharging firearms.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
The exterior upper covering, and its supporting structure, of a building.
A thick, viscous, black liquid obtained by the destructive distillation of coal or other organic substances used for preserving wood or rope and for covering road surfaces.
The part of a musical instrument in which notes resonate and increase the sound of the instrument.
An extra sole on a shoe.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 10040/41.
A building temporarily requisitioned for use as an auxiliary hospital administered by members of the Voluntary Aid Detachment during the First World War.
A piece of iron cut from blooms and lengths of bar, probably for transportation, which were then reworked.
A piece of machinery on which a railway engine, carriage or wagon can be rotated at a railway terminal.
An object which is going to become a key. It has the shape but has not been cut to fit a lock.
Stone, brick or wooden steps or stairs found in a garden.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.
A room used for the ritual cleaning of the body prior to burial
A major fortified place, often a town, capable of containing a large force. If Roman use LEGIONARY FORTRESS.
An apartment for the use of people of high status, often the owner of the building. Also a room adjoining, or close to, a hall and used as a drawing room or venue for private functions.
A strut which is at an angle between the principal rafter and tiebeam.
The plan on which a circular building is constructed.
A building in which animals are housed. For non agricultural use see ANIMAL HOUSE and narrow terms in RECREATIONAL class.

A building within a complex, such as a leisure centre, school, industrial site etc, often containing toilet and washing facilities, where individuals can change their clothes. For a changing room within a larger building, see Components.
A decorative moulding featuring a geometric pattern suggesting the crenelles and merlons of a battlement.
An object used to provide heat for various purposes eg to cook or to heat a room etc.
A clock with special mechanisms and dials to display astonomical information.
A C20th military building used to test the efficiency of gas protection equipment provided for drivers of all forms of vehicles.
A compact design of steam engine which eliminates a connecting rod by having the piston rod directly attached to the crank.
A place where current and former members of the armed services meet for social and recreational activities.
A building from which the administration of a county is carried out by the County Council. It is also, historically, the site where the county quarter sessions and assizes were held.
A route across a river, or lake. Use only for small inland ferries and index with LANDING POINT/STAGE/STEPS or PIER where known.
A wooden, stone or iron post for securing things to or for preventing vehicular access to pedestrianized areas.
Cluster of dwellings of medieval or later date (Scots)
A jar with a rounded profile merging into a rounded base with no discernible basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A room used for directing military operations and exercises.
A device for rotating a spit.

Land which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime land was requisitioned for various purposes, such as for argriculture or for military training/events etc.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 3156/41.

A hospital ward block, completely open on the south side apart from a low railing and sun blind. It was thought beneficial for the recovery of wounded soldiers as well as those with diseases of the chest.
A steeply pitched spire whose base is significantly narrower than the tower on which it sits.
Similar in design to the FROMSON HANGAR but designed to drawing number 3752/43 and used for storing aircraft with small wingspans.
A place where wheels and wheeled vehicles were manufactured, originally from wood.
A hard, unglazed earthenware, characteristically reddish-brown in colour, used in decoration and construction.
An inscription or illustration carved into the surface of a stone wall or other architectural element.
A road/carriage way giving access from the main road to the house, stables.
The measurement of the decay of radioactive uranium (U) isotopes. Particularly useful for dating calcite and sometimes bone, tooth and shell up to 70,000 years old.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
A container to receive milk during the milking process.
A camp for the temporary accommodation of uprooted civilians or foreign ex-service personnel, who had fought for the British forces during WWII (e.g.Polish).
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A container for holding votive offerings.

The supposed detection of subsurface features by employing a twig, copper rod, pendulum, or other instrument. Discontinuous movements in these instruments are believed by some to record the existence of buried features.
Workshop used in the the production of tripe.
A model village established by the chartists.
An area of the sea or coastline where vessels have been abandoned.
A machine for further attenuating a sliver of cotton after it has been through a draw frame.
Used for vessels registered in Malaysia.
A mid-1st century AD brooch influenced by the Thistle type, commonly with projections on the upper bow and widening to a triangular plate, often described as a fantail, below.
A long, narrow yard used for jousting.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of motor vehicles.
The residence of a keeper of a royal park etc.
Movements of men, munitions, and supplies in support either of naval manoeuvres and engagements or of terrestrial troop movements at home and abroad.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A 19th century spa building, usually consisting of a hotel with baths used for water treatment.
A truss in which spaces between timbers are filled, as between rooms and at the ends of a building.
A site where aircraft are stored, dismantled and processed for the recovery of serviceable parts.
A cord or handle which rings a bell when pulled.
A positive black and white image on film which can be projected onto a screen when light is shone through it.
Series of rooms in a workhouse complex where children were housed and looked after.

A rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound of Neolithic date, usually accompanied by flanking or encircling ditches, and normally associated with human remains. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
An object attached to a window which is removable.
A tread-wheel by which a crane was formerly worked.
Four iron spikes joined together so that when the caltrop is on the ground a spike is always pointing upwards. Used to disable infantry and cavalry.

A circular or octagonal building at the base of a post mill to provide storage space and to give protection to the superstructure. The roundhouse is not attached to the mill itself. Some roundhouses were later converted for domestic purposes.
A building where an officer of a county, district or municipality acting as a representative of the Crown holds inquests, including deaths through violence or accident and treasure trove.
Development relating to the construction of a new highway, or widening or modification of an existing highway.
A passage providing access to utility services or a larger tunnel for the purposes of monitoring and maintenance. May also provide be used as an evacuation route.
A circular toy which spins on a point. Can be kept spinning by whipping with a lash.
A shell-shaped moulded hood over an exterior opening, such as a doorway.
A market for the sale of cheeses.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
A pipe or channel to carry water outwards from a gutter or behind a parapet. If decorated with grotesque heads it is called a gargoyle.
That portion of the Pacific which stretches from the equator to Antarctica.

Combination of organic and inorganic material cohered to form a hard solid wall or covering. Use for structures created by the excavation and piling up of earth, such as ice houses. Earth may be used in combination with other materials.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
An area of land, usually enclosed, set aside for the breeding of hares.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote technology through lectures, research, etc.
A bridge, carrying a footpath or road, usually across marshy or waterlogged ground.
The measurement of the ratio of a radioactive potassium (K) isotope and the argon (Ar) gas produced as a by-product of its decay. Useful for dating volcanic material older than 1,000 years.
A funnel, connected to an opening in the floor of the tun encasing the grindstones in a corn mill, that carries ground meal away to a bin or sack.
A conical brick structure in which glass articles were made.
An enclosed area of land of varying size and shape which shows traces of defence.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
Instruments and their component parts used to produce music or audible signals of all forms.
A pit dug into the ground or a simple construction made of stone, brick or metal. Designed to contain a fire and prevent it from spreading, but can also be used to heat stone for breaking.
A kind of primary school kept by elderly women.
An object related to deaths, burials or funerals.
A thin, flexible material made from the pulp of wood or other fibrous matter which is then pressed and dried to form sheets.
A vertical structure, sometimes made of steel, often used in the manufacture of cement. Material is loaded at the top, burnt in the middle and removed at the bottom.
A building, usually circular, or containing circular rooms, for the exhibition of panorama paintings.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
Engineering workshop used for the final assembly of vehicles or structures from parts produced elsewhere in an engineering works.
A stand, either fixed or free-standing, usually with a sloping surface from which a bible, book or notes can be read, found in a church or lecture theatre.
A small vessel used to attack other vessels and setting themselves and then the enemy alight.
A tunnel running under a river or a hillside through which a railway line runs.

A very long, narrow, roofed building, often two-storeyed, used for the manufacture of rope. Often attached to warehousing, an engine house or offices. Can be included within the complex of a textile mill.
Large blocks of timber used to support railway tracks.
A raised platform or walkway connecting two buildings or a ship with the quay, etc.
A row of columns supporting an entablature.
Surface workings including shallow shafts, lode workings, open-pit methods and quarrying including some mines of stone, clays, compounds, etc. See also MINERAL EXTRACTION SITE.
A picturesque garden building decorated with tree roots, often serving as a HERMITAGE or ARBOUR.
A spandrel which supports a dome and aids the transition between the dome and its square or octagonal base.
An inscribed marker stone found on Hadrian's Wall.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A toothed, handled tool used to drag objects either to gather them together eg grass or hay, or to level them out eg sand or earth.
Positive image on continuous film strip suitable for projection of moving images.
A tool for creating holes in the ground in which to plant seeds or plants.
A roof truss supported by arcade posts in an aisled building.
An air-cushioned vehicle capable of travelling over land or water.
Factory for the production of safety fuses used in the ignition of gunpowder for blasting.

A highly decorated Anglo-Saxon Long Brooch, often made of silver or bronze, worn by women. Contemporary with the Cruciform Brooch, it features a large, square head plate and usually three rounded foot-terminals.
Waste resulting from the processes associated with the making of shoes.

A building with a range of facilities for the exclusive use of its all-male membership. Rooms were often provided as offices or short term accommodation, and the club could be used for business or social gatherings.
A small cargo vessel used on the West coast of Scotland.
Material consisting of at least 90% organic matter by dry weight. Formed from plant material under damp, wet or acid conditions where the rate of accumulation is greater than the rate of decay.
Trees, hedges and shrubs planted in the form of a medieval cathedral sometimes used as a memorial.
A substantial vertical member, usually a component of a main framework.
A hydraulically-powered crane where the jib and windlass are mounted on a central pillar.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
An interior wall, usually not load bearing, that divides a space.
One of a set, used as standards for specific coins, often bearing stamps and other marks of authenticity.
Dating to the reign of the Tudor monarchs.

An important two-seat, tractor biplane, initially used by the RFC in a reconnaissance role and by the RNAS as a bomber. Later converted to a single-seat Home Defence fighter and ultimately used as a trainer.
Although the proper term is square rod, for centuries this unit has been called a pole or perch or, more properly, square pole or square perch.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
An object placed to mark the site of a grave.
A strip of cultivated land situated against the exterior of a walled garden's perimeter, so placed to maximise usable wall space.
A fencing sword often used for recreational purposes.

Medium to coarse grained, green to dark red/black coloured igneous rock, mainly found on The Lizard, South West Cornwall. Due to its fragmentary structure, Serpentine is mainly used for decorative and ornamental purposes.
An object which has been bent and angled from which something else can be caught or suspended.
Pit for the depostion of ore sediment from waste water collected from ore washing.
A place where photographs are displayed for sale.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of wind power.
A building where motor cycles are assembled.
An instrument for measuring atmospheric pressure by its effects on mercury in a glass tube. It can also be used to measure altitude and depth and is especially used for predicting the weather.

The lowest of the three main parts of an entablature. Also the lintels, jambs and mouldings surrounding a door, window, panels or niche; or the ornamental mouldings around the exterior curve of an arch.
A levelled area of ground, circular in shape, used as the base on which a monument was built.Sometimes raised, a platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a monument.
Buildings, structures and sites directly associated with the operation of military airfields. See also AIR TRANSPORT SITE in the TRANSPORT Class.
A point of public water supply, including conduits, fountains, wells, pumps and standpipes.
A vase-like receptacle, especially a large bulbous one with a foot.

A building or site used to train civilians and members of the services in the skills designed to protect the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.
Dating to the reign of Queen Victoria.
A beam steam engine originating in Cornwall, first used for raising water from mines.
An educational establishment where the art and theory of building and construction is taught.
Purposely built camp with recreational facilities and individual chalets for accommodation.
An enclosure for wild cats such as Lions and Tigers
An individual section of panelling. Can form fences, ceilings, an outer layer to a wall etc.
Any object which bears an inscription.
A short trench used to protect troops or to provide defensive fire from, often dug for practice purposes.
A tall, multi storeyed building either used as business premises or, more usually, as residential accomodation.
A natural or man-made earth mound on which a gallows was erected.
A wooden cylinder or dowel used for pinning planks or timbers together.
A table found in a garden, often made of stone.
A flat level structure, can be part of a series, used to allow a person to move from one level to another, or can occur singularly on a threshold.
A stamp used to emboss paper.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A temporary, steel-framed transportable hangar developed by Teesside Bridge and Engineering Company to replace the obsolete Bellman hangars.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
Formerly included in the Historic England register of parks and gardens.
A railway which runs beneath the surface of the ground, eg. the London Underground Railway.
An establishment where chocolate was available as a beverage.
The large, pointed teeth, made of ivory, which are specially developed to protrude from the mouth of elephants.
A needle used to sew together thatch.
A piece of metal or wood with a hole through which a bolt can be screwed.
A building or set of rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls were held.
A container for sand which was used to stop ink from spreading.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A pit used for containing manure.
A hole or cavity in the ground, either natural or the result of excavation. Use more specific type where known.
A fuel store for the storage of dried peat.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
Hard, white/grey coloured liassic limestone. Quarried near Somerton in Somerset.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
Factory for the production of Pet Food.
A triangular sectioned rod probably used for making sparks.
A staff of office or authority.
A regular structural subdivision or compartment within a building, defined by dividing walls or the positions of the principal supporting members.
A burial ground for Roman Catholics.
Written or typed correspondence, usually between two or more parties.
A bowl with straight sides which are at an approximate right angle to the base, i.e. a roughly cylindrical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A building used to accommodate ducks.
Use for vessels registered in Germany or any of the states prior to unification.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
A working tunnel or gallery in a mine used for the extraction of ironstone.
A house with a pitched or gabled roof with a double slope and gables on two or more sides.
A target range used for rifle and small arms practice and recreational purposes.
A factory where rock gypsum is ground into a powder used in the production of plaster.
The vertical recessed face of a pediment, often decorated with sculpture.
A room intended for the purpose of teaching a group or class of students simultaneously.
An object worked on a lathe, usually the bi-product of such work.
Small building in which labourers, such as miners and tin workers. They are also associated with gardens where they provide on-site accommodation for gardeners and estate workers.
A large warehouse or store for upholstery.
An object which perforated the axle cap, passing through the axle and so keeping the wheel in place. Usually made of metal, though can be made of wood or antler.
A component of another building, often a house, used for storing nets.
A chapel dedicated to the Virgin, usually east of the chancel.
Decorative armour used for parades and display, not for combat.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.
A general name given to a series of machines which successively reduce the diameter of rovings before  the final spinning into yarn.
A building used to house members of the armed forces.
An example from which another object is made.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
A small stone blade with one edge blunted.
A trumpet type of instrument made from or in imitation of an animal horn.
A low lying area of land that is usually waterlogged at all times and is flooded in wet weather.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted under ground.
A compact design of engine in which a connecting rod is dispensed with, giving a short baseplate.
A residue, primarily lead oxide, formed during refining silver
REGISTER OF PARKS AND GARDENS DEREGISTERED
A rustic building of picturesque design, often associated with a model farm, country house or estate. Although ornamental in design they are intended to be functional.
Small vernacular building used by fishermen for the preparing of nets and storage of equipment.
A building or site used for the production of frameworks of beds.
A site where metal springs are manufactured.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one side of an open cattle yard.
A musket with a snaphance lock. This lock consisted of a flint and steel but the pan cover was separate to the steel unlike the flintlock.
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
An enclosed piece of land, generally large in area, used for hunting, the cultivation of trees, for grazing sheep and cattle or visual enjoyment. Use more specific type where known.
A building occupied by a club or commonly used for club activities.
A ticket booth in a theatre or cinema.
A vertical faced projection in the cornice.
Metal, either precious or base, in the form of bars and coins. Use more specific type.
Easily formed metal alloy composed of copper and zinc.
A small tool which pierces material. It has a flat cutting edge.
The court or enclosed space at the front of a building or structure.
Dating to the reign of the Hanoverian kings and queens.
A building or room where food is prepared and cooked.
A decorative moulding featuring a series of small, projecting, dome-like shapes each resembling a halved nutmeg.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with the knees brought up against the chest. This is a more extreme form of crouched inhumation.
A structure, often ornamental, in a garden, park or area of recreation, designed to reflect the style of Indian architecture. The most famous example of which is the Royal Pavilion in Brighton.
A lattice work bower or shady retreat covered with climbing plants.
Any vessel in use by the West India Company.

A Historic Landscape Survey can be used to identify the chronological relationships of the elements of a landscape to one another. By interrogating these relationships a relative chronology can be built up. This information can be used to frame further research, to inform site management or as the basis for public presentation.
A meeting hall of the Temperance Society.
A type of mace with bolster shaped stone or metal head on a wooden or metal shaft. Where the use is thought to be ceremonial, double index with ceremonial object.
A place of worship for followers of the teachings of Martin Luther.
A garden for the cultivation of herbs used for medicinal or culinary purposes.
The bark and wood of trees of the genus Aspidosperma used to produce tannin.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
An educational establishment where law is taught.

A form of Neolithic burial monument primarily found in Cornwall and the Scilly Isles. It comprises a round cairn, usually with a retaining wall or kerb, and an entrance leading directly into a chamber.
A site used by the Air Raid Precautions network. Use more specific term.
A feature found during an archaeological investigation which implies the presence of a monument, building, structure or human activity.
A house in a terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.
An encircling ornament for the head, usually denoting sovereignty.
A large trough or vessel commonly created from a hollowed out tree trunk for the storage of brine prior to processing for salt.
Clothing worn on the upper body.
A vessel lost having overturned due to severe weather or shifting cargo.
A settlement built to a pre-determined plan, including housing, infrastructure and associated amenities.
A short chain or chains attached to a woman's belt for carrying keys etc.
A rotary prime mover. Turbines may be steam, water or gas operated.
Grains of cereal used as food.
Stoving in or fracturing of lowest part of vessel's hull.
Two intersecting beams set on the ground to support a post, usually for a post mill.
A structure associated with forges, watermills, water-powered factories, etc.
A garden incorporating fountains and pools in which aquatic and other water-loving plants are grown.
A purlin that is threaded through a hole in the principal rafter.
A vessel that is deliberately run or dragged up the beach to save cargo and or crew. Do not use if the vessel is refloated.
Polished bone used to burnish objects eg pottery.
A crane in which, during any alteration of radius, an automatic device causes the load to move horizontally.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
A belt used to confine a hawk's wings.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the preserving of food.

Alabaster is a name applied to varieties of two distinct minerals: gypsum and calcite. The finer kinds of alabaster are employed as an ornamental stone, especially for internal decoration as it's softness allows it to be carved into elaborate forms.
A moulding which projects beyond the face of a panel or frame, usually found in panelling or in doors.
A sculptured likeness, portrait or image, often found on a tomb or other memorial.
An oval shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A kind of stone used in making ink.
A large tank or cask for storing or holding goods, whether liquid, such as chemicals or fermenting beer, or dry, often during a production process.
A prepared slope with rails on which boats can be transferred from one canal to another at a higher or lower level. The boats can either be floated in a caisson or carried in a cradle or sling.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A hospital department where research and treatment into the causes and nature of diseases or abnormal bodily conditions is carried out.
A covered arcade, often attached to a building, open on one or more sides.
An extant settlement which shows evidence of a shift in focus, eg. towards a new road, generally in the form of abandoned buildings or earthworks on the margin furthest from the new focus.
Swimming pool, usually part of a larger LIDO or SPORTS CENTRE complex. Medium size pool, between large pool and paddling pool, used primarily for learners.
An alloy of iron and carbon, its strength makes it suitable for load bearing purposes. It is primarily used in structural steelwork and concrete reinforcement.
Long narrow pieces of wood used for a variety of purposes.
A sample taken from waterlogged conditions.
A coarse grained metamorphic rock that is composed maily of green, brown or black amphibole minerals and plagioclase feldspar. Amphiboles are usually members of the hornblende group.
A pit where grain is stored.
A spout allowing water to spill away from a building. Usually carved in images of animals, people or grotesques.
A room for children to play in.
A terrace of houses built on a slope giving the roofline a stepped appearance.
A place of entry into a site, monument or building.
A single acting, non-rotative beam engine worked by atmospheric pressure.
An ornamental tablet of brass. Use a materials thesaurus where brass is a material.
Structured list of information about items of interest to a research project, for example monuments of a particular type.
A fairground ride, often a permanent structure, consisting of a tower with an internal staircase and an external spiral shaped slide.

Bordering the five continents of Antarctica, Asia, Australasia, North and South America, the Pacific is the largest of the world's oceans, and covers more area (63,838,000 square miles) than that of the combined seven continents.

Structural board comprising a core of thin layers of wood bonded together, which is faced on one or both sides with a sheet of metal, usually galvanised steel or aluminium. Mainly used for external wall cladding.
Machine readable files suitable for use in a geographic information system (GIS).
A tool for removing the core from an apple.
Apparatus using mechanical power for a particular function.
The application of colour and other materials to a structure to either conceal it from identification or to make it look like something else.
A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A hard, durable wood obtained from trees of the genus Ulmus.
A close fitting skull cap, usually worn under a helmet.
A transverse timber in aisled construction, joining aisle posts below tiebeam level, to allow rearing of pairs of posts.
The peg of a stringed instrument which, when tightened or loosened, tunes the string of the instrument.
A thin board forming part of a musical instrument and placed in a position to strengthen or increase its sound.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
A farmstead, often of linear plan, where the working buildings are placed opposite and parallel to the house and attached working buildings with a relatively narrow space between.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts and beams with infillings of pre stressed concrete planks and felted slabs. Initially used for military barracks in WWII and later for civilian housing. Manufactured by the Orlit Company.
A sculpted female figure carrying a basket on her head.
A holder for a candle, usually fitted to another object.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.
A horticultural site where trees, shrubs and plants are grown for sale and transplanting elsewhere.

A building as part of a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term from Components thesaurus if it is part of a building complex.

An end scraper which has a retouched end that is straight in form. If the tool blank is a blade or flake, and the retouch is abrupt retouch rather than scraper retouch then use either Truncated blade or Truncated flake. (Source: SARC)
A room, or part of a kitchen, for the cleaning and storage of kitchen utensils.
An area of land, usually planted with creeping plants and turf, laid out in a woodland landscape to produce the natural effect of a clearing.
An object which does not provide light but supports or is attached to lighting equipment.
A usually permanent defensive work. Use specific type where known.
An institution for the imprisonment of felons and debtors.
A tool for cutting substances eg wood, metal etc. Its blade has teeth down one edge.
A bowstring truss with the space between its members filled by a lattice of crossing diagonal rods.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A zoo building containing artificial ponds or tanks in which aquatic plants and animals are kept alive for purposes of observation and study.
A case or container for an amulet.
A written, drawn and photographic record, including a ground plan and elevations to produce an adequate record of the structure.
Piece of armour worn to protect the back, often permanently connected to the breastplate.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of children.
Hard, fossil rich, white to deep red coloured limestone, laid down during the Tertiary period. Used since Roman times because of its good durability and weathering properties.
Storage vessel, usually a two handled narrow necked jar.
A vertical iron bar fixed within a window opening to support a leaded light.

A maritime technique which involves the simple process of bringing up surface sediments from the seafloor for analysis usually using mechanical apparatus. As the process recovers a mixture of sediments it cannot be used to characterise stratigraphy.
Originally a metallic alloy of copper and tin or zinc, now used solely for an alloy of copper and zinc.
Round object used to carry cable or wire
A building or room, originally equipped for gymnastics or indoor sports but also, more recently, equipped with cross-training machines and free-weights for members to improve their physical fitness.
A building or room where beer is decanted from conditioning tanks, into casks or barrels.
A wickerwork basket for holding fish or catching lobsters.
A container used to catch blood during bleeding.
A measuring rule graduated in feet.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.
A small enclosure for cattle, sheep, swine, poultry, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A principal with a curved lower end that continues down the wall for a short distance.
A triangular piece of wood used to raise slates next to a wall or similar.
A building associated with rope manufacture, especially in naval dockyards.
A covered stall at a market or fair, etc.
An object carried about the person for religious purposes.
A lid with a carinated conical profile and straight vertical sides, surmounted by a conical top with and integral knob. (Source: MPRG)
A stone or metal head on a wooden shaft. Where the use is thought to be ceremonial multiple index with ceremonial object.
A place of worship for Baptists. The first Baptist church was formed by Thomas Helws in 1611 and gave rise to the General Baptist Movement.
A church, usually found in East Anglia, of early Medieval and/or Medieval date with attached or detached round tower.
Range used by the Navy with reinforced observation huts which housed quadrant equipment to record accuracy and damage.
A recess for holding the Holy Sacrament.
A drawing, generally on a transparent sheet, which can be placed on top of another image to combine information from both.

Planned &/or landscaped areas designed for aesthetic or recreational purposes. Includes all sites, buildings, structures & features normally associated with parks & urban spaces including street furniture.
A portable medieval container usually cylindrical or barrel shaped.
A vessel designed or adapted to sweep and explode mined areas at sea without prior detection. (See Minehunter for vessels that detect and destroy individual mines).

An image created by controlled exposure of light sensitive film.  Usually a static image in time and space.  For digital photographs double index with an appropriate term under MACHINE READABLE STORAGE MEDIUM.
a wooden, metal or stone post used to tether a horse, or other animals.
Other 8 (Dedicated to the display of a monument)
A roll of paper or parchment, especially with writing upon it.
A tool used to filter solid material from liquid by means of a mesh, net or sheet with holes.
A room used in a church to store vestments and for the clergy to dress in.
A purpose-built fisherman's house, eg. a house with a first floor dwelling and ground floor fish store, or a house with a watch tower for spotting shoals.
A vessel used for the underwater recovery of a ship and/or her contents or to assist vessels that are sinking.
An object supported by a crosspiece on a post, used by knights as a target in tilting.

A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific from mid 1980's to early 1990's.
A works where crude oil is distilled into its fractions or cuts.
A bank, often faced with stone, with a hedge planted on top.
A community of Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines, first founded by Moravian emigrants in Saxony, Germany.
A long loose fitting garment worn instead of a coat.
A sheet or cloth used to lay the corpse out in for burial.
A wall and area of ground where the game of fives is played.
A pit dug to protect a small group of infantry men.
Use for vessels registered in Cuba.
Housing provided for refugees. Similar to refugee camp but with the reuse of existing buildings rather than a temporary camp.
A technique for the dating of damage tracks in volcanic materials caused by the fissioning of decaying radioactive uranium (U) isotopes. Useful in samples more than 50,000 years old.
Small, heavily built coble, usually fitted with lugsail and oars, used on the north-east coast of England to assist, tow, pilot, provision or otherwise attend ships.
