The tower, generally attached to a church or other building but sometimes separate, where bells are hung and from which sound is emitted. Also applied to the upper chamber where bells are hung, or the wooden structure supporting them.
A tripod used to support pots over a fire.
An unprocessed mineral, collected for the extraction of metals or other substances contained within the mineral.
Items worn or carried as an adjunct to clothing, for example, headdresses, sashes, fans, masks etc.
A stick for digging up roots etc. Sometimes a stone weight is attached.
A tool with a cross handle at one end and a spoon shaped or gouge cutter at the other, used for drilling holes.
A room or building in which riding tackle is stored.
A site visit to ascertain the nature and extent of the site and its surrounding environs by means of a visual inspection from which a written and/or photographic record is made.
A heavy grating, often made of wood or iron, usually lowered vertically as a defensive barrier at the entrance to a gatehouse or barbican.
A building in which pottery ware is made by shaping plastic clay on a spinning turntable, known as a potter's wheel or throwing wheel.
Buildings and structures associated with canal transport.

A section of a building distinguished from the rest either architecturally or as a separate structure joined to the main building, often intended for entertainment, specialised functions or ornamental purposes.

A vertical vein of metallic ore, usually lead, occuring between walls of rock and cutting through the bedding. Often rakes have been worked from early times leaving deep trenches several km long, with adits leading off and shafts sunk at the side.
A wash room. Use with wider site type where known.
No longer used. Traditionally used for resources that could only be identified to a date range from the Palaeolithic to Iron Age. Included here to aid migration.
A container for drinking, with a base and stem but without handles.
An oil based derivative used as a fuel in diesel engines.
A place where photographs are taken of people or things on a commercial basis.
Objects primarily intended to be used as a medium of exchange, eg coins.
A tower containing a curfew bell. The bell was rung in the evening, as a signal that fires were to be extinguished.
A building, on a military airfield or base, in which motor vehicles are housed.
Remains of barley (Hordeum sp.) grain (caryopyses). These grains are sometimes itemised separately.
A passageway or corridor beteen two areas which is covered.
An office, particularly at a seaport, at which customs are collected.
A tower in which shot is made from molten lead poured through sieves at top and falling into water at bottom.
A device fitted and locked onto the head of a woman as a form of punishment, featuring a metal plate that fits into the mouth to impede speech..
A legally protected wreck that is no longer designated.
A piece of cladding in the form of a length of timber fixed horizontally to the building.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A shoe fixed to an animal, either permanently or temporarily, to protect the hoof and provide improved grip.
A place where the homeless are accommodated, permanently or temporarily.
A farmstead where the farmhouse and working buildings are attached and in-line. They can comprise the extension of linear farmsteads.

Archaeological monitoring of geotechnical pits and boreholes can provide a cost-effective means of establishing the potential for archaeological remains to survive on previously developed land or where deep deposits are anticipated.  It is usually used as part of a desk-based assessment or field evaluation.
A structure, building or site commemorating soldiers and civilians killed in war.
A wooden nail, round or square in section, used to fix a joint.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A place where letters and parcels are sorted before being distributed. Usually found at a large general post office.
Scaffolding intended to impede the advance of enemy armoured divisions. Often found in association with "one way" anti tank ditches.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
A tool used to notch, line cut or scratch into a surface.
Former terrestrial landscape of any kind now submerged through erosion, as at Dunwich, or historical inundation processes, eg. post-glacial submersion of the North Sea landscape ("Doggerland").
A vertical member dividing a window into two or more lights.
A garden devoted to the growth of vegetables.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
A site where metal is worked. Use specific type where known.
The hard, black, heavy wood of various tropical trees native to Africa and Asia, used in furniture manufacture and for making ornaments.
A cleansing house associated with Jewish burial ceremonies
Small revolving wooden chalets that could be turned with their backs to the prevailing wind so that hospital patients could recline in them on long chairs in all weathers.
Synthetic fibres and reconstituted materials imitating, or in the form of, timber created by a man-made process. Use carefully - do not confuse with mock and sham timber work.
To be used for the frame elements only, not for the bedding.

Armoured military vehicle with its own firepower, which operates on tracks for troop mobility over rough terrain. Some may be adapted, or purpose-built, to be amphibious, and may then be double-indexed as AMPHIBIOUS VEHICLE.
A place where gypsum is extracted.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
An ornamental panel or decorative structure situated above a mantelpiece
An enclosed area of parkland used almost exclusively for the hunting of deer.

Staircase whose moving steps are driven mechanically whilst remaining permanently in a horizontal plane allowing users or objects to be moved effortlessly from one level to another, within or outside a building.
A round barrow in which the mound and ditch are separated from each other by a berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
Equipment for the hunting and capture of animals.
A staircase for the use of servants, tradesmen or individuals not permitted to use the main part of a building or establishment.
A flat, oblong gaming piece marked with spots used to play dominoes.
A mound or structure on which targets are placed for archery practice or competition.
North American wood, the name being applied either to the American Larch; or to the Black or Ridge-pole Pine of inland areas; and the Scrub Pine of maritime regions.
A colonnette set in a corner or angle, such as the meeting of two walls or the place at which a doorframe meets the wall it is set in.
A long bed planted with mixed shrubs, usually found near the house.
Open-air area often terraced on which a range of ore processing operations are carried out.
A large building used for the transaction of the public business of a town, the holding of courts of justice, entertainments and other activities.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
Wooden or ferro-concrete tower for cooling waste, hot water from a power station. The water cascades from the top of the tower to a pond in the bottom.
This is the top term for the class. This class includes terms with very broad definitions which could be assigned to three or more classes. See UNASSIGNED Class List for narrow terms.
A prepared area used for the game of baseball.
For the collection of money by charities, churches, etc.
A warship used to provide an escort to other warships or merchant ships against attack.
A long hollow tube used to blow molten glass into shapes.

Collective term for the slates from Devon and Cornwall. Hard, fine grained metamorphic rock. Varying in colour from dark grey/green to blueish/grey. West Country Slate is geologically different from both Lake District and Welsh Slate.
A site, in which salt is obtained by boiling and evaporating salt brine or seawater in large pans. Often the only surviving evidence are the mounds formed from the waste produced by the process.
A building forming part of a complex or larger establishment, such as a workhouse, that serves as an entrance equipped with facilities associated with procedures undergone by new arrivals.
A representation of the crucifixion of Christ or related scenes as a sculpture, etc.
Ammunition manufactured for use in hand held firearms.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine Nuns.
An arched, or bow-shaped, segmental timber truss with its ends tied together by a straight or cambered member.
A structure with a roof to provide shelter from the weather for occupants or contents. Use specific type where known.
A craft used to deepen shipping channels, harbours and other water courses.

For example arthritis, club foot, back pain, amputations and loss of certain functions. Major dysfunction of a joint, reconstructive surgery, disorder of the spine, amputations, fractures of extremities and growth impairments.

Where archaeological remains are to be preserved in-situ within a development there will normally be a requirement to provide details of how this will be achieved.  Typically this would involve a design and methods statement for groundworks.  Where particularly important or vulnerable features are to be preserved there may also be a requirement to monitor their condition and take remedial action in the event of decay.
A small brewery, often situated in a public house, producing limited quantities of beer, for consumption locally and/or on the premises.
Pit for mixing raw materials with water in the preparation of a clay body.
A type of water pump used in the Wigan coalfields in the late 18th and 19th centuries.
A tray used for separating the grain from husks and straw.
An often highly elaborate water fountain, usually found in parks, gardens or urban spaces.
A piece of plate armour designed to protect the shoulder.
A sleeved garment worn on the upper body.
A jar with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body and a rounded, inward sloping shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A house with windows and doors on one side only; often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
A musket fired by a piece of burning match being held in the lock which, when the trigger was pulled, would contact with powder in the pan to set off the charge.
An area or series of tiles applied, usually to an interior floor or wall's surface, for practical or decorative effect.
A prison used for temporary detention. The typical village lock-up was a one-storeyed, one-celled building, sometimes of round or polygonal plan.
A large bag made of coarse cloth or thick paper.
A dwelling house forming part of a Chartist Land Colony.
An agricultural implement with sharp blades for cutting or turning over the earth.

Sites, buildings, structures & features used in the defence of the civilian population. Includes civil defence sites, weapons stores, training sites, military signals & active defence structures such as anti-aircraft sites.
A passenger vessel equipped to carry a large number of emigrants usually with large third class decks and plenty of cargo space.
A thick fabric cover used to provide warmth.
A room intended for the taking of refreshments, usually containing a counter from which they are served.
A descriptive account of the building supported by detailed archive research, annotated measured plans and elevations and a detailed photographic record.
A tool used for digging the ground.
An object to point at words whilst reading, eg the Alfred jewel.
A vessel with a lid, handle and spout used particularly for boiling water.
A classical order with metopes and triglyphs in the frieze. Greek Doric has no base and a fluted column but Roman Doric does have a base and may or may not have a fluted column.
A covered walk, walled on one side and usually arcaded on the other, surrounding or partly surrounding an open area in a monastery or similar complex of Christian buildings.
A megalithic tomb of Neolithic date comprising a chamber bounded by large upright orthostats, often only three or four in number, which support a large capstone.
Dried flower buds, used as a pungent aromatic spice.
Bells used either as a percussion instrument or for other purposes such as calling attention, marking time periods etc.
Pieces of bone used in a game, the pieces are thrown and then picked up between bounces of a small ball or throws of another piece.
A site where traditional public shows, in which the display of exotic animals, combined with feats of agility and comedy, were held.
A post box mounted in, or on, a wall.
A roof with a bow-shaped, segmental timber truss which has the space between its members filled by a lattice of crossing diagonal rods.
An abbey founded in 1415 for nuns of the Bridgettine order.
Decontamination and other work to render land safe for re-use e.g. previously in industrial use.
The west end of a church made up of a tower, entrance hall and upper room, usually with an altar.
A school attended by children between the ages of eleven and sixteen offering a vocationally orientated curriculum.
A building or range of buildings used for the cleaning, crushing and loading of freshly mined coal.
A building providing shelter for sheep and storage for fodder and shepherding equipment.
An all-steel end-opening, hangar with canted sides designed for folded-wing aircraft.
A part of a building joined to the core of the structure and at an angle to it.

Roman-era pottery, principally made in areas from modern-day France and Germany, for food use, with a characteristic glossy red surface and which may be either decorated or plain, and often produced in quantity as an export cargo.
A house in which a member of the Royal Court lives.
A building or group of buildings used for the raising of mink, a semi-aquatic mammal which is farmed for its fur.
Unspecified. Use specific type where known.
A religious cloth often used to cover coffins.
A passenger vessel equipped with recreational facilities for long voyages for pleasure and sight seeing.
A round container open at the top, usually to hold liquids.

Underwater investigation of the seabed, using side-looking sonar device that emits fan shaped acoustic pulses down toward the seafloor. The intensity of the acoustic reflections from the sea floor are recorded as an image of the seabed.
A chronological journal, generally showing appointments, or recording memories and impressions of a days events over a period of time.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply to DC supply for use by tramcars.
A mug with a rounded body profile below a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between the neck and the body. The neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
A massive structure, usually of stone, serving as a pier or breakwater, or joining two places separated by water.
Includes chemical and natural fertilizers and waste products. use more specific term.
An object that supports another in water, eg float on a fishing line or net.
A building, usually one-storeyed, for dyeing cloth.
A piece with one or more surfaces with either/both slightly convex shape appropriate for use in forming metal artefacts.
A wheel which is turned by a horse in order to provide power. Used in mines, manufacturing and farming.

A curved military aircraft hangar produced in 1939. The frame is steel which is then clad with steel sheeting and reinforced concrete and typically covered with a thin layer of concrete, earth and turf.
A construction designed to look like a pillbox in order to deceive or confuse the enemy.
A beam that has been applied to a wall face.
The structure across the lower end of a medieval hall containing the spere, its supporting posts and tie-beam.
A landing and taking off area for civil aircraft, usually with surfaced runways and aircraft maintenance and passenger facilities.
A thin piece of wood used as a roofing material.
A metal fastener used to hold a tile or stone against a spacer and driven into a wall thus forming a flue between the wall and the tile or stone. Also used to hold timber together.
Any of the pieces of hard tissue consisting largely of calcium phosphate that make up the skeleton of a vertebrate animal.

Traditionally, dating from the medieval period, this was an area on the north bank of the Thames where the Merchants of the Hanse conducted their business. Now includes a similar establishment in a provincial town.
A place from which clay is extracted.
A building used by an organization or society to promote the study of oriental languages and history through lectures, research, etc.
Timber or metal structure consisting of upright and cross members designed to support climbing plants.
A horizontal, riven board, tapered in section, used for external cladding.
A place from which chalk is extracted.
A circular bank of stones and turf, sometimes accompanied by a ditch, surrounding a natural outcrop of rock, usually a tor, or an earthfast boulder.
A place for keeping vestments and sacred vessels.
Use for vessels registered in Belgium.
A strap from the reins to the girth of a horse, preventing it from raising its head too high.
An uncommon form of a regular courtyard farmstead where the buildings are arranged in a Z-shaped form.
A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to orgainic material by measuring the amount of carbon 14 it contains.
The seeds of the palm Phytelephas macrocarpa, the albumen of which, hardens resembling ivory in colour, texture and toughness and is used to make ornamental buttons etc.
A clamp in which alum shale was burnt in the initial stage of processing.

An area of land incorporating bodies of water, either natural or manmade for use in water sports activities such as canoeing, rowing and sailing. Usually includes a leisure complex with facilities for the users.
Building material made by combining gravel, cement, water and sand. When hard it forms a stonelike surface, used for paving and building.
A covered walkway attached to a building.
An entablature consiting of an architrave, usually a frieze and cornice.
Use for ticks and true mites. Related to spiders, mites are widely present in archaeological deposits but are rarely studies in detail as they can prove difficult to identify.
A permanently occupied position or building designed primarily for defence.
A mill used for grinding textile rags.
An area of cultivated, managed woodland producing wood which is used for a variety of purposes.
A crane deriving its power from steam generated from solid fuels.
A stone which has a socket for an unknown function. Use specific term where known.
The area directly in front of a fireplace or the floor of a firecplace itself.
A tool used to incise or ipress images.
Coarse, hard Chalkstone, light grey to white coloured, containing shell fragments.
A machine that uses liquid pressure to exert a large force on two platens so that items placed between them are pressed to a shape, compressed, or forced together.
A mould in which an ingot is made.
A residence of the Bonhommes brethren, who followed the Augustinian rule.
Mercantile vessel converted during the First World War for the purposes of examining and boarding enemy vessels.
A watertight reservoir or tank that receives sewage, and by sedimentation and bacterial action effects a process of partial purification.
A type of concrete bridge, developed in the 20th century, that consists of reinforced concrete deck slabs that sit on the supporting bridge piers and/or abutments.
A vertical timber in a truss, descending from the ridge, and projecting below the lower transverse timber, normally used  with scissor beams.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of metal ores.
Equipment for turning wood, metal, bone etc.
A temporary settlement or encampment erected by construction workers (eg for reservoir construction).
Buildings, sites and structures associated with sporting activities.

A jug with a pierced bunghole just above the base. the bunghole can be made through an applied knob or disc of clay, or simply a hole in the vessel wall. In use, the hole would probably have had a tap or spigot attached. (Source: MPRG)
A shaft cut to facilitate the extraction of salt from halite deposits by pumping water into the deposit and pumping out brine from which the salt is later extracted.
A small chamber or private room.
Traditionally a mineral that could be used for striking fire but now a term commonly used to refer to various sulphides, especially iron disulphide.
A screen, with a wide central opening, or multiple narrower openings, spanning the lower end of a medieval hall, screening the cross entry and defining the screen, or cross, passage.
Residence of a leading land-holding family within the district.
A type of shield, usually wooden and circular.
A horizontal pierced metal object upon which to hold the coals of a fire.
A tunnel with a canal running through it.
A religious receptacle, especially Jewish where it contains four Hebrew texts worn during morning prayers.
Merchandise wrapped in canvas and tightly bound with cords or hoops to form bales.
A non-structural covering, such as tile, slate, wood etc., applied to an exterior wall.
A workshop used for the production of pottery moulds.
Where several minerals produced, use with other products and MINE, eg. ARSENIC MINE.
The framing of a door or window with two columns piers or pilasters which support a lintel,entablature etc.
A building housing the engines used to power equipment used by a searchlight, anti-aircraft or coastal battery.
A sailing warship armed with one or more heavy howitzers or mortars and used for bombarding shore positions. The modern equivalent is the MONITOR.
A fishing vessel employed exclusively on the Grand Banks cod fisheries.
A pillbox built to a design by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.
A steam engine in which steam flows in one direction only at each stroke, as opposed to the commoner contra-flow engines.
Place where tanned leather is dressed and coloured.
A pedestrian passageway, often elevated, connecting two buildings or sections within a building.
A high tower, attached to or detached from a building such as a church, with a belfry stage containing bells.
A container used to hold ammunition.
Small tower projecting from a castle wall, or other fortified wall. Allows defenders to fire along the length of the wall.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.

Nowadays a hospital where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical care and treatment. Traditionally they were often places where psychiatric patients were kept confined away from society receiving minimal medical care or attention.
A piece of furniture containing a chamber pot or wash basin.
Equipment or tool used to compress an object into a desired form, a flatter appearance etc.
A written extract taken from a published newspaper.
An excavation made in the earth for the purpose of digging out metallic ores, coal, salt, or precious stones etc. Use specific type where known.
Use for cargoes which are not specified.
A school where Jewish children are educated.
A compound consisting of potassium and silica, used in various processes.

A cylindrical bomb, designed by Barnes Wallis in 1941, containing hydrostatic pistols measuring water pressure for detonation at a depth of 30 feet.  Dropped whilst fast revolving at a height of 60 feet at 240-250 mph to maximise the bouncing effect.
A workshop used for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes.
A building or buildings used for the production of pens.
Goods stowed in barrels and therefore indicating that the barrels were in use as containers with goods stored therein, rather than as cargo in their own right.
A Roman sanctuary, devoted to the Graeco-Roman cult of Mithras.
A small bowl on a pedestal base, which may be solid or at least partly hollow. It may have a wick lip at the rim or a lug handle. (Source: MPRG)
Large mammals of the genus Bos, domesticated to provide milk, beef and materials eg. leather. Use only for live animals.
An upright timber standing on a tiebeam to support a collar or purlin. Once used as an alternative to king post, this term is now restricted to the shorter post ending at collar level.
A lock, often containing a fish ladder, which allows fish to swim upstream bypassing a weir or other obstacle.
A tall chimney terminating a CONDENSING FLUE, used to extract metal from the smoke produced by a lead smelter.
A shafthole adze with additional hammer knob, normally polished stone.
A point in a village providing water for drinking and washing.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in shoe making.
A small enclosure containing cold frames, often of brick and glass construction, usually situated against the exterior of a walled garden's south-facing garden.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
A ship used to process whales into saleable products.
A schematic depiction of the results of an archaeological excavation.
A surgery where patients who pay for medical treatments are seen and treated.
A device controlling the passage of liquids or gases.
A fine grained rock which splits easily into plates. Used for the manufacture of roofing tiles etc.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A settlement without any obvious evidence for a boundary. Use specific type where known.
A building where non-commissioned aircrew are housed.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A collared urn with a heavy rim or collar on top of a straight-sided or slightly bowed body narrowing to a small flat base. Decoration may extend for a short way below the collar, but this is rare.
People who have paid to travel on a vessel without having to work their passage.
A passage or road closed to traffic at one end.
Use for vessels believed to come from Central America but where the precise nationality is not known.
A building in a zoo or wildlife park used to accommodate giraffes.
A garden in which flower beds are the primary focal point.
A building or room containing a collection of preserved plants (usually pressed and dried specimens).
The area surrounding a monastic house including conventual buildings, outbuildings, cemetery, fishponds, etc, usually marked out by a bank and/or ditch or precinct wall.
Manmade structure that contains water that is heated to a high temperature and sometimes has bubbling air jets. Meant to be used for therapeudic purposes.
A site containing a tennis court, changing facilities and a club house.
A building with an aisle along one or both sides. Usually a row of posts separates the main space from the aisle.

A building used by the society, fraternity or order organized under this name with initiatory rites, mystic signs of recognition and various degrees of dignity or honour, for social or benevolent purposes.
A machine tool capable of creating a variety of forms and surfaces in materials by way of a spinning cutter positioned over a movable table.
A vehicle used to transport passengers. Cars usually have four wheels and an internal combustion engine.
Equipment, including uniforms, small arms and field pieces, used by the armed forces.
A building where students study theatre and the dramatic arts.
An image of a deity used as a focus for worship, usually used for non Christian images.
Clasp for fastening together two loose ends.
Use for vessels registered in Morocco.
A place where shoes and boots are mended.
A vault shaped trellis on which climbing plants are trained.
A building or complex where cork is treated and processed to be used in various products.
A longitudinal member in a roof, running beneath the collar beams and intended to give stability to the roof.
A wall plate used by insurance companies to identify insured property.

The non intrusive processes by which information is collected about the location, distribution and organisation of past human activities that are now submerged by water. The approaches can be either extensive or intensive depending on the objectives.
A device with hooks or claws attached to a rope and used for dragging or grasping.
An extension to a building, though sometimes contemporary with it, housed under a lean-to roof.
Matting manufactured using the fibres from the outer husks of coconuts.
Length of timber boarding (usually elm, now pine) fixed horizontally or vertically to the exterior of a structure which may be 'tongue and grooved' or 'feathered' to provide external protection.
A post or pillar set up alongside a road to mark the miles from or to a place.

Active sonar systems are based on the behaviour of sound waves in water; acoustic energy is transmitted and the time for the returning echo is measured to allow submerged seabed features to be mapped. Use specific type where known.
Reproduced image derived by mechanical printing from an image engraved or carved on a suitable surface.

Structured & carefully executed scanning of the ground surface with a metal detecting device in order to recover surface scatters of metal objects & plot them spatially within the study area as part of an archaeological survey or metal detecting rally.
Sites and structures associated with the storage of water and waste water. Use only where the exact form or function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
A structure found on lighthouses, piers, etc, capable of emitting a loud noise to warn shipping in foggy weather.
A large building used for the storage of finished cloth.
Railway engines designed to travel under its own power and to draw railway carriages and rolling stock.
A paper form used to record specific information in a systematic way.
A place of worship for the followers of Jainism

A man-made construction or object (such as a gravestone) which has been moved from its original site either through active human intervention or natural processes such as erosion. For buildings which have been moved use MOVED BUILDING.
A building used as emergency accommodation and food distribution centre for people displaced by a natural disaster or conflict.
An upright post with projecting arm from which the body of a criminal would be hung in chains after execution.
A tunnel with strengthened construction, used as an emergency exit from a civil defence building.
Tools used to maintain a fire.
Equipment used in the making of tools.
Outerwear designed to protect the legs from weather.
In which coniferous and deciduous are present in roughly equal proportions. Specify in Description whether currently managed, neglected, unmanaged or management not determined.
The area between the base and the cornice of a plinth.
A large natural or artificial body of water, sometimes covered, used to collect and store water for a particular function, eg. industrial or public use.
Structured descriptions of an archive or collection used to assist retrieval and management, or presentation to the public.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
A hospital block where patients come for day-care medical treatment.
A small crane fixed to the wall of a warehouse or similar building.
A narrow flake which is the by-product of making a burin.
Specially designed/fitted carriers of crew and/or supplies to offshore oil platforms.
A three masted vessel with a square rig on the fore and main masts and lateen rig on the mizzen mast.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
A flat floating framework of planks or other materials used for supporting or carrying persons or goods.
Rock fragment (diameter 4-64mm) larger than gravel and smaller than cobble, combined with other material e.g. flint, for decorative effect.
A place of accommodation for a stablehand.
A rafter set at the corner of a hipped roof, to take the upper end of a common rafter.
Expanding storage tank for gas, often includes a meter for measuring the amount used.
A microlith retouched to a half moon or crescent shape. (Source: SARC)
A small blade for moving earth, applying liquids such as plaster, smoothing etc.
A vessel equipped with water tanks and pumps for fighting fires at sea or on the shore line.
A strong durable wood originating in India and south-east Asia.
A sash or belt worn over the shoulder to the hip for carrying a sword.
Site types normally or frequently associated with burials which in some instances may have had solely religious or ritual functions.
The principal house of a manor or village.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
A communal dining room, especially in schools, colleges and monasteries.
An object designed to be the end of a lace or simimlar to aid the insertion of the lace through a loop or eyelet.
Use for vessels registered in Yugoslavia between 1918 and 1992.
An arboretum devoted mainly to the growing of conifers.
A large cross designed to be carried in a procession.
Objects used for, or associated with, the production of heat and light.
A concave sided jar made in tin-glazed earthenware. (Source: MPRG)
A building used to coordinate movement of railway engines and rolling stock in the event of war.
A polygonal or semicircular recess projecting from an external wall, often with a rounded vault.
A hand held device with bristles or hairs used for cleaning or painting.
A hydraulically-powered crane constructed from open box girders.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
A building, situated on the coast, used for observing the movements of enemy shipping.
A measuring rule not graduated in feet.
A channel dug, or built up, to carry away surplus water from a river or waterway to prevent it bursting its banks and flooding.
The area where the act of Offertory, where bread and wine are placed upon the altar, takes place.
Use for vessels registered in Peru.
A site where ores are smelted. Use more specific site type where known.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.
The debris resulting from the production of glass.
A measure for dry substances. A quarter of a bushel.
Religious Society Of Friends Burial Ground
Decorative ornamentation in the form of an upright, stalked trefoil used in Tudor architecture.
A stone with a concave upper surface on which grain was ground by using a rubbing stone.
A land based establishment armed with torpedoes and used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 7790/40.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A residence of two or three monks dependent on a foreign mother house sent to exploit a distant estate. Alien houses were officially suppressed in 1414.
Steel, usually unworked, in the form of bars.

A place of worship for members of the Congregational Church. These churches, the first of which was founded in 1616 in Southwark, practised self government. Most of them were merged to form the United Reformed Church in 1972.
An abbey or priory of Premonstratensian canons.
A threshing barn, usually timber framed which is raised on staddle stones.
A flat heavy slightly curved blade.
First practical submarine design. The first to use a combination of battery power and internal combustion engines.
An iron plate connecting two or more timbers together.
Bordered by the continents of Africa, Asia and Europe, the Mediterranean covers some 967,000 sq miles. It is linked to the Atlantic Ocean by the Straits of Gibraltar.

A piece of wire or similarly flexible material shaped to form a clip for fastening papers together; invented by the Norwegian Johann Vaaler in 1899.  The familiar double-oval 'Gem' clip was developed by Gem Manufacturing Ltd. in England the same year.
Accommodation in hired rooms or a lodging house.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the conveyance of goods &/or passengers.  Includes man-made routeways, mechanical structures & some vehicle types where it is deemed necessary to record such as monuments.
Use for vessels registered in the former Czechoslovakia between 1918 and 1992. See also CZECH and SLOVAK.
The base to a door or window frame or of a wall.
A building in which silk was dried.
Ore containing a high proportion of zinc.
A square, concrete pillbox-like structure with 36in thick walls and a single large embrasure used to emplace a Vickers Medium Machine Gun. The entrance was protected by an external blast wall.
A jug form characterized by the addition of three applied feet. The feet are usually short and stubby. Double index with the appropriate profile type. (Source: MPRG)
A house of Roman Catholic nuns or canonesses.
An axehead of flint or other stone, commonly used for Neolithic types.
Use for vessels registered in Austria.
The line of a flat rod system transmitting power from an engine or waterwheel.

A design of steam engine in which either three cylinders, in the case of vertical engines, or four cylinders on horizontal engines, permit steam to be expanded three times as it passes through the installation.
A container for one or more candles.
A semicircular crypt below the apse of a church.
If managed at all, then only to a low intensity, e.g. mowing, spraying etc., involving operations which are not archaeologically damaging.
An ornamental contour given to the angles or features of a building, whether a projection or a cavity, such as a cornice, an architrave or an astragal.
Any earthworks, walling, bastion or fortified outwork, or combination of these, generally with ditch or moat.
An interior or projecting shelter surrounding an entrance to a building.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
An airfield, and associated structures, used by one or more bomber squadrons.
An establishment for the preparation and selling of food to be consumed off the premises.
River principally lying between the states of Maryland and Virginia, USA, with its outlet to the sea in Chesapeake Bay.
Equipment used to pierce or puncture other objects through the use of a point.
A square of fabric tied around the neck.
A crane, located in an engineering workshop or similar establishment, which can be moved on rails and thus used anywhere within the workshop.
A Mark 1E aircraft which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
Equipment used to create objects through the use of a pattern or matrix which shapes the object.
An area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or other similar barrier. Use specific type where known.
Reproductive process for non-photographic media in which the image is created by transferring ink from a plate, block etc.
A piece of metal, usually cast, struck or stamped, with a definite value.
A bead or group of beads used in prayer.
A centre in which the public donate blood that will be used for the care of patients in hospitals.
A roof with one side longer than the other, continuing at the same pitch over an extension to a building. Commonly found in New England Colonial architecture.
An outdoor or indoor place where flowers were sold.
A site which has been bombed but where there is no crater, eg. bombed buildings.
An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
The highest judicial court where appeals can be heard and whose rulings are not subject to further review by another court.

A pointed arch which, on a plan, is shown to be constructed around four arcs: two centred below and two centred upon the springing line, which is the level at which the vertical sides of the arch begin to curve.
Central functional building of a gas works. Coal is roasted in retorts producing gas and coke.
A plan in which the staircase is placed at the centre of the building.
A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.

A type of transportable aircraft hangar patented by Miskins and Sons in 1939. The arched hangar was constructed of steel or wooden ribs and generally clad in steel sheets. The hangar did not require any foundations and could be anchored by iron stakes.
A building, similar to a cart shed, but used to house traps, gigs and coaches.
A fence or row of stakes, often with nets attached forming an enclosure within a river or harbour and used for catching, or holding, fish.
Small submarine with a two or three man crew. Used for special missions such as sinking warships in heavily defended harbours.
A row of houses whose facade in plan follows the concave arc of a circle or ellipse, eg. The Royal Crescent, Bath.
An object which has been carved. Use more specific term where known.
A pillbox constructed of prefabricated concrete panels. Double index with specific type where known.

A building which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime buildings were requisitioned for various purposes, such as temporary hospitals or headquarters.
A small carved figure, usually female in appearance, probably representing  fertility charms, found on Romanesque churches in the West of England, eg. Kilpeck.
In use for fruit growing. Includes former orchard retaining trees etc.
A structure consisting of a vertical mast and a horizontal boom operated by cables on a separate engine or motor. Used for hoisting and moving heavy loads or objects.
A standard latine block on RAF airfields.
A large building used for the storage of grain.
Warship or trading vessel, three masted with a low forecastle.
A band worn around the head to denote sovereignty.
Any vessel operated by Trinity house masters and brethren in the maintenance of lighthouses, lightships, buoys and other navigation aids.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic iron.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
An item with both secular and religious signifigance.
A spatially discrete group of pits usually containing artefactual material with little or no accompanying evidence for structural features.

A prefabricated structure of lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed for use as officers accomodation during WWII.
A building used to house apes and monkeys.
Part of the glass making process, the frit is broken up into a crucible and heated to create glass.
A metal pin, often with a screw thread and used in conjunction with a nut.
A path or area for exercise, usually taken in the form of walking. Can be partially or totally covered.
A plan featuring three foils or lobes radiating outwards from a central point.

A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.
A piece of written or printed matter providing a record of events, agreements, ownership or identification.
One of a pair of crossing braces halved or lapped across each other, tying a pair of rafters together.
A low, hemispherical cairn surrounded by a freestanding, continuous circle of boulders.
A building containing presses for the compaction of mill cake gunpowder as part of the gunpowder manufacturing process.
An institution for the detention of prisoners considered to be a major threat to public safety and/or to the security of the nation.

A land based installation armed with wire -guided and powered  "Brennan torpedoes" which were in operation beween 1890 and 1906. These torpedoes were invented by Louis Philip Brennan. The stations were used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A small room used as a study for the preservation of papers etc. Generally use for any small room appended to a larger one.
Plan showing a horizontal section, size and arrangement of rooms within a building, may include location of doors, windows and other features.
A marker, of stone, wood or metal, used to delineate the limits of a stretch of highway, river or canal subject to a toll charge.
A building where reptiles are accommodated at a zoo or wildlife park.
A small shovel for adding or placing coals onto a fire.

An institution created with the merging of Gaols and Houses of Correction in 1865. Nowadays term used for a prison to which people are sent whilst remanded in custody before trial or direct from court after conviction.
A small rake used to move the embers of a fire.
A shallow pond, often located near an ICEHOUSE, built to provide ice during the winter.
A chequered board used to play chess.
A garden incorporating Egyptian architectural features such as sphinxes and tomb-like features, etc.
A substantial structure supporting or surrounding a gate. May be ornate or monumental, and have associated structures such as lodges, tollbooths, guard houses etc.
A bench with a back, usually in a church.
A barrel-making workshop or factory, found in conjunction with a number of industries.
Auxiliary or support vessel used for the repair of naval craft.
6 DFW55373 projector emplacements spaced in a 3x2 rectangular gid, but each spaced 35m apart. No blast protection was provided at the shelters, which were placed between the projector emplacements.
A solid, spherical projectile, originally made of stone but later iron.
An uncovered area, surrounded or partially surrounded by buildings.
A wall constructed for the purpose of confining or supporting a mass of earth or water.
A cup with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
An outdoor theatre for the staging of dramatic productions.
A farm on which liquid sewage was regularly used for irrigation as a means of sewage disposal.
A pair of scissors used in circumcision.
A stone circle featuring a stone which lies lengthways between two of the upright standing stones.
A specially designed chisel for producing ornamental mouldings.
A place where beehives are kept.
A room or building used for the storage of fleeces.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.

All features of interest have been destroyed. No further information can be gained from future investigation of the site. Includes demolished buildings unless foundations, basements etc exist which are of interest, for which use very bad.

A reinforced concrete structure, which may be sited above ground or semi-sunken, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government from, in the event of nuclear war. Date specific to the early-mid 1950's.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A type of comb for flax or hemp.

A structure, based on drawing number (3329/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed above ground this design was found to be vulnerable and was superceded by the (11008/41).
A tile which covers the ridge of a roof.
A wooden bench with a back and ends, usually fixed and found in churches. The bench ends are often decorated.

A form used to record the details of a feature identified by archaeological investigation, generally including location, depth, colour, texture, inclusions and stratigraphic relationship to other contexts.
A terrace of BACK TO EARTH HOUSES.
A nail of distinctive form, specifically used in the shoeing of animals, eg horses, donkeys, oxen.
A building where onions are laid out to dry.
Aluminium coated by a protective film of oxides created by electrolysis.

A small, circular Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age enclosure which bears a morphological resemblance to henges, but may belong to another category of circular earthwork-defined monuments, or is enclosed by something other than a bank and ditch.
An alloy where the predominant component metal is copper.
A thin vegetable based sheet used for writing, drawing, printing etc.
Deposits that accumulate at the bottom of a slope, at a break in a slope, or where a barrier is encountered.
Narrow strips of wood which can form the groundwork for slates, panels or plaster work.
A graduated post or pole adjacent to an area at risk of flooding to indicate the depth of water during a flood.
Where secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. LEAD MINE.
An object to sit upon. Use narrower terms where known.
Hand held instruments which assist in the holding, cutting and eating of food.
A form of cement originally named since it was said to be like Portland Stone in appearance.
An airfield, and associated structures, used by one or more fighter squadrons.
A hollow, concave formation or place, which has sometimes been dug out.
A room or group of rooms in a building.

A commercially manufactured air raid shelter, using prefabricated parabolic concrete panels which could be combined to produce any length of shelter.Usually semi-sunken and covered with earth they were mainly used on RAF sites.
An indoor play area for the game of badminton.
Soft limestone consisting almost entirely of calcite.

A concrete arched military hut constructed by pouring concrete over hessian cloth that had been stretched over a temporary steel framework. Semi circular in section usually with end walls of brick. Designed by the Waller Housing Corp in 1943.

Originally denoting a Byzantine vessel, powered by oars, from the 6th century onwards, this developed into a large Mediterranean ship with oars and a single mast, used for trade or for war transport, (e.g. during the Crusades) until the 15th century.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.
Armour formed from thin pieces of metal fastened together or on leather or some strong woven material.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
A site where a single large balloon was attached by fine wire cables to the ground to form an aerial obstruction to attacking enemy aircraft.
Use for vessels registered in Russia.
A straight mine entrance, driven on a constant downwards slope.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine designed to Air Ministry drawing number 5342/42.
Soft sandstone stained by iron oxide often used in the Surrey area.
A monastic cattle ranch with associated buildings, paddocks and pastures.
A latrine built into, or projecting beyond, the wall of a medieval castle featuring a stone or wooden seat situated above a pit or the castle moat.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of water power.
One of the component tiles used in the construction of a tile hearth, being the floor of, or area in front of, a fireplace.
A container used to hold substances for dying or painting.
A structure with semaphore arms and/or coloured lights used as a means of warning on railway systems.
A room or building used for recording and broadcasting radio programmes.
Wood, cut and seasoned for use as a constructional material.
A box containing tinder, any dry inflammable material, usually also contains flint and steel for lighting fires.
An opening through which missiles or combustible materials could be dropped upon attackers. Usually through the roof of an entrance way or in a projecting parapet.
Another title for a bibliographic source which differs from the recognized official title
A dark blue powder, obtained from plants or synthetically manufactured, used as a dye.
A building, department or shop where postal business is carried on.
Unpowered flat bottomed vessel, used for carrying cargo from ship to shore or as a working platform.
A site where cobalt is mined
An apartment contained, wholly or partially, within the roof space of a house.
A hand held weapon used to throw missiles such as stones or bullets.

Derived from the Colchester in the mid to late 1st century, particularly in south and east Britain. Characterized by the attachment of the separate spring and pin through two holes in a lug behind the head, which projects to form a crest atop the bow.
A plinth or pedestal, sometimes decorated, and sometimes supporting statuary, placed at the apex and lower extremity of a pediment.
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
Threads prepared for use in a manufacturing process such as spinning, weaving etc.
A cable laid under the surface of the sea, often on the seabed, for various purposes including telecommunications.
A piece of material worn around the neck. Where it is a collar for an animal use animal collar.
An artificial paved bank or solid landing place built parallel to, or projecting out from, the shoreline to serve in the loading and unloading of vessels.
A place where fish are processed after being caught.
A waterside depot for coals brought from the collieries for shipment, furnished with staging and chutes for loading vessels.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
A closely mown piece of ground used for the game of lawn bowling.
In a truss, a rafter used to stiffen the principal rafter by doubling it.
A factory principally engaged in the  manufacture of the propellant explosive cordite.
A yard intended for the purpose of taking exercise, for example within the grounds of a prison.
A buttress which encases the corner between two walls.
German port on the River Ems.
A purlin that passes a principal rafter
Use specific type where known, eg picture frame.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A site where granite is excavated.
An institution for the imprisonment of vagrants and misdemeanants.
Sand consisting of a mineral common in igneous rocks.
A sloop used for carrying weapons and ammunition to warships.
Casual scribbles or pictographs on ancient walls, stones or other surfaces. In more recent times applied to humourous, satiric or obscene writings or drawings executed anonymously in public places.
A rectangular recess along the edge of a timber to receive a shutter, door or window.

The residence of a preceptor, officials and servants, etc, supervising the estates of the Knights Templars military order. Includes the mother house styled the Temple, London. The Order was suppressed in 1312.
A low bank on the edge of a defensive ditch on the side away from the main rampart.
The sill beam of the jettied upper floor resting on projecting ends of joists or on jetty brackets.
A fatty substance rendered from animal fat and used in the manufacture of soap, candles and for dressing leather.
An instrument used for making a loud sound for information or warning.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.
A room before a larger room which is often used as a waiting room.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a canal, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A marker stone used to demarcate the boundaries of peat cutting grounds and indicate who held the rights for each particular parcel of land.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
A building in which engineered metal products are finished and polished.
An object fixed to the door or floor to limit the amount a door can open.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of more than 90 degrees.
A processing house where surplus water is removed from gunpowder after incorporating.
A large room for large numbers of people, eg for balls, meetings etc.
A form of compass, sometimes with a screw for setting to small intervals.
A net worn over the hair to hold it in place.
Containers identified by function rather than by form.
A fragment of the base of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
A vertical structure usually made of stone, brick, timber, etc.
A room containing copper or steel vessels in which hops are added to the basic beer mixture.
Component: Use wider site type where known.

A place of worship for members of the United Methodist Free Church. Formed in 1857 by the amalgamation of the Methodist Reform Church and the Wesleyan Association they later became part of the United Methodist Church in 1907.
Type of footwear which covers a minimum of the foot and ankle.
Royal Naval Air Station Control Tower
A small hole for a lace, cord or hook to be passed through.
Warships constructed of iron plate or with wooden hulls covered by iron plates. Used as a generic name for the first examples of armour plated warships.
A tube to produce drops of liquid.
A priory of the female Order of Knights Hospitallers.
A sulphide of copper and iron, reddish brown in colour.
A small piece of metal used to mend ceramic, glass or metal plates and vessels.
A residence for all clergy having the sole or subordinate charge of a living.
A pediment with a gap at the centre of its base.
A court, usually with only 2 walls, used for playing pelota and its variants.
A base on which pews or benches can be placed.
A small coastal fishing vessel peculiar to Kent, cutter rigged.
A manufacturing complex incorporating furnaces, calciner and condenser flues. Use SMELTERY for more modern type of plant.
An end scraper made on a flake that is wider than it is long. (Source: SARC)
Use for vessels registered in Liberia. Often used as a flag of convenience.
Pieces of timber shaped for use in the construction of buildings, barrels etc.
Dating from the 15th century, it is a hard alloy of iron and carbon, melted and shaped into various moulded forms.
A tool used to pull down burning structures.
A neck band or necklace worn tightly around the throat.
A pestle used specifically for grinding cosmetics.
A lockable box for holding money and valuables.
An establishment where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness.
A comb or slide used to hold hair in place.
A residence of two or three monks of the Order of Tiron dependent on a foreign mother house.
A handheld lamp used to send morse code messages ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore.The lamp and its reflector can be covered/uncovered by a trigger operated shutter.
Workshop for the manufacture of master parts from working drawings which are then used as patterns for mass manufacture.
A metal disk with a turned rim, giving a resonant note when struck.
A platform for storing winter fodder.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
Man-made, roofless edifice or construction visible as substantial above-ground remains retaining evidence of architecture and materials, but which has been substantially destroyed.
A triangle of metal which, when struck, produces a note.
A hospital department for the medical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
A specialist school for the teaching of blind people.
Auxiliary Unit Special Duties Control Station
Long piece of silk etc worn around waist or over one shoulder often as a symbol of rank.
A building or site used for the manufacture of pins.
A balance with unequal arms where the contents of a pan on the short arm are weighed by a weight or weights attached to the long arm.
A cylindrical container, usually bulging outward in the middle and usually held together by metal hoops.
A piston mounted horizontally supplying power via a valve gear directly to a crankshaft or flywheel.
Equipment used in the grinding of cereal to produce foodstuffs.
The measurement of chemical alterations in the amino acids in protein molecules from bones, shells and teeth. Date range can be between 1,000 and several million years.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.
A concrete, circular concave dish 30 feet in diameter used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.
Large concrete letters representing the ground-to-air airfield code. It has been used to show pilots in WWII the name of the airfield they were above e.g. DW for Dunkeswell.
A building used for storing tree bark.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
Aggregate, cement and mortar combined with structural elements of iron or steel mesh or rod reinforcement to form stonelike masses for load bearing, structural building work.
Use for vessels registered in Argentina.
A vertical or inclined plane, channel, or passage through which objects are moved from a higher to a lower level by means of gravity.
Traditionally any food preserved by boiling with sugar, salting, pickling etc. Nowadays used specifically for fruit which has been preserved with sugar.
A late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age earthwork enclosure distinguished from a henge primarily by its larger size, irregular shape, and greater complexity of internal features.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.

Ground-based or marine subsurface mapping of archaeological features using different sensing technologies. Most commonly applied are magnetometers, electrical resistance meters, ground penetrating radar, side scan sonar, and electromagnetic conductivity.
Long parallel soil ridges less than 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
A pillow or cushion for lace making.
A two or three wheeled motor vehicle.
Use for complexes where services (eg. restaurants, shops) are provided in addition to facilities for buying petrol.

An artificially constructed wall with recessed and projecting grips for hands and feet and places to attach ropes. Used for practising rock climbing. If the wall is situated within a sports centre use term from Components thesaurus.
A small shelter used by a man employed to carry links (torches) to light people along a street.
A horizontal brace linking tiebeam and wall plate, or adjacent wall plates at the corner of a hipped roof.
An arch which is half an ellipse.
A training college for the instruction of military trainees in the theory and practice of warfare.
A recess or cupboard within a church, usually positioned near the altar, used for the storage of sacred vessels.
A light, open structure for the sale of newspapers, tickets, etc.
An inn, with an integral courtyard, for the lodging and entertainment of travellers. Often with open galleried wings overlooking the courtyard.
The lower area of a interior wall between the skirting board and the dado rail
A track consisting of flanged strips used in early colliery railways.
A container from which liquid is drunk.
A way made for pedestrians, especially one merely made by walking (often not specially constructed).
A school which combines the functions of both Infant and Junior Schools, teaching children up to the age of eleven. Use specific type where known.
A flat stone, often sandstone, used for paving.
An educational establishment, often privately funded, for young women.
Any building, group of buildings, or site at which tungsten ores have been converted to sodium tungstate by means of the Oxland Process. This was first used at Drakewalls Mine, Cornwall, in 1850.
Series of rooms within a workhouse where elderly men were housed.
This does not include food or liquid storage.
An unbleached cloth of hemp, flax or other coarse yarn.
A chamber in which minerals, metals, etc, are subjected to the continuous action of intense heat. Use specific type where known.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote the study of mathematics through lectures, research, etc.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
The limit line of a medieval local administrative unit of a hundred.
Building housing a form of early steam engine using steam at atmospheric pressure. Chiefly employed in mine pumping.
A chapel in a church for penitents.
A short principal rafter that that rises from a tiebeam to a collar.
A jar adapted by the addition of a straight handle and three feet. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A shelter on a firing range from which the wepaons testing can be viewed in safety.
A circle made out of stones, which is used for making wheels.
Buildings in London formerly used as hostels  for law students.

The local heritage asset may provide evidence about past human activity in the
locality, which may be in the form of buried remains, but may also be revealed in the structure of buildings or in a designed landscape, for instance. Heritage assets with archaeological interest are primary sources of evidence about the substance and evolution of places, and of the people and cultures that made them.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the process of distilling.
Between 40¡N and mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal13
Movable, usually functional, articles in a room. Use only for objects believed to be furniture where more specific term is not identifiable.
A balance measuring weight by the tension of a spring.
A residential home for older people or people with physical and/or mental disabilities who need care provided by registered nurses.
A building, or part of a church, used for baptismal rites, usually containing a font.
A plinth or pedestal, usually of concrete, to which an anti aircraft or coastal battery gun was fitted. Holdfasts are often the only evidence for a weapon which survive.
Kingdom of living things, lacking chlorophyll, that obtain their food from organic matter, usually by absorption. They include mushrooms, moulds and yeasts.
A child's bed, usually without rockers.
A private garden established primarily for growing vegetables and herbs for domestic consumption.
Decorative motif in the form of an ox skull.
Hard, corrosive resistant alloy of copper and tin.
A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
An area or site used for the landing and take-off of aircraft, often including associated buildings, equipment and other installations.
A shallow place in a river or other stretch of water, where people, animals and vehicles may cross.
Any building, group of buildings, or site in which antimony was smelted. Mainly 18th century.
An opening in a wall, roof, door, etc to allow light to enter. Usually used to include all component parts.
A feature formed by water falling from the roof of a building and creating a linear or curving indentation in the ground.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.

Synthetically manufactured stone made from natural stone aggregate or reconstituted ceramics or clay, and made to appear natural. Used as solid stone for masonry or for sculptural and architectural ornament.
Two-wheeled vehicles for personal transport with pedals for propulsion by the rider.
A building used to store fodder for deer.
A metal collar or cap to strengthen the end of tubes, sticks, shafts, etc. Use with specific object name where known eg spear and ferrule.
An establishment, often forming part of a university, for higher or tertiary education.
A casement, usually wooden, in a mill enclosing the grindstones and preventing the loss of ground material before it is channelled into sacks.
An object, often including gems and ornamentation, used as an adornment, usually on a person.
The principal storey of a building, containing the main reception rooms, when not situated on ground level.
A small narrow pointed missile that is thrown or shot.

An early warning structure built during and after WWI along the south and east coasts of England. Sound detecting acoustic dishes and walls could detect the sound of approaching enemy aircraft at a distance of 8 to 15 miles.
Cutting or copy from published work
An armoured fighting vehicle. Often survive as commemorative monuments, targets and coastal wrecks.
A specific form of cauldron, generally of rounded profile made in the Low Countries. (Source: MPRG)
A small dish, often with a handle, for soup, porridge etc.
An area of hardstanding for parking aircraft, in a state of readiness, usually around the perimeter of an airfield.
An instrument for writing or drawing with ink.
A building in which works of art are displayed for sale.
Factory or workshop making bits, spurs and other small metal objects associated with horse harness.
The heraldic bearings or shield of a person, family or corporation.
The SI derived unit of Area

A site, building or structure used for the detection of approaching hostile aircraft, shipping or missiles early enough to allow a counterattack or defensive measures to be taken. Use more specific term.
A plan featuring a lobby entry, situated at one end of a side wall, which provides access to one room only.
A linear groove worn into the surface of a road or thoroughfare by the continuous passage of wheeled vehicles. Usually expected to occur in pairs.
An attached plaque, inscription, mural or display commemorating nations, actions, soldiers and/or civilians that served or died as a result of conflict.
Items which are part of or added to footwear.

A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of lithic artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context. Use particular types where appropriate.

An operations room, built to drawing number 367/41, to control the lighting arrays of the DREM type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. Unlike earlier designs it was surface built and then covered in earth to protect against flooding.
An airlike, fluid hydrocarbon suitable for burning to produce light, heat or power.
A large, convex moulding, sometimes ornamented, set at the base of a column and above its plinth.
A truss with two curved kerb-principals, which are the short principal rafters rising froma tiebeam to a collar, placed either side of a crown strut.

Test pits dug by geotechnical engineers or engineering geologists to obtain information on the physical properties of soil, sediments and bedrock around a site to design earthworks and foundations for proposed structures.
An enclosed, high-sided seat, sometimes entered through a door, usually found in churches as one of a series of box-like compartments.
A small open boat, usually a very light craft propelled by a paddle.
A press used to extract the juice from apples, which was then used to make cider.
A building in which goods or items are stored. Use more specific type where known.
Edible fruit of the vine, which may be either red or white.
A site where rough stone is processed, shaped, worked or formed into finished products.
A precious metal characterized by its yellow colour and resistance to tarnishing.
A stone blade with one edge blunted.
A mechanically operated lift used to transfer rolling stock from one level of track to another.
A vertical, pointed structure usually resembling a pyramid or cone. Use for component of a larger building type where it is now used as a freestanding ornament.
A large vertical stone forming part of a structure. If the structure is roofed, the orthostat will stretch from the floor to the roof as a single slab.
A rounded or convex moulding, such as an ovolo or torus.
An early power loom in which  the shedding actions of the machine were controlled by tappets, or wipers, which received their motion from a rotating cam shaft positioned at one side of the loom.
A container, usually metal, used to water plants.
A factory where matresses are made.
A stand by set house designed to drawing number 13244/41 and comprising of 4 rooms; a fuel storage room, a transformer chamber, a switchgear chamber and the main engine room with 2 diesel engines.
A rod, often of antler, with a hole through it and decorated.
A joint in which a dovetailed timber's surface is proud of the receiving member on one side.

A place of worship for General Baptists, a movement established by John Smyth in 1603 and which grew out of the original Baptist church. They believed in free will and are often referred to simply as Baptists.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.

A building where fish are stored. Often taking the form of a single storey building with one room, but also may provide living accommodation for a fisherman above. Found mainly in the South West of England.
Solid masonry slabs (tiles) of terracotta which are usually used as a cladding by bedding in concrete. Faience also refers to decorative glazed units.

Controlled intrusive fieldwork which examines, records and interprets archaeological deposits, features and structures and, as appropriate, retrieves artefacts and ecofact remains within a specified area or site on land or within the inter-tidal zone.
A device for raising miners individually from a shaft consisting of two rods, raised and lowered alternately, fitted with small platforms and powered by a waterwheel or steam engine.
A place where umber or oxide of iron and manganese, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A building or site used for the maintenance and repair of motor vehicles.
A railway worked by the propulsive force of compressed air or by the formation of a vacuum.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.
A trough or watercourse constructed to collect rainwater from a roof and channel it towards a drain or pipe.
A component of salt works containing flues and drying areas where salt blocks are dried before being crushed and bagged.
A load carrying horizontal structural member.
Mine for the extraction of bismuth, which usually occurs in small quantities in the ores of other metal ores, particularly lead, and some copper ores.
Materials or goods which have been produced wholly or in part from oil, e.g. petroleum.
A deciduous conifer native to Britain and Europe supplying durable and waterproof timber suitable for shipbuilding features such as masts.
A winch powered by a steam engine.
A hospital block where pregnant women are accommodated and receive medical treatment before and after child birth.
A building plan in which the principal fireplace is positioned on the side wall.
A house plan with a hall and a single wing.
The SI derived unit for acceleration

A building or structure used to provide protection to an Air Raid Warden or firewatcher during an air raid, thus enabling the identification of the locations of fires caused by incendiary bombs in comparative safety.
A building or site where bloom iron or cast iron is forged into wrought iron.

Used by Ordnance Survey to record high accuracy height above Ordnance Datum Newlyn. Marked by a low concrete pillar, and maybe surrounded by railings, they comprise an underground chamber protecting the reference point, built directly onto stable bedrock.
A form of blast furnace. Steel is smelted in an open hearth while the waste gases are used to preheat the air blast.
A small garden enclosure within a BOSQUET or surrounded by clipped hedges.
Use for craft, such as logboats and punts, powered by pushing a pole against the riverbed in inland waters.
A flail used for the mortification of the flesh.

A 19th century establishment for the provision of work for the unemployed poor of a parish; later an institution administered by Guardians of the Poor, in which paupers are lodged and the able-bodied set to work.
A dwelling built on marshy, boggy or waterlogged land using timber piles driven vertically into the ground to raise the floor above the ground to prevent flooding.
Mark, usually consisting of a horizontal line above an arrow, cut by the Ordnance Survey as part of the survey of Britain and referenced to a known height above mean sea level.

A specific type of hook used in textile production, also known as a sheer board hook. Harbicks were used in pairs to secure a cloth to a cropping board so that the nap (of the cloth) could be sheared.
A terrace house sharing a common wall with its neighbours.
A ship or brig peculiar to the Mediterranean.
Block of flats within which the individual dwellings are accessed by narrow external balconies.
A horizontal member along the length of an aisle wall to receive the ends of rafters.
A lid comprising a shallow flared dish with an integral knob rising from the centre. (Source: MPRG)
The lower surface of a room.
A purpose built trench designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy glider-borne and airborne forces.
An object designed to hold food for birds.
A short timber set diagonally in the spandrel of an arch brace, between the brace and the corner of the main frame.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
Use only where the date is unknown or has not been verified.
Loss of vessel due to deployment of explosive charges set to detonate at a predetermined depth.
Geologist's term for any dark coloured, slightly metamorphosed igneous rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
A porch which is sufficiently large enough to allow a vehicle beneath it.
A column set on a pedestal and decorated with the bows of warships to celebrate naval victories. Originally a Roman form, it was revived in 17th and 18th century decoration.
A building used by members of the Womens Institute, an organization which meets regularly and engages in various social and cultural activities.
A building used in the preparation of manure.
A public house offering lodgings to the passengers, and stabling for the horses of stage coaches.
SHINE - Selected Heritage Inventory for Natural England
A tile used within a floor.
An instrument in which air is made to vibrate by a cane reed.
A defined portion of a surface, often a wall lining or door, usually rectangular, which may be recessed, level with or proud of its surrounding surface and may be framed by mouldings or channels.
A place where dead bodies are buried together. Often unconsecrated ground.
