A shallow dish or plate used to serve main meals off or to serve sweetmeats, these usually being painted with devices and riddles.
Depicting the nature and arrangement of strets and buildings within a built-up or urban area. For views within a singel street use STREET SCENE.
An instrument composed of several pipes in which air is made to vibrate by blowing across the top edge.

The monitoring of the excavation of a hole made by a non-archaeologically trained person. Any archaeological evidence that comes to light is recorded by the archaeologist during the course of the work although he/she cannot suspend the groundwork.

A modern building system in which both steel and concrete are utilized together to carry the load in ways that neither material predominates over the other. There are many varieties e. g. a steel frame surrounding a concrete core.
Wet soil, sand or other earthy matter combined with ballast and bonded with straw or other binding material. Walls are built in the absence of shuttering by the simple process of pitching in layers.
Buildings, sites and structures used by mariners for purposes of navigation.
A mine countermeasure vessel built to detect and destroy individual naval mines. (See Minesweeper for vessels that sweep and explode mined areas at sea without prior detection).
A joint in which the dovetailed member is proud of the receiving member and is not finished flush with it.
A residue left as the result of the burning of material.
A tower at the mouth of the harbour to defend the end of the harbour boom.
A building housing a Russian-style steam bath or banya.
A piece of wood attached to a thong that makes a roaring sound when the thong is whirled.
Specify in Description using: golf course, playing fields etc.
Application of earth based plaster to a backing of lath or wattle used in internal or external walls. Composite mixture which may include clay soil, dung, straw, lime putty, sand or horsehair.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A deep, square or rectangular, flat slab of clay, the upper surface of which has two or more cup-shaped holders cut into it. (Source: MPRG)
Sedimentary rock consisting of angular fragments naturally cemented together.
A stone inscribed or marked with runes.
A band worn around the wrist as a bracelet.
A garment used to wrap around a person.
A rough table usually for working upon.
A large building where iron is stored.
A vessel designed or adapted for the task of keeping shipping lanes and ports free from the threat of naval mines. Use specific type where known. of

Any object, often made of ceramic or 'porcelain' used for the purposes of personal cleansing, especially fittings such as toilets, baths and basins. May survive as fragments in the archaeological record. Use more specific term where known.
An unhewn piece of felled tree, or similar rough mass of wood.
A child's bed, usually with rockers.
A winch powered by a small steam engine used to drag barges, boats and other vehicles up an inclined plane.
School built by the local Education Authority to provide residental schooling at the seaside for children from urban communities.
Long poles or spars, usually set vertically, on sailing boats and ships to support the sails.
A two storied open fronted structure comprising a cattle or cart shelter on the ground floor with a hayloft above. Most common in South West England.
A microlith retouched to a rectangular shape. (Source: SARC)
A housing estate comprised of housing stock owned and let by a local authority.
A tool with adjustable jaws for gripping and turning objects.
An aisle within a chancel providing access to, and around, the High Altar and surrounding cells.
A large block of wood used to support the roof of a mine.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores  and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a military base.
A shop which sells vegetables and fruit.
A decorative, spiral scroll form, thought to have been based upon the shape of a ram's horn, employed in consoles, modillions, the capitals of orders such as the Ionic, Composite and Corinthian etc..
Solid bars made from pure lead.
A room where the public can sit, often in hotels and airports.
A school attended by children between the ages of seven and eleven.

Extremely thin foil made out of ethyltetraflouroethylene, a modified copolymer which is extruded into a thin film and which is related to Teflon. It has a very high level of light transmission in visible and ultra violet range. Used instead of glass.
A ship belonging to a shipping company which carries passengers on a scheduled route usually applied to steam ships only.
A purpose-built firing platform on which an anti-aircraft battery could be emplaced.
A strap or series of straps and or bars worn over the mouth of an animal to prevent it biting.
New Connexion Of General Baptists Chapel
The SI derived unit for density or mass density.
Hard, compact, unprocessed, fibrous cellulose substance. The roots, trunks and branches of trees and shrubs consist of this tissue.
A site where chalk is extracted from the ground.
A trench cut around a building or structure to prevent the spread of fire.
17th to early 19th century muzzle-loaded long guns.
A series of connecting metal links.
Transect or area-based arrangements of drilled auger-holes used to describe deposits and collect samples.
A group of buildings and satellite dishes used to transmit and receive signals relayed by satellites.
A chamber where discussions of issues take place, often found at universities.
Use for vessels registered in Wales.
A thin scoop used for cleaning the ear.

A site used for the safe storage of the art held in the national collections. During the Second World War many paintings, sculptures and works of art were moved to modified mines for safe keeping to protect them against bomb damage.
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.

A small tower or bartizan, which was often placed at the angles of a castle, to increase the flanking ability, some only serving as corner buttresses. Also used to describe the small rectangular towers situated between the milecastles along Hadrians Wall.
Equipment used to compress or break through compression.
A photographic slide of a black and white (monochromatic) image.
The case containing the charge for a firearm.
A custodial institution for offenders below the legal age of responsibility.
Use for vessels believed to come from Europe but where the precise nationality is not known.
A window with a frame for holding the glass, capable of being raised and lowered in vertical grooves.
Pipes used to carry water or hydraulic fluid for power transmission within a hydraulic system.
A stone or stone platform in a fire upon which cooking vessels are placed.
Imported Italian marble varying in colour from green, blue, purple to white.
A tool with an edged head and a wooden shaft, used for a variety of purposes. Where the function is known use the more specific terms of AXE (TOOL) or AXE (WEAPON).
An object used within a divinational process.
A cutting through a wood to open up a view or establish an allee.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
Fine grained, iron rich, liassic limestone, found in Dorset, Somerset, Oxfordshire, Northamptonshire, Leicestershire and Rutland.
A block on which objects are chopped or cut.
A factory where buttons are manufactured.
A joint in which the end of one timber is cut in V- form and rests on the edge of another timber, frequently found between common rafters and wall plates.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which experiments and observations are undertaken to gather and record information about the weather.
A sea within a sea, the Andaman Sea consists of that part of the Indian Ocean bordered by Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

A forcing house used for various types of fruit which first appeared in the 19th century. Lean-to houses were used for wall-grown fruit and free-standing houses for fruit grown in pots or for trees planted in the ground.
The warm room in a Roman baths.
Use only where stone is natural or where there is no indication of function.
A structure, often within a CHURCHYARD or LYCH GATE, on which a coffin could rest prior to burial.
Mark 16 or the sixteenth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
An inner defensive area within a castle.
A friary belonging to the Pied Friars also known as Friars of Blessed Mary or St Mary de Arens.
A semi-circular opening or window divided, by two mullions, into three sections, the central section being wider than those either side of it.
A form of hat, usually does not cover the forehead nor have a brim, and usually worn by women.
Objects associated with cultivation, the rearing of livestock, gathering, hunting, fishing, horticulture and the primary processing of foodstuffs.
An institution for the imprisonment and training of 16-21 year olds first established officially in 1908. Replaced by Youth Custody Centres in 1982.
Areas of land used primarily for agriculture. See also GARDENS, PARKS AND URBAN SPACES.
A mechanically operated display board used in greyhound racing, which showed the state of the Tote, or cumulative betting on individual greyhounds.
Use for the remains of any part of a fish.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (7345/41

Device for extracting juice from apples, usually crab apples, for use in cooking and medicine. Consists of a stone base carved with channels in the upper surface which was used with an upper weight, often secured with a wooden beam wedged into position.
A roofed, lightweight structure, usually attached to a house, provdiing access from and to the garden.
A hall built as part of a complex and used for the recreation of the workers or inhabitants. Usually associated with model estates, factories, flats etc.
A building housing a double inlet fan that was used for the ventillation of mine shafts
A workshop where tapestries were made.
That portion of the Pacific which stretches from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the equator.
Mechanical reproductive process using photographic, electrostatic and dry powder techniques.
An arch associated with the portion of the stage between the curtain and the orchestra.
A concrete, circular concave dish 20 feet in diameter used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.
A piece of metal in front of a fire to stop embers rolling onto the carpet.
A report which represents an initial synthesis of the data collected from an excavation ahead of the production of a full publication report.
A private chapel for a royal court.
A specialized form of truss bridge that extends or cantilevers from both sides of the pier, the inner 'arms' usually supporting a central span.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the practice of rituals & religious beliefs, including funerary rites. Includes ancillary buildings, structures & features of uncertain use, which are thought to be ï¿½ritualï¿½ (eg. hill figures).
A village laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
A room for personal rather than public use.
A building, or part of a building for the boiling and preparation of animal feed, usually attached to pigsties.
An undershot waterwheel, developed by General Jean Victor Poncelet (1788-1867) in France, which improved efficiency through the replacement of flat, wooden paddles with curved, metal vanes.
A building or site incorporating equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy aircraft or ships. Radar Stations can also be used to aid aircraft navigation in dark or poor conditions.

Machines for mechanical sewing, as opposed to sewing by hand. Victoriran and early 20th century examples are usually constructed of metal and operated by a hand wheel or treadle. Later examples may be electrically operated and/or have a plastic shell.
Use for vessels registered in Norway.
A step or ramp in the bank of a canal to enable horses to climb out of the water.
A conspicuous object, such as a beacon, used by mariners to aid navigation at sea.
An object used in combat to attack or cause damage to an opponent.
Animal skins, either raw or dressed which are used in the tanning industry to produce leather.
A hospital which has been built either wholly, or partially, underground in order to protect it from attacks by enemy aircraft.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to the surface of a ceiling.
A drawing which depicts to scale a feature within the landscape. For drawings of selected features of a site use SCALE DRAWING..
A building plan that features a hall lying between, and at right-angles to, two projecting wings.
A place where students live, sometimes on a college campus.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings are arranged around scattered yards which can be loose or regular in their form.
A fully automatic mounted or portable firearm, usually designed to fire bullets in quick succession from an ammunition belt or magazine.
A wall, usually perforated to allow free passage of air, supporting the ground-floor joists of a building.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
Photomechanical or photolithographical reproduction process representing a photographic image as a series of dots or lines.
A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
A assembly room or rooms in which a collection of nominated persons meet to transact business of relevant purpose.
A coal-burning power station where domestic electricity for an area is produced, eg. Battersea Power Station, London.
A full written presentation of the details of a particular event or investigative technique, often including illustrations and appendices.
A Byzantine bell-type capital, ornamented with carving resembling wicker-work or basket-weave.
A single or pair of figures or plates attached to a joist or bar either at the time of construction or later and built into the wall to provide support.
Mountings, often decorative, attached to a book.
A processing house containing equipment for sieving caked gunpowder to produce graded granules.
All or nearly all features of interest are well preserved for the period they represent and are clear at the time of survey. No sign of active damage.
A room in which food is prepared.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
A road or track specifically used by drovers or herders to drive their animals to market.
An enclosure containing a dock, boat yard, warehouse, etc, in which canal vessels are built and repaired, and all sorts of stores and merchandise for transportation brought together.
An object used for counting, keeping count or marking the position of a player in a game, usually in the form of a small circular-shaped piece of bone, metal, wood, plastic or other material.
An object used in the transmission of the written word or drawn image.
Sorting offices constructed during the Second World War designed to rapidly move goods from the vulnerable docks and ports via the rail network.
Use for a man-powered watercraft operated by wooden oars.
An iron cover for a manhole
A pier made up of several columns clustered together. They can be attached through their whole length or only at top and bottom.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A machine tool for producing flat surfaces and slots on small work pieces by cutting away surplus material.
A factory in which varnish is manufactured.
A object fitted to an item or garment for the purpose of display or decoration.
A mechanism used to turn a tram around.
A container to hold and/or apply grease.
Equipment used on a bird of prey for hawking.
A kiln used for extracting salt through the evaporation of salt water.
A building housing a set of bellows used to provide the blast of air to a blast furnace or similar installation.
An early to mid 20th century school designed to effect maximum ventilation and sunlight for its pupils.
Horizontal timbers laid parallel to each other on which flooring is laid and to which a ceiling is fixed.

Single-engine, two-crew multi-role aircraft designed for RAF Army co-operation. Entered RAF service in 1938. Noted for its role dropping agents into Europe, also served as a night-fighter, day ground-attack aircraft and target tug.
Civil building in Cornwall and Devon for assay and sale of tin ingots.
A decorative feature, or non-heraldic badge, representing the name of a person connected with a building, often in the form of a graphic pun on the name.
Mineral ore comprising mainly aluminium ore and mined for aluminium extraction.

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
An atrium or open court, surrounded by porticoes, at the west end of a church.

In the glass industry, material spilled or raked from the top of the crucible during melting:important for assessing the methods of glassmaking and a common find on furnace sites. Roman period onwards.
A stone or brick structure that projects into, or out of, a room and contains the flue.
A structure which allows aircraft fitted with radar equipment to 'home' in on an airfield in the dark or in poor visibility, and land safely. Radar beacons can also be used as navigation aids.

A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which young and domesticated animals are kept for public exhibition, especially for children. Children are given the opportunity to come into close contact and handle animals.
A place where material used for burning is stored.
A compact, free standing steam engine introduced circa 1810 and built mainly in small sizes.
Paper made for writing or drawing underwater.
A vessel designed for the transport of persons and goods from one place to another an a regular schedule of sailings. Use specific type were known.
A pump used to move water.

Unspecified defensive structure like a mound of earth, a rampart, an embankment or a wall-like fortification. Also used as an early term for a bastion or blockhouse. Use more specific term where known.
Use for vessels registered in Denmark
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelenght of 1.5m established to provide radar plotting of both shipping and aircraft movements.
An instrument in which air is made to vibrate by the player vibrating their lips and blowing into a mouthpiece.
An institution for the detention of prisoners, surrounded by a wall and/or fence as a barrier to escape. The level of security depends on the category of inmate detained.
A stringed instrument with a very rounded body.
The open space surrounded by a cloister.
An isolated building, circular in plan, generally consisting of one apartment with a domed roof, eg. Mausoleum at Castle Howard, Yorkshire.
Linear or curvilinear construction of earth, turf and stone, often, but not always accompanied by a ditch. Use specific type where known.
The inner rafter of a compound rafter.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A truss with a transverse timber like a hammer-beam, but braced to a principal or collar without a hammer-post.
A long stick or rod used as an aid in walking, climbing etc. Where it is a weapon use quarterstaff or staff weapon. Where there is another use, use the appropriate term eg surveying staff.
Clay used in the manufacture of fine ceramics especially porcelain.
A latrine, or privy, situated at the rear of a monastery dormitory.
A room or group of rooms usually reserved for use by the monarchy or government.
A visual representation of a physical object, place or person. [DC] Use a more specific term where appropriate.
An early form of lead furnace, set upon a hilltop or crest to utilize winds in smelting.
A vessel withdrawn from active use and awaiting disposal or reuse.  Vessel subsequently becomes derelict.
Sites and structures associated with the disposal of waste water and waterborne refuse.
A mill with machinery used to cut slabs of metal into rods, or thin sections, for use in nail making or wire drawing.
A piece of material, eg metal, cloth, leather etc, added to a button to enhance or embellish it.
A pipe in which air is made to vibrate by blowing across an edge, including transverse flutes and recorders.

Periodic visits being made to a site by an archaeologist to record archaeological deposits and recover finds that have come to light since the previous visit. An archaeological presence is not maintained during groundwork as it is with a watching brief.
An area within a hospital used for the isolation of patients. Patients were isolated if they had an infectious disease or suffered from a psychiatric illness.
An object with a broad enough blade which catches the wind and so is pushed until it shows the direction the wind is blowing in.
Use a term from the Archive Format list.
For example asthma, Cystic Fibrosis, Pneumoconiosis, Bronchieactasis, mycotic and other chronic infections, sleep related breathing disorders and lung transplant.
An object worn on the head.
The principal stand at a sporting ground, eg. at a racecourse.
A metal ring which joins the jess to the leash. The owner's name is often on the vervel.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A half-pier, corbel or other architectural element, usually situated at the end of an arcade, attached to a wall to support an arch.
A Roman market hall principally selling meat and poultry but also other provisions.
A managed small wood or thicket of underwood grown to be periodically cut to encourage new growth providing smaller timber.

A pass, vulnerable to attack from the enemy but essential for the movement of troops and which, if captured, could divide a defending force. As a result such passes are defended with anti invasion defences such as pillboxes.
The receptacle at the top of a rain-water pipe which gathers the water from one or more outlets or gutters on the roof.
A building used for an agricultural and/or subsistence purpose. Use more specific type where known.
A site used for the manufacture and finishing of querns.
A man-made passageway, which is built through a sea- or riverbed.
A decorative moulding depicting an animal or bird head with a tongue or beak that overlaps the moulding set below it.
A spa building to which water was pumped from springs or wells; usually also serving a social function as an ASSEMBLY ROOM, eg. as at Bath.
A fan designed to fan the coals of a fire to increase the oxygen around the coals and thus to help the fire burn.
A chamber for the incarceration of one or more prisoners.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
The festival for the first day after Ramadan.
A building or complex, housing powered machinery and employing a large workforce for manufacturing purposes. Use specific monument type where known.
A small concrete turret placed on top of a standard 4 ft. diameter concrete pipe sunk into the ground. Intended for use in defending road junctions, airfields and beach exits.
A pointed instrument for writing, usually on wax tablets.
A specialized lantern, with a reduced glare, for use in air raids.
A rural cross erected to show the way.
An area or defined space believed to have been used for trades and/or manufacturing activity. Only use when evidence for more specific site type is lacking.
A decorative feature of a shield for armorial bearings.
A bowl with concave body walls. Wide-mouthed, narrow-based examples, particularly those in larger sizes, have been termed Pans or Pancheons. (Source: MPRG)
A tool with a curved blade used for pruning.
A curb-roof with curved or steeply pitched lower slopes and a hipped or pitched roof above. Named after the French Classical architect F. Mansart.
A pulley block and metal ring used to guide a line or rope and cause it to run easily without chafing.
A long handled weapon which has a long blade in line with the shaft, sharpened on both sides and ending in a point.
A column of the Tuscan Order featuring a plain, unfluted shaft.
A ship acting as a base for smaller vessels and or submarines.
A set of small pincers used for gripping and plucking.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a domestic site such as a city and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing counterfeit targets.
An arrowhead which has a straight cutting edge.
A single line, or two or more roughly parallel lines, of standing stones set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes.
A maritime monument where the remains of a vessel are known to exist but where no detailed information is available.
An arch produced by two curves, usually each with a radius equal to the span, which meet at a point.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
A chapel for a prison, either attached or in a separate building.
Sacred Jewish texts and appurtenances buried within a Jewish cemetery.
A rectangular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.
A small spoon used with incense.
A building where violins are manufactured and the art of violin making is taught.
Buildings and structures associated with the performance of musical, oratory and dance events.
A composite beam of timber strengthened by an iron plate, or plates, used in the construction of 18th and 19th century timber framed mills and warehouses.
A small warship engaged in patrolling coastal waters.
A winding path in a garden or park, common in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.
An amber like substance derived from pine or turpentine.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
A cable railway with ascending and descending cars counterbalanced.
A shop which dispenses medicinal drugs and other health-related items. Can include an area for the preparation and manufacture of medicines and other drugs.
An ornamental moulding consisting of a series of small, regularly placed squared or rounded blocks.
An underground vertical cylindrical structure for the storage and launching of ballistic missiles.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War.
A wedge shaped stone or brick forming part of an arch or vault, with its radiating sides coinciding with the radii of that arch.
An associated group of toilet articles.
A projecting, sometimes decorated, finish to a moulding, chamfer, label, hood-mould or string-course.
The tool used to create a mark on pottery by the potter.
An underground foot tunnel primarily constructed to allow for the passage of pedestrians beneath an over ground obstacle.
Mushroom-shaped stones used to raise the floor of barns, granaries etc. above ground level, to prevent vermin gaining access to stored grain and fodder.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.
A single seat with back and arms and usually upholstered.
A building or group of buildings used for the making, processing, storing and selling of milk and other dairy products.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
Timber manufactured from fir or spruce trees.
A commercial premises offering advice on destinations and other travel arrangements, and where travellers may purchase flights,make hotel reservations or book package holidays and tours.

A horizontal surface separating the base of a rampart or earthwork from an associated ditch or moat. Can also refer to a continuously sloping bank of earth against a wall, as in a fortified city wall.
A truss which does not subdivide a space, as in the centre of a hall of two bays or in an undivided building such as a barn.
A freestanding building, or a room or recess serving as a place of Christian worship in a church or other building. Use more specific type where known.
A figurative or decorative object made of corn, used as a charm for luck or to ward off evil spirits.
Conelike spikes of the hop plant used in the brewing industry to give a bitter flavour to beer and malt liquors.
A chapel dedicated to our Blessed Lady, often placed to the east of the High Altar, sometimes in other positions.
A large, usually unroofed building with tiers of seats for spectators built in various shapes and enclosing a field used for sports events.
Use for a craft powered by a steam engine. Use also for a vessel employing a steam engine as its principle source of motive power.

A Roman under-floor heating system in which hot air heated by a stoked furnace, flowed through channels, created by either raising the floor on pillars of brick and tile or cutting channels into the concrete floor and tiling over them.
Armour designed to protect the leg or parts of the leg. For specific foot protection use FOOT GUARD
A wedge shaped stone used in an arch.
North of 40¡N; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal04
A complete written work including books and anthologies.
A hospital for the care of patients with incurable illnesses.
A medium containing microphotographic images, usually reproduced on film, requiring magnification to render them readable.
A small house or a portion of a house used as a self-contained apartment.
A large portable container used for carrying items such as clothes, papers etc.

Areas within the urban environment with their surfaces open to the sky, that have been consciously acquired or publicly regulated to serve urban shaping function, in addition others may provide recreational opportunities.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
Mediaeval-17th century mining method which involved exploiting an exposed surface vein. Rarely associated with waste.
A bowl with a sharp change of angle in the vessel wall, generally at the point of maximum diameter. the carination may be in the upper or lower half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)
A monument consisting of parallel lines of banks, ditches, stones, timber posts or trees which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments. Use specific type where known.

A device for telling the time by the sun, using the shadow cast by a gnomon, or sometimes a spot of light through a small hole. They were often used for checking the accuracy of clocks. They range from panels on the sides of churches to pocket watch size.

A coin struck, cast or stamped imitating an official coinage issue of contemporary or slightly later time period. The piece may consist of a similar alloy or a base core with plating of varying thickness.
A machine used in the worsted industry for cleaning woollen slivers after gilling and cording.
A series of arches, linked together, often made out of clipped hedges or trees with the trunks forming the uprights
A bell-shaped pit used in early coal mining. Use with functional type if known, eg. COAL WORKINGS.
Specify in Description using: river, stream, estuary above tidal (saline) influence etc.
A compound steam engine with provision for bleeding off some steam after it has passed through the high pressure cylinder and before it enters  the low pressure cylinder.
A building used for housing, and protecting from the weather, carts, waggons and farm implements, often open-fronted.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.
Buildings or sites used in the preparation, treatment and working of raw animal hide into leather products such as gloves or saddles, etc.
A film strip or roll containing reduced images.
A sign, often mounted on a post next to a roadside, giving directions or other instructions.
A half gable or half pediment concealing the lean-to roof of an aisle.
An opening within a structure to allow air and light in and or to allow a sight outside or inside.
A hook on harness to help attach items.
A site or building where ore is processed to obtain metal.

Historic England's Science Advisors provide support and science advice to local authorities determining planning applications affecting archaeological sites and the archaeological units carrying out these excavations. The input of a Historic England Science Advisor is available at all stages of the planning process and covers all aspects of the investigation and analysis of the historic environment to enhance its understanding and management.

A square pillbox with loopholes for four light machine guns with 18 in thick walls. Probably designed by DFW branch 3 although it may have been adapted from an external source as Southern Command correspondence refers to the type as 'Stento'.
Fabric of fibrous materials consolidated by heat and mechanical action so that the fibres are matted together.
A works using sealed retorts to produce charcoal. Wood distillates may be produced as byproducts of this process. They may be found at separate works or comprise part of a gunpowder works.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
Small seeds of the leguminous plant Lens culinaris, eaten in stews and soups.
An underground chamber, store room or passage.
A perforated strip of metal for shoeing the bifurcated hoof of an ox.
T shaped piece of bronze imitating a key and hung from a chatelaine.
A type of bowl designed to be suspended, usually from the roof.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.
A small stone structure, usually at a spring or bog, in which dairy products were kept cool on slate shelves.
Natural feature or area deliberately enhanced to construct a monument, eg rock carving, cave, rock shelter.
Buildings, sites and structures associated  with the manufacture of lace.
An alcoholic drink made from fermented apple juice.
A burial ground for followers of the Eastern Orthodox church.
The weapon end of an arrow, often shaped for particular uses.
A warehouse, usually under the charge of CUSTOM HOUSE officials, in which goods were stored before the duty had been paid. Often found in dockyards, harbours, etc.
Each of a pair of long narrow pieces of wood, usually pointed and turned up at the front, fastened under the feet for travel on snow.
A place where public sales of goods are made by competitive bidding.
Report prepared by a specialist in a particular field, often as a contribution to a wider project.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of shoe and leather polish, etc.
An establishment where books, periodicals, music, etc, are produced from original manuscripts and distributed to booksellers, dealers and the public.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
A large, metal or wooden structure, used for raising, lowering and moving heavy objects. Use more specific type where known.
Powder made from particles of stone used in mining to make the coal dust in the air less combustible.
A long seat usually without a back.
A processing house or room in a brewery.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.
A building, site or structure associated with the demonstration and testing of weapons and military equipment.
A cruck blade, sometimes jointed, set in the centre of a gable wall, usually of a cruck-framed building.
A sandglass that runs for an hour.

There are certain units, which are accepted for use with the SI. It includes units which are in continuous everyday use, in particular the traditional units of time and of angle, together with a few other units which have assumed increasing technical importance. There are also units which are currently accepted for use with the SI to satisfy the needs of commercial, legal and specialist scientific interests or are important for the interpretation of older texts.
A vessel used to carry supplies and equipment needed by recreational or deep sea divers.
A small vessel used as transport for customs officers.
A large stopper, often of cork.
A building used for the storage of picked fruit.
An embanked shute, often stone paved, allowing carts to tip their loads of coal from the road into a storage area.
Use for deposits formed in estuaries.
An arrowhead with its base hollowed to allow it to fit onto the shaft of an arrow rather than having a tang that fits into the shaft.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A place where silica or silicate, the most common mineral component of rock, is extracted from the ground.
A hard, coarse grained, durable igneous rock. Can be used decoratively or as a main material. Found throughout the country.
Mixed house of nuns and religious men.
A room intended for the placement and use of a billiard table.
Knapped or ground stone/flint tool where the specific type is unknown. Use more specific type where known.

A first century AD one-piece bow brooch, one end of which is drawn out to form a spring and pin, characterized by its long, narrow, tapering bow, a small crossbar in front of the spring and a forward hook which holds the spring chord.
A board indicating the name of the railway station.
A type of public building common in the 18th and 19th century, serving as an educational and/or learned society institute.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
A metal spur fitted to the leg of a fighting cock as an aid in fighting.
A place where marble is extracted from the ground.
Two discs at the end of a short shank, used to fasten shirt fronts, collars etc.
A building of unknown purpose found at a military site. Use more specific type where known.
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.
A temporary brick building, based on drawing number (2901/43), used for the repair, packing and storage of inflatable liferafts.
A flat bottomed drinking vessel with no handle or stem.
A place of meeting and worship for Brethren, a fundamentalist puritan sect founded in Ireland in the late 1820s and established in England in Plymouth in the 1830s.
A pit which appears to have been dug for, or which contains, objects apparently deposited for reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction. Index with principal object types.

A flour milling machine which uses horizontal steel rollers and dressing machines � seives and purifiers � to gradually reduce wheat grains into constituent parts or �streams� which millers call a �gradual reduction� process.
A long usually cylindrical object usually made of wood.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of timber.
Dating to the reign of the Stuart kings of England (including the Commonwealth inter-regnum)
The remains of the fine powdery substance produced by male elements of flowering plants, uniquely identifiable to the species it came from.
A shed, often found at a quarry, in which rough stone is shaped or dressed.

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
Usually a L or T-shaped tumbler lock key which allowed the bolt to be pulled across by a cord.
A hospital department for the identification and treatment of skin tissue disorders.

A site which has produced evidence of in situ working of stone for the manufacture of tools, weapons or other objects. Such sites will usually, but not always, be of prehistoric date. Use object material where known.
Goods and equipment used to supply a navy.
A semi circular jewelled headdress for formal occasions.
A lid for a well. Well covers are often ornate and can be made of various materials.
A church established by a religious community to propogate its faith.

An asset with strong communal or historical associations, or because it has especially
striking aesthetic value, may be singled out as a landmark within the local scene.
A place where tree trunks were sawn into planks by hand.
A projectile discharged from a weapon, usually a firearm.

Use where a section of the vessel has been recovered from where she lies, either at the time or subsequently, leaving behind substantial remains (unlike RECOVERED, where the entire vessel has been removed from the site).
Use for deposits formed as a result of construction activities undertaken by humans or animals.
A bowl adapted by the addition of three or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of gunpowder.
A vessel to contain holy water located near the entrance of a church.
A modern fodder store on a farm.
Metal spikes used for fixing one object to another.
A craft designed for use on canals and inland waterways. Usually 70ft long x 7ft wide though can be longer and broader.
A shallow outdoor pool, usually rectangular in shape filled with water which when frozen was used for the sport of Curling.
Use only for features assumed to be archaeological but which cannot be identified more precisely without further investigation .Use more specific term where known
A covering for the leg which fits closely.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A knife prior to undergoing the processes of sharpening or finishing, consisting of a single piece of metal from which the blade and tang have been shaped.
An area of a carriageway, usually delimited by road markings, for the sole use of bicycles.
A late 12th Century capital featuring large, unribbed leaves growing outwards from each angle before curving up towards the abacus and turning inwards at the top.
Remains of the group of animals characterized as being radially symmetrical in form, such as sea urchins, sea cucumbers and starfish.
A vessel to contain wine or water used in the Eucharist.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War.
A type of late 19th century tenement block for tenants of a higher social status - usually reflected in the more ornate facades.
Medium-sized animals domesticated for their wool, skin, meat and milk.
A protective covering applied to the top of a wall, chimney, gable etc., usually curved, sloping or ridged to prevent rainwater settling.
A Roman mixing vessel with a gritted inner surface.
Use for vessels registered in Pakistan.
An engine house which used air pressure to power trains on the experimental atmospheric railways of the 1840s.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently high to be seen at a long range and above low lying cloud or fog. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a High Light is usually accompanied by a LOW LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
A core with more than two distinct platforms usually including one or two striking surfaces and the the traces of former platforms. Usually restricted to flake production. (Source: SARC)
A fertilizer containing nitrogen, derived from sodium nitrate.
A piece of grassland, often near a river, permanently covered with grass which is mown for use as hay.
The support from which a lamp was hung.
A structure, often sunk into the ground, for the purpose of allowing total bodily immersion in mineral sprinwater or similarly beneficial substances.
A cruck truss whose blades are composed of two pieces of timber joined near the wall head in a variety of ways.
A written work being one of several found in a monograph or serial
Graves known to be of shipwreck victims buried close to their site of discovery, as was customary until the 19th century, rather than in consecrated ground.
A lobby or chapel at the western entrance of a church. Sometimes a place of burial, an area reserved for women, or a place where monks could meet female relatives.
A tall holder for candles which stands on the floor.
A bag stuffed with soft material used to support the head whilst sleeping.
This period follows on from the Neolithic and is characterized by the increasing use of Bronzework. It is subdivided in the Early,Middle and Late Bronze Age.

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
A container in which weapons are put for storage and or transportation.
An enclosed piece of land adjoining a house.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
A soft, lustrous low-melting crystalline metallic element that is malleable and ductile at ordinary temperatures and that is used as a protective coating, in tinfoil, and in soft solders and alloys.
The retrieval of samples for laboratory analysis from buried features that have been sampled using boring equipment.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 1.5m. Chain Home Low Stations were intended for use in locating low-flying aircraft but was also capable of detecting high-flying aircraft.
A flower bed, usually circular and convex in form, edged with wicker basketwork, iron hoops or terracotta.
A subterranean feature entered from a hillside, cliff face, etc. A cave may have been used for occupation, storage, burial, refuse, or as a hide-away. Index with site type or objects where known.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for Lemurs, including shelter.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of a horn filled with fruit etc.
A report written as a result of archaeological monitoring during development work.
A court in front of a church, usually open.
A building, often located in a park, where players can change and store equipment and from where spectators can watch the game.
A house or hut for a nightwatchman; including parish watch houses in churchyards and private watch houses, eg. in dockyards, factories, etc.
Ore containing high proportions of Iron.
A mine used for the extraction of zinc bearing ore. Use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where necessary, eg. LEAD MINE.
A path across a road, usually marked as a crossing for pedestrians.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
Buildings and structures associated with the mining industry.
A building where people pay to see films and 'moving pictures'.
A specialist hospital where women receive medical and surgical treatment.
A building, usually containing several dormitories, used as a cheap, short term residence. Use more specific term if known.
A small timber one-roomed dwelling where holiday makers could rest after a day spent sunbathing, swimming and playing on the beach.
A tall structure, high in proportion to its lateral dimensions, often rising in stages, free standing or part of another  building, surmounted by a clock.
A length of cord usually made from twisting fibres together which increases the strength of the rope.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.
A hospital department which treats patients without keeping them in overnight or for a longer period.
Equipment used in the care and upkeep of animals, usually used directly on the animal.
A building used to accommodate elephants at a zoo or wildlife park.
House owned by the church, often used for meetings.
A short published document, often a single sheet, describing a particular place, feature or service to assist visitors and users.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often a component of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
An area of a garden with a semi-circular backdrop formed by an ornamental, architectural structure or a natural feature grown to the required shape eg. a hedge
A building in which a view is projected onto a wall by means of a lens.
A building or group of buildings used for the storage and issuing of rations and equipment to an army unit.
Solid spherical objects, manufactured from stone or metal, fired from cannon.
A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which panels could be slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation (BCF) during WWII.
The flat end of a barrel.
Features of interest are not surveyable at the time of the survey, e.g. obscured by cloud-cover, vegetation, ongoing building work etc. or the monument could not be located.
An open circular area where avenues converge.
A store belonging to a cooperative society.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A place of worship for followers of Emmanuel Swedenborg who believed he was the medium through which the New Jerusalem would be founded on earth. The church was formed in 1787.
A building used for the administration of a squadron.
A musical instrument that produces sound through the passage of air through a number of pipes controlled by stops, pedals and keyboards.
The timber from genus Betula, found in Europe and North America, particularly in northern regions.
An associated group of manicure implements.
A steam engine which produces rotary motion.
A substantial piece of timber which is part of, and integral to, the structure of a building.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
A straight-grained, durable and often resinous timber obtained from trees of the genus Pinus.
Soft coverings and associated objects for walls, furniture, floors and windows. Also items such as chairs, beds, and cupboards.
A building, on an airfield or military base, used for the maintenance and storage of motor vehicles.
The outward curve at the top or bottom of a column where it joins the base or capital.
Mill incorporating water-powered hammers for beating brass sheet, etc. into vessels, pots, etc.
A boat roofed over and fitted up as a home for living in permanently or temporarily.
An installation used to store ammunition and equipment ready for the mobilization of armed forces in the event of a war.
Shed for grinding rags, eg. for use in mungo and shoddy mills.
An area attached to a house, or part of an estate used for pleasure and recreation.
A pit from which sand is excavated.
A school that is established, run and supported by a private, non-governmental body.
A place providing social, recreational, and educational facilities for a neighbourhood.
A pound for the accommodation of livestock.
A natural or man-made gap in vegetation or other combustible material that acts as a barrier to slow or stop the progress of a fire.
Buildings and structures inhabited by agricultural workers.
The fine, keratinized, flexible filaments that grow from follicles beneath the surface of the skin in mammals.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A form of round barrow intermediate between the Bell Barrow and the Disc Barrow. Only use where it is not possible to determine specific type.
Durable wood from a non-native, evergreen conifer.
An anti tank wall constructed specifically to be used for training purposes.
A vessel used for carrying weapons and ammunition to warships.
A decoy site designed to simulate permitted lighting, such as locomotives, furnaces and tramwire flashes, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.

Loss due to cumulative damage sustained during acts of warfare, capture, piracy, privateering etc. Use in instances where a more specific manner of loss (e.g. SCUTTLED, GUN ACTION) cannot be assigned.
A defence work, either a detached fieldwork or an outwork built as part of a fortification as a last defensive position.
A large stone laid horizontally to form the roof of a chamber.
Flood defence and coastal erosion works, extending inland to include estuaries and tidal rivers.
Use for vessels registered in Japan.
An embankment or cutting on a railway system, surfaced at a uniform gradient, up or down which materials were hauled by rope.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
A bed or border in which different species and colours are mixed.
A small tower, usually round or polygonal and attached to a structure. When a separate building, treat as a monument.
An ornamental building, usually decorated with or displaying shells.

A detached building without an operations block and crew briefing room designed on modern lines similar to, but smaller than WATCH OFFICE (12779/41). Began appearing on new stations from September 1941.

A gate, made of wood, used as a livestock barrier by continuing a fence line across a river or stream. The gate usually consists of a series of  droppers, that can float up and down depending on water levels, attached to a length of cable or wooden pole.
A report detailing the results of an archaeological event were the ground surface has been studied and any visible archaeological material collected.
An inscription on illustration applied to a wall by carving into its plaster to reveal a different colour beneath.
Sodium carbonate, usually derived from common salt, used for a variety of purposes including the manufacture of glass and soap.
A firm beach or foreshore used for landing and loading of ships and other vessels. In more recent times hards have been reinforced with concrete.
A room in which disused items, such as furniture, are stored.
Acts of vandalism, or deliberate damage by owner or other parties, which result in the `Constructive Total Lossï¿½ (CTL) of vessel, or contributes to CTL of an abandoned vessel.
Use for craft built with no engines or masts and designed to be towed by another craft.
A row of columns that carry arches or an entablature.
Monument type/interpretation is inferred, based on informed speculation eg by comparison with similar monuments, proximity to other monuments, topography, site character etc.
A colourless, thick sweet liquid used in the manufacture of chemicals.
Articles of value particularly those made with precious metals and precious stones, usually worn for adornment.
A small structure providing cover and protected accommodation for a sentry.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
A light plough used to break up the earth. It does not have a mouldboard to turn the earth.
A structure, often concrete or brick, used as a shelter by members of the British citizen army during watch or patrol duties, or air raids, in wartime.
A room or building used for the making of films, television or radio programmes and musical recordings (CDs, LPs, etc).
A horse-powered winding engine used at mining sites.

A missile or aircraft that obtain its thrust from a rocket engine. Some rockets will exist as monuments for example, in the form of gate guardians. Double index with the monument type where appropriate.
A workshop or factory for casting metals.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
A store for keeping undressed meat.
An area of privately owned land attached to, and incorporating, a country house and associated buildings.
A component part that is designed deliberately for decorative purposes.
A book containing information about a place that has been produced for the use of visitors or tourists.
Threads of material used to form cloth.
A vessel (often small obsolete cruisers or pleasure steamers) equipped with batteries of anti aircraft guns as its main armament.
Oil produced from the pulp of olives.
An informal garden attached to a cottage where flowers, vegetables and fruit trees are grown.
The powdery residue resulting from the combustion of a substance eg. wood and used for various manufacturing processes.
A brace which is cut to a double curve.
Fishing Industry Protocal for Archaeological Discoveries (FIPAD)
A car park situated beneath the surface of the ground.
A place where railway engines are kept.

The fertilized ovules of a plant, often occurring in an archaeological context, in the form of small roundish bodies or grains. Seeds are dispersed naturally or collected for sowing to produce a new generation of plants.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
Goods, including portable objects and furniture, commonly found in the home.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
A projection from the inner angle of a building around a court or with advancing wings, usually containing a staircase and often crowned above the roof line with an ogee dome.
The administrative office of a transport company who provide a service for the conveyance and transportation of either goods or people.
Small two or three masted ship used as trading vessels in the medieval mediterranean.
A small, open air bowl-shaped furnace, in which the flames are fanned by bellows. Used for both ferrous and non-ferrous smelting.
A building or site incorporating sonar equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy ships or submarines.
Deposits laid down as the result of river action.
A building at an airport from where passengers embark and disembark from an aircraft.
A crosspiece fastened over the necks of two or more animals, often oxen, and attached to the plough or cart to be drawn.
A window set within a curved projection from the face of a wall.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.
Unsorted sediment (i.e. containing everything from clay to boulders) laid down directly by a glacier.
A room within a house or building used to exhibit artworks, often decorated and lit accordingly.
A type of seaplane, with one or more slender pontoons (known as "floats") mounted under the fuselage to provide buoyancy.

Specific English quarryman's term for any limestone abundant in shell fragments. Use this term with care. When only Gritstone is mentioned, unless otherwise specified, assume it to be Gritstone (Sandstone), since this is the most common usage.
A strategically placed aperture in the wall of a fortification through which guns and cannon can fire upon an invading force.
An instrument for measuring the angle of slopes, usually in inches per yard, consisting of a weighted graduated wheel with movable sights.

Amoebae which are partially enclosed in external shells, or tests. Found in wet soils, freshwater, decaying organic matter and on vegetation such as mosses. Used to examine environmental factors such as water acidity and moisture content.
A garden incorporating features of traditional Japanese gardens - a pool, an island, stepping stones or a bridge, cherry trees and other shrubs and flowering plants grown with the emphasis on line.

A tower or structure, with a powerful light or lights at the top, usually erected at an important or dangerous point on or near the sea-coast for the warning and guidance of mariners, but can also be erected inland for the guidance of travellers.
A machine for creating bails of straw.
A prime mover which is rotated by the reaction from forcing a moving fluid to change direction.
The end of a timber post made wider than the rest of its length on one face to accomodate tiebeams, wall-plates etc..
Use only for buildings which house motor vehicles. Includes garages for vehicle repair. For petrol sales use PETROL STATION.
A complex or network of earthwork or cropmark linear ditches, banks or other features. Use specific type where known.
The barrel of a feather, usually goose, used as a pen.
A craft employed to harpoon whales and bring them in to be processed.
Material, stone or wood, lining the inside of a grave.
Man-made building, edifice or construction of assembled material parts.

A large circular defence work surrounded by a brick revetted ditch and sunken below a glacis. Usually built out of brick with the embrasures lined with granite blocks. Armed with ten or elven guns. Early 19th century as part of coastline defence.

A pilaster terminating the side walls of a temple whose capital and base differ from those of its associated columns. Such an arrangement, where the columns do not project beyond the faces of the antae, is said to be 'in antis'.
An island, partly or wholly artificial, built up by dumping timber, earth and stones onto a lake or river bed. Often revetted with timber piles or palisade.
A factory, works or structure used for the manufacture and purification of gas.
An axe used by the Saxons and Franks for throwing.
Recovery and removal of grease (lanolin) from raw wool.
An amulet containing a charm in the shape of a scarab.
The undressing room in a bath house or similar.
Containers used to serve food and drink. Use appropriate term.
A pit, sometimes found close to a church or cathedral, where bells were cast in medieval times.
A vessel to contain the wafers used in the Eucharist.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
A hospital for the reception of women during their confinement.
A place where swans are bred and reared.
A device used to throw projectiles, can vary from a small forked stick for hurling stones to a large engine of war to hurl large projectiles.
A cutting tool for shaping and carving materials, often used in conjunction with a hammer or mallet.
A coloured fluid used for writing, drawing and printing.
A container, usually ceramic, used to water plants.
A brick, stone or iron receptacle for baking bread or other food in.
An area or wing of a hexagonal plan workhouse or prison from where the supervision of the inmates is carried out.
A decorative or ornamental structure purposefully situated in a garden. Such as sculptures, sundials, bird baths, gnomes etc.
Partially decomposed granite used to produce a glaze for porcelain.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
A large storehouse where wholesale goods are stored.
An engaged column, that is one attached to a wall.

An archaeological watching brief involves observation of groundworks and investigation of features of archaeological interest which are revealed.  A suitable working method with contingency arrangements for significant discoveries will need to be agreed.  The outcome will be a report and archive.
A long spear designed to be thrown in order to injure or kill a given target.
A bridge whose trusses or girders form parapets on either side of the deck.
A container filled with musket balls, metal fragments, nails etc. Designed to kill or maim the enemy at a close range.
A pit dug for the extraction of brine.
Transparent, hard substance made by fusing soda-silica which solidifies from a molten state.
A device, monogram or symbol incised in stonework by a mason as a means of identifying his work. Particularly common in Romanesque and Gothic buildings.
Two masted merchant vessel, rigged as a brig.
Data suitable for processing using computer aided design (CAD) packages.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
A collection of items presented in a protective folder.
Mark 8 or the eighth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A building used for the storage of explosives of a non-military function, eg. mining explosives, signal explosivres etc.
A fountain erected specifically to supply drinking water.
A weight used to hold down thatch.
A circular pillbox designed by the Croft Granite, Brick and Concrete Company, with six loopholes. With no roof or door access was gained through the roof.
A term used to describe a vaulted roof where the vault goes from either the newel of a staircase to a wall or from one wall to another where the walls are circular in plan.
Soft, porous objects used in bathing and for cleaning. Originally made from the dried skeletons of marine sponges but now more commonly manufactured from synthetic foam.
Buildings and sites associated with the production of materials made from minerals.
A protective piece of armour carried in the hand to protect the bearer from weapons.
A wooden, or wooden soled, shoe.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
An early design of pump featuring a series of pistons, or sometimes bundles of rags, passing through a barrel on a continuous chain, forcing water upwards.
Onyx is a cryptocrystalline form of quartz. It is a semi-precious stone that is usually cut as a cabochon, or into beads, and is also used for intaglios and cameos.

Collective term for the Scottish Slates including the Aberdeen/Baniff and Ballachulish/Easdale groups. Fine grained, varying in colour from brown to dark grey/blue. Geologically different from Lake District, Welsh and West Country groups of slate.

Any vessel in the service of one of the historical or modern agencies concerned with the prevention of inbound or outbound smuggling: namely the Preventive Service, the Coastguard, or the Customs and Excise. Use more specific term.

A sculpture, drawing, or other representation of a face surrounded by or made from leaves and branches or vines. Green Men are frequently found on carvings in both secular and church buildings, and are though to represent pagan fertility deities.
A voluminous garment worn over other clothing.
A small ornamental case, usually on a necklace or chain, that holds a picture, keepsake etc.
Material derived from living things. Use more specific term where known.
1⁄100 of a chain and  1⁄1000 of a furlong.
A very fast small warship, armed with small calibre guns and torpedoes. Used for attacking enemy vessels, escort duties and anti submarine duties.
An expansion period stand by set house designed to drawing number 607/36 and containing a single generator set and switch board. Constructed in reinforced concrete.
Mass produced iron framed shed usually clad in metal sheeting.
A crane operated by a treadmill turned by the walking action of men placed within it.
A small sailing vessel armed with guns.
A container used to serve food from.
A bound collection of paper or other materials.
Horn is a hollow, bone-like projection consisting mainly of keratin, found on certain animals (sheep, cows, goats etc.)
A German stoneware form of conical mug. (Source: MPRG)
Semi precious stone or glass engraved with a design and used to make an impression on wax or clay.
A woven or bonded fabric or cloth. See TEXTILE Class List for narrow terms.
A pulley running on the outside of a belt to improve the effectiveness of a drive.

Type of leaf-shaped socketed spearhead with two small holes or loops on either side at the base of the blade. Possibly meant to assist in securing the metal spearhead to the wooden shaft, or to tie streamers of some kind to the top of the spear.
A room in a church to receive the congregation's offerings.
A base on which a statue, column etc. stands.
A missile base armed with the Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile. Thor Missiles were deployed in Britain under joint British/US control between 1959 and 1964.
Buildings and structures associated with the creation and use of hydraulic power.
A platform which moves laterally on wheels, by which boats, railway carriages and engines may be moved from one place to another, eg. from one slipway to another parallel to it.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder.
A place at a school where children receive medical advice, health checks and treatment.
Metal cylinder for producing charcoal using the retort method
An inclined member used to support laths under a roof covering. Normally one of a pair.
waste resulting from the working of wood or associated with a carpenter's workshop.
A large cargo vessel, either purpose-fitted or converted, for the transportation of slaves.
The fibrous stalks of the plant, Linum usitatissimum, which can be processed and used to manufacture linen.
A building used, as a meeting place and administration block, by an organization run for the benefit of students at a school, college or university.
A simple machine, worked by horses, to provide a power take-off for driving agricultural machinery.
A steel framed seaplane hangar designed for Royal Navy Air Stations by the admiralty in 1917-1918.
A large dish-like structure designed to observe the invisible outerspace phenomena detected by radio waves, eg. Jodrell Bank.
A type of temporary transportable aircraft hangar designed in 1936 by N.S. Bellman. It was designed for ease of installation, and was composed of light rolled steel sections.
A small moulded bracket found on the Corinthian and Composite orders, and in plain form in the Ionic.
A hard material formed by firing clay. For pottery, use POTTERY.
A representation of a monument or landscape based on historical or archaeological information.
A chamber built into the side of a covered reservoir to enable the water level to be inspected.
An artificial mound created by the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
A grave or sepulchre including a monument.
An internal door flush with, and decorated to match, the wall it is set in for the purpose of concealment.

A place of worship for Strict Baptists, a sect who broke away from the Particular Baptists and kept up the practice of denying communion to non members after the union of General and Particular Baptists was formed in 1891.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.
A fragment of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
A mill which is powered by a turbine.
Worked or unworked block/boulder/cobble, on which grain was ground by to-and-fro motion, resulting in a deep smooth elongated hollowed area.

A pit dug to extract Sarsen stones from the superficial geology in which they occur. They range in size from one dug for the extraction of a single boulder to pits from which multiple boulders are extracted & date from the Neolitic to the mid 20th century
A part of the chancel of a church where the altar is situated.
A solid material which is combustible distilled from petroleum.
A building, group of buildings or space within a building, where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artefacts are housed and displayed.
A small ball, usually of glass or porcelain, used in games.
An iron, stone or concrete tower built up from the bed of a reservoir. From it the control valves of the pipes which draw off water at different levels are operated.
An elevated platform on which a criminal is executed.
A place where vehicles can be filled up with petrol, oil, water, etc.
A form of belt or sash worn to hold in garments.
A rail used to suspend objects from.

An emplacement housing mobile sound locating acoustic dishes/horns for the detection of incoming enemy aircraft and the triangulation of their positions so that they could be targeted by Anti aircraft guns.
Extremely hard, fine grained, grey to brown silica rich sandstone. It is often found on the surface of the South Downs and has been used, as found, since prehistoric times.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A bowl adapted by the addition of two handles, generally opposed. (Source: MPRG)

For example mood disorders, agoraphobia, anxiety, bipolar disorder, chronic depression, eating disorders, dissociative identity disorder, multiple personality disorder, obsessive-compulsive or paranoid personality disorder and schizophrenia.
Outerwear covering the upperbody, including the arms. Covers to the waist.
A structure housing machinery for crushing coal. Usually found at the pithead of a colliery or coal mine.
A by-product usually from the smelting process.
A vessel with a specially adapted mouthpiece, to assist in feeding young animals and humans.
A soft, powder used in the manufacture of bread and foodstuffs, obtained by grinding wheat or other grain.
A wooden or stone plinth for depositing milk churns on.
A combination of spear and axe on a long handle.
A jar that contains an offering.
Ceramic vessels produced out of wet clay which is shaped ad dried or fired to harden. In some cases other materials like sand are added to the clay.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of textiles.
A container within which a body is placed for burial, usually made of lead or wood.
A short, broad bladed oar used without a rowlock.
A handheld weapon that fires missiles by means of explosives.
Mark 14 or the fourteenth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
General term for images used to represent a particular place or item, or convey information.
A vessel in which incense is burnt.
A meeting hall, sometimes equivalent to a GUILDHALL, but also associated with some early mining industries.
A laundry situated within the estate of a manor or country house.

A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions surrounded by a concentric arrangement of annular or pennanular grooves. More complex designs may also occur.
A long rope with a noose at one end for catching animals.
A large building where fish are stored before sale.
Thick, black liquid distilled from bituminous coal, and containing many organic chemicals.
A steam driven winding engine house for raising coal to the surface.
The main current address for the building or monument.
A piece of land, sometimes man-made, completely surrounded by water.
A plate used in the Eucharist.
A slight structure built for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, either attached as a lean-to to a permanent building or separate. Use more specific type where known.

A list of English battlefields maintained by English Heritage. Inclusion in the document does not confer any statutory status. It lists and records the details of battlefields to preserve their nature and survival.
Monument visible on the sea, lake or river bed, either totally submerged at all times, or exposed at low tide, low water conditions etc.
Vehicles owned or used by the armed forces. Includes tanks, armoured vehicles as well as civilian vehicles in use by the military eg. ambulances.
A sculptured group comprising a chariot drawn by four horses.
Wood from non-coniferous trees, eg. oak, known for their hardness.
A machine for cutting down cereal crops.
A gate on a toll road where travellers had to pay a toll to the toll-keeper.
A building containing equipment used for the polishing of grains of gunpowder and extraction of the resulting dust.
A decorative ornamentation of interlaced bands in the form of a plait.
A storage area usually for naval weapons and stores.
A tower-like structure of wood or brick with a wooden cap and sails which are driven around by the wind producing power to work the internal machinery. Use with product type where known.
A building containing a machine tool for boring out large cylindrical holes in items such as steam engine cylinders, pump barrels, etc.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
For commercial or non commercial use. See narrow terms in each class.
A room within a building or complex used for storing clothing.
A tube through which missiles are blown.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A stone on which Runes have been inscribed. Often used as memorials though not always associated with a burial.
A waterwheel where the water enters below the top of the wheel but above the axle.

A strategic food store, directly operated by, or on behalf of, the government. The stores were used to store a variety of foodstuffs. They were in operation from the end of the Second World War until the early 1990's.
A room in general use for persons to meet, often found at institutions such as colleges.
A place where inmates of a workhouse or prison carried out stone breaking.
Implement with a shallow bowl at the end of a handle used to eat with or to stir food etc.
A flight of steps leading from one level to another.
A shop selling a variety of goods and merchandise.
A building or room where business, administrative or professional activities are conducted. Use specific type where known.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War. The U Boat had 5 torpedo tubes (4 bow/1 stern) and carried 10 torpedoes as well as an 88mm (or in some cases 105mm) deck gun.
A school where no fees were charged.
A wind-powered pump for land drainage.
That area between high and low water levels. Specify in Description using; sand, shingle, mud flat, estuarine silt, rock etc.
An ancillary building to a synagogue, used as a place of worship at the feast of the tabernacle.
A ramp or incline between differing levels constructed to allow carriages access.
A place where metal-cutting hand files were made.
A siren used to warn of an impending attack by enemy aircraft.
A cross erected by the side of the road.
A raised floor along the side of a line at a railway station, for convenience in entering and alighting from a train.
A place where telephones and their components are manufactured
A framework used as a support upon which fruit-trees or climbing plants are trained.
A steam generator comprising a pressure vessel, and/or rows of tubes arranged to receive heat from a firegrate.
