A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto textiles.
A comb used to comb fibre before spinning.
Cotton which has not been processed.
A field system which appears to have developed in an organic, or piecemeal, fashion over time.
A curving, upright timber brace used in roof construction, found in pairs, forming an arch.
A screen that separates a tomb or a chapel from the main body of a church.

A limited programme of intrusive fieldwork which determines the presence or absence of archaeological features, structures, deposits, artefacts or ecofacts within a specified area or site on land or within the inter-tidal zone.

A design of beam steam engine introduced circa 1800 in which, instead of a single overhead rocking beam, there are two beams positioned alongside the cylinder, one either side, giving a lower overall height.
An underground structure for the storage of mineral oil.
A farmstead where the main range of working buildings are attached in-line and form a long row often facing a series of yards.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder. Extensively used as mine winding engines.
A report depicting the results generated from an intensive survey of a large area of land including field recording, measured site surveys and land history.
A carved bust, figure or representation usually fixed to the bow of a ship.
An engine which uses air or the products of combustion as its working  medium.
A purlin that sits in a trench cut in the back of a principal rafter.
A hearth used for the reheating of metal slag to extract further metal.
A boat, ship or other vessel either whole or in part. Watercraft often survive as commemorative monuments or have been reused as floating restaurants, museums, hotels etc.
A stable, on two or more levels.
A range of buildings used to house abandoned or stray dogs.
A wooden, metal or stone strip attached to the floor between the door posts in a doorway covering the joint between two floor surfaces.
A container holding materials used in writing.
Savoury ingredients, such as herbs, used to add flavour to food.
Bridge for carrying pipes between buildings or working areas.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, incorporating an operations room.
The residences of people involved in transport work.
A mortar used specifically for grinding cosmetics.
Equipment including diving suits, wet suits, oxygen tanks etc. used to enable people to undertake underwater activities.
A building where milk is deposited and stored before it is despatched to the consumer.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.
A room where a class of pupils is taught.
A commercial premises where clocks are sold and repaired.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
A building where animals are deliberately fattened before being killed for their meat.

Observations made by antiquarians (Those who studied sites and landscapes prior to archaeology and architectural history becoming established disciplines in the 19th century) and reported through publication or from unpublished manuscripts.
A precious metal of lustrous white colour with great malleability and ductility.
A small knife used in surgery.
A barbed spear head used to catch marine life, usually has a rope or line attached to it.
Molluscs found in salt or brackish water. Use more specific term where known.
A structure, part of a structure or area constructed from plain bricks.
An iron bar or ingot of distinctive form with a pinched end previously thought to have been used as a medium of exchange in the Iron Age but is now believed to be a roughout for a sword.
A single piece of apparatus that uses mechanical power for a particular function.
A place where a yearly or half-yearly court of record is held by lords of certain manors.
An outer wall of a castle or similar fortification.
A kiln that is octagonal in plan. Use with functional kiln type where known.
Includes equipment for the consumption of food.

The earliest subdivision of the Palaeolithic, or Old Stone Age; when the earliest use of flint tools appears in the current archaeological record. A hunter gatherer society is a defining characteristic.
A rigid frame type of airship pioneered by Count Zeppelin and used by the Germans in WWI for military purposes: do not use asa generic name for airships
A strip of lead holding small pieces of glass (quarries) in a window.
A fluid substance. Use for unspecified liquids only, where known use more specific type.
An extended arbour, eg. the beech arbour at Hampton Court, Middlesex.
Use of a quarry or other area as a dumping ground for domestic or other waste.
Straps fastened around the legs of a hawk.
Use for vessels registered in Algeria.

The non intrusive processes by which information is collected about the location, distribution and organisation of past human activities. The approaches can be either extensive or intensive depending the objectivies that need to be addressed.
An early washing machine used in bleaching works for washing calico and other textiles.
A vessel carrying square sails on all masts and having three or more masts.
Sites used for the manufacture of aircraft.

A roughly circular monument featuring a low, more or less level platform of stones surrounded or retained by a low stone kerb. Some may feature a small central open area, thus resembling a ring cairn.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.

The room housing the looms in a domestic handloom weavers cottage. In general, wool loomshops were above the living quarters, whereas cotton loomshops were often below in a cellar, since the floor was usually kept damp to aid the weaving of the cotton.
Various flavoured aromatic and savoury substances, such as herbs, salt etc, used to impart flavour to food.
A knife used to rub grease into a hide and to force dirt out of it. The knife is symmetrical with a handle at each end.
A hospital for the treatment of venereal disease.
A structure of wood, stone, iron, brick or concrete, etc, with one or more intervals under it to span a river or other space. Use specific type where known.
A hoist suspended from a girder within the roof of a building or workshop.
A structure consisting of combustible material, typically wood, on which a body is placed and then cremated, sometimes with accompanying grave goods. Use only when evidence of structure exists.
A mill for the processing of rice for use in food products.
A county judicial building where the Quarter Session and the Assizes for the County were held.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of food.

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A workshop in which textile fibres were spun into yarn by hand.
A mowing implement with a large curved blade and a long handle.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
Visual, descriptive and analytical record of a building, usually interior and exterior. Equivalent to Historic England Level 3.
Line, cord or thread, especially that used for tying up parcels, etc. Also use for "twine", i.e. twisted thread, for the same purpose, and medieval equivalents, e.g. "packthread".
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.
The second subdivision of the Bronze Age.
An underground, or partially underground, vault or crypt beneath a church or other building.
A surface made up of small pieces of hard material such as stone or tile, often in a decorative pattern.
An elevated table or podium on which to place, or sacrifice, offerings to a god or gods.
A secondary or incidental product of a process.
A building in which purified charcoal was produced by distillation of wood in sealed cast-iron retorts heated in fire-boxes. Tarry by-products were sometimes recovered by condensation flues.
A heavy substance, usually gravel, sand or lead, placed in the bilge of a ship or boat to provide stability.
A capital with a half figure projecting from each corner
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
Wooden boxes or cases for carrying fruit and other similar goods.
A site on which rigs, towers and other associated structures and buildings used for the testing of helicopters and helicopter parts are located.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of hunting.
A space in a Buddist building that is used for teaching Dharma/Dhamma - the teachings of Buddha.
A fortified river or river bank forming part of the anti invasion infrastructure.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A ring used in the marriage ceremony.
A place where coal is mined.
A turret, tower or look out occupying a prominent position to provide a view, either a separate building, or part of a villa.
A garden ornament, usually of stone or metal, designed in the the form of a vase used to receive the ashes of the dead.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.
A highly defensible gateway, usually of stone with two or more storeys, built into the defensive walls of a town or city.
A press in which the juice is extracted from grapes in the manufacture of wine.
An alloy, traditionally of tin and lead but now of tin, antimony and copper, used for domestic utensils.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
A free-standing building with enough space to hang and dry nets.
A pole projecting to the rear of a post mill to allow the sails to be moved into the wind.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
Smelting furnace into which compressed hot air is driven.
A building in which coal slurry, produced in the coal washing process, is recovered.
A building complex with hangars and slipways built adjacent to a body of water where seaplanes can be stored and maintained.
Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons
A part of a coffin that is removable eg handle, mount etc.
The area of the Basilica, especially in the early church, in which the altar resides.
A type of buddle used as an ore-cleaning device for seperating metallic ore from waste material by washing the dirty ore in a continuous flow of water.
Cob type construction typical to Buckinghamshire using a local clay with a high chalk content to produce walls of notable inherent stability.
A continuous series of ornaments within a horizontal moulding.
A designated area of land, usually closed to the public, used for military exercises and training purposes.
Room within a building or complex used by a porter.
A bishop's court for ecclesiastical causes and offences, formerly having wider jurisdiction in matters of moral discipline.
An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
Containers filled with high explosive, which can be fired from artillery pieces, thrown, dropped by aircraft or placed by hand and detonated in various ways.
A moulded bar or baton dividing the panes of glass within a window light.
A large stone used to grind grain or similar.
A detached fort covering a strategic point.
A workshop for printing textiles in a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.
A joint between two timbers meeting end to end.
A stone with a rectangular depression into which molten metal, usually tin, was poured to create ingots.
An enclosed furnace used for the continuous casting of plate glass.
An area of land, with associated buildings and targets, used for practicing the dropping of bombs and other aspects of air warfare.

The unplanned observation of archaeological features or the recovery of artefacts of interest, for example either random finds by members of the public or the unplanned observation of archaeological features during the course of unmonitored developments.
A plant where freshly mined coal was washed down and any dust removed before loading for transport away from the colliery.
An enclosed area, often surrounded by walls or buildings.
A place where military personnel parade, practice marching, assemble or muster for a march or any other special purpose.
An iron striking plate used to create sparks to ignite a fire.
An observation tower is a structure used to provide panoramic views of the surrounding area. They are often used as attractions at seaside resorts e.g. Blackpool Tower.
A stone or platform on which lumps of ore are manually broken up.
A place where the game of skittles is played.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A vertical timber resting on a hammer beam and forming a triangle between it and a principal.
Fish of the Salmonidae family, caught for food.
Cottage provided for guests to a country house.
A piece of military ordnance, of sufficient size to require mounting and used for firing projectiles, traditionally cannon balls but more recently high explosive shells.
A stepped, roadside platform, usually of stone on which a sedan chair was placed to allow the porters to lift the chair without having to bend.

Defined as species present after the last glaciation e.g. oak, ash, elm, beech, birch, alder, hazel, hornbeam etc. Specify in Description whether currently managed, unmanaged, or management not determined.
A type of light fixture affixed to a wall in such a way that it uses only the wall for support, and the light is usually directed upwards.
A barn with steam powered threshing.
A site for the storage, preparation and launching of missiles.
A craft of uncertain function over 30 metres long.
A decorated beam, above the dais or high table, attached to the partition at the upper end of a hall.
A stone that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
A bottle for the confinement of evil spirits.

Plain clay tile suspended, loose, from the top edge of a tiling lath or batten so as to overlap two courses below. It is held in place by a small wooden peg wedged into, or passed through, one (or sometimes both) of two holes in the head of the tile.
A Neolithic monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by frequent causeways, and often accompanied by an internal bank, also causewayed.
A pavilion used for exhibitions, e.g. the exhibition pavilions at the Great Empire Exhibition, Wembley, 1925.

All physical evidence for a monument has certainly been completely destroyed (allowing no future reinvestigation) by activity implying substantial ground disturbance. Eg quarrying, road cutting, or natural disaster, erosion, acts of God etc.
A stone (including standing stones, natural boulders and rock outcrops) decorated with carved motifs.
A sheet of glass coated in a light sensitive substance on which a photgraphic image can be developed.
Circular enclosure featuring an enclosing bank with no accompanying ditch. Use specific type where known.
A container for a pyx which is often a canopied niche in a wall.
A covered gateway, at the entrance to a churchyard, where during a funeral a coffin could be set down until the vicar arrived.
A stone found on route to a churchyard on which the coffin is rested during transportation.
A building to house waterwheels, attached to a WATERMILL or water-powered factory.
A container for holding or pouring liquids, usually having a handle or lip.
A curved blade used by the Romans and Greeks to scrape the body after bathing.
A large, vertical revolving wheel with passenger cars or pods on the periphery used to give a bird's eye view of the surrounding area.
An observation post used by members of the Home Guard.
A buttress placed at the exterior corner of a building, forming a 135 degree angle with the walls it supports.
A machine used for spinning cotton powered by water.
Pipes manufactured from iron and used for a variety of purposes.
Collective name, in a true geological sense, for a metamorphosed limestone eg. Carrara marble. In British sense, any decorative stone that will take a polish, eg. Purbeck marble.
Isla Grande De Tierra Del Fuego
A training college for chefs and other catering students.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.

An institution for the imprisonment of prisoners who can be trusted to serve their sentence without likelihood of escape and of being a threat to the public. There is no physical barrier designed to prevent absconding.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.
An opening in the ridge of a roof intended to provide ventilation or an outlet for smoke; also the hood on such an opening that prevents rain entering.
A head covering, usually with a brim.
A machine consisting of a continuously moving band of fabric, rubber, or metal used for transporting people or objects from one place to another.
A bowl-shaped cavity or depression created in the subsoil by the long term presence and growth of tree roots or when a large tree is blown over or has its stump pulled out.
A tool with one or more serrated edges.
Establishments responsible for the research into and the design, development and manufacture of chemical weapons
A garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of deceased infants are scattered or buried.

Monument either never or no longer visible above ground surface, but whose presence is indicated by proven below ground stratigraphy revealed by deliberate investigation, including geophysical survey, or other surface disturbance.
That portion of the Atlantic Ocean which stretches from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the Equator.
An office or central station of a local telephone system where the various lines are brought to a central switchboard and communication between subscribers is achieved.
Originally partially covered baths shaped somewhat like a slipper, now usually a number of single baths of the modern domestic style installed for hire at public baths.
A vessel, purpose-built or requisitioned, used for patrolling inland or coastal waters, e.g. Coastguard and Customs vessels.
A site where slate is quarried from the ground.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.
An instrument used for surgery, which is the treatment of injuries by instruments and manually.
Large warship equipped with turret mounted guns. Intended for independent action for trade protection, reconaissance and fire support for amphibious operations.
Any of the pieces of hard tissue consisting largely of calcium phosphate that make up the skeleton of a vertebrate animal.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.

A collared urn with a heavy rim or collar on top of a concave neck or cavetto zone, which may or may not be decorated, and this in turn leads down to a straight-sided but narrowing body. Decoration may extend below this cavetto zone, but this is rare.
An object used to burn incense in.
A type of fabric often used to trim clothing.
Buildings incorporating a high degree of protection against damp for the bulk storage of salt.
A conduit or pipes, used primarily for conveying petroleum from oil wells to a refinery, or for supplying water to a town or district, etc.
A place of worship for followers of the Pentecost (ie. emphasising the gifts of the Holy Spirit).

Although local heritage lists have long been developed successfully for buildings, all
heritage asset types, including monuments, sites, places, areas, parks, gardens and
designed landscapes may be considered for inclusion.
Aerial photography using infrared sensitive film or sensors to reveal soil and vegetation characteristics not apparent in photographs derived from conventional aerial photography.
A centre used by the Air Raid Precautions network to co-ordinate reports of air raids in an area.
A substantial monument attached to a wall and often standing on the floor.
Development relating to the construction of a new railway, or associated sidings, depots etc, or modification to existing railway.
A place where meat is displayed for sale.
Use type of instrument where known.
A piece of material, usually glass, which has been ground into shape to enhance vision or protect the eyes.
A cereal of the genus Triticum, which can be ground to manufacture flour for bread and pasta.
The cutting part of an auger.
An underground cell, usually hidden and accessed only through a trapdoor, in which a prisoner was confined and then allegedly forgotten about.
A container, usually round and deep.
A fixed object to sit upon. Use narrower terms where known.
A tool with a handle and curved blade designed to cut through grass sods.
Use for Insectivores (hedgehogs, shrews, moles), Chiroptera (bats) and rodents (squirrels, rats, voles, mice, dormice).
Fixed instrument to measure altitude of stars and planets.
A pin or bolt, especially one on which some other object turns.

The assessment of the age of a hedge based on its nature, condition and the number and type of woody plant species present. Most surveys make use of Hooper's hypothesis which states that for every 27m a new woody species invades a hedge every 100 years.
A turf-covered mound in a curvilinear E-shape, and hard-standing to take an aircraft. There were usually an access point to an air raid shelter at the rear. In use during WW2

Source from which stone utilized for the manufacture of non-flint artefacts, including axes, was obtained. Applied only to sources exploited during the Neolithic and earlier Bronze Age. Do not use for flint mining or knapping sites.
A hook to join parts of clothing together.
A tool used to hit fabric, eg to remove dust or dirt.
A stall, often within a cow house, where cattle are kept individually.
A brush used to disentangle hair.
A port situated on a river, often associated with a town or overland goods transport facilities.
A preparation made from the evaporated juice of the rhizome of the plant Glycyrrhiza glabra, used medicinally and as a sweet, usually in the form of a black, chewy substance.
A concave groove or series of grooves.
A decorative form consisting of two upright S-shaped curves positioned opposite one another with their concave sections placed at the top.
A beam steam engine, reciprocating or rotative, powered by two steam cylinders side by side.
A barrier, usually in the form of a small wall, set to prevent people falling over the side of a bridge, balcony, roof etc.
A triangular gable usually above an entablature.
A winding walk, common in early 18th century Rococo gardens and parks.

Some damage or part destruction of features of interest apparent, or the features of interest are obscured by more recent additions/alterations. For buildings, indicates structurally sound, but in need of minor repair.
A device with a funnel-shaped entrance designed for catching eels.
Distinctive clerestory-roofed building, used for the drying and storage of military parachutes.

A place of worship for members of the New Connexion of General Baptists,an orthodox Baptist church which broke away from the General Baptists in 1770 when the latter became influenced by Unitarianism.
A short beam that projects into a roof space from the foot of a principal rafter to receive a hammer post and, often, an arched brace.
Items made from cloth, wool etc used as a covering for the human body.
Dung or compost, carried either as an export cargo or as waste to be dumped out at sea.
A garden or collection of potted plants on the flat roof of a house or other building.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A building used to house peacocks.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.
Instruments for measuring and displaying time. Often manufactured as a piece of furniture e.g.a grandfather clock.
A small merchant ship or warship with concealed weapons, intended as a trap for enemy submarines.
A sedimentary rock primarily composed of silt sized particles.
A hollow case containg explosive, incendiary, smoke-producing, poisonous or other offensive material, designed to be deposited, dropped, thrown or shot froma mortar.
An opening or cavity through which a stream or natural watercourse disappears underground.
A fortified structure used to protect civilians and military personnel from enemy bombing.
Metal knives, forks and spoons, carried either as an export cargo or for crew and/or passengers.
A large building used for the accommodation of paying travellers and guests.
Also use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A resource which requires interaction from the user to be understood, executed, or experienced.  [DC]
Buoys used to direct craft on water along the correct route or away from a hazard. Usually used in coastal areas.
Container with a handle, spout and narrow neck.
The seed of the flax plant pressed into cakes and used as cattle fodder.
One of a series of chapels which project symmetrically from an apse or ambulatory at the east end of a church.
An area of a building or complex specifically housing the kitchens, sculleries and services.
A hinge composed of two parts: a u-shaped hinge attached to a door which slotted over an L-shaped staple in the door jamb.
A building in which cordite dough is stored before extrusion.
A covered way or passage especially in a cathedral or monastic church, leading east from the cloisters between transept and chapter house.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
Receptacles, including boxes, barrels etc., designed to contain something.

A stone core which is irregular in shape. It can have numerous usuable or abandoned striking platforms. It is the most common core type and it is often the last attempt of a knapper to extract the final usable flakes form the core. (Source: SARC)
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions, generally created by chipping or pecking.
A bracket that is shaped to form an angle.
A bell worn by a cow to identify its location.
A necklace holding charms or being itself a charm.
Stones used to edge a pavement or raised path.
An ornament made of thin plates of gold or silver, with repousse ornament.
A piece of ground on which athletes race.
A waterwheel where the water enters at the same level as the axle.
A bobbin where thread is wound around it, used for example in spinning and weaving
A flat bottomed boat or hollow float of which a number are used to support a temporary bridge over a river.
A priest's private entrance into a church, usually found on the south side of the chancel.
A flat bottomed ditch flanked by mounds running to the south of Hadrian's Wall for much of its length, marking the boundary of the military zone.
Removal of samples from insitu deposits for dating analysis by studying the remnant magnetism contained within the deposit.
A North country memorial imitating a wattled hut decorated with formalized bears or snakes.
A smooth, flammable liquid, produced naturally or from plants or animals, and used for a variety of purposes.
An expansion period stand by set house designed to drawing number 974/35 and containing a single generator set and switch board. Constructed with brick cavity walls.
A moveable covering, usually to a window, made up of a frame containing slats set at an angle. Allows air to circulate but limits light entering.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of patients suffering from epilepsy. Originally epilepsy was seen as a mental illness.
100 links, 4 rods or  1⁄10 of a furlong. The distance between the two wickets on a cricket pitch.
A bowl whose form resembles two cones joined together at their widest points, forming a carination.
A Very High Frequency device to allow aircraft to pinpoint their position as an aid to naviagation. Built as part of the Rotor programme.

A place of worship for Presbyterians, a movement who started off attempting to reform Anglicanism before breaking away in 1660. Sometimes referred to as moderate puritans, they joined with the Congregationalists to form the United Reformed church in 1972.

An underwater technique used to create 3D terrain models and to record objects on the seabed through the comparative analysis of reflections from high frequency sound waves emitted in multiple beams allowing large swathes of the seabed to be surveyed.
Small 'drops' or conic projections under the mutules (a repeating block motif) and triglyphs (rectangular blocks embellished with vertical grooves) in a Doric entablature.
A tool for scooping loose substances, usually with a handle and a curved blade partially covered at the handle end.
Controlled investigation, recording and removal of archaeological deposits under threat of destruction from building development. A pre PPG 16 activity, usually under strict time constraints.

Baggage, plate, money, clothes and other personal belongings of all kinds. Use only where the vessel is a cargo vessel conveying the goods of a person of consequence, e.g. a noble or diplomat, rather than for a general passenger vessel.
A textile mill where felt is produced.

Any animal other than livestock (animals carried as food); animals used for transport (horses; mules); and domestic pets. Such animals may be exported as specimens, for zoos, menageries, and circuses, or as unusual pets (e.g. elephants, monkeys).
A wood or metal dowel for joining objects together eg for securing roofing slates.
A decorative fitting of mid to late 11th century date, exclusively of copper alloy, and mostly zoomorphic. Arranged in pairs, on each stirrup either side of the footplate.
Living quarters for animals, birds, etc, as pets or for observation, entertainment, etc.
A sliding metal bar, often fixed to a door or similar, which moves through staples so that its end fixes into another staple or hole which is attached to a fixed object, eg a door frame.
Wax used to seal letters, envelopes, documents, etc.
A building plan consisting of three rooms placed in a straight row.
Particulars of a property for sale.
A building used by an association of persons for social and recreational purposes or for the promotion of some common object.
A way between different places, used by horses, travellers on foot and vehicles.
A dockside crane with a solid curving jib made out of rivetted iron plates.
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of  the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
A hospital department where heat, light, sound, electricity, etc, is administered to patients suffering from muscular or skeletal disorders.
An object used in the lighting of an area.
A grave marker in the form of a casket.
Production of steel by reheating wrought iron in charcoal filled containers.
A type of steam engine in which the steam cylinders are placed above the crankshaft supported on a robust frame.
Photographic transparency mounted for use in projection equipment.
The residence of a dock worker.
A plan type, usually for a church, having a rectangular core with one apsidal end wall.
Bordering the continents of Africa, Antarctica, Asia and Australasia, the Indian Ocean covers 28,364,000 square miles.
A lock or a dam in a river.
A ditch associated with a palisade.

A bronze axehead of middle or late Bronze Age date in which the side flanges and the bar/stop on both faces are connected, forming a single hafting aid. For palstaves with side loops use looped palstave.
A usually temporary earthwork or fortification, the latter constructed by military forces operating in the field. Use more specific type where known.
A body which has been interred in boggy or marshy ground or other similarly waterlogged environment. Interment may have been deliberate or accidental.

A monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by several causeways, surrounding a central circular area used for funerary activities, often concealed originally beneath an earthen mound. Index with barrow type where known.
Old ship converted to a floating coal store.

A railway, usually by the sea, linking the beach with the cliff top. Various mechanisms were used the most common being that the cars were attached to a cable and winding drum and were balanced so that one travelled up, as the other came down.
An inhumation burial in which the body is covered by a shroud, placed in a coffin of stone, wood or lead and covered with gypsum, plaster or lime. Roman and early Medieval.
Use for vessels registered in China.
Sedimentary rock consisting mainly of calcium carbonate. Varying in grain size, colour and hardness, quarried and used throughout the country.
A place where ropes are made.

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
A site where tin ore is extracted from suspended fire waste in tin mine spoil heaps.
An artificial stretch of water, usually rectangular in shape, used decoratively, particularly in formal gardens, eg. Long Water, Hampton Court. Occasionally used to supply water to cascades.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land, both natural & man-made, which cannot be assigned to a particular class (for example, railings).
A signal station incorporating equipment for visually conveying coded communications.
A man made terrace, often constructed in concrete, built to allow spectators a view of organized outdoor events or activities.
A circular building for housing and repairing railway locomotives.
A type of spur with the goad in the form of a rotating disc.
A bowl used to contain and burn incense.
Compact grained, brown/yellow/green/grey blue, coloured liassic limestone.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
A knife that is used for circumcision.
A venue, with a boxing ring and associated facilities, which is used to train for and undertake amateur or professional boxing.
A passage constructed within the thickness of a wall.
A slab of stone, either standing or recumbent, inscribed with a cross. Usually found in association with burials.
A folding circular cover on a stick held in the hand for protection against rain.
Pieces of metal money usually small in size and circular in design. Manufacture from a variety of metals including gold and silver but more recently manufactured from base metals and alloys.
One of a pack, or deck, of cards used to play games, each distinguished from the others by markings on its face.
An ornamental bracket on either side of a doorway supporting a cornice.
A pumping station for draining a mine or colliery.
A treadwheel using a donkey as motive power. Usually found operating wells.
Pairs of canal gates (also called Brindley gates) designed to rapidly shut off  a section of a canal to prevent flooding
Building for testing the condition and strength of textiles.
A place where domestic refuse is collected for disposal.
A wooden rod passed through a spindle whorl. Used to handspin fibre.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of stones. Use more precise term where known.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of fuel.

Raid or assault by ships upon a terrestrial location, typically a settlement or town, which may involve a terrestrial incursion and damage to buildings and/or capture of people. It is distinct from a battle or naval skirmish.
Mark 12 or the twelfth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A trench, usually linking two or more rows of trenches, enabling the conveyance of messages or equipment safely from one trench to another.
A telegraph pole, tree trunk or similar erected on the side of a road, or in an open space, to prevent the landing of hostile aircraft
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
Meat precooked and then sealed in cans made from steel, tin or aluminium plate to preserve it.
A vessel used for inspecting vessels entering port during wartime.
Includes bleaching, dressing, dyeing and printing.
Hollow cylinders or tubes of ceramic, wood, plastic or metal used to convey liquids, gases etc. Used in a variety of industries.

A site, usually with an airfield, hangars and control buildings, used for the storage and deployment of military aircraft or the administration of the Royal Air Force. May also include accommodation buildings for personnel.
A building for miners to change their clothes.
A building used for the storage of rope made from the fibrous stems of the hemp plant.
Use only for historic state of Czechoslovakia, where new state is known index with CZECH REPUBLIC or SLOVAKIA.
Small furnace, used to create an upward draught of air in mine workings.
Fixed equipment, such as slides, swings and climbing frames for children to play on. Often found in playgrounds, parks and school grounds.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
An inclined plane built to allow tanks to be loaded and unloaded between rolling stock on the railway network and vehicular low loaders.
A building or complex where soft skins are produced by tanning with alum.
A garden seat covered in clipped, camomile plants which release a fragrant smell when sat upon.
Piece of work to test eventual pattern, sometimes small and used as a demonstration of crafter's skill.
City Of London Coal Duties Boundary Marker
The seed of a cereal plant used in the manufacture of foodstuffs.
A horse-powered apparatus, for the crushing of commodities such as ore or cider apples, consisting of a stone wheel running over a circular iron or stone bed.
A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of soft drinks.
A decorative moulding cosisting of two ogee-forms with joined faces.
A designation under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 that encompass the remains of a military aircraft or a vessel sunk or stranded in military service within the last two hundred years.
A sheet of flat film, 105 x 148mm in size, carrying a matrix of micro images.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to plasterwork whilst the plaster is still damp.

A short, tapered, vertical stone supporting a rough stone disc so resembling a toadstool, often forming one of several uprights on which a timber structure, such as a granary  rests, protecting the building from damp and vermin.
Prior to 1822 a vessel used by the customs department involved with the prevention of smuggling.
Corrosive, dense, oily acid, usually in aqueous solution, used in the chemical industry.
A path running by the side of a canal or navigable river for use in towing vessels.
Art applied in pigment to rock wether in the form of a free-standing stone or the walls of a cave.
A natural flow or current of water issuing from a source.
A site used for the separation of oil into its constituent parts by heating in an enclosed vessel(s).

Accommodation given rent-free along with or as part of a corrody, which is a provision of an annual allowance of food and money by a religious house to an individual, usually in return for service or by purchase. Term used until mid 16th century AD.
Loss of a vessel or aircraft through accidental contact with another or a structure. Do not use when contact is with natural feature or rocky shore.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.
A room or cupboard usually used for the storage of garments.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine monks.
All linen used at the table, including tablecloths.
An oblong mass of hardened clay or mud, used in building.
A room or a building set aside for infants and young children.
A fine, soft fibre produced by silkworms and used to make thread for textiles. Also the cloth made from this thread.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A prefrabicated home sited in parks where a pitch fee is charged. Although technically mobile they usually only make one journey before being permanently installed.
An area where the sport of wrestling takes place.
A place where railway trains regularly stop for taking up and setting down passengers or for receiving goods for transport.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
Glass that has been coloured by fusing glass with a metallic oxide film or by burning pigment into the surface.
A garden specifically planted with sweet smelling, fragrant plants.
A large container for holding or storing liquids.
A building or complex in which visitors to a prison can meet with the inmates under the supervision of the prison staff.
A building used for the collection and storage of electricity using large lead-acid batteries (accumulators).
A vessel used to put down and pick up moorings on the sea bed for large vessels.
A building where civilians are enlisted to join the military forces.
A burial site for an animal, usually commemorated by a gravestone or other structure.
An excavation from which stone for building is obtained by cutting, blasting etc.
A steam engine in which the pistons are long relative to their diameters, and there are no piston rods and crossheads.
A four-armed metal coupling, positioned at the centre of a windmill's sails,  connected to the front of the striking rod and the shutter bars of all the sails, causing the shutters to open and close.
A Roman Bow Brooch dating from the mid-second to mid-third centuries AD, characterized by the pronounced curvature of the bow, resembling a knee. Usually used by military personnel.
A container in which needles are held.
A nodule of iron pyrites used to create fire in combination with tinder and flint or another nodule of iron pyrites.
One of a pair of large circular stones used for grinding corn in a mill.
A prepared area of ground used to play the game of golf on.
An engine in which the power is provided by electricity either in the form of batteries or direct from the mains supply.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to the surface of a ceiling.
A building with a regulated moderate temperature for the cultivation of plants.
Items of crockery and cutlery which are used whilst dining, either to eat with or for table decoration.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
A range of techniques that use the build up of charge stored within a crystalline material to estimate its age
A furnace for holding hot steel ingots to equalize their temperature before they are hot-rolled in a steel-making or rolling mill complex.
A small hut erected over a mine shaft.
A moulding on a flat or vaulted ceiling, suggesting a structure or forming a pattern derived from vaulting..
A building owned by a constituency political party which provides a meeting place for local political activities and also provides entertainment facilities for its members and guests.
A reinforced concrete block designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Use more specific type where known.
A lawn planted with camomile plants which when walked upon release a fragrant smell.
A shallow, ornamental recess, often arched and semicircular in plan, set in a wall or pier and usually containing a statue or ornament.
An alcoholic drink made by the fermentation of malt and flavoured with hops or other bitters.
An all timber constructed watch office with meterological section. Similar in design to 2328/39 and 5845/39. There were only two known examples built in the UK at Wick and St.Eval.
Timber framed construction where a box of horizontal and vertical members is created to support the roof.
A workshop in which products are made using wood and timber.
An object consisting of a vertical member with a transverse member. Usually there is a religious or ritual significance to such an object.
Equipment used to sharpen other objects.
The top of a cornice in an entablature.

A building within a gunpowder works complex, where the mill cake (pulverised and incorporated ingredients of gunpowder) was broken down. It was crushed or broken down by passing it between pairs of revolving gunmetal rollers in a breaking-down machine.

All features of interest are damaged beyond use for survey purposes or are missing. For buildings, this indicates structural failure or evident instability, loss of significant areas of roofing, or a major fire or other disaster.
The stem of the plant Zingiber officinale, with a characterisitc hot and peppery taste, used in cookery and medicine.

Damage to the majority or all of the features of interest is apparent, or significant features of interest are missing. Some features of interest remain. Active damage apparent (e.g. for buildings water penentration, rot etc).
A metal, shankless bit, with a ring on either side used to control an animal (usually a horse) by exerting direct pressure on the  tongue, lips and the side of the mouth.

A unit of weight in the avoirdupois system equal to 2,240 pounds (1,016.05 kg) in Britain (the long ton) and 2,000 pounds (907.18 kg) in the United States (the short ton). 
As a unit of volume it is equivalent to 100 cubic feet (the register ton) or 40 cubic feet (the freight or measurement ton)
A decorated, hanging sign, bearing the name and also often a pictorial representation of the inn or public house to which it is attached.
Remains of wheat (Triticum sp.) grain (caryopyses). These grains are sometimes itemised separately.
Coastal base for the docking, launch and maintenance of submarines.
A room usually set aside for the provision of materials used in a household.
A power driven machine or device for raising a liquid or forcing it along a pipe, or for compressing a gas.
A reversible device for measuring time by the transfer of sand from upper to lower glass bulb.
Includes all forms of paper and any products manufactured from it.
A type of Roman lodging house, frequently sited near the town gate.
A building or site used for the manufacture of whiting either from crushed chalk, limestone, marble or through chemical preparation.
Internal combustion engine powered by diesel fuel.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.

Building block (often a temporary brick structure or Nissen hut) comprising office accommodation for flight commanders and flight sergeants as well as pilots' rest rooms, storerooms and locker rooms. Some flight offices have central corridors.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).
A motor vehicle designed to transport cargo.
The staff or crook of a bishop or abbot.
A tippler, a machine for loading wagons at a pithead, operated by hydraulic power.
Substances, either natural or man-made, used to make soil more fertile.
A building where beer was sold or displayed.
An apparatus worked by hand or mechanically for weaving yarn into textile.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the control, accommodation, service and testing of aircraft.
Vehicle either adapted, or purpose-built, to operate on both land and sea, for example a tank or DUKW.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic lead.
A medicinal or mineral spring often with an associated building.
A turbine driven by gas flow or the gas from combustion.
Layer of grass with earth and matted roots cut from the ground and used for earth buildings and as a covering material.
A stone-lined pit or tank, sometimes circular,  for concentrating ores by sedimentation.
Hard, coarse grained, grey to red/brown coloured granite. Used predominantly for tombstones becasuse of its ability to take a polish, but it is also in demand for underwater construction.
Narrow necked containers, originally of leather but now usually made of glass or plastic. Used for storing liquids.
A sweet, crystalline subtance obtained from sugar beet or sugar cane and used in cooking, brewing etc.

This term is appropriate to official notifications of a monument or area whether they are statutory or purely advisory. Where possible the specific document type should be indexed for example Scheduled Monument Notification.
An often light and airy garden building in the Moorish style used for recreational purposes.
Buildings and structures used for sending and receiving signals.
The stalks of cereals separated from the grain br threshing and used as fodder, basket manufacture, thatch etc.
A wall used in the game of handball.
Horizontal masonry or timber work at the entrance to a dock.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a trapezoid and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A strong container, usually metal, secured for storing money or valuables.
Monument with a roof and walls or evidence of these.
Medium grained, hard, white/grey coloured stone consisting of quartz and often silica, produced by the metamorphosis of sandstone.
A university or college building set apart for residence or instruction of students. They can be located either on or off campus.
A pond used for dissipating heat by evaporation from steam engine condensate. Mid 19th century to mid 20th century.
Large granite stone used as the base stone of a stamping mill against which ore was crushed. Contains distinctive striations from the crushing process.
Decorative ornamentation worn in the hair.
A small shaped container designed to bathe the eye.
A school where theological subjects are taught.
A long, slender, flexible tube for inserting into a body cavity for the introduction or withdrawal of fluids.
A pipe allowing the passage of water through it and designed only for this.
A small cargo craft, usually with two masts and a lateen rig.
A form of tandem compounding of early beam engines, with a high pressure steam cylinder mounted on top of a low pressure one, introduced in Cornwall the 1840s by James Sims.
A jar with a profile that slopes inwards from base to rim. Particularly shallow examples have been term Peat Pots; this is a term with a restricted distribution in northern England. (Source: MPRG)
A battery equipped and ready to fire salutes
Non-military maritime flood and erosion defences.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of football.
An area of land used for producing renewable energy, which can comprise a solar farm, wind turbines or biomass facility
A school for the teaching of poor children, often the recipients of Poor Law relief.
An instrument to remove the seeds from flax.

Recording using specialist equipment that allows discrete wavelengths in the visible spectrum and beyond to be recorded. The combination of different spectral bands allows features to be identified that would not be visible to the naked eye.
A building situated next to a horse racing course with facilities for participants and spectators.

A maritime investigation that records depth data which can be used to map submerged topography utilising echo sounders which emit a short acoustic pulse. Depth is calculated by measuring the time taken for the pulse to be reflected back to the transducer.
The edible tubers of plants of the family Ipomoea Batatas eaten as a vegetable.
A room where a committee meets to discuss matters put before them.
An institution for the imprisonment of military personnel convicted under military law by a military court.
A kiln used to reduce the shells of shellfish to calcium carbonate.
A type of helmet with a hinged visor.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of sailing. Often situated by a MARINA.

The light emitted from sedimentary minerals or mineral inclusions in bricks when stimulated in the laboratory by light of a different wavelength. Used to date samples up to 250,000 years old; especially appropriate for geological sediments.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
A piece of ground used for motor racing.
A water-drain connected to a stone bowl within a niche in the south wall of a chapel, used to receive  the water in which the priest washed his hands and rinsed the Chalice.
A piece of cast metal obtained from a mould in a form suitable for storage.

Dutch coaster of the late 17th to late 19th centuries with a square hull and 2 masts, generally having a heavy keel and round stern and bilges, although later examples were built on more refined lines.
Machinery and parts for the manufacture or assembly of military tanks, i.e. armoured vehicles.
A circular or sub circular brooch with an attached pin. There is a gap in the circular part of the brooch.
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
A photograph taken from the air.
No longer used. Traditionally use for resources that could only be identified to a date range from Neolithic to Iron Age. Included here to aid migration.
A hall in a village used for meetings and other functions.
A vault used for the storage of cider.
An institution for convicted prisoners held under a regime which strove to reform by means of silent isolation and labour.

An artifically constructed wall with recessed and projecting grips for hands and feet and places to attach ropes. Used for practising rock climbing. If the wall is a free-standing external structure use term for the Thesaurus of Monument Types.
Normally an unpowered vessel, moored in places where the construction of a lighthouse is impractical.
Use for vessels registered in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
A building or complex where corks and stoppers are made for use in bottling.
Manufactured goods, including shells, dynamite etc., containing substances which can be made to explode.
The bracket under a jetty bressumer.
A natural compound used as in the building and medical industies.
17th century Dutch vessel built for naval or East India service, with a relatively flat bottom and narrow hull; sometimes rendered into English as `fly-boat'.
A narrow aisle that pierces an internal buttress.
A vessel used to transport bombs and depth charges from the shore to flying boats during the Second World War.
An open space or area, usually square in plan, in a town or city, enclosed by residential and/or commercial buildings, frequently containing a garden or laid out with trees.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A tool of flint or other stone, usually worked bifacially, and thought to be a fairly general purpose tool.
Celebrates worship of the Hindu goddess Durga.
The lowest part, or base, of a structure, sometimes built into the ground, on which the weight of the whole rests.
Use for the remains of any part of a human.
A boat fashioned out of a section of tree trunk.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.
A flint tool for piercing holes.
Use for vessels registered in the Faroe (also spelt Faeroe) Islands, e.g. at Torshavn

A circular pillbox designed by the Engineering and Metals Company using 'Armco' corrugated iron sheets as the inner and outer skins into which concrete was poured, giving a 12in wall thickness. The design was taken up by DFW and assigned a drawing number.
One of a pair of posts, placed symmetrically on a tie beam,  supporting a collar purlin or plate.
A hooked blade used to cut crops. All the blade is to one side of the handle rather than being on both sides as in a sickle.
A casement  window, carried down to floor level, and opening like two-leafed glazed doors to a garden, veranda or terrace.
Planks or boards manufactured from softwood timber.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
A small house in which leeches were bred for medical purposes.
A panel, usually wooden or stone, painted or engraved with an illustration or inscription.
Photographic plate, on glass, developed using a wet process.
A building housing a gas engine, used as a power source for driving other machinery.
A thin timber, usually sloping on both sides, fixed to the floor between the jambs of a doorway.
A purpose-built, or modified, building where organizations and associations meet for presentations and consultation.
Equipment used in the production of textiles.
A hospital where more 'natural' means of treatment are used rather than conventional methods.
A room in a library or institution providing periodicals, newspapers, etc.
A sculptured, carved or moulded representation of an imaginary creature with a human head and breast combined with the body of a lion.
Term used by the RAF to describe an open walled structure built of concrete, brick or sandbags which enclosed one or more machine-guns mounted on pintels for light anti-aircraft and ground defence.
A place where saltpetre, the chief component of gunpowder, is kept.
Oil used to lubricate moving parts, particularly in machinery.
The storage of material (text, images, files etc) in an electromagnetic format.
The plant, Allium cepa, whose bulb is used, usually for culinary purposes.
An Ionic base with a lower disc with horizontal fluting or reeding, above which is a torus, also reeded.
A school used by the children of settlers at a Chartist Colony.
An internal combustion engine powered by the combustion of vapourized oil.
An open floor surface for dancing.
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.
A building for the housing of trams.

The extraction of wood samples for dating analysis. Tree ring dating is the science of dating cultural and environmental events in the past by comparative study of the growth rings in trees and aged wood.
A hall normally reserved for holding feasts on special occasions.
A concealed passage or room for the purpose of hiding and protecting a (Roman Catholic) priest during times of religious persecution.
A device for catching eagles, falcons and hawks.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the farming of fish.
An educational establishment where the art of garden cultivation is taught.
A container to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A site used for the manufacturing of steel. Use more specific type where known.
A hall built for the use of people living within a parish boundary.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief, made by chiselling stone, carving wood, modelling clay, casting metal, or similar processes.
A room with special ventilation used for the slow drying of foodstuffs.
Stone used to line a furnace or oven.
An aeroplane with two wings, or planes, placed one above the other either side of the fuselage.
A signal usually mounted on a gantry, be it mechanical or electronic, to provide guidance to traindrivers on access to sections of track.
A factory where flour was produced for use in food products.
A horizontal iron bar set in a window opening to which a leaded light is fixed.
A semicircular niche or recess in a wall.
A place, where a corpse could be laid whilst being carried on its way to a burial, to allow the bearers to rest.
A shop where fish is sold.
A building in which a society or organization is instituted to promote science, art, literature, education, etc. Use more specific type where known.

Any building or site in which silver was refined and/or extracted by smelting, cupellation, liquation or by the Parkes Process. IA-C20. Don't use for lead or copper smelters at which silver has been extracted unless silver-related features survive.
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
A mineral, Sodium Chloride, obtained by mining or the evaporation of brine used as a seasoning and for preserving food.
A power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 1380/24.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.
A ring with separated, often ornamented, terminals.
A render including an aggregate of gravel or stone chipping thrown rather than trowelled onto an external wall.
The place where metallic ores were crushed and washed to remove waste, forming a concentrate which could be used in a smelter.
A place where two or more railway lines meet.
Machinery and equipment used in the manufacture of aircraft.
A flat, horizontal strip, block or moulding, sometimes decorated, on a facade or interrupting an architectural feature such as a column.

Usually dating from the early 20th century these cabinets, sited alongside public highways, were used for the distribution of electricity for street lighting control and later for domestic use. In Wolverhampton these boxes also serviced the tram system.
An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Auxiliary Units to relay information gained from the various out-stations back to headquarters.
A channel, usually placed upstream of a mill, that carries water from a river or other water source to a waterwheel.
Dried seedless grapes used in cookery.
A formal garden consisting of lawns, walks and borders belonging to a college or university, eg. Oxford or Cambridge.
A fixed seat, often enclosed, usually found within an ecclesiastical building and frequently arranged in series to accommodate a congregation, choir or clergy.
An inclined plane with a cradle designed to lift a ship from the water onto a slip.
A machine for cleansing flax, hemp or cotton and forming the fibres into a continuous wide lap or sheet in preparation for carding.
An alcoholic drink made from fermented grape juice (or occasionally other fruits).
Fat from an animal used to lubricate objects.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders and diseases.
A sour tasting liquid, produced from wine and other liquors, used as a preservative, in pickling, or as a flavouring for food.
A graduated vessel or instrument for gauging or measuring the force or quantity of a fluctuating object, such as rainfall, tide, wind etc.
A shaft or pit dug in the ground over a supply of spring-water.
A bowl with straight sides which turn outwards, forming an obtuse angle with the base, i.e. and inverted, truncated, conical shape. (Source: MPRG)
An engine in which the mechanical force of steam is made available as a motive power for driving machinery.
A garden that has been specifically created to be accessible to both disabled and non-disabled visitors. They may contain scented and edible plants and features designed to make sound etc.
A hospital department where surgical and medical dental treatment takes place.
A small, fast boat used for carrying orders between sailing vessels.
A ward for receiving new paupers upon entry to a workhouse. They had to remain there until checked by medical officer.
A road junction where two (or occasionally more) roads cross each other.
The blade or sharp-pointed head attached to the end of a spear's shaft.
Specialised fermenting vessel consisting of a two-storey system consisting of a shallow chamber approximately 2m high above which is a walled deck.
A temporary overnight camp enclosed by a shallow ditch and palisade, constructed by Roman troops on campaigns or manoeuvres.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A cube-shaped capital with its lower corners rounded to facilitate the transition from the circular shaft below to the square abacus it supports.
A field system with one prevailing axis of orientation, in which most field boundaries are either aligned with this axis or run at right angles to it.
A building where advice and aid appertaining to physical and economic wellbeing of disadvantaged members of a community are made available.
A building or group of buildings owned and operated by a governing body and often occupied by a government agency. Use specific type of building where known.
Moorings for a seaplane not part of a seaplane base.
A room, usually at ground level or below, housing the tank in which water is heated as part of a building's heating system.
A parallel or axial-flow reaction water turbine invented in France in 1843, in which water descends through fixed curved guide vanes which direct the flow sideways onto curved vanes on the runner.

A secure, bomb-proof, undergound complex designed to be used by the government in the event of a national emergency such as nuclear war. Usually equipped with communications equipment, emergency rations and water and air filtering plants.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of beer.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with health (for example, treatment of the sick) &/or social welfare (for example, alleviation of poverty), including all charitable foundations & all forms of state defined social welfare.

Calcium Oxide obtained by heating limestone in a kiln. Used as a constituent of modern mortar, or as slaked (non-hydraulic) lime in lime putty, daub, limewash and traditional lime plaster, mortar and renders.
A detached vertical structure acting as support to a superstructure. Where a pillar is a separate monument, use a monument type thesaurus.
Mechanism for turning around vehicles in a confined space.
A light, often suspended from a lamp-post, to illuminate a street or road.
Malleable metal used for roofing and for alloys such as bronze.
A plan featuring a doorless entry to a lobby in front of an axial chimney-stack.
Use for vessels registered in Spain.
A stone block set into a wall to support a truss or beam.
An ornamental shoulder piece, usually a badge of military office.
In Orthodox churches, the screen that divides off the sanctuary, usually decorated with sacred images (icons). (Source: Pevsner Glossary)
A part of an arch between the apex and the springer.
A single-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich (drawing number 4178/44). Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
A depot or warehouse for the storage, distribution and repair of shoe making machines.
A place where tobacco is made into cigarettes, cigars, etc.
A tool used to produce a polish on an object.
A craft available for public hire for short journeys.
A training ship to which boys who had committed petty crimes were sentenced for 4 to 5 years to be reformed and trained as sailors.
Scale drawing showing the horizontal extent, height and arrangement of an excavated layer or feature on an archaeological site.
An arch built by corbelling or cantilevering in from both sides with horizontal joints.
A small transportable hangar built by the Teesdie Bridge and Engineering Company. Mainly used on RNAS airfields for folding wing aircraft.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.
The white, fibrous substance surrounding the seeds of plants of the genus Gossypium, which can be spun and used in the manufacture of thread and cloth or used in its raw form as wadding or packing.
A building, often close to a churchyard, used for the entertainment of poor people on their wedding day.

Includes all stages of production process of textiles, eg. wool, cotton, linen, etc, and textile products. Use only for sites where there is evidence of textile manufacture but no specific monument type, otherwise use more specific term.
A volatile, colourless distillate of petroleum used as a solvent and paint thinner.
A fall of water. Use for artificial waterfalls if naturalistic in form, otherwise use CASCADE.
One of a pair of inclined struts that meet at the bottom to form a V shape.
A farm building in which cattle are housed before slaughter.
A line or track consisting of iron or steel rails, on which passenger carriages or goods wagons are moved, usually by a locomotive engine.
A stone used to cover a grave.

A two-storey, structure with a brick ground floor and a reinforced concrete upper floor with balcony and large windows to the watch office and control room. This became the most common building design for air traffic control in the Second World War.
A structure used for the secure storage of bicycles.
A necklace or armband made of metal.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A stone channel sunk into the ground, employed from the mid-19th century, to carry away gases produced during smelting.
A manmade chamber cut into a rockface.
A room or hall designed for an audience to listen and view, as in a theatre, concert hall, lecture hall etc..

Any unspecified items without utility or function and prized for personal or domestic decorative value. Examples might be unspecified metal objects from the Bronze Age or Victorian Staffordshire china dogs.
A building or site where bodies are burnt, and the ashes collected for burial or dispersal.
Ornamental garden building constructed within the branches of trees.
A device used in the production of hard cheeses that exerts pressure upon fresh curds in order to remove and drain away excess whey.
A large shed for the housing of aircraft, etc.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
Objects used to measure time, distance, weight, number or natural forces.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, often found on the promenade or pleasure pier at a seaside resort or at a site of scenic beauty.
An enclosing structure composed of bricks, stones or similar materials, laid in courses. Use specific type where known.
An indoor market used for the sale of antique goods.
A series of flat-topped structures, usually wooden or stone, on which a person places their feet when ascending or descending, facilitating movement from one level to another.
A two-piece Bow Brooch, derived from the Colchester Brooch, dating from the later first and second centuries AD and so called due to the decorative stud on the upper bow.
A toothed comb used to beat the weft against the cloth in weaving.
The central part of a road between the pavements or the verges.
A greenhouse for the growing of figs.
A small, pierced, often spherical or cylindrical, piece of glass, wood,etc, which may be strung together with others to form a necklace.
Part-decomposed vegetable matter formed under waterlogged conditions into a firm, brown deposit resembling soil. Used as a brick for infilling in timber framed walls.
A small, often of about two inches or less in length, version of the Long Brooch usually made of less expensive materials than other brooch types and frequently worn in pairs.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
Use for a craft powered by a rocket engine which uses stored rocket propellant mass for forming its high-speed propulsive jet  eg. Flying bombs
A burial ground for Nonconformists. Use more specific term where known.
A circular range of houses dating from the 18th century, eg. John Wood's Circus at Bath.
An anti-personnel device consisting of a 40 gallon fuel drum placed on top of an explosive charge and detonator. When detonated the barrel would explode sending burning fuel over the intended target.
A tool used to examine or explore a cavity eg surgically for exploring the depth and direction of wounds.
A concave moulding where the profile is a quarter of a circle.
A mill where china stone is grinded.
A tray on which an offering is made.
An ancient Egyptian gem cut in the shape of a scarab beetle and engraved with symbols on its flat side.
A house, enclosure or large cage for the keeping and breeding of birds.
A site available to the public for the pursuit of leisure and recreational activities.
A field and desk based assessment of heritage asset condition and vulnerability so that informed decisions can be made regarding how best to manage the resource.
A receptacle for spittle, usually used in a public place.
A short piece of track lying parallel to the main railway line enabling trains and trucks to pass one another. Sidings can also be used to park trains which are not in use.

An aircraft lifted by gas bags, containing hydrogen or helium, but propelled by engines. Also known as a dirigible balloon, firm and streamlined in shape and incapable of high speeds. Used extensively during World War One.
A gallery or platform within a place of worship housing the organ.
A large building used for the storage of leather goods or processed animal skins.
A structure in a garden used to house gardening implements, etc.
A place where people were put to death. Use narrower monument type where known.
Thick material, usually woven, used as a covering for the floor.
Penannular objects of late Bronze Age, usually gold and too small to be worn on arms.

Generally rectangular structure normally used for burial purposes, and formed from stone slabs set on edge, and covered by one or more horizontal slabs or capstones. Cists may be built on the surface or sunk into the ground.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
A long wooden shafted weapon tipped with a metal point.
A refreshment house in a public park or country house garden.
A staple foodstuff made with flour, water and usually yeast, which is kneaded and then baked. Can include unleavened (no yeast)  varieties.
A row of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
A secondary rib usually springing from the junction of two other ribs, or one that rises between a main diagonal and transverse rib, from the springing to the ridge rib.
A castle surrounded by two or more lines of walled fortifications.
A keystone decorated with a relief sculpture, usually a cartouche
Moving images made available through projection, video or other methods.
A small boat of wickerwork covered by a watertight material.

A sunken, circular, concrete pillbox used on airfields. They remained flush with the surface to permit the free movement of aircraft but, if attack threatened, could be raised hydraulically or by a counterbalance, and manned to give covering fire.
Views across or along the sea and seafront, lakes and rivers.
General merchandise and saleable commodities. Use more specific type where known.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
Letter D1 - Pre app recomend condition EAS version
A settlement area that combines a harbour and terminal facilities at the interface between land and water transportation systems.

Standard rectangular block or tablet bonded on mortar joints in a regular arrangement or pattern for strength or decoration. Made from clay or brick earth which may contain varying quantities of chalk, lime or iron oxide which effect colour or density.
A small building used by the keeper of a castle, park, etc.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.
Rock or hard minerals used as a building material and for carving etc.
Use for deposits representing material discarded or remaining as a result of a process or processes.
One tenth of a nautical mile. Equal to 100 fathoms under the strict definition.
A machine producing mechanical power by the internal combustion of gas.
A horizontal stone placed across a grave.
A small, usually inexpensive, restaurant with a limited menu of light meals served at counters or tables.
Use for smaller forms of mechanical propulsion, such as diesel, electric and outboard motors.
A sports pitch usually with a synthetic surface (ie. not grass).
A stamp, made of clay or stone, used to mark bars of eye ointment.
An official residence of an abbot during the summer months.
Articles used in charging guns and ordnance.
A straight road lined with trees along either side, also straight lines of trees found in parkland usually leading to a landscape feature.
Collective term for the building limestones formed during the Lower Jurassic period.
A barrier consisting of a horizontal rail supported by uprights.
A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.
The vertical side of a window, archway, doorway or fireplace.
A gentry house in a town or city, either detached or in a terrace.

An arrangement by which panels, screens, vaults or windows are divided into parts of different shapes or sizes by means of moulded stone bars or ribs, called form-pieces or forms in the Medieval period.

The first transportable aircraft hangar developed by the RFC/RAF, which comprised a kit of timber and canvas that could be assembled in 48 hours. The canvas doors open one end only. Also known as Type H hangar.
A long thin piece of wood,
The lower, or inner, curve of an arch
Use for vessels registered in Uruguay.
A room or building for hand knitting garments on simple hand frames.
Obstacles, including scaffolding and anti tank blocks designed to impede an enemy's attempts to land forces onto open beaches.
A mechanical component or device that can change the direction of motion of a pump rod from the vertical to the horizontal plane and vice versa.

A small stone core with a conical form and a single core platform which may or may not be prepared. Microblades are removed form the circumference of the platform. The end opposite the platform usually tapers to a point. (Source: SARC)
A type of spur which ends in a point, blunt or sharp, which is used to aid control of an animal eg a horse.
The residence of a chauffeur or driver
