A microlith retouched to a triangular shape. They can be sub-divided into scalene and isosceles triangles. (Source: SARC)
Mark 7 or the seventh variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A fob can consist of a chain and or a ring.
The hides of animals, either untreated or tanned.
A specific type of small rounded jar. (Source: MPRG)
A powder made by grinding the edible part of various grains, and used as a foodstuff.

A decorative design or illustration, often an anthropomorphic or geometrical image, carved into a stone surface, such as a cave wall or free-standing stone. Usually, though not always, of Prehistoric date.
A small work shop for nail manufacture, most commonly situated at the back of a nailer's dwelling.
A private chamber usually in a Royal residence.
Sites and structures associated with the cutting and processing of peat.
A vessel that has sunk at sea: Double-index with background cause were known, e.g. LEAKED, COLLISION.
A factory where fruit and seed oil is produced by an oil machine.
A barn in which a central space is separated from side aisles by posts and braces.
A walk bordered by trees or clipped hedges in a garden or park. Made of gravel, sand or turf, it is different from a path or avenue.
A building used for the treatment of victims of chemical, gas or other forms of contamination.
A centre where patients suffering from venereal and associated diseases receive treatment.
Purpose built accommodation for members of the armed forces and their families.

A site where flint seams within chalk have been exploited by digging deep vertical shafts, often with horizontal galleries radiating out from the base. Use for Neolithic examples and for Post Medieval gunflint industry.
A flat object which is broad and rounded at one end and tapers to a handle at the other.
Sporting venues and competitions in progress.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where cargo vessels can load and unload large storage containers. May include a rail terminal for containers which have been transported to the port by rail.

A monument within a church or cathedral representing one of the stations of the cross. Usually images or pictures of successive incidents of the Passion, they are intended to be visited for meditation and prayer.
A shore establishment for the teaching of maritime theory and practical skills.
A vessel comprising two or more dishes, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
A building in which photographers, taken for aerial reconnaissance purposes, are analysed and interpreted to provide intelligence on enemy activities.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A public house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers, etc.
A window in a spire, often in the form of a dormer.
A pressure vessel used to store gasses at above atmospheric pressure.
A post mill in which the drive is taken down to the base of the mill by putting an upright shaft in the hollowed post.
Glazed and decorated, patterned earthenware tile combining different coloured clays which are inlaid and burnt in. Mainly used for flooring and external decoration.
A place where working men could educate themselves through lectures and the use of a reading room with newspapers, etc.
A factory in which logs are converted to timber by running them through a series of saws.

A complex of buildings used as a headquarters and training base for Royal Navy personnel. Even though they are buildings on land shore establishments are deemed to be shipsand are designated 'HMS' eg. HMS Dolphin in Portsmouth.
A small, flat band or fillet around a shaft or column.
"Looking glasses", up to and including the medieval period made of polished steel or other reflective metals; later a piece of glass with a reflective coating, e.g. silver or aluminium.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
Used for orthographic drawings in the horizontal plane, generally from above generally depicts localised areas.
A climbing plant (Rubia tinctorum) which was formerly cultivated for the reddish-purple dye obtained from the roots.

An element such as a window, door or wall decoration, usually associated with a larger monument but which may be found in isolation. For example a stained glass window or panelling saved from a demolished building.
A site, containing installations and machinery, used for measuring the power of explosives.
A device on a boat's gunwale serving as a fulcrum for an oar and keeping it in place.
A narrow strip of land where a plough and team could turn. This usually remains higher than the ploughed land.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
Objects used or associated with sport and games, eg gaming piece. This class includes toys.
A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An excavation from which stone for building and other functions, is obtained by cutting, blasting, etc.
A shelf that is behind an altar.
A measuring container to measure dry goods.
A horizontal member cutting through the corner formed by two walls to act as a support to a hip rafter to support jetties on two adjacent sides of an upper floor.
This is the top term for the thesaurus.
A tray for separating grain from chaff.
Posts with hooks attached to allow drying new cloth to be stretched out between them.
Signs or badges of office, honour, membership, occupation etc.
A self-contained establishment (out-patients) where pregnant women receive check-ups, counselling and medical treatment.
An item designed to cover, decorate or enhance a wall.
Stone used for grinding or polishing during the manufacture of lithic implements
An ornate public house that developed in the 1830s after the passing of a law to encourage the drinking of beer in alehouses licensed for the sale of beer only.
A component building of an explosives works where cartridges were filled with explosives with the aid of cartridging machines.
A principal that has been reduced to the same thickness as a common rafter where the roof has clasped purlins.
A costrel with a barrel-shaped body and a centrally placed neck. One end is usually flat and the other domed. Two opposed strap handles or lugs join the rim or neck and shoulder. (Source: MPRG)

A shaft which appears to have been dug for, or which contains objects apparently deposited for, reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction (eg. of stone, water, etc). Index with principal object types.
A building or group of buildings, incorporating radio masts, built to intercept radio transmissions from enemy vessels and aircraft during WWI and WWII.
A vessel with a lug sail rig. A lug is a four sided sail set on a lug or yard. Modified from square-rigged vessels from the late 17th century. Became a popular fishing boat rig in the 19th century.
A structure, usually well concealed, used to store explosives intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organization) in the event of an invasion.
Stonemason's term for any coarse/hard stone that is not easily worked. Index with specific stone type where given. Not to be confused with Kentish Ragstone.
An appliance for producing motion by the stepping of men on movable steps on a revolving cylinder. Used as a form of punishment in prisons.
A room or building where a pump is worked.
Narrow, rough tracks often over upland routes used by packhorse trains to carry goods.
Use for vessels registered in Venezuela.
A window usually spanning the full width of the north side of a roof allowing the maximum amount of direct and indirect light to enter.

A pit used for the re-burial of disarticulated human remains from many individuals, occasionally displaying sorting of remains, eg. grouping of skulls or long bones. Distinct from mass burials which contain articulated skeletal remains.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.

Composed of sand, stones or other aggregate and cement mixed with water which sets in a hard mass. The material is usually associated with modern building but was developed by Romans where cement was obtained from quicklime.
The name of a class of excavations, found in chalk formations in England, consisting of a shaft sunk to the chalk, and there widening out into one or more chambers.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
A Roman brooch dating from approximately 50 to 150 AD. Derived from the earlier Aesica Brooch, and fitted with a hinged pin, the body widens to a triangular plate below the bow.

A costrel with a flattened spherical form: the back is flat and the front domed or mammiform. The base may be slightly flattened or rounded. Two opposed strap handles or lugs join the rim or neck and shoulder. (Source: MPRG)

The New Stone Age, this period follows on from the Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic and is itself succeeded by the Bronze Age. This period is characterized by the practice of a farming economy and extensive monumental constructions.
A specific form of globular jar with a rounded or very sagging base and an inturned, generally simple, rim. (Source: MPRG)
A bracelet or necklace formed by hammering gold onto a triangular-sectioned bar and twisting the metal to form a spiral pattern.
A vessel used to carry supplies to warships.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where a container vessel docks to take on or unload its containers.
A garden designed to display sculpture, publicly or privately.
Any factory or site using machine tools in a manufacturing or processing capacity.
Use for vessels registered in Poland.
Photographic film responsive to infrared radiation. Used to record temperature variations in the subject, indicative of hidden archaeological or architectural features.
A slim piece of wood used to ignite fires, lamps, ovens etc.
A Mark 3 aircraft which has undergone slight modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A tall, narrow window with a pointed arched head.
An abbey of the Bridgettine double order of nuns and religious men.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an E-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
A machine used for lifting materials.
A device for operating a lock.
Buildings, structures or sites used for the production of chemicals used in agriculture, such as fertilizers and weed killers.
Sedimentary clay with smectite mineral properties, originally used for the cleansing ["fulling"] of cloth; in the 20th century it was used for a wider range of industrial applications.
Usually distilled alcohollic drink but also used for liquids where a substance is in solution with alcohol.

An enclosed structure of brick, stone or metal in which material is heated or burned, or, in a domestic context, food is cooked, through the continuous radiation of heat from its floor, walls or ceiling.

A natural spring located within a, usually small,  man-made structure, such as a niche or a box. The structure is so placed to accomodate use for a specific non-religious function, such as communal bathing.
A reinforced and padded item of clothing designed to protect the upper body in sports associated with physical contact or possible injury from sporting equipment. For military uses use BREASPLATE.
A decorative, framed tablet, usually bearing an inscription or coat of arms, in the form of a scroll or curving piece of parchment.
A building in which pack animals could shelter.
A hiding place for a (Roman Catholic) priest.
An engraved stamp used to impress an image onto another object.
A control tower designed for use on Very Heavy Bomber Station Airfields. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 294/45 they were the first to be have a Visual Control Room
A commercial building used primarily as a trading place for breweries and hop merchants.
Small port on River Trent, North Lincs.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
A form of granite found in Cornwall
An area of a church, often a free-standing building, in which baptism is administered
A rustic garden building made of wood with moss pressed between the wall slats. The mosses could be of different types, forming a mossery.
A circular bank surrounding an area where burials were placed.
A depot for the depositing, storage and dispatch of plant or other resources associated with the delivery of local government public services.
A school attended by children between the ages of eleven and sixteen.
Wood, cut and seasoned so forming or capable of forming any part of a structure. May be treated with preservative before use.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
Early Bronze Age assumed to be a neck ornament, crescent moon shaped, often gold and elaborately decorated.
A school founded in or before the 16th century, for teaching Latin, later becoming a secondary school teaching languages, history, science, etc.
A covered pit into which raw sewage is discharged.
Cubes of solid concrete, usually with sides of 3 feet 6 inches or 5 feet which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A multi-storey building in which individual blocks of flats cluster around a central service core.

Objects used in, or which are created as part of, a manufacturing or production process, including the by-products of such processes. This does not include finished items, these will appear in other appropriate classes.
A joist which rests on top of a beam.
An object used to hold offerings to a deity.
A plaque attached onto, or a line incised into, a wall face or other surface to indicate the height of flood water inundation.
An assessment of a known wreck or underwater archaeologcial site through diving.
A kiln in the form of a pit dug into the earth which was used for the the production of white coal prior to the Industrial Revolution.
A place of worship for members of the Church of Scotland which has been Presbyterian since 1690. It is the national Church of Scotland and is free and endowed.
A tablet, often made of lead, on which curses are written. Sometimes the tablet is transfixed with a nail.
A schematic diagram showing the relationships of the composition and strata of layers identified during excavation or intervention.
Animal skins which have the outer pelt of fur on them.
A dish in which an offering is made.
A device for hoisting, or operating pumps, using water displacement as a lifting and balancing medium.
A stringed instrument usually played with a bow.
Traces of food observed adhering to, or found within, an object or another material.
A heat engine prime mover in which hot gases or hot air expand as they pass through and rotate vanes attached to a central shaft, enclosed in a chamber.
A passageway within a building providing access to rooms.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A rectangular pier projecting slightly from the face of the wall it buttresses.
A bar or rod, usually of metal, used to push another object into place eg to push coals within a fire.
Use as an external architectural feature only.
An ornate, openwork fabric made by twisting, knotting or looping threads. Originally made by hand but more recently manufactured mechanically.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
A covering for the head with a peak to shade the eyes.
Coarse grained, dark coloured granite, quarried in the Peterhead and Cairngall areas of Scotland, but used throughout the North.
A receptacle to hold water used in baptism usually found in a baptistery or nave of a church.
An artificial area of open water, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
An area used for the training of personnel in civil defence procedures.
A strip of cloth used for binding a wound.
A vane usually combined with crossed rods to show the four compass points. Used to indicate the direction of the wind.
A truss comprising principal rafters and wall-posts secured by knee-braces or sling-braces, but lacking tiebeams.
Any material, including gold, silver, copper, tin etc. which is ductile, malleable, usually lustrous and a good conductor of heat and electricity.
Soft coverings and associated objects used within buildings.
A place set apart to contain books for reading, study or reference.
Buildings and structures used to monitor the accuracy of bombs dropped on a bombing range
A building used for the daily administration of the Royal Air Force.
A pawnbrokers shop or place of business.
A structure comprising two upright spars, joined at the top to form a triangle, with a hoisting tackle suspended from the apex. Used to lift cargo or other weights.
A type of tomb in the form of a slab raised on freestanding legs.
A building housing computers and information technology equippment e.g. for a business, factory or other instituion.
Sixth Rate Ship Of The Line
Accommodation in a monastery for new monks.
A purpose-built triangulation pillar used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
Reinforced concrete blocks, walls or ditches designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
An attachment to furniture that can be detached.
A covered passageway projecting into or across a ditch of a fortified place to provide flanking fire to the ditch in which it stands or for the purpose of sheltering communication with outworks.

A type of temporary military aircraft hangar introduced in 1940; of steel welded and bolted construction typically clad in galvanized corrugated iron sheets. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF in World War Two.
Seats or benches covered in turf, built against a wall, tree or fountain,  were a common feature of medieval enclosed gardens.
Large mammals, domesticated for riding and as draught animals.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.
The pelts of beavers used for the manufacture of fur coats and hats.
A structure which protects a beach or harbour by breaking the force of the waves.
A building containing a flight siumlator used to provide safe training for pilots.
A strap passing underneath the animal to hold saddle in place.
A marker stone showing the extent of a measure of land containing a vein of ore.
A building used for the dissemination to the public of such items like tourist brochures, travel maps, guide books and other documents, etc.
Rolls of barbed wire with supporting metal posts designed to impede enemy advance.
A mixed earthy substance consisting principally of clay mixed with calcium carbonate and sand in very variable proportions.
A pan with a long handle which would be filled with coals and drawn over sheets to warm a bed.
A small garden building used to store equipment used in the game of croquet.
A vertical, circular member, usually load-carrying. Where separate, use monument type.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55422.
A small metal ring through which a nail or rivet is passed and fixed.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
An area of either natural or artificial stone arranged to resemble a rocky outcrop or cliff face within animal cages/enclosures of a Zoo.

A specific form of rounded jug with a wide mouth, a large parrot-beak spout and three handles in the form of wide straps that spring from the rim to the girth.The spout may have a lug applied to the outside. (Source: MPRG)
An area of land consisting of the lord's demesne and of lands from whose holders he may exact certain fees, etc.
A decorative feature in the style of a formalized rose.
An apparatus designed with a large vaned wheel rotated by the wind in order to generate electricity.
A large pot used for boiling.
A steam vessel propelled by rotating propellers called screws.
An inscribed marker stone found on Hadrian's Wall.

Structures, traditonally consisting of a long shank with two arms at one end and a ring to attach to cable at the other, used to hold a ship in one place by mooring it to the bottom of the sea. Usually made of stone or metal.
Floatable vessel used as a floodgate in docks.
A steam-powered machine used for raising materials such as ore or water from a pit or shaft.
A decorative tile incorporated into the front of a tile stove.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
A furnace for smelting ore in which the fuel and ore are mixed.
Parts of a building's fabric, structures and associated services, eg drain pipe. If the structure is complete use a monument type thesaurus.
Hard, transparent, brittle substance manufactured by fusing soda or potash with other ingredients. Used for glazing windows and in the manufacture of drinking vessels.
The fittings or parts on a strap.
A column that is equidistant, with intercolumniations, even at the corners, with two or more triglyphs over each  intercolumniation.
A musical instrument producing sound by the use of strings.
A trench dug to contain a sill beam, a horizontal timber beam used as a foundation for the wall of a building. Use wider site type where known.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.

In the glass industry, a furnace of Lorraine Type, comprising a central rectangular melting furnace with ancillary structures at each corner, adjacent to the fires. Post-Mediaeval until superceded by coal-fired furnaces.

An Anglo-Saxon disc brooch featuring an upturned rim. Usually decorated with zoomorphic or geometric designs either chip-carved directly on the face or applied to a thin bronze plate affixed to the brooch's floor.
An inclined plane connecting two different levels, used to accomodate the movement of vehicles, wheeled apparatus,livestock etc.
A market where cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry are bought and sold.

A decoy site designed to replicate the layout of an RAF satellite airfield, complete with dummy aircraft, simulated runways and simple structures intended to fool enemy aircraft during daylight raids.
A gable with sides shaped like a flight of steps.
A powder made from charcoal, sulphur and potassium nitrate and used as an explosive in fireworks, flintlock guns etc.
A building or site where aircraft can be stored and maintained.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
For use when a vessel, already lost through other causes, is dismantled or dispersed by means of explosives to render it harmless to other shipping.
A workshop used for the manufacture of statues, either cast or carved.
A light, soft, moderately-strong wood obtained from trees of the genus Picea.

Traditionally a mew was a building housing hawks when they were moulting, however since the C16th the term has been used for a series of stables grouped around an open yard or alley, often with rooms above. Use only for stables otherwise use FALCONRY.
Three-masted fishing lugger built in and operating out of Yorkshire on the North Sea fisheries; so named as it was crewed by five joint owners, plus two or three paid hands.

A structure over an opening usually formed of wedge-shaped blocks of brick or stone held together by mutual pressure and supported at the sides; they can also be formed from moulded concrete/ cast metal. A component; use for free-standing structure only.
Dried produce especially, hay, straw etc. used to feed cattle.
A building or room where nets are made
Hard, protective covering made largely of calcium salts secreted by soft bodied invertebrate animals.
A cup adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
The residence of a Royal Navy or Merchant Navy officer.
A chapel built on, or at the end of, a causeway.
A pointed arch in which the arcs comprising it are centred on points both outside and inside the arch so that the point takes the form of a double S, or ogee.
A site in which one or more searchlights and their accompanying structures were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
A furnace constructed as a shaft with the fire at the bottom and the fuel and ore added from the top.
A building used for the preparation of animal skins and hides prior to the tanning process.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55483.
A tall, usually steel, structure used to receive and transmit radio signals in order to determine the height, distance and number of aircraft approaching.
Fruit which has been preserved by drying.
An open roofed structure on which climbing plants are grown in order to provide a shaded walkway or seating area.
A long bed planted with perennial flowers and plants.
Dredging of waterways or channels to remove obstacles to navigation. Where the intention is to recover aggregate from the seabed use: mineral extraction.
Garden comprising rockwork features including grottoes, cascades and arches, often in different architectural styles ie. Gothic, Chinese and rustic. In use from the mid C18.
A commemorative stone inscribed with a dedicatory inscription to a person or event.
A cigar shaped implement used to release knots and tangles in weaving.

The measurement of the ratio of the radioactive Carbon 14 (C-14) isotope and non-radioactive carbon isotopes. Useful for dating organic materials such as wood and bone between 500 and 45,000 years old.

A building containing a series of seats for use by the clergy during services. The seats are usually placed in the church and as such this is a very rare monument type, being purpose-built. An example being St. Germoe's Chair in Germoe, Cornwall.
A well with a superstructure, either partially or wholly enclosed with an access door, designed to protect the water source.
Drawing of the vertical face of an excavated feature or features depicting the vertical extent and stratigraphic relationship between identified layers or deposits.
Magnetic tape used to record sound. Includes both cassette and reel tapes.
A medallion, as on a brooch or ring, with a stone which is often semi precious with a device carved in relief.
A site equipped for active defensive action against an airborne enemy assault.
A mechanical lift or elevator, used to lift goods, etc.
A recess, often containing shelves and usually fitted with a door or doors, used for the storage of items.
A stage in a church tower where bell ringers stand.
A building or room where motor vehicles are exhibited for sale.
Chamber built into underside of a structure to exercise demolition.
A factory for the manufacture of military tanks.
An area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
A floor area, covered in sand, onto which hot metal from a furnace is cast.
A site containing plant and machinery for the manufacture of steel.
A reddish metal used in alloys, coins and the construction and electronics industries.
A chair fixed to the end of a plank, in which scolds or dishonest people were tied and ducked in water as a punishment.
Easily formed metal alloy composed of copper and zinc.
Fixed or hardened installation for machine guns. Temporary soft installations are possible as well.
The constituent parts of a kiln.
A tower, containing a gate, built into the walls of a town, castle or similar fortification.
A room used by those who have to wait at railway or bus stations, etc.
A small building, often inhabited by a gatekeeper, gamekeeper or similar. Use specific type where known.
A yard or enclosure attached to a farmhouse, usually surrounded by other farm buildings.
A building which has been fortified, often as a temporary measure rather than as part of the original design
An alignment of stakes or stakeholes of unknown function
A pit where bears were housed for baiting and entertainment purposes. If not used for baiting use BEAR ENCLOSURE.
Transport vessel, usually a hired vessel of mercantile origin, used for the exchange of prisoners-of-war; sometimes, specifically a hospital ship with such prisoners.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
A container used to assist in cooling wine.
The part of a column between the capital and the base.
An early type of steam engine, similar to a Cornish Engine, designed by Edward Bull.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
The cutting or chopping part of an adze; bifacially worked, longitudinal section symmetrical, cutting edge  parallel to the direction of the hafted tool as swung.
A room in a public house, hotel, club etc. containing a bar from which alcoholic drinks are served.
This dates from the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain to the Norman invasion in 1066 and is to be used for monuments of post Roman, Saxon and Viking date.
A monumental burial place, usually for a single person or family.
A concrete, cylindrical pedestal on which a spigot mortar was mounted. The pedestal is often the only evidence for a Spigot Mortar emplacement to survive.
Pit for soaking animal hides as part of the tanning process.
A light, ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation built in the Chinese style.
A leaf or diamond-shaped arrowhead with shallow retouching at the edges.
Monument visible as remains of former earthworks.
An explosive-proof vaulted chamber used for the storage or ordnance.
A room for the storage of bread, biscuits, flour etc. Often part of a buttery in medieval times.
A vessel used for storing and issuing gunpowder, usually moored well away from the dockyard.
A design of vertical steam engine patented in 1802.
A collar, usually metal, used to signify slavery and to inhibit freedom, usually with a chain attached.
A pick with a point at one end and a cutting blade at the other end.
A medieval high status farmstead, acting as the centre of the estate, directly controlled by the lord and used for the benefit of his household and dependents.
Sedimentary rock consisting of rounded pebbles naturally cemented together.
A place of worship and residence for Anglican nuns.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
An instrument which has a cupped mouthpiece and may have a straight, bent or curved tube. It includes slide trumpets like the trombone.
A boiling vessel used in the direct boiling process, or the sleeching process, used for the manufacture of salt. For evaporating features associated with SOLAR and PARTIAL SOLAR sites use SALT POND.
A site where coal is processed.
A building used to store military equipment and ammunition.
A mine used for the extraction of tungsten bearing ore. Use with other mineral ores extracted and MINE, eg. TIN MINE.
A factory where packaging products, such as cardboard boxes, are produced.
Use for a craft powered by a steam engine that uses three expansion stages of progressively lower pressure, to extract further energy from the steam.
Fragments of wrought or cast iron broken up for reprocessing.

An area used for the deposition of human remains where the principal funeral rite is the burial of the corpse complete. Generally indicated by the discovery of articulated human skeletal remains, occasionally with evidence of coffins and/or grave goods.
A steep-sided pit formed by, and for, the extraction of gravel.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mine or bombshell.
A band or bracelet worn around the arm.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with road transport.
A waterwheel turned by the force of water falling upon the top of the wheel into buckets placed round the circumference.
A long narrow two edged sword with a guarded hilt, used as a thrusting weapon.
A complex of buildings where electricity is produced using steam-powered turbines.
A container with a religious, ritual or funerary use.

A structure or building used in the manufacture of the explosive cordite. After the cordite had been pressed to extract moisture it was placed on racks within the stove prior to being taken to the reeling house for winding.
A channel for taking a rapidly flowing stream of water away from a canal lock, or away from the canal itself.

Also spelt "oszemundt" and other variants. Low-grade cast iron in the form of balls or spheres, produced in small workshops and exported across the North Sea and Baltic region. Particularly associated with 16th century Sweden.
A wooden frame with holes, through which the head and hands of an offender were thrust, in which state they would be exposed to public ridicule and assault.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
Examination, recording and plotting of variations in the electrical resistivity of soils in order to locate and define buried features.
A dwelling cut into the rockface of a cliff or hillside, often with a built frontage. Many date from the Medieval period and are still in use in some areas of the country.

A human constructed underwater structure, usually built to promote marine life in areas with a generally featureless eas bed but have also been built to control erosion, block ship passage, or improve surfing.
The age of an asset may be an important criterion, and the age range can be adjusted to take into account distinctive local characteristics or building traditions.
A structure used for the lifting of boats and other water craft.
A lid with a shallow domed profile and a central knob. (Source: MPRG)
A site or structure on which a signal, especially a fire, could be placed as a warning or means of communication. Use for beacon sites or surviving beacon structures.
A projecting wall or structure, such as a parapet or battlement, supported by a series of corbels.
A flat tile with raised or flanged edges, used with imbrex for roofing.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
The spanning of an opening without the use of a lintel.
A hammer designed to fight with, often has a hammer side and a spiked side.
A covered tank in which rainwater is stored for use when required.
A heavy grade, water proof plastic film used for the preparation of technical drawings.
A painting executed directly onto a wall.
Movable stand for carrying a body to its grave.

Class of elements and alloys that are characteristically lustrous,ductile, fusible and malleable. These are extracted from ore minerals originally existing in nature and processed before becoming a recognisable metal. See METAL Class List for narrow terms
A clip used to attach pieces of harness together.
The subsoil traces of cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of a plough to till the soil.
Materials used in the manufacture of objects.

A trench dug through topsoil in an arable field in order to extract underlying clay which was then spread on the field and ploughed in to improve soil fertility. Usually found in peaty soil areas such as the Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire fenlands.
An object used in smithing to enlarge holes, consists of a tapered square rod.
A shallow pond, often artificial, fed by the condensation of water from the air, occuring on high land which has no other adequate water supply.
Residues from ore-processing operations; intact tips and deposits may preserve considerable evidence on the processes used. A high rpoportion have been destroyed by reprocessing.
Obstacles like concrete cubes, cylinders or pimples erected in the defence of Britain.

Inshore craft used for carrying troops and military equipment used either for beach landings or as a ferry; as cargo smaller landing craft could be carried aboard larger craft in the D-Day operations, for example.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
Hanging drapery used to cover an opening eg a window, often decorative.
A joint in which the tenon passes completely through the receiving timber.
A white ductile metal used, for example, in alloys, for instruments, and in aircraft construction.
A strip of ground forming a fringe to a garden. Use more specific type where known.
A stony mound containing or concealing deliberately deposited human remains. Use specific type where known.
A stone, of unidentified function, showing evidence of great heating at some point in the past, leading to vitrification.
A gate leading to water, either a river or the sea. Used as a means of supplying castles, for example, with goods brought by water transport.
A market where fish is sold.
The gearwheel on the upright shaft within a windmill from which secondary drives operating other parts of the machinery are powered. are taken
Sites where minerals are extracted from the ground.
This period follows on from the Bronze Age and is characterized by the use of iron for making tools and monuments such as hillforts and oppida. The Iron Age is taken to end with the Roman invasion.
Remains of one of the groups of animals characterized as lacking any form of backbone or spinal column.
A metal mouth piece used to control an animal, usually used on a horse.
A branched, hanging light fitting, often ornate in design, provifding illumination from a number of candles or lightbulbs.
A church, the plan of which is based on that of a Roman basilica.
A house having four rooms of equal height on each of two floors; in larger houses there are often two parallel and equal roofs.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.

The controlled measurement of natural and artificial landscape features to produce a measured plan or a 3D data set reading as a plan. Features are depicted by either hachures, symbols or contour lines.
Beams of wood, iron, steel etc., used in the construction industry.
A subscription club, usually with a library and newspaper room, established from c.1815-1860, their educational function gradually taken over by the public libraries in the later 19th century.
Flat bottomed vessel used as a platform for a pile driver.
A crane for lowering loaded coal waggons onto a ship.
A border put around a picture to enhance it and ususally to hold in place the picture and any covering, eg glass.
A place devoted to the cultivation and exhibition of rare trees.
A building with malt kilns for the malting of grains and with other similar equipment for brewing work.
A painting executed directly onto a wall.
A channel that returns water that has been used to turn a waterwheel back to the river or source from which it came.
A site used for the production of anaesthetic gas.
A building housing equipment for the process of distillation.
A miniature lead phial worn around the neck as a religious pilgrim sign, generally medieval.
Small ornamental pyramid or cone, often decorated, crowning a spire, turret, buttress etc.
A pavilion at the end of a PLEASURE PIER.
Blue-white metal, obtained from ore, and used commercially for roofing, galvanizing iron, or in alloys. Also used in the 19th century as sheathing for ship's hulls.
A site where a periodical gathering of buyers, sellers and entertainers, meet at a time ordained by charter or statute or by ancient custom.
Long parallel soil ridges in excess of 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
The bottom part of a sleeve, can be ornamental.
A building housing a steam engine.
The round, firm fleshed fruit of the apple (Malus Domestica) tree. Grown in numerous varieties throughout the world.
A wall mounted, hydraulically operated crane or winch, sometimes used to operate lifts.
A horn containing gun powder used for priming a firearm.
Organised and documented collection of the records made during the course of a project.
Use for deposits formed by the action of the sea or under marine conditions.
A building, or first-floor room in a building, for the dry and secure storage of grain after it has been threshed and winnowed.
An item used to fasten, bind or join one item to another.
A building, either purpose-built or modified, used for the co-ordination of the Fire Service.
A stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 4238/44.
A site, often in a woodland clearing, used for the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
A room in a house, hotel, business premises etc. where guests or visitors are received.
A large building, situated by or near a dock, canal, road or railway and used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation.
A bridge in which the load is carried by a single beam, or beams, spanning the space between two supports.
Building used for children to play in.
A type of ferry that is designed to carry wheeled vehicles that can be driven on to and off the vessel.
A series of cages in which hens are confined for intensive egg laying.
Use for the historic region of Flanders only
A kiln in which the contents are protected from the fire, usually by a lining of tiles or refractory bricks.
Use for the remains of any part of a mammal, except for humans.
An object used to retrieve birds used in hawking. Consists of feathers tied to a rope, food is contained in the lure whilst training the birds.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
Woven or felted fabric used in the manufacture of garments, tablecloths, towels etc.
A military camp providing training facilities.
A civic building housing fire engines and a permanent fire-fighting force.
A steam motor in which rotory motion is produced by steam impinging directly upon a series of vanes upon the circumference of a revolving cylinder or disc.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
A room in which cloaks, coats, hats etc may be left and often including coathooks, hat boxes and similar fixtures and fittings.
For reheating of worked metal or glass to make it malleable or to harden it after use for toolmaking, etc.
Studding in which the studs are at an inclined angle to the posts.
A convex, finger-like moulding, usually applied in a series to form a pattern of ridges.

A building designed specifically for handling tobacco. This may be a bonded warehouse containing facilities for removing tobacco leaves from the hogsheads in which they were imported, and pressing them.
A large one handled drinking vessel, sometimes fitted with a hinged lid.
Coarse grained, metamorphic rock in which the colour is dependent upon the predominant mineral.
An object used to weigh something down or to measure the weight of another object.
Pertaining to or deriving from a botanical living organism. See VEGETAL Class List for narrow terms.
A road, used traditionally for the transportation of a corpse to a place of burial.

Includes the processes for investigating and recording historic buildings. Differences in terminology may apply to the recording of buildings due to the approach taken. As such, concepts in this hierarchy may be country specific.
A medieval court established for the administration of forest law.
The original pattern/type of an object.
The residence of a person entrusted with the management of a great house or castle.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
A chapel attached to, or inside, a church, endowed for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.
Soft mineral, colour varying from black/purple to yellow/green. Commonly found as a mineral vein.
A machine used for combing wool. Use more specific term where known.
The British Admiralty in practice used a fathom of 6 feet. This was despite its being  1⁄1000 of a nautical mile (i.e. 6.08 feet) until the adoption of the international nautical mile.

A device or engine powered by one or more horses or donkeys walking around a circular track and harnessed  so as to turn a large toothed wheel, either in the same plane or above, which turned smaller  wheels operating machinery.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (13079/41)
A rod around which fibre is wound for spinning
An 18th century garden with a Chinese layout and ornaments.
A diagonal or arched member placed across rafters to stiffen and support a roof structure.

A site which is known, or believed to be, where an aircraft crashed. It is an offence to interfere with the wreckage of crashed military aircraft without a licence (Protection of Military Remains Act 1986). Index with AIRCRAFT TYPE where known.
A written work for publication, being one of several found in a serial, monograph or magazine.
Reuse of timbers or hull of a vessel in construction. For example sinking of hulks as harbour foundations or recycling of timbers in domestic contexts.
A complex of buildings where barytes is processed for industrial use.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the mining explosive sabulite.
The slab or place on which a fire is made.
Items which are used in clothing but which are not necessarily a separate item of clothing.
Third Rate Ship Of The Line
An iron bar used as a lever.
A mill in which sets of rollers were used to roll metal to set thicknesses or shapes such as rails, beams or rods.

A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of rowing. An area of the building may be used for the storage of canoes, sculls etc. Often situated by a river.
An embankment of earth alongside a tramway.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of cement.
Dried or partially dried grapes eaten as a fruit.
A tall, thin pillar of wood, stone or metal on which a lamp could be fixed.
A tool for gripping with, often used to pinch objects together.
A maritime monument where the remains of a vessel are scattered over a wide area.
A building where animals are slaughtered.
A small private chapel in either a house or church.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.

A structure consisting of three stretches of tramline joined by points. The tram is able to go forward, reverse and then go forward again changing line each time until it has turned around completely.

World War II-era British merchant ships used in convoys as an emergency stop-gap until sufficient escort carriers became available. They were equipped with a rocket-propelled catapult launching a single Hawker Sea Hurricane plane.
A base embellished with horizontal reeds and other mouldings.
Found in early churches this was a part of a church on the south side of the chancel where there were bookshelves and storage for vestments.
A lap joint which has a notch cut in one side.
Thick, viscid liquid, obtained by the distillation of wood, coal or other organic substances, chemically a mixture of hydrocarbons with resins.
The exercise hall of a Roman baths complex.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of cotton.
A reverberatory furnace used for forging wrought iron from pig iron using coal as fuel.
A circular, metal or wooden cover, covering a hole in the pavement where domestic coal deliveries were dropped into a store below.

Loss of a craft, especially aircraft, resulting from the malfunction of registering or measuring apparatus vital to its navigation or operation. In the case of structural or engine failure use MECHANICAL FAILURE.
Bed coverings, usually of woollen or similar natural or artificial fabrics.
Weights used on a type of vertical loom to hold the warp threads taut.

Detailed survey using photographic images to record archaeological and architectural sites or features of interest. Record photography is an important aspect of recording such features before they are destroyed.
A tall, tapering pillar with a pyramidal top, generally square on plan. Used in England from the late 16th century as a public, funerary or garden monument.

Where the land on which the monument stands is dedicated to the monument itself: this may include Guardianship sites displayed, also sites which exclude any other Land Classification e.g. Cross, Commemorative Monument etc.
Use for vessels registered in Canada.
A simple type of hinge used for large gates.
A small arched hangar built by the Canadian company Fromson of Byfleet to drawing number 3971/43. Used only as storage sheds on RNASs.
Small landing craft often armoured, designed to carry infantrymen and their equipment ashore from larger vessels offshore.
Part of a large church, east of the nave, appropriated for singers and clergy.
A mill in which textile rags were ground, either to enable the fibres to be respun or to use the pulp in the manufacture of paper.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, where ambulances can be parked and stored.
An underground channel with a vaulted roof. Use specific type where known.
A site where alum (hydrous sulphate or salt and alumina) is quarried.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
A box in which letters are posted or deposited for dispatch.
Soft, very fine grained, dark coloured, sedimentary rock which splits easily.
A place of worship for members of the French Protestant church of the 16th and 17th centuries.
Preparations for beautifying or enhancing the body, face, hair or skin, e.g. creams, and coloured "make-up" items, e.g. rouge, lipstick, etc.
A garden incorporating features of Moorish-influenced Spanish gardens - water features, patios, benches, walls and compartments, evergreens, etc.
House, where destitute Jews converted to Christianity after the expulsion. Latin for "House of Converts".
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
A slate situated at the end of a terrace for a coal company employee to wake the miners for their shift. The slate had the time of the shifts written on it.

A programme of assessment of the known or potential archaeological resource within a specified area or site on land, inter-tidal zone or underwater by the consultation and collation of existing written, graphic, photographic and electronic data.
A site intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organisation) in the event of an invasion. Use more specific term.
The junction of two timbers at right angles which involves chamfers or mouldings meeting on a diagonal line and where the timbers meet on the 45 degree line of the chamfer or moulding junction.
A structure composed of two large upright stone supporting a third, lintel stone.
A place where specific skills are taught on short courses.
A place of worship for Welsh Presbyterians. Formerly known as Calvinistic Methodists, the Presbyterian Church of Wales separated from the established church in 1811.
An abbey or priory for nuns ofthe Benedictine order.
Tablet of a uniform shape. Used as finishing or covering materials which fit together in a regular format.
An area used for the breeding and rearing of rabbits.
A discoidal flint tool often has a ground edge.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Benedictine order.
A place where radio programmes are produced and broadcast.
A capital with an abacus, ovolo, neck and astragal.
A diagonal brace running from an end of a cross tree to the vertical post to support this.
A room dedicated to the drawing or letting of blood, a procedure once thought to possess medicinal properties.
A small object designed to hold together the two ends of a cuff.
A waterwheel turned by the weight of water discharged into buckets placed around its circumference from an outlet positioned above it.
Buildings and structures associated with lifting and winding at the site of a mine.
A modern building in which the load is carried by a reinforced concrete framework. Use for reinforced concrete buildings.
A long handled fork with two or three long curved tines for tossing straw or hay.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons, usually at a pithead.

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.
A metal basket, mounted on a pole, in which oil or pitch was burned for illumination.
A walkway around the parapets of a castle or the roof of a church.
An instrument for measuring angles, usually in the form of a graduated semi-circle.
A type of cast chisel with a sharp, concave edge for shaping wood, stone or metal. A particular type of British Bronze Age tool.
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.
The principal church of a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.

An enclosure of Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age date, related to henges, defined by a circular arrangement of pits, probably none of which originally held posts. More than one circle, concentrically arranged, may be present.
Land owned and managed by the National Trust.
Dating to the reign of James I of England (VI of Scotland).
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting weapons with a larger calibre ammunition such as the QF 3.75 inch (94mm) gun.
An object for making an offering to a deity. It includes objects concerned with curses, sacrifices, and prayers and their related objects.
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A pump for removing condensed steam from the condenser of a steam raising plant.
A modern piece imitating an ancient coin in an attempt to deceive, usually for financial gain.
A small slab in a Doric cornice.
A building or complex where animal hair is processed, using a variety of means, for use in products such as brushes, mattresses etc.
Metal used primarily for roof coverings and window fittings. It is easy to work, can be worked cold and does not rust which makes it suitable for holding or repelling water.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.
A friary belonging to the Friars of the Sack also known as Friars of Penance or Penitentia.
The first driven gearwheel on the vertical shaft within a corn mill which meshes with the brake wheel in a  windmill, or the pit wheel in a watermill.
A hollow, cylindrical structure or tube made of clay, lead, steel, wood etc. through which gas, oil, water or other liquids can be conveyed.
A bridge which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.
A large body of water surrounded by land.
A gate or mechanism designed to allow animals which are being raced to start at the same time.
A Hall where billiards was played.
A herbaceous plant grown for its fibre and marijuana, a drug derivative. The fibres are used in the manufacture of rope.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
Outer cases for ammunition shells, e.g. Howitzer shells; not "live" ammunition, i.e. either at the first stage of manufacture, or having been expended.
A building in which works of art are displayed, permanently or temporarily.
Fused ash from furnaces used as aggregate.

A material or combination of materials manufactured by human effort, or fashioned into shape by man or a man made industrial process (excluding metal). See MAN MADE MATERIAL Class List for narrow terms.

A steel pipe driven into the ground at a shallow, oblique angle and packed with explosives. They were intended to be detonated on the approach of a hostile amroured vehicle or tank in order to create an obstacle directly in its path.
Worked pieces of stone. Use more specific type of stone where known.
Objects used to secure buildings, furniture or objects or used in the finishing and (non-structural) decoration of buildings, equipment and furniture.
A horizontal member spanning an opening and providing support to the wall above the opening.
A small hole filled or vacated by a stake, normally driven into the ground.
A furnace or oven used for drying items or materials. Use specific type where possible.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
A building or site used in the production of japanned goods. Japanning was the process of covering a material with a hard, black lacquer in imitation of Japanese lacquer work.
Objects used or associated with the transmission of ideas and information through the written medium.
A path, barred to vehicles, reserved for riding horses.
A tool used for digging where the blade is at right angles to the handle.
A crude, stone built structure, often roofless, used by tin miners to store equipment.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of concrete panels. Produced by during WWII as barrack accommodation and as emergency housing. Similar in style to Maycrete huts.
Buildings or sites used in the production of items derived from the parts of animals not used for consumption.
An abbey or priory of Cistercian monks.
A hostel used to accommodate members of the Womens Land Army who undertook essential agricultural work during the Second World War.
Originally a large tract of wooded country, owned by the Monarchy, for the purpose of hunting. The royal parks of London, eg. Greenwich, are all open to the public and have been for centuries.
An area of ground used for children to play on, often attached to a school.
A plant for bottling manufactured goods, as opposed to a BOTTLE WORKS where bottles were made.
Weapons used for cutting and thrusting, consisting of a blade and a hilt.
A hard, gritty, grey/green coloured form of chalk.
A paved area, generally found at the back of a house.
A combination of timbers to form a frame placed at intervals and carrying the purlins.
A piece of metal or timber holding two elements together.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Gilbertine order.
Plant for the processing of uranium ores, such as pitchblende. Uranium is the principal extract, but radium may also be recovered as a by-product
A structure sited within the grounds of a fire station used for drying hoses.
A triangle of cloth worn by ladies to cover the shoulders, neck and throat.
An establishment where beauty treatments and associated therapies are provided by professional practitioners.
A device which automatically controls a particular funtion within a machine or mechanism, such as regulating the gap between millstones in a windmill.
Includes excavation, research and general notes.
A hot steam bath introduced from the East, in which heavy perspiration is followed by soaping, washing, massage and cooling.
A private school offering term time accommodation for pupils being taught there.
A library where books may be consulted but not taken away.
Royal Flying Corps Side Opening Aircraft Hangar
An engineering works that produces tufting machinery especially for use in the manufacturing of carpets.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
Pond for storing cut lengths of timber to prevent them becoming seasoned.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
Use for vessels registered in the Netherlands.
Fish of any kind preserved by salting, for example salted cod such as bacalhau or bacalao.
A tract of land, often including a farmhouse and ancillary buildings, used for the purpose of cultivation and the rearing of livestock, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A motor in which rotary motion is produced by steam power.
An earthwork or structure on a rifle range used to mark a set distance from the rifle butts (usually at 50 or 100 yard intervals).

A formal programme of observation and investigation conducted during any operation carried out for non-archaeological reasons that may damage archaeological deposits. This will be within a specified area or site on land, inter-tidal zone or underwater.
Photographic negative using nitrate process on a film base material.
A fortified tower designed to house a number of artillery pieces and a small garrison. Artillery towers first appear in England in the 16th century.
A timber placed horizontally in a cob or stone wall to support the foot of a post or cruck blade.
An area of ground used for the game of quoits.
In Roman architecture either 1. A block of buildings enclosed by four streets or 2. A large tenement house or apartment block.
A house used to accommodate Llamas at a zoo or wildlife park.
A linear open working along a lode vein, worked directy from the surface. Survives as a gully or ravine, normally with closed ends.
A key, usually with a long stem, its terminal is generally hooked or looped, and bit set at angle to stem with radiating or looped wards.
The cutting part of a drill. Often bits are interchangeable.
A recess, usually situated in the north wall of a chancel,  often canopied, containing a decorated tomb chest representing the burial and resurrection of Christ.
A building used for the testing of steel.
The use of knapped flint applied to a wall to form a decorative pattern.
A medieval plan with the hall situated at one end of the main range.
Working area for rag sorting and grading.
A place where the game of squash is played.
A funerary vehicle used to carry a coffin from a church or funeral home to a cemetery.
A simple, lean-to structure, such as those built by the dock companies to provide shelter for dock workers waiting for work.
A tool with a pointed head for breaking ground.
Not a round barrow ploughed out at one end, but a specific type, the flat edge being additionally defined by stone slabs.
This class of documents confers statutory designation on the monuments listed within them. It usually is restricted to legally defined national or local notifications of designation.
A factory used for the processing of isinglass, a product obtained from the swim bladders of sturgeon and used in the brewing industry as part of the  process for clearing wine and beer.
A craft used for the transportation of cargoes. Use specific type where known.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specifications (drawing number 2243/41). Constructed from prefabricated A-frames and clad in corrugated iron.
A wheeled open box for carrying loads.
A structure erected for the processing of shale, to extract oil through heating.
A flat nail of the same thickness that tapers in width to a point.
Building or buildings housing  equipment for generating heat for a building complex.
Terms covering features of a monument or building which imply the previous presence of a component or structure. Use for negative evidence of a component or structure.
An endowed school providing a liberal education for such as can afford it.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
Grain from a cereal of the genus hordeum, often used in the manufacture of alcoholic spirits.
A place where hops are stored.
A site used by a carrier to accommodate his horses and vehicles and store goods awaiting transportation, etc.
Originally a reception room where visitors come come to talk especially in a closed establishment such as a monastery or school. Later used to refer to any room used for entertaining guests.
A form of tumbler lock key which pushes the bolt.
A factory concerned with the commercial manufacture of cider, as opposed to domestic production.
A building used for the storage of equipment.
A door divided horizontally into two parts, independently hinged.
An artifical head of hair worn to disguise baldness, for adornment, for ceremonial or theatrical use etc.

Articles intended for personal adornment, usually to be strung on items of jewellery or sewn onto clothing. They may be made out of worked raw materials (eg. shells) or be manufactured goods, for example glass beads.
A centre used to train Air Raid Precautions wardens.
A trough for containing moulding sand for use in casting metal artefacts.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of shoes or boots.
A vase used on the altar.
Generic name for a small steam or power boat often carried on board a larger vessel.
A projectile or group of projectiles fired from a weapon, usually solid rather than explosive.
A passage, usually horizontal, leading into a mine to allow for access or drainage.

A mill for the processes of grinding, balling, couching, drying and packing of woad. The mill can be demountable, enabling it being located close to the fields, as woad crop has to be rotated and move to new fields as soon as the ground is exhausted.
A place of worship for Protestant Methodists, a group who broke away from the Methodists to form their church in Leeds in 1828.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around all four sides of the yard.
A glasshouse for the cultivation of ferns.
A device for holding a lamp in a fixed position. These could take many forms from a simple bracket fixed to a wall to an onrate candelabra.
A ship of the line mounting between 90 and 98 guns on three gun decks
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
An instrument in which air is made to vibrate by a cane reed, which may be single or double, and may or may not be contained in a reed cap.
Recorded interview intended to preserve the recollections of persons whose experiences or memories are representative of historical life.
Sites, buildings or structures involved in passive air defence, usually by forcing hostile aircraft to fly high or drop their bombs on the wrong targets. Use more specific term.
A number of small iron balls, each about the size of a cricket ball, often numbering nine, wired together and bound in a canvas bag.
A building or complex producing umbrellas, parasols and canes.
A surface interpreted as a buried cultivation layer, for example an agriculturally cultivated field.
Fine grained, acidic, light-grey/white/ brown/red-coloured igneous rock.
A building used to house railway engines.
A decorative pattern, as used in tracery or a Gothic arch, featuring six lobes, or foils, separated by cusps.
A mound kerbed with wooden stakes or boulders.
A small warship with a shallow draught. Used for patrol duties and shore bombardment on major rivers.
The ridge formed at the intersection of two vaulted surfaces.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution lighter than air gases for use in barrage balloons.
The residence and office of an archdeacon.
A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A large approximately triangular stone at the foot of a gable, cut to have a horizontal bed and a top conforming, wholly or in part, to the slope of the gable.
Corrosive chemical compounds, usually liquids, which are neutralized by alkalis.
A place where lead ore is extracted from an open cast mine.

A room, particularly in a house or theatre, intended for dressing or changing one's clothes and furnished with wardrobes, dressing tables and other facilities for the application of make-up, styling of hair etc.
A road whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
A hospital for the medical or surgical treatment of domestic or wild animals.
A rib placed at an angle to support timbers.
A thin opaque, slightly absorbent material, generally made from processing of plant or other fibres, for use as a medium for writing, drawing and printing.
An area of a building or complex, such as a workhouse, hospital or prison used to house infirm inmates suffering from fever.
A hoop or band of material put around a wheel to protect it and, when filled with air, to provide a more comfortable ride.
An mill in which manganese was ground to a powder between two horizontal millstones.
Hard, corrosive alloy of copper and tin.
Deposits formed under conditions present adjacent to ice masses during glacial periods.
An arch with jambs that do not stand at an angle of ninety degrees to its face.
A bowl with a single loop handle crossing over the top of the vessel from one side of the rim to the other. (Source: MPRG)
A pot for drinking hot milk curdled with ale and flavoured with spice used as a remedy eg for colds.
A defensive or protective covering for the head.
A material resulting from the smelting of iron ore.
A flammable liquid that occurs naturally and is also now distilled.
The courtyard of a castle, ie. the area enclosed by the rampart or curtain. Use with wider site type where known.
Production of smokeless domestic fuel by roasting anthracite in a type of kiln.
An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers of ocean liners can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A massive structure designed to transfer canal boats between different canal or river navigations, eg. Anderton boat lift.
An artificial lake, often made by damming a stream. A common feature of landscape parks.
Coast Defence Chain Home Low Station
A short or long term residential home for people not requiring medical intervention or nursing care, usually for older people.
Seaborne assault landing troops ashore with resultant fighting on land, examples being the Battle of Maldon, 991, the Normandy landings of WWII and so on.
A detached block within a hospital complex used as sleeping accommodation for patients.
A building for the manufacture of condensed milk.
A detached subordinate building. Use specific type where known, eg. DAIRY.
A small building housing a mechanism used for winding a cable.

Collective term for a hard, fine grained, dark coloured metamorphic rock, which splits easily; hence its common use as a roofing and flooring material, and a functional description for any rectangular, sheet, roofing material.
A hand-operated loom on which figured cloth could be woven, also known as a drawing engine.
Squared block of glass, tile, stone or marble used in mosaic.
The structure consisting of a series of balusters supporting a rail or coping, and sometimes a base and pedestal, on a parapet, balcony or staircase.
Small square rigged ship with a narrow overhanging stern.
A place where perfume is sold, as well as manufactured.
An arrangement of railway tracks, stations and other buildings that together form a railway transport system.
A movable stucture which enables or prevents entrance to be gained. Usually situated in a wall or similar barrier and supported by gate posts.
Sailing vessel generally with three masts square rigged on the foremast only.
A stock exchange dealing in the prices for coal and shares in coal production.
Sites, buildings, structures & features relating to the provision of knowledge and skills.
An interment of a human body that displays unusual burial practice such as positioning of the body, decapitation, dismemberment or over-secure burial.
A multi sided object usually used to obtain a unique value in games of chance.

A type of aircraft hangar from the closing years of WWI either of steel or wood utilising a type of lattice work roof support known as a Belfast Truss, which features diagonally interlaced pieces of thin pine. The roof appears as a smooth curve.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A porch with columns and pediments.
Fresh And Brackish Water Mollusca Remains
A fishing vessel specially designed to operate and trawl for the catching of bottom lying fish. Use with power where known.
An item hung over a window, usually can be open or shut to allow light in.
A facility where the exterior of a motor vehicle can be cleaned.
A place for strolling, public walks, etc. Usually associated with coastal resorts.
A burial in which the body is placed in, or covered by a boat, which is then covered with earth. Use with barrow type where relevant.
A transept in which the two wings that extend beyond the walls of the nave are lower than the nave and the crossing of the church.

A large rectangle roof tile in the form of an upstand on one side followed by three rolls, the last of which fits over the upstand of the adjacent tile. The name does not denote a relationship with the Roman period.
Rock of definite form and size, usually artificially shaped. See STONE CLass List for narrow terms.

A mask worn over the face to protect the wearer from inhaling airborne pollutants and toxic gases. The mask forms a sealed cover over the nose and mouth, but may also cover the eyes and other vulnerable soft tissues of the face.
A public music or dancing establishment often with facilities for gambling.
A side scraper with a short concavity retouched into an edge. This may be achieved by a single blow. (Source: SARC)
A room which contains, wholly or partly, a staircase.
A purpose-built tenement. Use specific monument type where possible.
A mechanism used for lifting and lowering weights, operated by hand.
A building or room used for the practice and study of dance.
A piece of fabric worn tied or knotted around the neck.
A stone edge-runner grinding machine or mill used for mechanically grinding and mixing the ingredients of gunpowder.
Mark 10 or the tenth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
A coupled timber built end-opening First World War aircraft hangar.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.
The principal Eastern Orthodox church in an area.
National Record of the Historic Environment Number
A building housing the services of professionals with an expert knowledge of the law such as the offices of solicitors, barristers and lawyers.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of the essential logistical requirements of the Royal Navy.
A complex or ornate lid which cannot be easily classified according to the main forms of lid. (Source: MPRG)
Small fish, Sardina pilchardus, common to European waters and eaten as a food fish.

Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of pottery. Use only for sites where there is evidence of pottery manufacture but no specific monument, otherwise use more specific term.
A pit from which marl, a mixture of clay and carbonate of lime, is excavated. Marl is used as a fertilizer.
Military provisions, traditionally of all types but now used specifically for projectiles and propellants such eg. bullets and gunpowder.
A plant incorporating a range of ore processing operations such as buddles.
A house consisting of a single storey hall with two storey domestic ranges attached to either one or both ends.
A long-handled implement designed to allow the user to scratch their own back.
Use for vessels registered in South Africa.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
An object showing signs of being worked. Use more specific term where known.
A warehouse used for the storage of fruit and/or vegetables.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

An outlying farm or estate, usually belonging to a religious order or feudal lord. Specifically related to core buildings and structures associated with monastic land holding. Use specific term where known.
A curfew consisting of a half section of an inverted bowl. The form has been adapted for use against a wall. (Source: MPRG)
Use for vessels registered in the Philippines.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
An instrument made of a hollow cylinder or hemisphere covered at one or both ends and sounded by striking.
A distillery for the manufacture of perfumes from herbs.
A terraced field usually found on hillsides. Comprising a flat strip of land, called the tread, and a steep, scarped lynchet or edge, called the riser.
WWII secret bases, sometimes partially underground, intended for use by the British resistance in the eventuality of a foreign invasion.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine.
Originally gold coins issued in Florence, but later used for various coins issued on the continent. In modern Britain, the two shilling piece.
French Banker, fishing vessel for the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, generally three-masted or of brig type, from the late 19th and 20th centuries.
Official currency printed or written onto paper which can be directly exchanged for goods, services or coins.
The month of pilgrimage to Mecca.
A school where handicrafts are taught.
An aircraft hangar designed to house seaplanes.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.
A site or building used for processing shale. Shale can be fashioned into goods or, if bituminous, distilled to produce oil, naphtha or tar.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.
A capital featuring stylised, often projecting, three-lobed leaves.
A school for pupils with physical or learning difficulties.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
An indicator of the extent and or ownership of a property.
A mobile piece of equipment used by the Royal Observer Corps to track the movements of enemy aircraft.
A cover for an object, usually designed to fit the object.
A group of colleges and associated buildings belonging to a university.
