A small convex moulding, often decorated with beads and reels.
Components within a religious, ritual or funerary site directly connected to the sacred practices involved at the site.
A shed in which delicate plants are reared from seedlings for planting out later.
A cruck with its feet sitting on a ceiling beam on the first floor.
Levelled or terraced area of ground presumed to have been the site of a house or hut.
A building plan in which a passage crosses the axis of the building, often at one end of a hall, with an external door at each end.
Very Heavy Bomber Station Control Tower (294/45)
Building or structure housing a buddle.
A simple, pointed implement for piercing.
The main hall of worship within a Sikh Temple.
A building or group of buildings, often enclosed by a system of fortifications, used by an armed force for the storage and distribution of military equipment.
A general tool used to beat objects with.
A dial for showing the hours of the night by the moon.
An industrial manufacturing complex producing bricks.
Instruments for determining position at sea, e.g. compasses, sextants.
A piece of prepared ground on which the game of polo is played.
An aircraft, either whole or in part. Aircraft often survive as commemorative monuments, gate guardians or crash sites.
An arena for bull-baiting, not a tethering ring.
A handheld serrated device for grooming horses.
A small and powerful vessel used to assist vessels that are sinking or disabled at sea.
A hut used by a person who makes items from wood. Often found in a woodland setting.
A roller used in the fulling process to felt cloth.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of racket sports.
A section of roadway attached at one end to a harbour or dockside and ending at a landing stage, rising and falling with the tide, for the loading and unloading of vehicles and pedestrians.
A building, usually at a sports ground, with facilities for players and spectators.
A building housing the generator set and associated equipment supplying electricity to a radar station.
An area or route marked out for the site of a race.
The systematic use of portable X-Ray Fluorescence equipment to retrieve information on the different chemical elements present in the soil.

A small clinker-built craft, dating primarily from the 19th and early 20th centuries, fitted with oars and often a sail, usually found on the north-east coast of England and used for fishing or pilotage.
A stand or tray for ink bottles and or pens
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A subsidiary member, usually vertical, in a framed  wall or partition.
A shaped or decorated raised panel below the sill of a window or a niche.
A series of steps designed to enable fish to ascend a fall of water or a dam.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
The carriage house or garage for a fire engine - especially those built by insurance companies or industrial concerns.
The ocean which surrounds the continent of Antarctica, and includes the most southerly regions of the three largest oceans, the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian.
Castles constructed between 1481 and 1561 for defence using heavy guns.
A hard, silica rich rock, black or brown coloured, commonly found in nodular form.
An alcoholic spirit distilled from malted barley or barley and maize or rye.

A permanent military RAF aircraft hangar type, designed in 1924. It features a steel frame (with longitudinal ridge and valley trusses for the roof) reinforced concrete and brick infilling for the walls. Typically 122 foot span by 249 foot in length.
A building used for the daily administration of an army.
A glazed opening in a roof or ceiling.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows an almost rectangular course.
A pier which supports a gate.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.

Measures the remanent magnetisation direction of magnetic minerals. Useful for dating fired structures, in-situ since their last firing, and for sediments settling from non turbulent water bodies. In the UK, calibration data extends back to 1000BC.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
Plans of structures, particularly ground plans, and divisions or elements of structures that form part of these plans.
An area of land, in the shape of a D, enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A semicircular niche in the wall of a mosque used to indicate the Qiblah - the direction to be faced during prayers. Qiblah is set as the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca.
An area of land and associated buildings where vines are cultivated. The grapes produced are then used to make wine.
A factory for the manufacture of vehicles
A reading desk usually placed near the west end of the choir.
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
A secondary title associated with a bibliographic reference.
Small fish, common in European waters, caught for food.
A pen or enclosure used for containing sheep.
A small, ornate structure in which candles were placed either during masses for the dead or to indicate the position of the cemetery at night .
A square or cylindrical pipe at the top of a chimney which helps the draught of air.
A barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor.
A construction of wood or metal used to enclose an area of land, a building, etc.
A chamber usually used for sleeping.
An object used to grip together objects.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
A chapel where the followers of the Anglican tradition worship.
The first court which is before the principal court.
A market hall where cloth merchants can show their wares and conduct business.
A pump used for moving brine (salt water).
Areas of land that have been designated as national property where habitation and commercial activities are restricted to preserve their outstanding landscapes.
A three dimensional representation usually done in wood, ivory or stone.
A form to record the details of a monument or site found during the course of a field survey or visit.
A small detached building used to accommodate patients with tuberculosis.
The transverse portion of a cruciform church, or the arms on either side of the crossing, often with chapels at the east sides and possibly with aisles as well.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the large-scale production, processing and preserving of food and drink.
A hall, often associated with a synagogue, used for studying the Torah and other religious texts.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
A small one masted craft, often using oars as well as sails.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
Usually a small, two or three man trench, dug as an isolated fieldwork rather than as part of a defensive system. A WWI and WWII feature.
A plate on which an offering is made.
A mill used for the manufacture of narrow strips of woven fabric used in the closing or fixing of garments, or for binding the edges of fabric goods.
An area of ground which has been cleared of plants and other obstruction.
Items that have been through a manufacturing process. Use specific type where known.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
An area of the floor, wall or ceiling of a building, which has been painted, carved, sculpted or decorated.
A machine consisting of a number of moving parts designed to produce a specific physical effect, such as the powering of a craft or other device.
A centre for the teaching of crafts.
A rescue station serving a number of mines in the immediate area.
Steam engine, usually, driving a centrifugal fan to provide an air blast for a blast furnace.
Stadium housing a track and associated buildings and structures for the public racing of greyhounds.
A small gate swinging in a U or V-shaped enclosure, which allows only one person to pass through at a time.
A medium speed anti submarine escort vessel built from World War II

A convex, usually round, piece of metal or other material mounted at the centre of a shield. Originally serving  a practical purpose in deflecting blows and providing a mounting for the grip, it later developed into an ornamental feature.
A mill used for the production of cardboard and other similar products.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A prepared area of ground, featuring a 'mini' golf course with obstacles, used to undertake the leisure pursuit of miniature golf or 'crazy golf'. Often popular at seaside resorts.
An instrument using lenses to magnify the object being viewed.
A container used in growing plants, either to contain or for use in their cultivation eg watering cans.
A terrace with windows and doors on one side only, often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
An establishment dedicated to the study of God and religion.
A building providing accommodation, dining and recreational facilities for commissioned naval officers.
A place with organized amusements for people on holiday.
Support or 'mother ship' used for the repair, maintenance and refuelling of submarines, specifically 20th century submarines.
A communal residence of secular priests and/or other clerics sometimes with the condition of learning and education attached.
A by-product of the production of microliths.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A factory or plant used for the manufacture of electrical machinery or components.
A box with one transparent side within which a picture, jewel etc can be displayed.
A weight used with letter scales for weighing letters or parcels and establishing the required postal rate.
A method of grinding cereals where one stone is rotated on another by hand.
A type of warehouse, usually one-storeyed.
A pillbox constructed for use in training exercises forming part of a simulated defensive position
A stone tool, often only polished on the edge.
Second World War defence work usually consisting of securinng points for a boom defence, associated gun, and searchlight, emplacements
A solid ball fired from cannons, size and weight would depend on the calibre of the cannon.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
A kiln in which Iron ores were heated before smelting in order to drive off the impurities such as sulphur.
A factory producing metallic aluminium by an electrolysis process.

A candlestick in which the socket is above a drip tray or grease tray, placed on a pedestal base which is generally hollow. There may be a vertical loop handle and one or more secondary drip trays. (Source: MPRG)
A small self-contained rotative Beam Steam Engine.
A village cemetery where cinerary urns were buried in large numbers during the Bronze Age.
Oil produced from the seed of the flax plant. Used in the production of paints, varnish etc.
A workroom or apartment, often with a north-light, used for the creation of artwork by painters, sculptors etc.
A dimensional check on a building or site giving detailed measurements.
A set of two or more pins joined together by a chain.
Materials used for the construction of buildings, vehicles or other objects.
A long handled scoop usually used with liquids.
A small paved area attached to a building.
A container which holds a set quantity of a substance, can be graduated to show quantities.

An engine which operates machinery via a pivoted, horizontal beam with a piston located at one end and a reciprocating pump beneath the other, resulting in a rocking, seesaw-like motion. Variations featured the steam piston placed above the beam.
Twin blades each with a sharpened edge connected together by a pivot which cut when opened and closed on an object.
A bowl divided into two or more compartments by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)
A track inlaid into the road surface of a street or road, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers.
A wide-mouthed, narrow based flared bowl associated with dairying activities. (Source: MPRG)

A large room, similar to a dormitory, within a hospital, and used for the temporary or permanent accommodation of patients, either waiting for or recovering from operations or undergoing long term treatment.
A clay cone, part of a furnace.
A cheap eating establishment traditionally serving jellied eels, pies and mash.
A cup with a rounded body beneath a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between neck and body and the angle of the neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
A building where the bones of the dead were stored.
Animal remains bearing evidence, such as knife marks on bones, that they were slaughtered and used for food.
An object in the sea bed detected by marine survey equipment that shows the contours of the sea bed beneath a vessel.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
A system of overhead cables from which cars or containers are suspended (usually driven electrically).
A moulding on an entablature that is between the frieze and the corona.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
An upright timber similar to a crown post, but not supporting a plate.
The main title of a bibliographic resource.
A white, caustic solid obtained by heating limestone and used in the preparation of mortar and cement.
A terrace, balcony or room exposed to the rays of the sun which were thought to be beneficial to recovering from an illness.
An object used in the Eucharist.
An open area within an exchange building (e.g. cotton exchange, corn exchange, stock exchange) where goods are traded.
A sculptural or decorative representation of an animal. Includes mythical and fantastical animals such as dragons, centaurs etc.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A building for housing deer overnight.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
A marker used to represent a gambling stake.

Use to identify a feature, previously thought to be a monument but now disproved, or to avoid erroneous identification as a monument in future. Where a feature is regarded as an antiquity, but is unclassified, use SITE.
A farmyard or enclosure containing regularly built stacks of hay, corn, peas etc.
Vertical screens made of wood or steel framing mounted on concrete blocks were built to protect airships from cross winds when entering or leaving the airship sheds.
An area within a hospital where children are accommodated during the period of their medical or surgical treatment.
A monument where the evidence that defines the type of the monument derives from the nature of surface markings. Examples include graffitti on quarry walls.
A basement or cellar, usually within a house, leased as a separate dwelling.
Collective name for the seeds of various cereal grasses.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A decorative fitting of mid to late 11th century date, mainly of copper alloy, often traingular or trapezoidal in shape. Mounted at the junction of the stirrup and stirrup strap.
Urn containing a cremation. Where component use with wider site type.
A projecting stud which fastens into a socket.

Type of furnace used in the glass industry to pre-heat glass in crucibles, prior to the main melt. This may have been a separtate structure, or may have been part of the main furnace. All periods from the Roman onwards.
The taking of photographs from above using photographic equipment mounted on, or used from an aircraft or other airborne vehicle.
A site used for the sport of badger baiting using fighting dogs.
A closed chamber used for heating or baking objects.
Explosive devices which produce spectacular visual effects when ignited.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of non ferrous metal ores.
Documents relating to the administration of planning applications.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
A long bed containing rose plants.
A layer of stone, brick or boards, etc, on which people tread. Use broader site type where known.
The seed of the flax plant used to produce oil and, in LINSEED CAKE, as fodder.
An establishment where tickets/reservations for events, journeys or entrance to a site can be purchased.
A type of updraught intermittent kiln of rectangular plan and battered sides, but with an open top.
Triangular concrete pyramids with 6 feet long sides and 5 feet high, intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Thought to be confined geogaphically to Southern Command.
An industrial building, plant or site where crude substances, such as sugar, metal, oil etc., are purified or refined.
An instrument used to create and link loops of yarn to produce a garment.
A garden building or greenhouse, containing pools in which Water Lilies are grown.
A bolt for fastening metal plates. One end is put through prepared holes and then beaten flat.
An enclosure where ewes are kept at the time of lambing.
A house provided for the treasurer of a cathedral, palace or similar.
A fishing vessel that catches fish by using a Seining net, that is a large net that is made to hang in the water by attaching weights along the bottom edge and counteracting floats along the top.
A burial ground for victims of cholera.
A red dye made from the dried bodies of the insect Dactylopius coccus.
A truss with transverse timbers, like a tie-beam from which the middle section has been removed, supported on braces and carrying hammer-posts and braces that carry the open structure of the roof.
A fastener used within a cavity wall to hold the two sides together.
A small dome on top of a larger dome, roof etc.
Stones placed in the bed of a stream or on wet ground, to enable crossing on foot.
A small cap for protecting the finger or thumb whilst sewing.

An artificial harbour, constructed using prefabricated, concrete caissons, floating breakwaters and blockships, which were towed across the channel and assembled off the coast of Normandy to assist the allied forces after the D-Day landings in June 1944.
Any church of the Anglican Communion.
A stone set up on a road or path to mark the miles from or to a place.
A building in which oxen are accommodated.

A place of worship for the sect known as 'Cokelers', formed circa 1850 by John Sirgood. Most aspects of Dependent belief are fairly orthodox within the Arminian traditions of Protestant dissent. Chapels can be found in Sussex, Surrey, London and Kent.
Any of large class of polymers based on synthetic resins or modified natural polymers which may be moulded, extruded or cast while soft or liquid, which then set rigidly or slightly elastic in form.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around three sides of an open cattle yard.
A protected chamber for investigating the controlled detonation and burning of explosive compounds, typically associated with a protected control room and high speed visual recording facilities.
A report detailing the results of archaeological fieldwork that has been produced in advance of a full synthesis of the collected data.
A water tank, often raised on stilts, used to supply water to steam trains.
An object which is attached to or connected with a door.
A canopy or building to cover the platforms in a railway station.
A factory where security safes are manufactured.
A place where graphite is extracted.
A monument whose presence is inferred from verbally delivered information drawn from the speaker's personal knowledge.
A site where sugar beet was processed before being washed and dried to form granulated sugar.
An ore containing sufficient quantities of a mineral as to make its extraction profitable.
A building used for the storage of artillery pieces.
A screen dividing one part of a church from another.
Use only where evidence is specific, ie. copper/tin alloy. For working of copper based alloys of unknown composition use COPPER WORKING SITE.
A building with small observation ports used for plotting mines dropped by parachute.
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.
A protected building or site used for the safe storage of chemical weapons
A building in which cows are milked.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A place where two artificial waterways meet each other.
Sites and structures associated with the manufacture of bricks and tiles. Includes sites associated with earth extraction and preparation.
A crane mounted on a large metal gantry, used for the lifting of large-scale building materials, etc.
A building in which horses are accommodated.
Sites for the manufacture of substances or items by controlled chemical reactions.
A concept dating in England from the second half of the 18th century, when hardy North American plants were relatively easy to obtain.
An object projecting out of the sea bed detected by marine survey equipment that emits and receives high frequency sound waves projected sideways from a boat or towed array.
A defensive structure or site where an anti-tank gun is emplaced.
Unbaked clays and/or soil material often mixed with, or performing the function of an aggregate or binder. See EARTH MIX Class List for narrow terms.
An object, usually wood or metal used to force open or keep open another object. Often used to split timber by striking the thick end and forcing the wood apart.
A housing for racing pigeons usually situated in allotments of back yards.
A support projecting from a wall.
A structure inclined towards the water on which a ship may be built or lowered into the water.
Traditionally the premises of a chandler, a maker and seller of candles. Now, a shop for the retail of groceries and other provisions.
A tool for pounding or grinding.
A vault created by the intersection of two other vaults set at right angles to each other and of equal size.
A complex of buildings using Radar or satellite tracking to monitor and detect enemy missile launches early enough to allow a counterattack or defensive measures to be taken.
A fibrous silicate mineral used to manufacture incombustible items.
A raised platform at the end of a hall on which the high table sat, though sometimes used to describe the table itself.
Feature exists but has been infilled.
A factory used for the production of acetate.
A plant used to sterilize water for use in public bathing establishments, not to be confused with desaliation or  purification units for drinking water.
Silver rings believed to have been used in the Hebrides and Irish Sea regions during the Viking period, and derived from Hiberno-Viking arm rings.
Sites, buildings and structures for the control and mounting of anti aircraft artillery. Also, structures for passive or indirect defence against enemy aircraft.
A 17th century garden in the Dutch style: usually flat and compact, with an emphasis on small canals, hedges, topiary, lead statuary and flowering shrubs and bulbs.
A room or building used for curing fish or meat.
A large, luxuriously appointed building used as an official residence by a member of royalty.
A trinket worn as a protection against evil.
Armour designed to protect the torso, and consists of both back and breast plates.
A structure used for drying yarn in open fields.
A room equipped with apparatus to facilitate physical exercise, gymnastics or indoor sports.
A pointed, two centred, arch whose span is greater than its height.
A rock carving, especially a prehistoric one.
A building with facilities for playing snooker.
A tool used in processing the fibres from coconuts.
A brace, parallel to another, in wall framing or arcading, or in trusses between post and tiebeam; also referred to as a duplicate brace.
A tool used to pound, crush or beat an object.
Lantern slide developed using a dry process.
A multiple, parallel arrangement of linear earthwork ditches, usually accompanied by banks, and often of considerable territorial extent. Usually of later prehistoric or Roman date.
A vessel used for medical purposes.
A beacon, firmly embedded on the sea floor, consisting of an iron mast, with ladder steps leading up to the refuge cage considerably above high-water mark, and capable of holding several people.

A funerary site, either totally or partially underground, for the depositing of the dead. Often found in cemeteries in the form of a circular or semi-circular sunken area comprising of several galleries with vault entrances built into the side.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A form of pilaster without base or capital.
Oil obtained from the rendered blubber of whales, used as a fuel in old oil lamps.
A building or room, where business and/or administrative activities to do with the canals was conducted.
A room used for the display of merchandise for sale.
A Mark 1B aircraft which has undergone further modification to enhance performance or armament.
A building housing a number of power looms.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.
The major tower of a fortification, often acting as its last defence.
A building containing pans in which salt water or brine was boiled to produce salt.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
The consecrated ground immediately surrounding a tomb or grave.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
A distinctive magistrates court established by legislation in 1980, dealing with civil family proceedings.
A building or cage in which parrots are bred and kept.
A court of summary jurisdiction formally recognized by statute in 1848. Renamed Magistrates Court, following legislation, in 1949.
A staircase divided into two parallel flights joined by a landing with no well between the outer strings.
A place used to hide something or someone.

A container to hold a liquid in honour of a deity.

Ore containing high levels of lead, eg. galena.
A dome shaped building, housing training apparatus, including a projector, for training ground gunners in the art of airfield defence.  (WWII).
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
An indoor or outdoor market where leather and untreated animal hides are sold.
One of a set used in pharmacy to measure volume or weight for dispensing.
A building or school where music is taught.

Coring can assist in a variety of situations to map stratigraphy (borehole surveys) and collect samples. It is mainly undertaken when the deposits of interest are too deep for conventional digging, or when large areas need to be mapped. In developer-funded evaluations, borehole surveys should not be seen as a replacement for conventional trench evaluation, but they can be used as a first phase where the results need to characterise the local sedimentary sequence and help pinpoint trench locations. This technique is also very helpful in establishing the presence of waterlogged deposits with potential for palaeoenvironmental evidence (see also Hydrological impact assessment).
